headline: NO CHURCHES / CATHOLICS CLOSE DOWN IN MEXICO.
text:
WHIPS AND CANES

All the Catholic Churches close at noon to-day and all the priests will withdraw as decreed by the Mexican Episcopate as a protest against the new Mexican religious laws.

In order to maintain peace and order a cordon of Police surround Mexico $ ^{®} $ City Cathedral.

Deportatlon orders were served on the Papal Envoy yesterday evening.

The Government is closing, sealing, and guarding all structures containing Church property, which will be handed over to Citizens' Committees.

Some disturbances occurred last night.

headline: U.S. INDUSTRY. / BRITISH COMMISSION IN SEPTEMBER.
text:
A PRESS REPORT

The Daily Mail says that the Government has decided to send a small Commission composed of leading employers and labour workers' representatives in September to study industrial relationship in the United States. — Reuter.

headline: ANOTHER SHOW.
text:
PROF: LANGSNER TO GIVE MATINEE.

NOTE DATE AND TIME.

In response to many requests for another public demonstration, Professor Maximilian Langsner, M.L.L.C. has consented to appear at the Theatre Royal for a matinee on Thursday, August 5 at 5.33 p.m. prompt.

The Professor's powers in occult science are too well known to need repetition. Those who were unable to be present on the occasion of the first show will welcome this opportunity, while many will want to go again.

Booking opens at Messrs. Moutrie's to-morrow.

headline: DEBT OF. HUGO STINNES'S FIRM.
text:
BRITAIN AS "UNCLE."

Hugo Stinnes's firm, which owes the German Banks about £4,000,-000 as the result of the winding up of the late Herr Hugo Stinnes's affairs, intends to pay off the amount, for which it will raise a foreign loan.

The Volks Zeitung (Cologne) says that negotiations have been proceeding for some time with a British group of financers to grant the loan.—Reuter.

headline: CANTON STRIKERS.
text:
COMMANDING GENERAL SAYS "MUST STOP."

A VAGUE REPORT.

Disobedience to National Government

A castle received by the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" makes the rather startling announcement that Canton's present military chief intends to deall drastically with strikers on the ground that strikes contravene the rules of the Revolutionary Government. On General Chang Kai-shek leaving for the Northern front, General Li Chai-sum was appointed commander of home defence. The Brief statement as cabled does not say whether General Li refers to strikers strictly of Cantanban, or the so-called "Hongkong strikers." The message is clear to the extent that military force will be used in putting down strikes.

Post and Press Strike.

Advice from Canton is that the postal strike continues and that all (native, subordinate?) employees were to have come out during the week-end. It being the end of the month.

The Commissioner is quoted as having stated, in reply to a request from the employees' union, that the "demand for an increase of pay must go to the chief commissioner in Peking.

It is interesting to note that mails which were expected here from Canton on Saturday and yesterday have not come to hand, ostensibly through delay in the post.

The end of the newspaper strike has not been reported. On the other hand, it is believed that proposals have been advanced for a settlement and these...it is stated...

headline: Hero Welcome
text:
Detailed accounts have reached Canton about the arrival of General Chang Kai-shek in Shikwan and Lokcheong, on his way to the battle front.

Four Russian advisers, a big staff and several aeroplanes are with the commander-in-chief. The people of the various towns accorded General Chang a very cordial reception.

One report is that the mere fact of his personal arrival has caused order to be restored and outlaws to disappear from haunts where they exacted toll from the populace.

General Tang Sang-chee, the pro-Canton commander in Hunan, has announced that another advance will be made immediately, from Changsha, into Wu Pei-fu's territory. Ping-kiang is stated to be his first objective. The Hunan Government is said to have been remodelled on the style of the Kwangtung provincial government, with General Tang as chairman of the military department.

The Hunan Provincial Assembly is reported to have denounced General Tang. One accusation against him is that he has levied from the wealthy classes, 50 percent, of property and 20 per cent. on rental of fields. Non-payment will be severely punished, states the report.

headline: A $ ^{1} $ WHARF SCENE. / ALLEGED PICKPOCKETTING INCIDENT
text:
CRIMINAL SESSIONS CASE..

Incidents at the ferry wharf in which a passenger, alleged pick-pocket and a district watchman figured led to the appearance at the Criminal Sessions this morning of Chan Chung, charged with stealing from Leung Sau-shan $21 in Canton currency and $7 in Hongkong currency.

The accused created somewhat of a stir when he alleged that he had been the victim of a trumped up charge brought by a watchman who knew he (accused) had been convicted on several other occasions and had fabricated the story for the purpose of his advancement. The jury, however, found the accused guilty and Mr. Justice Wood sentenced him to eighteen months' hard labour.

Detailing the facts, Mr. H. K. Holmes, Crown Solicitor, said that the complainant landed on Hongkong side and was about to get into a mesha when the accused brushed past him. Complainant noticed that he had a tope with him which he carried in his hand, for the purpose suggested the Crown Solicitor, of shielding his movements.

Complainant at the same time felt a tug at his breast pocket and was about to seize the accused when a district watchman in plain clothes, who was on duty, came and stated that he had had the accused under observation and had seen him take something from compliant's pocket.

The watchman opened the hand of the accused, continued the Crown Solicitor, and in it was found $2 in Hongkong currency and $21 in Canton currency. The complainant had had $7 in Hongkong currency and $21 in Canton currency in his breast pocket. This was missing.

Serious Allegation. In a statement made to the police, the accused denied taking the money. He said that the complainant had observed nothing and when asked by the watchman how much he had had in his pockets he could not say. Accused affirmed that the complainant had been taught by the watchman what to say. The complainant had not been willing to go to the police station but the watchman told him he must go.

After evidence had been called, the accused made a statement in which he alleged that the watchman who stopped him at the wharf-knew-that-he- (the accused) was a "bad character" (having been convicted of theft on several occasions) and that he had "trumped up" the charge with the hope of getting promotion. The facts, according to the accused's affirmation, were that the watchman had seized hold of him and taken him to the complainant who was sitting in a riesha, asking the complainant if his money was alright as he (the watchman) had reason to suspect that money had been stolen from his pocket. The complainant replied that his money was alright and on being asked to examine his pockets and see, he refused. The watchman then examined the complainant's pockets for him, continued the accused, and although the complainant was not desirous of going to the police station he was made to go by the watchman.

The watchman and the complainant were both called in the course of the hearing of the case this morning and completely denied that the facts were as stated by the accused.

Sentence was passed as stated above.

headline: COAL INDUSTRY. / NUMBER OF WAGE EARNERS AT WORK.
text:
NEARLY 100,000.

Questioned in the House of Commons as to the number of wage earners at work in coal mines, exclusive of safety men, Colonel Lane-Fox, Secretary of Mines, said that on July 24 there were 93,870 wage earners employed of whom 36,800 were employed in mines not producing any coal or producing coal for collery consumption only. — British Wireless Service.

Two causes of enteric fever (both Chinese) were reported during the 3 days ended August 2.

A Chinese snatcher was sentenced to six months' hard labour at the Central Magistracy yesterday. He was caught by a P.W.D. meter render at Li Chit Street while escaping with $100 which he had taken from a Chinese girl at Queen's Road East.

headline: GUNNER CHARGED.
text:
TRAMWAY EMPLOYEES AS COMPLAINANTS.

ASSAULT PROVED.

Gunnar James Money, of the R.A., Lyceum Barracks, was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindgell at the Central Magistracy this morning on two separate charges of assaulting tramway employees, the complainants being a traffic regulator and a Chinese inspector.

Evidence in the first charge was that the defendant along with two others entered the tramway shelter at Causeway Bay shortly after 11 p.m. yesterday and pointed his fist at the traffic man's nose when he was told that there were no more cars to Shaukiwan but only one for Quarry Bay.

"Itness further stated that a troley cools inside the shelter was "knocked down" first and witness was attacked next. He was seized by the neck and felled to the ground by several blows. Witness got up and ran away with the defendant behind him.

The inspector's evidence was that he arrived at the terminus shortly after and received a complaint from the other man. On approaching the defendant to investigate, witness said that he was kicked at by the defendant. The blow missed and soiled his clothing.

A Chinese constable who came on the scene on hearing police whistles blown said that he suggested that the defendant should go to the police station. Defendant went with him quietly followed by the complainants.

In a statement on oath, defendant denied that he assaulted the men. He explained that he went to the Queen's Theatre along with Gunners Brien and Pepperel, left before the show was over, had supper and drinks at the Naval Canteen, and took tram to Causeway Bay intending to continue the journey to Shaukiwan.

While waiting at the terminus, defendant said that a number of Chinese gathered round them and one of them knocked off Brien's cap. On stooping to pick it up defendant had his own cap knocked off. He chased the man who did it, but failed to catch him.

Gunners Brien and Pepperel gave corroborative evidence.

Sub-Inspector Goble, who was present when the parties came to the police station, said that the defendant appeared to be a sober but a little excited. "No mention was made of the attack by the Chinese and, in fact, the other two Gunners told him they were not there at the time.

His Worship held the evidence for the prosecution to be substantially correct, while the story for the defence was contradictory. He convicted defendant on both charges, imposing fines of $5 and $5 compensation on each charge.

headline: CANTON'S STRIKES.
text:
RAILWAYMEN & SEAMEN TO COME OUT?

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS.

Latest intelligence from Canton is that a settlement do not appear in sight for the postal and newspaper strikes.

A cable to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" indicates that the employees of the railways and the seamen have declared their sympathy and support for the employees of the Postal Administration. The same message adds that the strike of postmen is extending and may "get out of hand."

In the vernacular newspaper offices—all closed with the exception of two alleged officials orans

—a decision has been announced whereby expenses will be reduced to a minimum, this to include the cutting down of present staffs. The object, as stated, is to be able to hold out against the employees' and their demands, for a long period.

headline: TRAFFIC CASES. / REGULATIONS SET AT DEFIANCE. / THREE OFFENDERS.
text:
Several traffic summonses were dealt with by Major C. Willson at the Central Magistacy this morning.

Mr. D. Clow, tramway inspector, gave evidence in a charge against a taxicab driver of-cutting-past-a-stationary vehicle. Witness said that he and two other European ladies who were alighting from a tram car had a narrow escape. Defendant was fined $20.

Another taxicab driver was fined $25 for dangerous driving. The case against him was that he got in front of a tram car near Murray Road and suddenly stopped, an accident being narrowly averted by the motorman applying his emergency brakes.

A “speed demon” was fined a similar amount. It was stated that he raced along Praya East near the Lee Garden at 24 miles an hour.

headline: CANTON'S WAR.
text:
MANY PROVINCES JOINING IN FRAY?

IMPORTANT DESPATCHES.

From a batch of important despatches to hand, it is evident that Canton's allies still holding Changshu, a town in a strategic position in Central China, while Wu Pei-fu's faction are yet in possession of Yochow. The messages read:—

Governor Yang Sin of Szechuan province had instructed two generals to assist Hunan province (against the south?).

Twenty field pieces have been assembled at Yochow and the cruiser (or gunboat) "Yung Kien" is proceeding thither. An offensive (against the south) will be launched in a week.

Wu Pei-fu has appointed a subordinate as commander of the Yangtsze Flotilla. He has ordered a general attack on Changsha.

To assist Chao Hang-teh is restoring himself to the governorship of Hunan (as against Canton's nominee, Tang Sang-chee), Wu Pei-fu has allotted Chao $100,000 and Sun Chuan-fang (Tupan of Kiangsi) is remitting $50,000. Chao is waiting for the re-capture of Changsha before reassuming the governorship.

Steps have been taken by ex-President Tsao Kun to ask Wu Pei-fu to return to the south. Wu replied that Canton's Northern Expedition is more in the shape of propaganda. His military and naval strength is converging in great number at Yochow and Sun Chuan-fang is assisting his campaign. When Nankow is taken (from the Christian general's former army) he will return to Hankow.

Of Sun Chuan-fang's subordinates it is stated that he is sending a division and two autonomous brigades into Fukien (the province to the north of Kwangtung). His 76th brigade at Nantung is also ready to march. On August 2 Yang Wen-kai passed Hsuchow en route for Kiangsu province.

The gist of these reports is that activities are hinted, if not having actually taken place, by the various warlords whose domains are close to Canton's sphere. Meanwhile Canton is quiet about General Chang Kai-shek's taking the command in person but it is felt that far-reaching developments, with possible influence on the whole of South China, are imminent.

headline: CANTON'S STRIKES
text:
The strikes of postmen and newspaper employees at Canton are not reported ended, nor is a settlement in sight, according to latest messages to hand.

There is no mention of the seamen and railwaymen coming out in sympathy.

headline: STREET DANGERS.
text:
FIRE ENGINE DROPS IN A PIT

TWO HOURS' LABOUR

Following the usual custom, the engine turned round in front of the No. 2 Police Station on the return journey but one of the front wheels got stuck in a trench temporarily covered in with earth for the night.

The engine got clear by working on reverse gear, but must a worse fate, as the rear left hand wheel broke through some planking placed over a deep hole and fell in with a crash. The planks which were replaced over the pit as protection for the night collapsed owing to the weight of the fire appliance.

Assistance was summoned by telephone from the Central Fire Station and with the combined efforts of the firemen the engine was extricated about nearly two hours' work.

The mudguards of that portion of the appliance would have been smashed but for the fact that the ends also went into the pit and further progress was stopped by the ladders stays at the rear and the tool box fixed along the dashboard. There was little apparent damage and the appliance returned to the depot none the worse for the mishap.

Profiling by this experience, the pit was again closed with planks and two lanterns placed over it to warn traffic.

headline: COOLIE FIGHT. / HIT ON THE HEAD WITH A SHOVEL.
text:
POLICE COURT CASE.

With blood stains on his clothing and head "in bandages," a truck coolie looked on passively at the Central Magistracy this morning while another man explained from the dock the cause of the trouble.

The defendant, also a truck coolie, alleged that he was struck on the leg with a bamboo pole when he questioned complainant's right to precede him with a truck. He retaliated when another attack was premeditated.

Div.-Inspector Grant said that the defendant nursed a grievance and took the opportunity when he met complainant again in the afternoon to hit him on the head with a shovel.

Defendant was fined $5 and ordered to pay a like sum as compensation.

headline: TRAMWAY
text:
EXPLANATIONS IN COURT.

Two Chinese, brothers, were brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning for an infringement of the Tramway Company's by-laws. One was charged with transferring his July monthly ticket to the younger boy and the latter with using a ticket not in his name.

The elder boy explained that he sent his brother to exchange his ticket for a new one, but Mr. A. Gillard, of the Tramway Company, mentioned that the ticket holder lived in Bonham Strand, and the boy was found on a car between Causeway Bay and Quarry Bay. Further, that the boy did not appear to have any money when brought to the depot.

The younger said that he wanted to watch the swimmers at the North Point beach first and when arrested he was too frightened to mention about the renewal of the ticket.

Each of the youths was ordered to pay a fine of $10.

headline: ALLEGED THEFTS. / EUROPEANS CHARGE HOUSE COOLIE.
text:
MISSING "VALUABLES.

A house coolie long wanted by the police authorities, at last fell in the trap yesterday afternoon, having been arrested at No.10 Albion Terrace, Kowloon Dock. He is charged with kureny under three charges.

Mr. A. Thompson, an engineer at the Tai Tam Tuk Reservoir, who is the first complainant, alleges that while the accused was in his employ, on October, 1924, the accused stole $350 from him, and then disappeared.

Mr. J. R. Haywood, solicitor, who is the second complainant, alleges that while the accused was in his services on February, 1924, the accused stole a silver cigarette case.

Mr. Haywood representing his mother-in-law., and third complainant, alleges that while his mother-in-law was living with him at Derrington House, Garden Road, during which period the defendant was in his employ, the latter stole from his mother-in-law a gold wrist watch.

The wrist watch and the cigarette case were found in the possession of the accused, and were duly identified by the complaints.

The case was remanded until next Tuesday.

headline: TELL-TALE CLOCK. / STOPPED WHEN IT WAS. STOLEN.
text:
TIME IN COURT CASE.

Many things happened in the course of half an hour yesterday morning.

While a caretaker of the Glass makers' Guild at Water Street left the premises at 11 o'clock and returned in just that time, a thief sneaked in and removed a wall clock and a large vase.

At the other end of the street, at 11:30 o'clock, a wary detective had caught a man stalking behind the stalls with a gunny sack containing the stolen articles.

All parties met at the Police Station and the clock pointed to 11.10, the time it was taken down from the wall.

The arrested man was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with breaking into the premises, but the probability being that the caretaker forgot to lock the door through which he entered, he was convicted only on unlawful possession.

His explanation was that he was employed to carry the bag for another man who disappeared when he was stopped by the detective. The sentence was four weeks' hard labour.

headline: SENTENCE “CUT.” / MAGISTRATE REVISÉS HIS. DECISION.
text:
COXWAIN'S OFFENCE

There was an echo of the charge against the coxswain of the lighter 'Delaware' belonging to the Standard Oil Company in Hongkong, at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning. The coxswain was charged last week with stealing sixteen cases of tin plates, a part of an order coming from the States to the Company in Hongkong, and was sentenced to nine months' hard labour, upon conviction.

Mr. J. H. E., Ninth Magistrate, remarked that although the defence did not petition a rehearing of the case he was reopening it, because in reviewing the case he noticed that the section under which the charge was brought allowed a maximum sentence of six months dead labour

The convict's term was therefore reduced from nine months to six months hard labour.

Not that the Rents Ordinance will come again even though Sir Edward Stubbs first took the view that control was necessary when some landlord rashly increased the rent of premises at East Point for

My advice to the Government is to stop the dispensary altogether. If a property owner can be so heartless the authorities have no option. The public must forego such a boon if it does not have enough spirit to kick.

But I have no sympathy for the Government. No response has been made to the many suggestions for a Fair Rents Board. If a declaration is coming, on policy, that a Fair Rents Board is unnecessary, impracticable, or unadvisable, I sincerely hope that the Government will use the case I mention as an argument, not for the poor tenant, but for the landlord.

Yours, etc.,

headline: A FAIR CHARGE?
text:
MR. CROUCHER SUED BY ARCHITECT.

WANCHAI GAP HOUSE.

Regarded Plan As "Scrap Of Paper."

The question of what was a reasonable amount for an architect to charge for preparing a sketch plan of a house it was proposed to erect at Wanchai Gap arose out of a case before Mr. Justice Wood in the Summary Court. this morning.

Mr. H. H. Bourne, architect, of Prince's "Building, claimed $900 from Mr. N. V. A. Croucher, broken, of Messrs. Benjamin and Potts, for services rendered. The claim was made up of items for "taking instructions, preparing a sketch design and making approximate estimate of cost by public measurement, or otherwise for a house to be built at or near Wanchai Gap." The claim was based on 1½ per cent. on the approximated cost of house ($60,000).

Mr. H. C. Macnamara was for plaintiff and Mr. M. M. Watson for the defendant.

Mr. Macnamara, in opening, said that defendant had paid $150 into court but plaintiff was unable to accept it as it was totally inadequate.

In June of last year, said Mr. Macnamara, Mr. Croucher contemplated having a house built on an eminence near Wanchai Gap. He had been in negotiations with the Government to buy a certain plot of land and the land had subsequently been bought by him.

headline: COAL CRISIS:
text:
CAN ONLY BE SETTLED BY PARTIES THEMSELVES.

MINISTER'S STATEMENT

The House of Commons, by 173 votes to 195 defeated in Labourite proposal to adjourn for the Summer recess till August 17 instead of November 9 in view of the coal stoppage. The Labourites contend that the situation might change in the "next three weeks and the House should be in session in order

Sirn Austen Chamberlain said that sixteen days of Parliamentary time had been devoted to coal discussions without powerfully contributing to a solution of the dispute, which could only be ended by the parties thereto.

Thereafter practically an empty House, on a motion for adjournment, debated the British American debt settlement, coal stoppage, and other matters.

The House of Commons meets "at brief intervals at the end of August, September, and October to renew the emergency regulations if the coal dispute is still in existence.

headline: VOTE AMONG MINERS.
text:
Prospects of Acceptance Good.

Before Parliament adjourned to-day for the Summer recess, Mr. J. Ramsay MacDonald, the Labour Leader, asked what the Government was going to do in regard to the coal stoppage. He said that so far from the situation being nearer a settlement to-day, than it was a month ago, it was much further away from a settlement. headline: PROF. LANGSNER ILL.
text:
To-day's mutinee demonstration in occult science, which was to have been given at the Theatre Royal at 5.83 p.m., has had to be cancelled.

The "China Mail" is informed that Professor Langsner is ill with malaria and fatigue and is therefore unable to conduct the demonstration. It is hoped to fix up another data for the matinee, the date to be announced in due course.

headline: CANTON'S STRIKES.
text: The strike of postmen in Canton has extended to other parts of the territory under the control of the Nationalist Government which has not announced any official action in the matter. The newspapers are still suspended as the workmen remain “out.” A vernacular report states that the printers employed by the political administration have also come out. The writer poignantly asks if their “strike” will be interpreted as an act contrary to the interests of the Canton Government?

headline: OUR POST OFFICE.
text:
RECORD MAIL HANDLED IN JULY.

STAFF DIFFICULTIES.

Canton Strike Has An Indirect

A department of the local public service which receives little publicity except when the annual report of its working is published is that concerned with the Post Office administration. Yet, needless to say, the work of sorting, delivery and transhipment and the supervision and administration proceeds daily — sometimes nightly—with demands on the time and labour of the whole department particularly heavy at certain times.

A correspondent to-day refers rather "belatedly to delay in the delivery of newspapers arriving on Saturday morning and received on Monday holding that if the department is under-staffed steps should be taken to make up the deficiency.

A “China Mail” representative who made enquiries was informed that the delay referred to was on account of the staff having to prepare for an outward mail to Europe on the day in question as well as two inward Europe mails and other smaller mails both ways. As it was the end of the month, some 200 men had had to be paid, this also leading to a certain amount of interruption.

For normal times the present staff of the Post Office is sufficient, he was further informed, although the especial difficulties faced by men who were comparatively new to the work had to be taken into consideration. A large percentage of the clerical and outdoor staff consisted of men engaged since the strike and although they were doing their best it stood to reason that they were not yet as conversant with the technicalities as men who had been engaged on the work for ten years or more (as some of the men who left during the strike had been). A great deal of extra supervision work was required. A Record July.

Further interesting facts with regard to the amount of mail handled by the department were given to the newspaper representative. Hongkong acts as a sort of “Clapham Junction” in regard to transhipment of mail in the Orient and transhipment involves a considerable “and growing” demand on the time of certain of the employees owing to fewer ships going direct from Shanghai to Canton since the strike and the growing use of the postal service in regard to communications between those ports and between Shanghai and Yunnan.

This will be more fully appreciated when it is stated that during July of this year over 21,000 bags of mail were received here, this number being a record for one month within the memory of members of the staff who can go back over many years. Considerable extra work has had to be undertaken as an indirect outcome of the Canton strike, mails which have been transhipped to boats for Canton having to be brought back in certain cases, unloaded and transferred to other boats. Although Shanghai has been cabled with regard to the impossibility of parcels to Canton being handled by the depleted staff there, a considerable number had had to be stored here which had left there prior to the notification.

The Siberian route, it would appear from further answers to the "China Mail" representative's enquiries, is being very extensively used at the present time particularly for the despatch of newspapers and periodicals, from Europe here, although, naturally enough, the quantity despatched from here via that route is considerably less. The opening up of the Tientsin-Pochow railway enabling mail for North China and Europe via Siberia to be forwarded to Harbin by the rail route had enabled the local authorities to make more regular air reliable connections in Shanghai.

headline: TEASED 2 GIRLS.
text:
VIOLENT COOLIE CAUGHT BY CONSTABLE.

FRIENDS JOIN IN.

On asking an earth coolie not to molest two Chinese girls who were passing Kowloon Tong, yesterday, an Indian “constable was assaulted by the coolie and about 35 friends, it is alleged, who threw stones at the constable.

morning—before—Mr. J. H. B. Nihill at the Kowloon Magistracy. He said that the constable, without any reason whatsoever, approached the matshed where he was working and threw away his shoes, (the defendant's), and because of this he protested. He denied having assaulted the constable.

"You are a violent boy," said Mr. Nihill, who passed sentence of ten strokes with the birch.

headline: FELINE SAGACITY.
text:
LOST CAT MAKES FRIENDS AT “COURT.”

POSSESSOR IMPRISONED.

"The cat on whom the court "sat" in solemn conclave yesterday to determine whether the coolie in whose possession it was found was the rightful owner made another appearance at the Central Magistracy this morning, when it was mentioned to Major Willson, the Magistrate, that a Japanese who had noticed the report had paid a visit to the station to see the cat.

The Japanese in question, said inspector Pain, had been unable to say whether it was his cat or lot.

Major Wilson expressed surprise and the Inspector said that the man had gone back to consult his wife and bring her to identify it if it was the same as the one they had lost. He had not put in an appearance again.

After adjourning the case to see if the man returned His Worship again questioned the defendant as to what means he came by the cat. Defendant replied that it was his own cat which had run away during the "flood."

Commenting that this was a different story to that given yesterday when he said that he had been asked by a friend to find a cat which had run away. His Worship sentenced defendant to 14 days' hard labour.

No order was made as to the ustody of the cat but it is understood that it has already made riends at the police quarters and will not lack for a home.

headline: CHURCH FIGHT. / EXTRAORDINARY AFFAIR IN MEXICO.
text:
CLASH WITH TROOPS.

México City, August.5.

The new religious Ordinances have provoked widespread disorders, accompanied by bloodshed, the most serious of them occurring at Guadalupe. The people inside a church fired on General Aguirre, who was passing by. Troops were summoned and the inmates barred the doors, mounted the towers, and fired down on the soldiers. The latter battered the doors in and routed the inmates, who nevertheless returned and tried to recapture the church.

A fight between troops and Catholics at Guadalajara resulted in six persons being killed and 14 wounded.

Milder disorders occurred at other centres, including Iraputs, where a. Protestant woman was beheaded, it is alleged, by Catholics. A band of crooks, profiting by the situation in Mexico City, are divesting women of their gold crosses and necklaces on the plea of their illegal display of religious insignia.

Senor Siaz, Secretary of the National Episcopate, in a statement, says that the Church has never approved of an armed uprising, but if necessary it would go to Calvary with the present struggle.—Reuter.

headline: DEAR VEGETABLES
text: A vernacular report says that the price of vegetables in Hongkong has gone up this week on account of a strike of workers near Canton, the strikers preventing supplies from getting through.

An earlier Reuter's message from Peking stated: — The Canton-postal-strike-has spread to Swatow, but the cooperation between the foreign naval commanders there is ensuring that foreigners get their letters without interruption.

Mails are brought to Swatow by gunboats and are landed by marines. On the other hand, Chinese residents are entirely cut off from outside postal communication.

headline: POST STRIKE ITEMS.
text:
The Public Safety (Police) Department has sent out armed detachments of police to patrol the city on account of the tense feeling following the many strikes. The public has been assured of adequate protection. Various shipping interests at Wuchow have called to the Union of postal employees in connection with the transport of mail bags (from Canton7).—Wah Tsz Yat Po.

The Nationalist Government is mediating in the postal strike.—Kung Sheung Yat Po.

headline: CHINESE RADIO.
text:
AFTERTHOUGHTS ON LOCAL CONCERT. HONGKONG,

TIPS * FOR FUTURE.

Expert's Views On Possibilities of Music.

o [By Leung Kam-Cong]

Having been asked by the China Mail to give my views on the possibilities of broadcasting Chinese music I must begin by emphasising that I know practically nothing about radio beyond what I say and heard at Wednesday's test concert in which I was privileged to take a small part.

First of all I say emphatically that I think it of very little use to install apparatus in a theatre. The sounds, or music, or whatever one pleases to call it, emanating from a Chinese stage, are not in the least amenable to broad-lasting for entertainment, simply because of drama (or opera), is fundamentally different from that of the Occident.

"Here I should add that I am confining myself to the Cantonese theatre and music."

Four Instruments Enough. For broadcasting, whether as accompaniment to songs, or as selections, four instruments are ample. They should not be played at high pressure as is necessary on the stage because our theatrical acoustics are so poor and the audience so noisy.

For the singer's main guidance and support I would use the Woo Kum (a two-stringed fiddle of a mellow tone) instead of the Yee Yin (also a two-string-fiddle, but with thicker strings and therefore more penetrating), which occupies the place of "leader" both in a theatrical band and in an orchestra.

But nearer to the microphone, I suggest putting a dulcimer. A dulcimer is on the basis of a harp laid flat:—brass strings fastened on brass regulators which stand on a wooden sound-box, played by striking the strings with two thin strips of bamboo peel. Under ordinary auditory circumstances, the dulcimer is the sole accompaniment and it is played by the singer (soloist). Having brass strings which are very "soft" the dulcimer ought to be entirely free from blurs in reception, as the vibrations are so mild.

headline: CANTON'S TROUBLES.
text:
The Canton Government is reported to have settled the postal strike by offering a subsidy to the workers, who are expected to return to work on Monday.

Further open fights in the city, between rival labour factions, are reported.

headline: DESERTER.
text:
AMERICAN SOLDIER FROM PHILIPPINES.

LANDED DESTITUTE.

Rufus Horak, aged 24, an American who on his own admission had deserted from the Philippines army, was charged before Major Willson this morning on two counts.

The first count concerned the non-possession of a passport and the second his being without visible means of subsistence. Sub-Inspector Fallon applied for the withdrawal of the first charge as he had instructions from the D.C.I., Mr. King, to ask for an order for the defendant's expulsion from the Colony. The defendant had given himself up to the Police after being in the Colony for some six days.

In" reply to Major Willson, In- spector Fallon said that it was usual under the circumstances to apply only for an order for deten- tion.

In reply to another question, In-spector Fallon said that if such an order were made, the defendant would have liberty of action at certain hours. The principal object of the Police in regard to the accused was that they might have him continually under observation with a view to getting him deported when the opportunity arose. The Police were awaiting certain confirmation from Manila in the matter of photographs and papers of identification.

It was therefore decided to proceed on the charge of non-possession of passport on which defendant was convicted and sentenced to two months' hard labour.

headline: PICKETS SNUBBED:
text:
ALLEGED INTERVENTION OF SOLDIERS.

HONGKONG PASSENGERS.

An “incident” in which a detachment alleged to be soldiers took high-handed action and supposedly snubbed the Strike Pickets' clearing office in Honans reported from Canton.

It may not be generally known that the strikers have the use of a high building on Honam island, on the opposite side of the river to Carlton city, where they issue permits for certain cargo and passports for passengers to and from Hongkong. A lookout is kept on the Hongkong steamboat from the top of the building.

This week it was alleged that a motor-boat took off from the steamboat one male passenger, eight ladies and a quantity of luggage. The motor-boat had permission to call on the steamboat but not to take off the passengers and their effects.

Action was taken and the motor-boat, passengers and luggage were detained. Three men, dressed like military officers, accompanied by ten or fifteen men armed with Mausers, are alleged to have gone to the clearing office, conducted themselves high-handedly, and finally to have made off with the motor-boat, passengers and luggage.

The report states that the “incident” has been brought to the notice of the Strike Executive and picket headquarters.

headline: ARBITRARY STEPS / FOREIGN OWNED SCHOOLS IN CANTON. / CHINESE AGITATION
text:
Arbitrary steps are suggested in a resolution which was to have come before yesterday's meeting in Canton of the Executive Society on Education—steps which aim at the very root of "foreign" schools in Canton and territory.

The proposer is of the opinion that since the Nationalist Government is busy with the present war, decisive measures ought to be adopted by the Society. The proposals include:—

Administrative committees and positions of principals to be confined to Chinese (i.e., in schools now owned or controlled by foreigners).

Land and property vested in such institutions to be turned over to Chinese.

All schools managed by foreigners to be registered with the Government which will appoint one supervisor, from the educational departments, to be continually at the schools and to direct all matters and matters pertaining to administration.

(Syllabus, etc., to conform with Government regulations. Opposition to be overcome by forcible measures if necessary.)

headline: Hongkong "Zoo."
text:
The speaker on the subject of an iguana's tail, also told the "China Mail" man about a wild animal entrepot in Gilman Street, where a distributing agent received weird monsters from all parts of the world and delivered them to owners of travelling shows in all parts of China.

Seriously, however, an iguana, not unlike a chameleon, is the most aquatic of the lizard family. They live on marine vegetation, diving under water to do so; and they can stay under for some considerable time without coming to the surface to breathe.

Then somebody suggested that the otters may have been brought here by the Fanling Hunt. Such is not the case, the zoological gardens in Japan also being the destination in this case.

Snakes For Food.

The “Mail” reporter also heard that a tapir arrived a few days ago, to be sent on to San Francisco. Articles in previous issues of this paper have explained the uses to "which snakes are put by Chinese in this Colony and, of course, elsewhere. Snakes form an expensive item in diet—in fact more costly than a luxury. Even the poisonous variety have their value. The spleen is supposed to have great restorative attributes and the "meat" is considered a delicacy.

The import of snakes into Hongkong (from Canton "more far") has been restricted by the strike. But there is also a re-export business, Hongkong dealers sending on shipments to places where the Cantonese emigrate in any number.

As the winter is the snake feast season, it is thought that the batch of six baskets mentioned in the H.K.S.P.C.A. report were either for transhipment, or for making special snake gamshu.

headline: SEAMEN JAILED.
text:
REVOLVER

A CAPTAIN'S STORY.

Unruly Indians Who Had to Be Locked Up.

Order was only restored on board the S.S. "City of Corinth," when a few days from Hongkong, by the captain procuring revolvers to protect the loyal part of his crew against "picketing" by nine firemen who gave trouble as far back as June, when they adopted "a ca" eanny policy because they were tired. These nine Indian firemen were tried and sentenced at the Marine Court this morning. On the first charge of disobedience to the lawful commands of the master at Manila on August

After the master had given evidence, the Magistrate (L.T. (Com. G. F. Holt, R.N.), added a second charge of combining to impede the navigation of the ship; on this defendants each received an additional twelve weeks.

headline: Pay to be "Docked."
text:
Both sentences were, with hard labour," to run consecutively (meaning sixteen weeks in all), without the option of a fine. His Worship also ordered that "any wages that may be due, to be used for their subsistence while undergoing their sentence and the residue for their repatriation to Bombay."

Mr. L. R. Andrewes appeared for the prosecution.

headline: Previous Trouble
text:
Things continued till Manila where the men were refused shore leave because of the strict laws there regarding deserters from ships.

Trouble broke out, the men openly refused to work even when summoned before the captain. The British Consul-General went on board and explained the penalties to defendants. The Consul informed witness that the civil authorities in Manila could give no assistance and suggested that the men should be brought to Hongkong to be dealt with here. Subsequently the defendants, said Captain Burton, picketed the storehold door, "driving on deck the men who were working and refusing to allow any one to go below."

headline: Pút in Irons.
text:
"To safeguard the loyal men,' remarked Captain Burton, 'I procured revolvers."

Explaining that the loyal men were so intimidated, that they dared not work, witness added that defendants were put in irons. They were removed to the House of Detention and then brought to Hongkong.

Confirmatory evidence was given by Mr. W. Kirk (chief engineer) and Mr. T. McKinney (second engineer).

Defendants declined to cross- examine but one of them made a statement.

His Worship found all the men guilty on both charges and imposed sentence as stated.

The report of captain states that the crew consists of 18 British and 42 Asiatics.

headline: MAGISTRACY ITEMS.
text:
EXHIBITS IN COURT.

More than the usual number of assault cases and lareniess made up the charge sheets at the Central Magistracy this morning before Mr. R. E. Lindsell.

A blacksmith, from Shaukiwan with a wounded head was the complainant in an assault charge against a boat builder, the wound stated to have been inflicted with a wooden pole when complainant went on Saturday morning to collect the balance of an old debt amounting to $1.55. Complaintant alleged that he was attacked by the defendant and three others. Defendant was fined $3 and ordered to sign a personal bond for future good behaviour. He was further ordered to pay $2 as compensation to the complainant, thus satisfying the debt.

Two scavenging coolies were involved in another case, the aggrieved party appearing with a wounded leg. An iron bar was brought to prove the assault.

Complainant said that they had a dispute yesterday over a broom and he was attacked at Leighton Hill Road this morning.

Defendant attempted to prove that he was also assaulted, but he had to pay a fine of $5, or go to prison for seven days.

Sergeant James. of the Aberdeen Police Station, charged two women and a man with assaulting another women who was in hospital with a deep wound in the thigh.

The injured woman was unable to say how she received the wound, and Sergeant James thought it possible that she fell over an anchor which was found there, as alleged by the defendants in their statements to the police and in court.

Defendants were remanded to bail for one week.

In explanation of a charge of unlawful possession of a bundle of copper wire and metal, a Chinese boy told the Magistrate that he found them in a lane at Wanchai.

Div.-Inspector Blackman said that inquiries had been made since Saturday morning to trace the owner, but without success. The boy received eight strokes with a light cane.

An apprentice-failed to get away with a bucket containing ten pounds of tin soldier, the property of the Taikoo Docks. He was charged with theft. Defendant, who pleaded that he was pressed to commit the theft owing to starvation, was sentenced to four weeks' hard labour.

headline: STREET FIGHTS.
text:
CANTON CURBING MOB ROWDIES?

LABOURERS' DISPUTES.

Continual riots and fights between opposing bodies of workmen in Canton have led to about fifteen being arrested by the Department of Public Safety (Police Commissioner) on Saturday night.

The, trouble has spread to several Unions and the real_casus belli has now been lost sight of:

In different parts of the city rowdies have met and fought, causing considerable unrest. Most of the men were armed with all kinds of weapons.

The authorities have taken action and it is believed that the trouble is in hand. Armed police patrols were out again on Saturday, it is reported.

On the Taiping maloo, leading into the western suburb from the Bund, seventeen men are stated to have been killed or seriously wounded on Friday.

The postal strikers are expected to return to work today.

A correspondent to the "Wan Tsz Yat Po" states that the tea-house and (wheat) flour workers were mainly concerned; and that the strike of oilshop employees has been settled.

The s.s. "Szechuen" reports the suspected suicide of a second-class Chinese passenger from Shanghai. She left that port on August 8 and he man was posted missing the second day out.

headline: FALSE "ALARM.
text:
FIRE ENGINE COLLIDES IN CITY.

FIREMAN INJURED

Wiring Connections At Club To Blame?

Whilst proceeding to the Hong- kong Club at 9.55 a.m. to-day in response to an alarm which prov- ed false, the No. 6 fire engine ap- plince skidded on the damp road surface and collided with a pillar of the C.P.R. (Union) building at the junction of Pedder Street and Chatter Road.

Fireman No. 59 was jolted off the engine and sustained injuries to chest and neck which necessitated his removal to the Government Civil Hospital where he is progressing favourably.

The fire engine was damaged very considerably, the radiator being smashed in and the fire escape carried also being damaged. It was towed back to the station by another fire engine. It will be some time before the engine is again in commission but it is hoped to get the fire escape repaired and ready for use in the course of the day.

headline: Narrow Escape
text:
Although the impact was considerable the pillar shows little signs of the collision. Needless to say, if the engine had not first struck the pillar and had entered through the C.P.R. window there might have been many more casualties as there were a number of people in the office at the time and the engine was travelling at considerable speed.

This is the second false fire alarm-within-two months from the Hongkong Club and is believed to have been due to defective wiring. The Club is connected up direct with the fire station and as soon as the indicator falls the brigade immediately gets busy. The falling of the signal does not; however, open up immediate telephonic communication with the Club and as seconds may be precious the fire station on both occasions has immediately sent the machines away without confirming an outbreak.

headline: Boycott Effect
text:
The boycott and crisis which commenced in June of last year has caused considerable anxiety in the commercial sphere of this Colony. The facts are too well known to all and it is needless for me to make any comment except perhaps in connection with the effect of our chain of theatres. The situation naturally hit our Chinese theatres very seriously, namely, the Grand Theatre at Wanchai, the New Taiyat Theatre at Yaumati and the Cheong Lok Theatre at Sai-wan-ho, which are situated in the heart of industrial and labouring districts. Fortunately, however, the effect did not continue for long and after a few months, conditions returned to a more or less normal state.

Owing to considerably increased expenditure and overhead consequent upon our taking over two of the Colony's largest theatres your directors regret that they are unable to repeat the previous year's dividend of 20 per cent. but they are recommending a dividend of 15 per cent. which, I feel sure, in view of the company's increased overhead and the troublous period through which we have all experienced, will be a source of gratification to you just as surely as it is to them, especially as we are able to carry forward an amount of some $26,000—representing nearly 60 per cent. above last year's figure. We have every reason to hope that the immediate future will yield even better results.

Cinema Prices.

A few people have, from time to time, publicly expressed their indignation at our prices of admission and, as a matter of interest,

headline: China the Jail / POLICE BESIEGER.
text:
LABOURERS GIVE TROUBLE.

CADENTS CALLED OUT?

A substation in the 6th police district, Canton city, has been threatened and surrounded by workmen who insisted on the release of rioters. Reinforcements from police headquarters dispersed the rowdies.

Mr. So Shiu-ching (chairman of the Stilike Executive) and Mrs. Liao Chung-kai (wife of the Labour Minister who was assassinated last year) have issued an appeal asking Labour Unions, not to cause unrest and thereby prejudice the Government interests (through disturbing home fires while war is on). Mr. So and Mrs. Liao "ask that disputes be referred "to the Labour Ministry but the appeal has not yet had the effect of restoring order.

All city police are now armed. Special men on post duty have been sent to quell street fights. The Nationalist Government has sent a detachment from the Whampoa Academy to Canton to assist in preserving order." Wah Tsz Yat Po."

headline: CANTON NEWS.
text:
FINANCIAL SITUATION NOT ALARMING

FOREIGN REPORTS DENIED.

The Canton Information Bureau has issued the following “communique through Reuter's Agency:—

The postal workers resumed work this morning.

The reports appearing in foreign newspapers describing the financial situation here as alarming are entirely false.

The demonstration on Sunday against the resumption of the Peking Tariff Conference was attended by large crowds.

I would point out that approximately 21% million people visited all our theatres in a year and if we had charged 2 cents less per head for admission we would show a net loss of some $5,000—instead of a net earning of nearly $40,000—a fact which clearly indicates the very small margin on which your company is working.

As last year, we have budgeted for a bonus to be paid to Chinese theatre staffs, which will not exceed $960. You will, I am sure, cordially approve this recognition of faithful and arduous service.

I thank you, gentlemen, for the patient hearing you have given my remarks, and take pleasure in calling on Mr. J. M. Noronha to second the resolution now before you, viz., that the report and statement of accounts as presented, be received, approved and adopted.

headline: SMUGGLER CAUGHT
text:
HELPING TO ROB HIS OWN HOUSE.

$ ^{*} $ ARMS FOR CANTON.

Painter on "Futshan" Gets 3 Yenwa "Hard"

Mr. R. E. Lindsell and Major C. Willson sat together at the Central Magistracy this morning to deal with, the charge of unlawful possession of arms against a ship's painter of the s.s. "Fatshan" formally adjourned from Saturday.

The case was one in which an attempt was made to lower the arms which had been placed in floating containers when the ship was on the outward voyage between Capsuimum and Castle Peak. A "sampun" with a man's hat hoisted on a pole was to take possession of the arms as arranged by the smugglers. This sampun was, in fact, passed by the s.s. "Fatshan" after the discovery had been made by the ship's officers, also on the downward voyage, apparently still hopeful of the arms being lowered.

The arms taken over by Acting Inspector J. Moss, who had charge of the case, comprised 20 Mauser pistols, 42 Smith and Wesson revolvers, 40 magazines and 3,250 rounds of ammunition.

Defendant, who had stated to the police that the arms were given to him by a travelling trader to take to Canton, admitted the charge.

Mr. Lindsell: You were smuggling them to Canton?

Mr. Lindsell: You live in Hong- kong yourself?

Defendant: Yes.

Mr. Lindsell: You are encouraging armed robbers to come and rob your own house by smuggling arms to Canton.

Defendant: "It is not mine. Mr. Lindsell: You admit you are smuggling to Canton. It is the stuff armed robbers get hold of and come here.

Defendant, who appeared to contradict His Worship on this point, was sentenced to three years' hard labour, an order being made for the arms to be confiscated.

Marcato's fortnightly notes on music will appear in the "China Mail" on Friday, also the result of the competition.

On Page 4 of this issue will be found further interesting details about the fire on the Frenc. mail steamer Fontaine-bleau.

Developments following the resignation of the England cricket captain are repoted on page 9.

headline: Sinks in 90 Seconds.
text:
Mystery surrounds the sinking of H29 within a few minutes.

The Commander-in-Chief has arrived. He took charge of the special equipment which was rushed to the quayside to raise the vessel.

The submarine had just returned from tests, the hatches being open and the propeller had not stopped. When she came alongside she suddenly tilted and sank within ninety seconds.

The basin is comparatively small.

Pumping operations ought not to occupy many hours.—Reuter.

headline: BOYCOTT PARLEY
text:
RESUMPTION DEPENDS ON NANKOW?

EFFECT OF THE WAR.

Interesting Intelligence From Canton.

Few foreign residents in the Colony pay much attention to the fortunes of war in North China and even the Chinese themselves are at a loss to make out the precise position but from an unofficial source it is learned that the fighting at Nankow has considerable influence on the prospects of the boycott conference being resumed.

The gist of the intelligence gathered by a correspondent is that the Canton authorities are waiting to come to a decision. Some days ago, the conference adjourned. The Hongkong deligation came back to await instructions and the Canton Government was to consider the proffered loan of $10,000,000 for development work.

headline: Where the Rivals Are
text:
General Chang Kai-shek, commander-in-chief, is at "the southern China front while his civil officials are" mostly in Canton.

Hunan is the province separating Kwangtung from the Yangtze Valley (central China). The Nationalist Front is reported to be near Changsha and Wu Pei-fu's troops are near Yochow, a town on the railway between Changsha and Hankow (the latter erstwhile the capital of Wu Pei-fu). Operations on this front are partly restricted. It seems that Canton's forces are awaiting developments before making another advance. On the other hand, Wu Pei-fu's subordinates are marking time pending the return of their leader from the North.

Wu Pei-fu's Movements.

Marshal Wu has been quoted as having promised to return to Hankow so soon as the campaign in North China is concluded.

Further north than Peking, the army of Feng Yu-hsiang (the Christian general). known as the Kuominchun, are holding on to Nankow Pass, on the road to Kalgan, their main camp.

Vernacular cables report a continuous assault on Nankow and Reuter has stated that firing has been heard in Peking.

Should Nankow fall, then it is presumed that Wu Pei-fu will leave the North to Marshal Chang Tso-lin (warlord of Manchuria). The conclusion is that he will go back to central China where his presence will tend to a central command, and prestige—and possibly an extension of hostilities in Hunan, thereby engaging the attention of Canton.

headline: Canton Waiting?
text:
The correspondent remarks that Canton is waiting to see how things will pan out at Nankow. Should the Kuominchun win then it is likely that the Nationalists will push forward and consolidate their position before re-opening the conference with Hongkong to end the boycott. Victory for Wu Pei-fu (and Chang Tso-lin) at Nankow will adversely affect Canton's prospects in Hunan and may hasten the resumption of the adjourned conference.

The consensus of opinion in Canton, from a well-informed source, is that the interval before resumption may not end just yet.

headline: UNCHECKED.
text:
HOLERA AMONG SHANGHAI CHINESE.

RESULT OF GRATHET

As a result of the excessive heat on August 6, cholera is continuing, even checked among the Chinese community in Shanghai, says the "China Press" of August 7, which adds: "In spite of the heroic fight, carried on by the vicious hospitals against its spread, the epidemic is (sid) unchecked and no effective control has been gained over it.

Nesterday afternoon the Thibet Road infections Diseases Hospital reported two deaths from cholera and 45 out of 182 people received saline injections. The Tientain Road Red Cross Hospital treated

16 others, received saline injections. In the Buckill Road Summer Discases Hospital, no death was recorded, but 48 patients out of 226 attended took saline injection. The situation, in Horgkew district seems much improved, as the St. Luke's Hospital reported the admission of only two cases yesterday.

In the native city, Nantuo, a Chinese woman who was overtaken by cholera at two o'clock Thursday night died at five Friday morning. A cause of heat prostration occurred in the West Cateadistrict, when a Chinese ice cream hawker, while running about to sell his commodity, under the mid-day sun, suddenly fell down unconscious and died on the way to hospital. In Pointung, five more people succumbed to cholera on Thursday and in Chapel, more than seven deaths were recorded. Among the victims in the various places, the majority are boys and children. According to a report submitted to the Shanghai-Wosung Constabulary by the Second Police Station in the West Cate district five persons, three men and two women, became infected with cholera on Thursday and all of them died. In the night.

In order to combat the epidemic Dr. V. K' Ting has ordered officials to inaugurate the services of the newly-promised Shanghai-Woosung Health Bureau. The Bureau, as reported, has been under process of organisation for a considerable time and it is hoped that it will be opened by the middle of this month, Mr. Hsu Huang-chi, assistant director of the Bureau, has just come to Shanghai from Nanking and is now conferring with Dr. Ting and Central Yen Tsung-yang. Chief Director of the Bureau regarding the establishment and opening of the office in the near future.

Preventive Treatment. With the daily toll taken by cholera mounting steadily and a constant vigilance being applied to the situation by the health authorities, it is interesting to note the preventive measures, other than the usual cautions about contaminated food and water, which the French municipality is using.

According to Dr. R. Poupelain, Health Officer for the Concession, more than 2,000 doses of the Anti-choleric Billyaccin have been given to policemen, firemen and other employees of the French Municipality in an effort to prevent the spreading of the epidemic.

As explained by Dr. Poupelain this vaccine, which is known only as a preventive and not as a cure after the disease has been contracted, is taken in the form of six tablets and not in the usual way of inoculation. Three tablets prepare the digestive tract for the remaining three tablets containing the real cholera, vaccine and this form of inoculation is in line with the Pasteur Institute discoveries pertaining to local immunisation. As the intestines are affected in cholera, swallowing the anti-toxin rather than receiving it through injection carries out the principle of local immunisation. The vaccine is believed to be efficacious, not only in cholera, but in prevention of dysentery, typhoid and other disturbances of this nature.

Rules for taking the cholera vaccine are given on a sheet accompanying the medicine, as follows: "To preserve oneself from cholera a gall pill (round) immediately followed by a compressed tablet of vaccine (flat) must be absorbed each morning on an empty stomach, during three consecutive days. The previous ingestion of the gall pill is necessary in order to enable the absorption of: the vaccine by the intestine. After the ingestion of the entire dose (three gall and three vaccines) in three

days immunisation is complete and almost immediate. The absorption of this galled vaccine produces no disorder or discomfort.

During the week from August 1 to 5 $ ^{th} $ says the "N.-C. Daily News," of August 7, there have been notification of 75 cases in the French Concession, 74 Chinese and 1 foreigner (Russian). Of this number 25 have died.

In the Settlement, while notification of new cases are stated to have decreased, the number of deaths recogded from cholera have increased. Three foreign cases were reported on Monday (two Japanese and one Indian); on Tuesday, 74 Chinese, on Wednesday, one foreign case and 21 Chinese. In Chinese Territory, notification was made on Monday of 105 cases, on Tuesday 108 and on Wednesday 30. Chinese, of unknown, residence were reported on Monday as 13, and on Tuesday, seven.

Deaths in the Settlement were six Chinese on Sunday, and on the same day in the Concession one death was reported. In Chinese territory four deaths were recorded as well as two Chinese of unknown residence.

It is said, however, that the medical authorities have the situation well in hand and that should the next week see lowered temperature with rain in Shanghai, the back of the cholera epidemic could be broken.

headline: CANTON STRIKERS. / NEWSPAPERS STILL NOT PUBLISHING.
text:
POSTMEN BACK.

Canton's vernacular papers are still not publishing.

One report indicates the possibility of the two alleged Government organs being involved—not in the actual strike, but in the dispute. The report goes that a certain section of Labour is not now supporting the official publications because of the attitude taken up.

The Canton (vernacular) Press Association is stated to have asked the Government what policy it will adopt in the present dispute.

On Monday the striking postmen are said to have returned to work, without incident. No further street riots have been reported but a disturbed atmosphere still prevails.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
CLERICS' PROPOSAL TURNED DOWN.

BALLÓT'S SURPRISE.

Contrary to the expectations of the newspapers the district votes in the mining areas, which were considered to-day at a meeting of the Miners' Federation Executive in London, disclosed a majority against the proposals "for a settlement of the coal dispute, which had been advanced by the Industrial Christian Fellowship and approved by the Miners' Executive.

The statement issued at the close of the meeting gave no details of the voting.

It merely stated that the decision reported from the districts was against the recommendations of the last delegate conference, and added that the Executive had decided to call another delegate conference of their members on Monday next to give the report of this voting to them. British Wireless Service.

headline: LIKE OTHER NEEDS.
text:
Sir,—The Government exercise control over the electricity, tramway and telephone, services in order that the interests of the public may be safeguarded. It is hardly necessary to state that items of expenditure incurred in connection with these public utility companies play far less important a part in the household "budget than does that of rent. If the Government considers necessary in the best interests of the public that it should have the final say as to any increases in the price of the public services already mentioned how much more is it incumbent on them to set up machinery for safeguarding the tenant's interests in respect of one of the biggest items figuring in his budget—that of rent?

Dealing with a public utility company and with separate landlords are of course two very different things but if the principle is right in the one case then it is in the other and no consideration of the difficulties involved should influence the Government in ignoring the desirability of setting up a controlling organisation.

In June of this year a committee was appointed "to enquire into the general rise in the "price of foods sold in the markets and to suggest steps which may be possible to effect a reduction of "those prices." If such an organisation can be instituted in respect of food—and it is a very much more ticklish business to deal with multitudinous "stallholders than with landlords—it can be instituted in respect of rents.

The very fact that in many cases tenants have been obliged through lack of suitable alternative accommodation to endeavour to meet the increases demanded by the landlords is sufficient indication that the supply of such types of houses or flats has not overtaken the demand—rebutting the statements made in Council when it was decided to drop restriction. The "Government cannot wash their hands of responsibility in this manner and it is up to them to put in hand some organisation for the control of rents on a fair basis.

Alleged Exploitation of 1

[To the Editor of the "China Mail."] Sir,—There is one aspect of the Hongkong rents scandal that has received little publicity. Will you therefore be kind enough to accord me space in your valuable columns to make it known? Financiers who engage in mortgage on property are also to be blamed for putting rents unduly up. Does this seem strange to you, Sir? It may but the element of surprise will not be there if you have gone through what I endured. My house was hypothecated just before the strike began. Values have now fallen. When the year was short time ago the more foreclosed. Against that I no complaint it being his due. Then came the natural sequence, the sale by public auction. Suffice is it to say that I still owe a considerable sum to make good the deficiency because

the amount I borrowed equal to 8 per cent. of the value at that time.

Once that property was out of my hands, tenants received notices increasing rentals by an average, in round sums, of 55. percent. It is only now that I have discovered the fact that the buyer at the auction was acting in the interests of the mortgagee. What assumption can a business man make? I can only conclude that to get the best out of a bad bargain rents have been raised so that the present value of the property will go up pro rata. On the basis of value in ratio to revenue the mortgagee artificially puts up the price. He then recovers his outlay. I have lost all along the line. That is only a side issue but why should tenants suffer for an error of judgment by the mortgagee and by me? This aspect of the evil of non-control needs great emphasis. headline: HONGKONG, / EUROPEAN'S LOSS.
text:
JEWELLERY THEFT AT THE

OLD SERVANT SUSPECTED.

A Peak resident has lost a valuable diamond ring among other articles of jewellery from his residence.

The report of the loss made to the police by Mr. E. B. C. Hornell, of '204 The Peak, states that it took place between Monday and yesterday.

The missing articles comprised a white gold diamond ring set in platinum, a gold necklet with cross attached, and another gold chain with a sapphire pendant. These were taken from a jewel case in the bedroom.

Suspicion rests on a former house coolie who had been staying in the servants' quarters during the past two days and was found to have disappeared when the loss was discovered.

headline: OBITUARY:
text:
FUNERAL TO-DAY.

We regret to have to record the death of Battery Quarter-Master-Sergeant Jacobs, of the 38th Henry Battery, Royal Artillery, stationed at "Stonecutter's Island.

Death took place at the Military Hospital at 8.10 p.m. yesterday after a brief but acute illness lasting six days.

Deceased leaves behind a large family with whom the greatest sympathy will be felt. Besides his wife and six children (five sons and a daughter) who are at present in Hongkong, another son is serving with the British Army stationed in German territory.

The funeral will take place at the Protestant Cemetery at Happy Valley, leaving the Medical Inspection Room, Wellington Barracks, at 4 o'clock this afternoon.

headline: COLONY'S WEALTH.
text:
FIGURES WHICH SPEAK FOR THEMSELVES.

SUBSTANTIAL SURPLUS

An important statement with regard to the year's working, was made by the Colonial Secretary in Council this afternoon in moving the first reading of an Ordinance to authorise the appropriation of a supplementary sum of $832,249.52.

Certain troubles had occurred during the year, he said, and it was interesting to note that the actual figures for 1925 showed a revenue of $23½ millions and an expenditure of $28½ millions, a deficit of only $5,022,052.

Thus, in spite of the boycott the revenue had exceeded the estimate by $1,437,365, only just less than a million dollars below the record year of 1924, and well above that of 1921 and 1922.

The expenditure was of necessity to some extent curtailed and in spite of unexpected calls on the revenue of the Colony the expenditure was kept below the estimate by over two million dollars. It would thus be seen that the year closed with a very substantial surplus of assets over liabilities of the sum of $8,113,482, a figure which within the last ten years had only been exceeded on three occasions.

[Sec also page 6.]

headline: Elementary Education
text:
It was chiefly with regard to elementary education that the King, together with the Government, was most anxious that progress should be made; added the Prince, and his observations during his tour would be chiefly confined to this. He had hoped, however, that during his stay here he would have the opportunity of visiting the University and schools whilst in session. This had been impossible but he had spoken to H.E. the Governor, also the Vice-Chancellor of the University and the Director of Education who had been of considerable assistance to him.

The King of Siam, said Prince Dahni, was anxious to incorporate into the educational system of Siam methods which had been tried with success elsewhere and it was as a result that the present tour had been undertaken. Siam had its Department of Education and a special Minister for Education and any proposals which might arise out of the report would be submitted to them. Much had already been done in regard to higher education as the result of measures introduced based on the experience of students from Siam who had been educated in Britain, America, Germany, France and Japan.

headline: CANTON RIOTS.
text:
GENERAL CHANG ISSUES REGULATIONS.

STRICT PRECAUTIONS.

To stop street rights among workers and rival unions in Canton Commander-in-Chief Chang Kai-shek has issued a notification which reads:

I have been informed by the Bureau of Public Safety to the effect that of late fighting has been occurring among workers, that the rioters could not be suppressed by the police and that they sometimes assaulted the police and endangered the lives of the passers-by. Hereafter any workers who carry weapons and gathers in crowds to

Light with their rival workers are to be considered as frustrating the public peace.

I also consider them to be the best of our military operations. I have therefore instructed the Commander of the Gendarmerie of Canton as well as the Head of the Bureau of Public Safety to enforce the following regulations so as to put an end to further disturbances. 1: Except troops or the police groups "carrying weapons and roaming about the city are to be suppressed by military force and their weapons are to be seized and confiscated.

2. Ringhender's of groups making preparations for fighting are to be severely punished in accordance with military law.

97 "Search is to be made on passers-by." Any "one" secretly carrying revolvers or other weapons is to be arrested and severely dealt with.

headline: PRINTERS "CHOW."
text:
Pickets'Surround Newspaper

Three vernacular newspapers at Canton are reported to have resumed publication.

It is thought that the masters have submitted to the printers' terms.

A curious development occurred when the employers took steps to just strikers from the offices.

Instructions were given to the ebooks not to prepare any meals for the striking workmen. The workmen at once reported to their union. The union sent pickets who took up "stations" in the newspaper offices, warning the employers that meals would be provided by the union to the strikers at $1.20 per head per day, the cost to be borne by the owners.

Following the threat, the masters at once conceded the point. Food was again given the strikers, but then the pickets refused to leave and they also had to be fed. One paper's office had the appearance of being under siege, pickets standing on duty and a flag flying from the top.

The report goes that the three papers which resumed gave in rather than accommodate the pickets and striking printers.

headline: RIOT-PREVENTED
text:
Rival Union Men Separated By

Near the Little East Gate of Canton city, another labour riot was just nipped in the bud on Wednesday, thanks to reinforcements being sent by the Public Safety Department.

Over 200 men of the Oil-workers Guild were returning to work, under orders from the Police. A smaller number of workmen, alleged to be also in the oil trade, assembled on the route they had to take and formed a barrier. Anticipating trouble, armed police had been sent out and the rival gangs were separated and told to move on. Various crude weapons, bamboo poles &c. were seized.

The trouble among workers in the vegetable depots has not yet been settled.

The silk dealers in Ha Kau Po are reported to be reopening their doors to business, protection having been promised by the Police. In this trade two rival gangs of workmen are said to have been implicated.

In 1916 the Colony had the record number of rieshas, it is observed. With the advent of motor traffic, the Police Department has followed a policy of gradual reduction.

Since 1923, ricshas (the drivers of which?) have had three convictions registered against them for offences, have been withdrawn from off the streets. The numbers thus taken off are given by the “Kung Sheung Yat Po” as 120 in 1923, 100 in 1924, none in 1925 and over 60 in 1926.

A factor not mentioned by the vernacular paper is the permission of public ricshas on the upper levels a few years ago, but this addition is possibly included in the figures quoted above.

The licence for a public ricsha is $72 a year, it is stated. Including the licence fee and the hire charged by the owner ("or "farmer"), the coolies pay 45 cents a day for the privilege of drawing a ricsha. The man on day shift pays 24 cents and the night shift man pays 30 cents.

headline: FATAL DISPUTE.
text:
A quarrel between a number of coolies at Yaumati yesterday afternoon had a fatal ending

During the dispute a sanitary coolie's broom struck another man in the region of the spleen and he died shortly afterwards.

A man, alleged to be the ussailant has been detained by the police.

A bazuar is to be held on Sept. 2 to 4 inclusive, in the London Mission Society compound, Bonham Road, for the building fund of the new Church of Christ in China (To Chal Church). Further particulars will be announced later.

headline: OPIUM TRAFFIC. / DRUG SMUGGLED FROM WUCHOW. / $1,000 FINE.
text:
The smuggling of opium into Hongkong from the West River district was disclosed in prosecutions brought by Revenue Officer Pearse before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

One of the cases concerned Ho Kam, a seaman on the motor vessel "Ching Lung," who was charged with unlawful possession of 14 taels of prepared illicit opium.

Possession was admitted by the defendant, who said he smuggled the opium from Wuchow on a lighter belonging to the Asiatic Petroleum Company.

A fine of $1,000 or six months' hard labour in default was imposed.

One British case of diptheria in Kowloon and a Chinese case of cerebrospinal fever in the city were reported to the Medical Officer of Health on Thursday.

headline: LABOUR RIOTS.
text:
HOW TROUBLE SPREAD TO KONGMOON.

13 MEN INJURED.

Pakkai, Kongmoon, August 11. Kongmoon has been emulating Canton's example in the matter of labour riots and troubles. Recorded in order of occurrence these are:—

August 2: The postal strike began here and service in all stations in this district suspended. August 9: Postal strikers resume.

August 9: Drug shop workers went on strike. Pickets were posted round the shops and people were prevented from having medical prescriptions filled. Then a misunderstanding arose and the drugmen fought with members of the Tung Tack Coolies' Guild. Soldiers appeared on the scene and dispersed the rioters. The wounded comprised 3 on the drugmen's side and 10 on the coolies.

August 10: Employees of the Longmoon Electric Co. threaten to go on strike for better pay and privileges.

August 11: The strike of telephone employees was settled, the Kongmoon company giving higher pay. As a result the subscription was raised by $1 a month, to $8 a month.

[Trouble among oil-workers is referred to on page 2.]

headline: IS LOCAL OBJECTION ONLY SHAMMED?
text:
SHANGHAI AND HONGKONG.

[To the Editor of the "China Mail."] Sir,—The letter you reproduce by "An Optimist" only goes to show that the class distinction evil exists also in Shanghai as well as in Hongkong.

"An Optimist" prays for a lend in the big knobs giving approval for shorts and shirts. And by the way, why do you insist in calling them "Cissy" shirts when they are nothing of the kind? I most strongly object to such a denomination as will others who wear a sports shirt for comfort and for no other reason.

Will any Hongkong taiwan have sufficient courage of his convictions to insert the hong notice suggested:—

"During the summer months male employees are permitted to wear open shirts and shorts?" I know that if I turned up at office sensibly dressed to meet weather requirements my boss would send me home directly and tell me to be clad "decently" before I returned.

Another crisis will have the wonderful effect of making Hongkong—and Shanghai—less inclined to the “Thank God I am not as others” feeling. One will appreciate shorts and shirts if a man's work is done in a day.

Yours, etc.,
