headline: We allow 10% discount for Cash
text: This statement has aroused great national indignation in the Liangkuang (i.e., Kwangtung and Kwangsi provinces). Numerous meetings were immediately summoned in order to deal with this grossly provocative charge made at a moment when the negotiations between the Canton and Hongkong Governments are only adjourned and not ended. A big parade is announced for this week in order to prove that the Chinese people in the Liangkuang support the strike and boycott movement.

headline: ARE FRESH NEGOTIATIONS IMMUNANT?
text:
POSSIBLE MEDIATION.

London, August 22. While messages from the coal-fields report that many more miners are working, it appears that Mr. Cook's week-end campaign resulted in some indecision among the miners at Mansfield who had signed on on the local mineowners' terms of a 7½ hours day at approximately pre-strike rates of pay, and a big majority of whom had not yet resumed work. All roads leading to the pits in this district were picketed and many men who started from home intending to work have returned. Meanwhile, inquiries in Government circles show that there is no ground for Mr. Cook's suggestion that negotiations with the Government as a party may occur this week. There appears no probability of any actual negotiations in the near future, though the Government has informed Mr. Cook that one of the Ministers would be prepared to meet him at any time he desires.—Reuter.

The anticipation in South Wales of an early termination of the coal stoppage was reflected on the Cardiff Stock Exchange to day. Collery shares were very firm and in strong demand. All the leaders showed an upward tendency. At least 6,000 miners have resumed in Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire, whilst 740 more men are working in Warwickshire than on Saturday and 400 more at Cannock Chase.—Reuter.

headline: BATHING PARTY ROBBED.
text:
While a moonlight bathing party were enjoying themselves on the beach at Ting Kau (beyond Laichikok) on Monday night, a thief took advantage of lifting things from their motor car left unattended on the road. In a report of the theft made to the police by Messrs. Fremoulet and Foquet, residents of Nathan Road, they estimated the loss in ladies' clothing, keys and other property at a totall of $68.90.

A workman in the employment of Messrs. Trollope and Colls was severely injured in an accident at the Peninsula Hotel building yesterday. He was removed to the Kowloon Hospital in an unconscious condition.

headline: LORRY DAMAGE.
text:
GEARS MEDDLED WITH BY A COOLIE.

COURT SEQUEL

Acoolie in the employment of the Sang Lee contractors was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with damaging a P.W.D.O lorry to the extent of $70 by negligent tampering with the genres while the vehicle was loading earth at Stubbs Rond.

Defendant pleaded that he knew very little about a motor engine, but he had been in the habit of assisting the lorry drivers by cranking the engines. On this occasion in engine refuses to start and he moved a level which made the lorry run backward and damage another lorry standing further down. The driver of the lorry admitted that defend; he had frequently done the cranking for him. His Worship thought that the action was one for the Summary Court to decide if the contractors refused to pay compensation and discharged the defendant.

headline: Pickets Active.
parent_headline: COAL TROUBLES. / MINERS' AGENT IN COURT 3 ILLEGAL THREAT
text:
Whilst, generally speaking the number of miners working continues to increase, there has been a decrease in the Mansfield district of the Notts coalfield where picketing and intimidation is reported have been very active and large numbers of police are being drafted to protect those men who are willing work.

Acts of open violence are few, and so far the Police have detained only one man.

Mr. Cook is said to have a great deal of solid support in this district, where thousands of miners are attending meetings addressed by the leaders.

Emergency Regulations. It is understood that the Privy Council will meet to-morrow at Balmoral Castle, where His Majesty the "King has just" arrived, to issue a proclamation of emergency and a proclamation recalling Parliament on Monday for a brief sitting to confirm the Emergency Regulations.

A lively debate is expected. It is understood that the Labourites will try to induce Ministers to call a meeting with the miners or the owners.—Reuter.

headline: CANTON'S WAR.
text:
CAPTURE OF YOCHOW CONFIRMED.

AEROPLANE LOST?

Canton's capture of Xochow has been confirmed now by sources which---may ---be described as "strictly anti-Red."

Yochow is in the northern part of Hunan province, on that part of the Hankow-Canton Railway which runs to Changsha. (Note: the southern part of the railway runs from Canton to Shiukwan, and the middle section of the line is only "projected.")

In their present position, the southern Nationalists may launch an early attack on Hupeh province and the strongholds of Han-kow. "Wuchang, and the Hanyang arsenal.

Marshall Sun Chuan-fang (ruler of the central maritime provinces and hinterland) is reported to be moving troops into Kiangsi province, ostensibly to guard his frontiers against possible invasion by a flank movement of the

An aeroplane flying from Canton to the front, is reported to have landed in Kiangsi owing to engine trouble, and to have been captured.

For publicity purposes in the territory newly conquered by the Nationalists, a sum of $1,500,000 is said to have been voted by Communist agitators, the funds coming from Russia.

A vernacular paper in Swatow was raided, states a correspondent, for publishing the report of the capture of Nankow (in the North) by the allies.

Reports on another piracy in neighbouring waters "(that of the s.s. "Honan"), in addition to what of the Norwegian steamer, will be found on page 4.

headline: STOLEN CABLE. / FOUND IN MARINE DEALER'S SHOP.
text:
TWO MEN CONVICTED:

Acting on information received by the police, two Chinese were arrested and charged before Major C. "Willson at the Central Magistracy this morning with the theft of telegraph cable in the Albany nullah between the filter beds and May Road. They both pleaded not guilty.

Altogether 600 feet of cable, valued at $400, the property of the Eastern Extension Telegraph Company, disappeared between August 16 and 24, as stated in a report to the police.

Det-Sergeant Flaherty said that when he caught the two defendants, they took the police to a marine dealer where a part of the missing cable (between 300 to 400 feet) was found; but only the lead covering. It was discovered that the defendants had sold the lead at the rate of 15 cents and three cash per catty, realising a total sum of about $40.

Mr. C. W. Somers, of the Eastern Extension Telegraph Company, remarked that it was hardly possible to offer for sale

Questioned on this point, the dealer said "he believed the defendants' statement that they bought the lead from another dealer in the street:

Defendants were sentenced to two months' hard labour. His Worship deferred his decision as regards the disposal of the material found.

headline: ASSURANCE GIVEN.
text:
Object Achieved"; Resolution Withdrawn

Speaking of yesterday's Council meeting against the Hon. Dr. Koch's resolution for the appointment of a Committee to make investigation and report on possible measures for preventing such considerable rainstorm damage as was experienced recently, the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird said that he did not think "that any of the damage caused by the recent storm could have been foreseen and guarded against. Taking the case of the rock which demolished the No. 3 pumping station anyone examining it would have thought that its weight alone would have prevented any power except that of an earthquake from moving it.

The vulnerable parts of the Colony extended throughout the whole North side, said Mr. Bird, and to examine all the works above Conduit Road and decide which were dangerous would need not only the agility of a mountain goat but the possession of second sight in an advanced degree.

The Director of Public Works, after stating that the instance of the boulder constituting a danger to a house,'(referred to by Dr. Koch) and the alleged reply of the P.W.D. was unknown to him, said that extensive investigations were being made and data collected with regard to retaining walls which were being kept under close observation to ascertain if in any case movement was taking place.

Regarding Crown Tand sold for building purposes every care would be taken in future that such was reasonably easy of development without being a danger to adjoining property. The Government could not accept responsibility for work on private buildings but must continue to restrict its operations to periodical inspections of work in progress to see that there was no departure from the approved plans and to take action in all cases where defective workmanship was discovered.

Emphasising that prompt consideration was always given to any report from the public with regard to dangerous conditions of the hill side and that such reports were always appreciated, the D.P.W. said that in many cases the danger only arises in the course of a few hours and is caused by the diversion of a heavy flow of water from a water course or nullah which may itself have become blocked by small boulders following exceptional rain, and however expert an officer may be this is a danger it is impossible to guard against.

Dr. Koch Replies.

In replying to the remarks of Mr. Bird and the D.P.W., Dr. Koch said that he was not in a position to give the name of the architect who had furnished him with particulars of the hillside boulder which had constituted a danger but he would endeavour to get his permission to give the locality.

Mr. Bird, said Dr. Koch, had only begged the question and had merely stated what they all knew. He (the speaker), knew they were not like conics to skip about from rock to rock but human beings could see where the dangerous rocks were and it did not take pre-vision of double-magnifying power to see, where they were. They were patent, they called out to one.

It was evident that these boulders were on disintegrated soil and when there were series of heavy rains for thirty or forty days they soaked through the rotten soil and then when another heavy rain came the rocks slipped down.

Danger to University. It was a mercy that the rock which destroyed No. 3 Pumping Station did not take another angle and destroy part of the University. If some part of the University had been damaged a little more might have been made of it than only over five coolies being killed.

(Continued at Foot of Next Column.)

headline: COAL DEADLOCK
text:
FRESH NEGOTIATIONS ABORTIVE.

NO FURTHER MEETING.

A new development in the coal dispute has been created by the decision of the Miners' Executive to ask for a meeting with Sir A. Steel Maitland. This depends additional interest to the speech of Mr. Churchill on Saturday in which he indicated the dines on which, in his opinion, a Government settlement might be reached, namely a 7½ or 8 hours' day and district agreements, which, however, might be brought within the ambit of a national agreement, allowing a reasonable measure of elasticity to meet the difficulties of particular localities.—Reuter:

The coal negotiations have been resumed between our officials of the Miners' Federation that afternoon meeting Mr. Winston Churchill, Sir A. Steel-Maitland and Lieut.-Col. G. R. Lanerox at 10 Downing Street.

A delegation of fourteen, comprising two members of the Minors' Federation, Mrs. A. J. Cook several district agents and miners' wives are leaving for Russia to-morrow at the invitation of the Russian miners who will cover the expenses of the visit, which is expected to last a month.—Reuter.

London, August 26 The utmost secrecy is being maintained regarding the coal disusers at 10 Downing Street, which

"Marcato's" latest review on records and gramophone notes will be found on page 6. A new competition is a'so announced.

lasted ninety minutes, but there appears that no immediate good results are likely and no further meeting has been arranged. A full report of the meeting will be prepared as quickly as possible and sent by special courier to Mr. Baldwin at Aix Les Bains. The miners' delegation is visiting Russia for the purposes of col

The miners' delegation is visiting Russia for the purposes of collecting funds.—Reuter:

New Attacks on Baldwin. London, August 23. Mr. Baldwin's recent statement to the United Press saying that there was no suffering among the striking coal miners and that their families were better off as recipients of charity than they had been when their men were working, is "the meanest document ever penned by a minister of the British crown" says Mr. Lloyd George in an attack on the Prime Minister.

The original Baldwin statement which was intended to explain to the world the position of the British Government toward the strikers, has become a political issue of first importance throughout the country. Many leaders, some belonging to Mr. Baldwin's political party, have condemned the statement severely. — "United Press."

headline: DISPUTE POSSIBLE.
text:
CHINA DESIRES TO DENOUNCE TREATY.

BELGIUM'S FIRM STAND.

With reference to the reported Sino-Belgian dispute, M. Vandervelde, Foreign Minister, stated that there is no dispute but that a dispute is possible since China wished to denounce the Treaty of 1865 which was unilateral and could only be denounced by Belgium.

He declared that Belgian notified China that Belgium wished to conclude a new Treaty, which was not onesided, but this was impossible until there was a stable Government in China and the Customs Extraterritoriality Conferences had finished.

M. Vandervelde related subsequent Sino-Belgian negotiations, and added that China had not yet replied to Belgium's declaration agreeing to the modus vivendi providing that the clauses in the Treaty of 1865 were observed with the exception of Clause 46. M. Vandervelde said he hoped that mutual satisfaction would be obtained before October, "but if, in spite of all efforts at conciliation, we are unsuccessful we shall submit the question to the Hague."—Reuter.

headline: THE WEATHER. / OCCASIONAL RAIN FOR WEEK-END?
text:
OFFICIAL FORECAST.

Till noon te-morrow the official weather forecast reads:—

At 11 a.m. the Observatory reported:—

Pressure has increased considerably at Vladivostock and slightly from Chefoo to Formosa and Tonkin. It has decreased moderately at Tokyo and is nearly stationary at other reporting stations. The northern depression is passing into the Pacific.

The southern depression remains a stationary over S.W. China.

The name of the Tai Ping Steamship Company has been struck off the Register of Companies.

In the exercise of the powers vested in him by the provisions of the Rope Company's Tramway Ordinance, 1901, and otherwise His Excellency the Governor in Council has ordered and declared that the duration of the rights, powers and privileges granted, made and maintained under the provisions of the Rope Company's Tramway Ordinance, 1901, shall be extended for a period of one year from December 15, 1926.

Yes, or no, it is wasting D. Koch's time and your effort to dispute the reply. Suffice is it that the Government does not see fit to change its opinion. Then why not a referendum or plebiscite? I warrant there will be a bigger response than some may think. If the Kowloon community express a public want can the Government still adhere to its opinion? The greatest good for the greatest number, they say, and a voice for the people in the Government. An alternative argument is that there is no voice. The Briton's birthright must count for nought in this Crown Colony, but Kowloon! Wake Up!

Yours, etc., JIM SYD-JOY: ny: August 27:

headline: "CARRY ON."
text:
COAL WAR TO BE WAGED FURTHER

BITTER FEELINGS.

A verbatim-report of the conversations at 10 Downing Street yesterday contains the following passages:—

Mr. Herbert Smith said that the miners were anxious to see what good offices the Government could render toward a solution, also what temporary financial help the Government could give.

Mr. Winston Churchill replied that he estimated at the beginning of the coal stoppage that the country would lose ten times as much as it actually had done. The country had shown most extraordinary power in carrying on. Coal was coming in freely—nearly a million tons weekly. Furthermore, there was a certain domestic output. "We were undoubtedly in a position for carrying on the life of the country without difficulty. That was the most remarkable new fact."

headline: SWATOW TROUBLE. / HAS PORT BEEN CLOSED BY CUSTOMS?
text:
NO LOCAL REPORT.

Inquiries made locally to-day failed to confirm the previous report that the port of Swatow may be closed by the Chinese Maritime Customs to-day.

The local (Kowloon district) Customs office has received no official intimation, nor have the Naval authorities anything to say.

Messrs. Douglas Laprafk & Co., general managers of the Douglas S.S. Co., Ltd., have a steamer calling at Swatow to-day and due to arrive in Hongkong to-morrow when the facts should be known.

A. Router cable received late yesterday read

Swatow strikers have confiscated a cargo of tobacco belonging to the British-American Tobacco Co. The Customs Commissioner notified the strikers that he would be compelled to close the Customs, after referring the matter to Peking, if the cargo was not restored by noon of August 28. Up to four o'clock in the afternoon of August 28 the cargo had not been restored. — Reuter.

.

headline: TO END CRISIS? / DEFINITE MOVE BY
text:
FRESH RAY OF HOPE.

The Miners' executive sat for an hour and 45 minutes and decided to call a delegate conference for Thursday.

Reuter understands that important developments are pending and that the Federation will make a definite move in the course of the week to end the deadlock and enter on negotiations for a settlement.—Reuter.

[Other cables dealing with the coal crisis will be found elsewhere in this issue.]

headline: ROGUE CAUGHT. / ENTERED BUILDING TO COOL HIMSELF.
text:
NOW IN PRISON

What would be described in the wording of the charge sheets at the Central Magistracy as a rogue and vagabond was applicable to a Chinese who was brought before Major C. Willson this morning.

A police officer said that in consequence of frequent complaints by contractors of the loss of electric bulbs and fittings, six detectives took it by turns to stay inside the new Fire Brigade building at Des Vœux Road and keep a watch. Defendant entered the building at about 2 o'clock this morning and ran away as soon as he spled the detectives, but he was chased and caught.

After a detective responsible for the arrest had given evidence, the defendant said that he went into the building to cool himself, as he was feeling warm.

Sentence of three months' hard labour was imposed.

headline: YOUR / "FLOWERY" APPEALS BY TENANTS.
text:
AlLEGED INCREASES.

"Flowery" language is used profusely by two of the correspondents to the "China Mail" on the subject of rent increases in the Colony. One emphasises "secrecy" over a schedule he has prepared "for fear of reprisals" by his 'heartless' landlord.

Tenants—both Chinese and foreign—are invited to write to the "China Mail," giving particulars of rentals having been raised since the Restriction Ordinance lapsed on July 1.

A foreigner, who does not wish his "cuse" to be published, says that his rent, for a house in a "central locality," used both as offices and residence, with the basement as godown, has been the subject of a notice by the owner's solicitor. He is warned that he must vacate by a certain date, after which possession can only be maintained at a figure which works out at 70 per cent, more than the former rental.

A grocer at Queen's Road East, No. 158, alleges that his rent has been increased from $60 to $100 per month. After a reference to the decreased turnover, he prays that the Editor will see to it that his rent is again at the old figure for which his gratitude will know no bounds! He concludes with an enjoinder that business must be preserved by keeping rents down.

Other Chinese correspondents refer to the influence of the "strike" on trade.

The occupant of a tenement flat at West Point, in a row of about 20 houses, tells how an increase of $24 (on $46) was cut down by $10 to $14, after negotiation and “remonstration” with the landlord. He particularly requests that detail be not published as that $10 may be put on again.

Bank's Property. From Staunton Street, a tenant of a flat gives figures which may mean either an increase of $6 or $20. The omission of certain words —whether by intention or accident—makes his letter exceedingly vague. The owners are a local native bank. A phrase the writer uses is rather unique. Broadly translated, it reads:—I therefore respectfully request the gentlemen of your esteemed paper to give prominence to report by early publication.

Chinese correspondents should not be dealt with as they have little value. Where a request is stated, details will not be put in print. In no case will they be divulged.

headline: SQUABBLE IN EUROPEAN HOUSEHOLD.
text:
SERVANTS BOUND OVER.

Three servants employed at No. 3, The Albany, were brought before Major C. Willson at the Central Magistracy for disorderly conduct.

The first defendant, a house boy in the employ of Mr. E. R. Dovey, said that he was putting on his shoes when the second defendant, a coolie also employed there, flung a bottle at him which injured his hand whilst attempting to shield his face.

The second defendant alleged that he was assaulted without any provocation by the first defendant, who enlisted the aid of two other servants.

Only French Restaurant

No questions were put to the third defendant, Mr. Grantham's servant.

Mr. Dovey, who was present in court, thought there had apparently been bad feeling between the servants as to who had been the informer in a recent raid carried out by the police in the servants' quarters.

All the defendants were bound over on personal bonds of $50 to keep the peace for six months.

A Chinese youth was fined $5 at the Central Magistracy this morning for indulging in the dangerous practice of carrying a companion almost perched on the handle bar of a cycle. The youth was caught by a Shantung constable at Connaught Road Central shortly after 10 p.m.

To ALBERT'S 22 Queen's Road Central.

headline: FRIDAY
text:
AND

this batch were searching in the passenger accommodation for drugs and other possible contraband.

Det. Sub-Inspector K. Andrew, with two European sergeants, led a small detachment from the Water Police to carry out the routine search for arms.

The Police found arms and ammunition. Two of the crew were arrested in connection with the seizure.

Ugly Gestures Made. About fifty of the crew assumed a threatening aspect and the gangway was pulled up, the police and revenue officers being virtually prisoners aboard. Serious developments were averted, although ugly gestures were made.

In the interval between the arrival of further police, (the pulling up of the gangway had been noticed and interpreted as meaning possible trouble) accompanied by the French Consul who had been communicated with in the meantime, nothing serious occurred although the situation was pregnant with possibilities.

Strictly, the Revenue officers were not concerned with the taking into custody of the two seamen. But seeing their brother officers in difficulties, they had to stand by.

The “China Mail” is informed by eyewitnesses that one or two of the ship's complement were particularly truculent.

Even when the captain forbade them to hoist up the gangway, one man is alleged to have given the winch another turn to tighten things up, and then to have sulked away.

Order had been practically restored when Mr. C. G. Perdue, Assistant Director of Criminal Intelligence, boarded the ship.

The prisoners were held and it was decided not to proceed with anything in the nature of obstructing the police or attempting to evade arrests, etc.

No Extrairly Here. Upon the arrival of the Consul, the misunderstanding which had led to the attitude adopted by the members of the crew was made clear. It appears that the ship had, some time ago, been involved in similar trouble at Shanghai where, acting in accordance with the extraterritorial rights applicable there, the French authorities had taken the matter in hand and arrested the members of the crew in question.

The crew were under the impression that such extraterritorial laws applied equally to Hongkong as to Shanghai, not being aware that in a British port matters appertaining to law and order are the province of the British authorities.

Being Charged To-day. In view of the fact that a French gunboat was in harbour the crew believed that they were within their rights in demanding that any action taken in respect of the members of the crew found with arms in their possession

should be by the French authorities. As soon as the position was explained to them by the Consult the arrest of the two men was effected without further trouble and they were taken from the ship by the police officials. The two men in question are to be charged to-day at the Kow. loon Magistracy with the illegal possession of arms and ammunition.

In what amounted to a fracas, the Revenue party held on to their seizure.

Later in the day, a number of trunks and satchels were observed to be landed at the Imports and Exports office, where a grimly batch of men in blue dungarees turned out to be the revenue officers.

A Japanese passenger on the "Angers" was arrested. He is believed to have boarded the ship at Marseilles.

In connection with seizure of "dope," it is stated that the keys to the packages could not be found at the time but further developments are expected.

In the absence of an official statement, the estimate of $500,000 as being the value of the drug is given with reserve. At any rate, the quantity looked to be formidable enough to be "a record."

headline: ROCOCO BEATEN. / BROKE A MARBLE TABLE AT RESTAURANT.
text:
TO PAY COMPENSATION.

Rococo, the circus clown, found himself in trouble at the Kowloon Magistracy, this morning.

He was charged with damaging a marble table and a sugar bowl at a Chinese restaurant where he had gone to have

The Magistrate (Mr. J. H. B. Nhill) amended the charge to one of disorderly conduct, while under the influence of liquor.

Rococo pleaded guilty and offered to make good the damage by paying-in-instalments, as he was out of work at present.

His Worship imposed a fine of $10, or ten days' hard labour... He also ordered the payment of $20 as compensation for the damage, or two weeks' hard labour in default.

headline: HOLDING OUT. / ALLIES DEFENCE OPERATIONS SUCCEED.
text:
WU PEI-FU IN CHARGE.

The Allies are still holding the Tsing-Chichow line:

Wu Pei-fu has established his headquarters at Ho-Sheng-Chilo, whence he is personally directing the operations.

"Meantime" Allied _reinforcement" are constantNr arriving from the North_ _enter.

"working to relieve the poorer classes who will be greatly thankful for such acts of virtue." His case is that his rent has been $45 for thirteen years and now it is $75.

"Esteemed Government."

An anonymous writer who signs himself as "one of the rent-afflicted tenants" prays that the "China Mail" and the president of the "Foreign Tenants' Protective Association of Kowloon" will petition the "esteemed Government" to put rents down.

This letter contains the stereotype reference to the boycott and its effects, but some unique arguments are put forward.

The gist of his plaintiff is: Having to pay more for rent, tenants cannot afford to buy meats for food. Without meat, a man's breath becomes weak and his blood dull. He puts himself forward as proof and offers himself for medical examination to prove his contention.

Accordingly, he says, not only should the Government control rents but also forbid market stallholders from combining together to increase prices and therefore deprive the public of ment!

headline: MONEY EMBARGO / HOW MUCH ONE CAN CARRY AWAY.
text:
LOCAL REGULATIONS

It is from today the emergency regulation about carrying money out of the Colony ceases to take effect. It will be recalled that when the strike began an embargo was placed on persons taking with them more than $5 in coin or notes, on leaving Hongkong. This regulation is now deemed unnecessary.

Long before the strike began, there were orders in force which remain to-day.

One is not allowed to take more than $50 of the Colony's coinage away, and not more than one Hongkong (or Mexican) silver dollar. Of copper cash one can bring any amount to a Chinese destination. For other places, a permit is required from the Superintendent of Imports and Exports.

headline: MISSION HOSPITALS. / CANTON ORDERS INSTANT RETURN.
text:
TO PROTECT FOREIGNERS.

After a year or so of interference with foreign missionary institutions in Canton and elsewhere, an unexpected announcement has been made by the Nationalist Government which indicates that rights will be recognised.

One sequel to the “strike” has been the closing down of mission hospitals on account of intimidation by the pickets.

The communique to hand also refers to foreign buildings occupied by the military.

It will be recalled that statements have been made previously—not necessarily by any “inspired” body—that the control of certain institutions, by Chinese, would be aimed at. The Canton Information Bureau issues the following through Reuter:—

“The Nationalist Government has ordered the office of the commander-in-chief to instruct the Wuchow authorities to immediately return the Stout Memorial Hospital at Wuchow to the American Baptist Mission for a re-opening, and also to issue peremptory orders to all Nationalist forces in Hunan and elsewhere to protect the life and property of all foreign missionaries and evacuate all mission buildings now in occupation by the military.

“The Government has further instructed the Miscellaneous Workers' Union to open negotiations with the authorities of the Canton Hospital for a speedy re-opening of that institution.”

headline: KWONG HING CASE. / WERE THEY AGENTS OR PRINCIPALS?
text:
JUNK HEARING AGAIN

The question as to whether the Kwong Hangs acted as agents or principals in the shipment of goods to Mui Kong San Wui (Kwangtung) "which did not arrive at their destination owing, it is alleged, to a piracy, came before Mr. " Justice Wood again in the Summary Court this morning. The Ho Yuen firm claims $996.36 as the price of goods entrusted to defendant and monies on account of freight customs dues and coolie hire in respect of the shipment which the defendants failed to deliver or return to plaintiffs.

Mr. M. K. Lo, on behalf of the defendants, maintains that they acted throughout as... agents and not charterers.

Mr. J. A. Gordon Leask appeared for plaintiffs this morning, notifying a change of solicitors since the previous hearing.

So Chun, partner of the plaintiff firm, was cross-examined by Mr. Lo this morning. He maintained that the Kwong Hing had given an undertaking in respect of the safe delivery of the goods. The plaintiff firm, he said, had paid to the defendants 20 per cent. increase on the Customs, dues for guarantee of safe arrival in view of unsettled conditions caused by the boycott.

Plaintiff further stated that all the arrangements with regard to the taking on board of the cargo had been directed by the Kwong Hing firm although the junk owners had done a certain amount on their instructions

Mr Lo referred to the evidence which plaintiff had given in a case at the Supreme Court concerning another shipment of goods on the same junk when it had been held by the Chief Justice that not sufficient evidence had been made out for him to hold that a piracy had taken place.

Mr. Lo referred to what he termed "inconsistencies" in the plaintiff's evidence at that hearing and his evidence now.

His Honour said that he did not agree. There were no materials inconsistencies.

After hearing further evidence, His Honour found that the Kwong Hing firm (defendants) had only acted as agents in collecting goods. He gave judgment for defendants.

headline: DETECTIVE INSTINCT / CHAUFFEUR COMMENDED BY MAGISTRATE.
text:
A SMART CAPTURE

Smart amateur detective work by a Chinese motor car driver, Chan Chan, of No. 44, Robinson Road, was responsible for a thief being caught while he was getting away with five pieces of clothing stolen from the Government quarters at Breezy Point, near Park Road.

When the man was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with theft, Mr. S. W. Cressey, prison warder, identified the clothing as his property. He said "that the clothing had been ironed and left in assettee in the sitting room overnight, but the loss was not discovered until the defendant was brought to his quarters by a constable yesterday forenoon.

Chan Chan, the chauffeur, stated that he was driving his car along Park Road when he observed the defendant coming out of the quarters with a bundle under his arm. Witness suspected the man to be a stranger in the locality, stopped his car, and asked him what he was doing there. Defendant immediately dropped the bundle and bolted down Park Road with witness behind him blowing a police whistle. The man ran into the arms of an Indian police sergeant who was walking up the road. Defendant, who said that the bundle was given to him by a small boy who could not be found, was sentenced to four weeks' hard labour.

His Worship commended the chauffeur for his public spirit and directed Div.-Inspector Grant to bring the matter to the notice of the Traffic Inspector.

headline: NEGRO FIGHT. / SEAMEN FALL OUT AT TAIKOO.
text:
A COURT SEQUEL.

But for the presence of a man of the same nationality (a seaman on the s.s. "Strathbarne") at the Central Magistracy this morning, a serious language difficulty would have arisen in an assault case concerning two African negroes, who could speak only Arabic. Jama-war Sama, the interpreter, with a slight knowledge of English, did quite well in his new role.

The complainant, Abdul Ali, a native of Aden, was alleged to have been assaulted by Abdul Achmed, a Somaliland native, fireman on board the vessel, while alongside the Taikoo Sugar Refinery yesterday. Marks of the assault were visible on complainant's face. These, defendant, explained, were caused in a fall during a struggle. He added that he had good reasons for fighting, as complainant expected to get money for doing extra work as stoker when he only looked after his work as a lamp-trimmer.

The captain of the vessel, who was present in court, informed the Magistrate (Mr. R. E. Lindsell) that owing to a fireman leaving the ship at Java, the defendant and another fireman did the absent man's work in addition and were entitled to get extra wages. He thought the complainant had also helped them and when he tried to get his share the other turned on him.

His Worship imposed a nominal fine of $2 and further ordered him to sign a bond on personal surety of $50 to keep the peace while the vessel was in port, adding that any more trouble would result in the defendant being sent to prison.

headline: CONSTABLE JAILED. / HAWKERS VICTIMISED BY INDIAN
text:
TWENTY-CENT BRIES.

A police trap, with Sergeant Nolloth watching developments, was set for an Indian constable who was alleged to be demanding money from hawkers squatting at Lyndhurst Terrace. The officer watched for about an hour and marched the constable to the charge room after he had received two marked ten-cent pieces at 9 p.m. yesterday.

The constable admitted he took the money as a bribe when he was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Captain Bloxham said that a hawker complained that the constable took twenty cents from him or Thursday evening and informed him he would come again the next day for a further twenty cents. Marked coins were given over to the hawker and when brought to the charge room these were found in the constable's pocket. "A bad record, too," remarked His Worship in looking at a card which showed six reports, several of them serious, during one year of service. Defendant was sentenced to four months' hard labour.

headline: SOVIET SNUBBED. / DELEGATES BANNED FROM BRITAIN.
text:
TOMSKY FOILED

A letter has been despatched to the officials of the General Council of the Trade Union's Congress, which will hold its annual conference at Bournemouth next week, informing them of the decision of the Home Secretary not to permit M. Tomsky and other Soviet delegates to enter Great Britain for the purpose of attending the conference.

The newspapers state that M. Tomsky, who is President of the All-Russian Council of Trade Unions, had prepared a speech on the failure of the general strike in Britain in May.

The agenda of next week's conference indicate that no debate on the general strike will be initiated by the Council, but it will probably be discussed on resolutions tablely some of the affiliated Unions. British Wireless Service.

headline: BREAKING UP?
dateline: E FOR NEW MOVE. London, September 2.
text:
The miners' delegate conference heard reports from the districts. The report from Notts was perturbing. It stated that the country was divided and that only one portion was solid to the Federation. The opinion was expressed that it was impossible to arrest a big local breakaway unless the Federation abandoned its no compromise attitude.

The conference adjourned till the afternoon, when it is expected that the Executive will ask for plenary powers to negotiate to open a new conference.

A prominent leader said that feeling in the Federation was growing that it was time that the struggle terminated and that the Executive made a definite peace move.—Reuter.

The Miners' Executive by a majority decided in the afternoon to recommend the delegate conference to give them plenary powers and an open mandate to negotiate a settlement of the coal stoppage and approach the Government for a new conference with that object. —Reuter.

Result To Be Submitted. London. September 2

in contrast colours.

headline: Confirmed.
text:
London, September 2. The miners' delegate conference agreed to the Executives' recommendations, cabled earlier.—Reuter. Get the Best Terms.

London, September 2. Though a settlement of the coal stoppage is not likely in the immediate future in view of the amount of consultations necessary, the fact that the delegate's conference empowered the Miners' Executive to negotiate free of the old formula "not a minute on the da", not a penny off the pay" has changed the whole situation and the Executive has practically been told to get the best terms obtainable in spite of the opposition to any retreat on the part of the President, Mr. Herbert Smith, backed by the Yorkshire and Lancashire delegates.

The difficulty of a national agreement, to which the owners are solidly opposed, may be overcome by the establishment of variable district minima subject to the safeguard of ratification by a National Board.—Reuter.

headline: WALES WAYERING?
text:
Rugby, September 2. The miners' National Delegate Conference to-day decided by 557,000 votes to 225,000 to empower the Executive to negotiate a national agreement for the settlement of the coal dispute.

The conference was in session for the greater part of the day. It sat for three hours this morning under the presidency of Merbert Smith and received reports from every district as to the position. After discussion on these reports the conference adjourned to enable the Executive to meet and frame a recommendation to lay before the conference. The Executive met forthwith, and it was reported that it had by a majority decided to ask the conference for plenary powers and an open mandate to enter into negotiations for a settlement. This decision was communicated to the delegates late this afternoon. A further adjournment was taken to enable the South Wales and other district representatives to hold a group meeting to consider their attitude. On resembling, after some further discussion the motion was carried. British Wireless Service.

headline: BAD TO WORSE.
text:
POSITION OF GERMAN TRADE.

DYERS REVIEW

Berlin, September 3. The general depression in German industries and their inability to meet their increasing demands for raw materials unless there is a considerable expansion in export trade was emphasised by Herr Duisberg, Chairman of the Association of German Industriallsts and Chairman of the German dye industry, in speech at a general meeting of the Association at Dresden.

Herr Duisberg, who has just returned from a world tour, finds the position in the country generally worse than when he left Germany. He said that the engineering industry was in a worse position in July than in June. The position of the iron and steel industry was extremely bad, as was evidenced by the number of unemployed, whilst the dyestuff industry, which was the backbone of the chemical industry, was very unsatisfactory, the business being under 50 per cent. of the average turnover.

Hierro Duisberg accused America of dumping competition. He said that although the export from the mining and iron industry had rather improved as the result of the British miners' strike the home demand for coal remained very unsatisfactory.

Herr Duisberg said that he expected the impending conclusion of the iron and steel impact to bring to an end French and Belgian dumping sales in South Germany. The position of the electro-technical industry was generally satisfactory, but paper and textiles were not prospering with the exception of artificial silk, velvet, and silk. He concluded by recommending the strictest economy and an all round reduction it imports to the minimum.—Reuter.

headline: DOOR OPEN.
text:
MINERS' REQUEST TO CHANCELLOR

FRESH NEGOTIATIONS.

A letter addressed to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, signed by Mr. A. J. Cook, states that the Miners' Executive and the delegate conference request the Chancellor to convene and attend a conference of the Mining Association and the Miners' Federation. The latter are prepared to negotiate a new national agreement with a view to reducing labour costs to meet the immediate necessities of the industry.

Following receipt of the letter from the Executive of the Miners' Federation the Government has requested the Mining Association to resume negotiations.—Reuter.

The Miners' Executive, in consultation with Mr. Ramsay MacDonald and other members of the Parliamentary Labour Party, have spent most of the day in discussing and drafting proposals with a view to reopening the coal negotiations. It is stated that good progress was made.

When completed the proposals will be submitted to the Government, who will then decide whether they offer a basis for fruitful negotiations. If, as is hoped, the proposals show a definite advance the Government will invite the mine owners to resume negotiations and to display reciproce concessions.

Mr. Churchill, who will be responsible for any action taken by the Government during the Prime Minister's absence abroad, and the Labour and Mines Ministers are remaining in London during the week-end to deal with developments.

The Miners' Executive will probably approach the Government to-morrow. — British Wireless Service.

It is proclaimed by order of His Excellency the Governor in Council that Tsingtao is a place at which an infectious or contagious disease prevails.

headline: CANTON'S WAR.
text:
CONFLICTING REPORTS OF WUCHANG.

ATTACK ON KWANGTUNG?

News overnight as the fortunes of war in central China are apt to confuse the issue further.

Reuter passes on a Japanese despatch denying that Wuchang (the city on the southern bank of the Yangtse River) has been taken by the Nationalists.

On the other hand, local vernacular papers which have been anti-Canton in tone, admit that Wu Pei-fu has evacuated Wuchang.

The pro-Nationalist press claim the entry of the Canton troops even into Hankow, on the northern Bank of the river, and the general's route of Wu Pei-fu. "Occasional" sources give more details of the reported revolt against Wu Pei-fu.

headline: Charge.
text:
Alleging that on the instigation of Mr. A. E. Murphy, of the Kowloon Tong Development Company, they had been wrongfully arrested, falsely charged and detained for two or three hours, six collies engaged on the work of levelling ground at Kowloon Tong claimed $1,000 joint damages at the Summary Court this morning.

Mr. D. McCallum appeared for the "plaintiffs and Mr. R. A. Wadeson for Mr. Murphy, the defendant.

The plaintiffs' case was that one of the six coolies was proceeding from work at 5 p.m. on July 27, carrying some cement bags, the property of his employers, the Tung Lee Company. He was stopped by an Indian watchman employed by the Kowloon Tong Development Company and accused of stealing the bags.

The coome was then taken to the house of Mr. Murphy at 47 Kowloon Tong and Mr. Murphy ordered his detention. The Tung Lee Company, said Mr. McCallum, had a contract with the Government for levelling certain ground at Kowloon Tong. Mr. Murphy was employed by the Kowloon Tong Development Co. which had nothing whatsoever to do with the Tung Lee.

headline: Workmen Protest.
text:
Certain of the fellow workmen of "the man who was detained by Mr. Murphy went to the house to enquire into the cause of his detention and to protest. They also, it was alleged, had been detained and abused "within degree." Later, the police went to the scene, continued Mr. McCallum, presumably on information lodged by Mr. Murphy; the men were handcuffed, somewhat roughly handled, a revolver pointed at them and marched through the streets. "It was not until eight o'clock that they were released on the order of the police. " Subsequently, a letter was written to Mr. Murphy on behalf of the plaintiffs (by Messrs. Leo d'Almada and Mason) in which it was stated that the men were acting only in the course of their employment, that Mr. Murphy had obtained a revolver from his wife and, pointing at one of the men, had roughly pushed him towards his (Mr. Murphy's) office, at the same time directing the Indian watchmen to take the others to the same place. This, stated the letter, the watchmen had done, covering the workmen with their rifles in the meantime. After investigation of the charge the police had ordered their release. The letter concluded that it was difficult to understand such conduct and intimated that unless redress was made proceedings would be instituted.

To this letter there had been no reply, stated Mr. McCallum.

headline: Police Evidence.
text:
Inspector Stimson, in charge of Kowloon City Police station, said that it was shortly after 6 p.m. on the day in question that he got to the charge room. The six plaintiffs were there in the dock in charge of Indian watchmen. Mr. Murphy was not there and witness had difficulty in understanding what the charge against the men was. Some cement bags were produced which the plaintiffs were alleged to have stolen. In reply to questions, Inspector Stimson said that the sergeant interpreter was in charge of the station during witness's absence and it would have been he who ordered them to be placed in the dock. So far as witness knew the men were not handcuffed when he saw them but it was the practice to take handcuffs off when placing people in the dock. Witness made an entry in the charge book.

Asked why he had done this if no charge had been formulated against the men, witness replied that he gathered from replies to questions put through interpreters that the men were charged with the theft of the bags.

Mr. Wadeson, in cross-examining, said that witness had made a

report to the D.S.P. on the matter and in this he had stated that after having been to Tsimshatsui police station that afternoon he had returned by way of Hunghom where he had seen Sergt. Cunningham who had mentioned to him something about trouble at Kowloon Tong in the course of which an attack had been made on some Indian watchmen. Mr. Wadeson asked witness if it was not probable that he connected this with this appearance of the men in the charge room when he got there. Witness said that he might have thought of what he had been told. In reply to further questions he said he did not question the coolies or the watchmen as to the events of which he had heard.

Mr. Wadeson put it to Inspector Stimson that it was in consequence of a telephone message from Mr. Rouse, of the P.W.D. and an interview with the manager of the Tung Lee that the men had been released and that it had been put to the police that it would be very impolitic not to release them as otherwise there might be a strike of all the men working on the Government nullah. Inspector Stimson said that the men had been released as there was no charge against them. The plaintiffs' evidence and cross-examination occupied the whole of the morning and this afternoon the defence will open.

Hitherto passengers and cargo coolies going to and from British vessels at Canton and Swatow have had to run the gauntlet as the pickets opened fire indiscriminately. It is understood that such help has not been forthcoming for two or three days.

headline: BOLSHEVISM OPPOSED.
text: The vernacular paper state that the Cantonese recently sent an emissary to Sun Chuan-lang urging him to join the Southerners, but he refused all offers, declaring that he is strongly opposed to Bolshevism and Communism.—Reuter.

headline: WHARF INCIDENT
text:
Armed British bluejacket and marines landed on the "two wharves of the Hongkong, Canton and Macno Steamboat Co., Ltd., at Canton, on Saturday, and ejected a party of strike pickets and others.

Stones were subsequently thrown, states a report which has reached the “China Mail,” but it is almost certain that the missiles were not directed at the landing party.

It is believed that in the pell-mell which ensued when the tres-passers rushed on to the western bund, a coolie carrying two-wine jar's was bowled over, and his aamshu lost through the containers breaking.

A "row" followed, a bully being jeered. Stones were thrown at the bully but not on to the wharf.

headline: Dining Room Upset?
text:
There are two wharves, similar in appearance, on the Bund, which are the property of the company. The space in between is also British owned. Ropes have now been secured between the two wharves to prevent people landing there. A correspondent states that strike pickets have used the wharf as a refectory. This seems to be borne out by the observations of an eyewitness who saw the caterer to the strikers rapidly evacuating cooking utensils, bowls, chopsticks and "chow" that was in course of preparation for the evening meal.

It appears that the British Consul has been in negotiation with the Canton. Foreign Office about the occupation of the wharves—discussed since last year when the steamers anchored in the stream prevent agitators "getting at" the crews, etc.

headline: "Row" on the Bund.
text:
The Strike Executive is reported to have issued orders for bidding their men to enter foreign buildings.

Till noon on Saturday, the trespassers were given to leave. About 2 m. p.m., several British gunboats steamed into position and parties were landed from armed launches. The sailors soon got to work and were in possession with little or no trouble.

Strike pickets were alleged to have fallen out with two pedestrians on the road. These men were taken by the police to a police station in the vicinity; from whence they are believed to have been forcibly removed to strike headquarters.

The “China Mail” learns that a man was subsequently found on the street with grievous wounds in his abdomen. It is said that the man was so badly cut that his organs fell out! He is surmised to have been mixed up in the “row” among the Chinese, on the bund, during the confusion.

This incident, lacks confirmation and is only given for what is worth.

headline: MARITAL TROUBLE. / QUEER DEFENCE BY A HUSBAND. THREAT TO KILL.
text:
An extraordinary defence was put forward by a Chinese when he was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with causing grievous bodily injuries to his wife. He denied the assault, but stated that he had a Bamboo pole in his hand.

His Worship: And the bamboo pole happened to fall on her head? Defendant readily agreed to this suggestion.

Divisional Inspector Blackman in a statement said that the woman was apparently the defendant's wife, and they had had a dispute between them. It was alleged by the woman that she was attacked with a hatchet, but he thought this was hardly consistent with her wounds. Defendant was fined $5 and bound over to keep the peace.

On leaving court the woman informed the Magistrate that she had been threatened with death since his arrest. She was assured of protection by the police.

headline: CANTON'S PROTEST.
text:
THREAT OF RETALIATIONS.

Allegations About Help for Wu Peizfu

As Foreign Minister of the Nationalist Government at Canton, Mr. Eugene Chen has addressed a long protest to His Majesty's Consul-General. Exception is taken—arguments being advanced—to the landing of the British Naval party at the Steamboat Co.'s wharves on Saturday, and the clearing opt of the strike pickets thereon. Threat of retaliations—through the instrument of strike and boycott (a nation-wide economic weapon of Nationalist opinion, as it is called)—is made in the communique.

Further, the British are accused of din ulterior motive in hindering the Canton Government from pushing on towards victory against Wu Pei-fu.

Act of Aggression. The official communication ends:—

“I have the honour to protest against the forcible landing yesterday of,” armed British naval forces on the jetties in the West Bund of Canton—within a stone’s throw of the scene of the murders on June 23, 1925. This action is not only a violation of the Laws of Nations but in the actual circumstances of the moment it is an act of material and moral aggression that is calculated to lead to another British massacre of the Chinese in this city. Guns of your warships are trained on the busiest section of Canton’s great roadway. There also are the quarters of the strike pickets and a centre of the activities of the people who have been incensed by the notorious bandit and pirate’s speech of the Governor of Hong Kong.

Too Proud to Reply. “The latter’s outburst, it is well known, instantly aroused the intensest indignation here, because it was at once a misrepresentation of the objective facts of the situation and a signal affront to a Government whose accredited representatives were still members (together with official representatives of the Government of Hong Kong) of a Conference formally under adjournment and not at an end.

“The Hongkong Governor's exercise in vituperation was left officially unanswered because a reply to it invited and might have exacerbated public feeling and rendered impossible any further search for a new solution of the strike and boycott movement in this territory. And it is within your personal knowledge that during the past week I have been seriously considering an alternative solution which might bring about a speedy settlement on terms acceptable to both sides.

headline: Some of the Arguments.
text:
"It is in these circumstances that the British Naval authorities have thought fit to intervene. Neither in law nor on facts have they any right to do so. The jetties in question, besides being on Chinese territory, are Chinese public property which have only been leased to the Hongkong, Canton and Macao Steamboat Co. They have not been used by the Company for more than a year. They are constructed of iron and concrete and are admittedly in no danger of destruction. Nor is the Company under any risk of losing its property or leasing rights in them. No British lives are or have been in jeopardy or peril in connection with them. And proper Chinese authorities have never been notified or asked to afford protection to same."

"These are the facts of the case. But independently of these facts I have to remind you that there is no principle or rule of International Law nor is there any provision in any of the Treaties between China and Great Britain, or any other Treaty Powers, which can possibly justify or excuse the flagrant invasion of Chinese territorial sovereignty committed by the British Naval forces."

headline: MOTOR CYCLE PATROL.
text:
A report appears in a vernacular paper that the formation of a Police Volunteer Reserve for motor cycle patrol duty is under consideration. No confirmation of this report was available on enquiries being made this morning.

Canton were some British colonial port under coercion, but British Naval forces have gone about their job in a manner fitly designed to goad an indignant and inflamed public to retaliatory action and to create an incident that would infallibly disable the Nationalist Government from effectively prosecuting its present victorious campaign in central China against Wu Pei-fu, who is widely reported to be supported by the British.

“The creation of such an incident being, it is believed, the political objective of the British Naval operation the Nationalist Government is determined not to be drawn into it. Once recently at Wuchow the Nationalist Government had to protest against an attempt to create a similar incident planned (it is significant to note) by the same British Naval forces. It may be—it is—a grievous humiliation that Nationalist China is unable to repel by force of arms such British Naval acts of war.

But there is a powerful section of Chinese Nationalist opinion that believes in the application in a nation-wide scale of the economic weapon of the strike-and-boycott statesman in Britain's dealings with this country. But if it is true that England's foreign trade is her very lifeblood, it is clear that a real and national adoption of this view is immaterial to British policy in China then the rough-neck method of the sailor can continue to replace the mind and technique of the (?) in retaliation for the humiliations and insulting blows which England's "gunboat policy" is heaping on Nationalist China. What British Policy Should Be! “If an extension and fundamental change must take place in British policy in order to prevent the British Navy from serving the jugular vein of British trade and commerce in Nationalist China (words missing). It is a distinguished Englishman who warned men in places that a nation must learn or perish. Have the several events since May 30 at Shanghai and June 23 off Shameen taught the governing mind of England nothing? "Besides entering an energetic and indignant, protest against the action of the British Naval forces and reserving the right of my Government to indemnities, I have the honour to demand:"

(1) The immediate withdrawal cf the armed British detachment on the jetties;

(2) The instant cessation of all interference with the small craft traffic on the river by the British Naval forces; (8) And the retirement of the British gunboats now moored along the jettles to their usual anchorage off the Shameau.

headline: Only Four Arrests.
text:
This morning the labour agitators and students held a mass meeting at the west gate of the native city, after which. large crowds proceeded to. Nanking Road, creating a din and throwing pamphlets in the air.

" The Police, aided by special constables, dispersed all gatherings till noon, and succeeded in preserving order, only four arrests being made.

No acts of violence have so far been reported.

Half of the Volunteer Corps are standing by, but so far they have not been called out.—Reuter.
