headline: OPPOSITION REMAINS.
text:
Although the southern Nationalists have now occupied the cities of Wuchang, Hanyang and Hankow, they have by no means destroyed all opposition. Marshal Wu Pei-fu must be regarded as on the decline. It is true that he has other military adherents further North but they will have been disheartened by the trend of events and especially by the treachery of Liu Tso-lung, defender of Hanyang.

For days the Nationalists hampered at the gates of Wuchang without getting in. As soon as the "bright sky, white sun" flag of the Cantonese was hoisted by one brigade of the Hanyang garrison, the other Northern divisions retired. Wuchang and Hankow were evacuated and order has been restored by the southerners now in control.

River Crossed Under Cover.

Chinese reports indicated that Wu Pei-fu may have gone down the Yangtse River on one of his gunboats but it seems more probable that, as cabled by Reuter, he went north with his troops.

General Chang Kai-shek, commander-in-chief, was on the Wuchang sector. Keeping the northerners occupied, he paved the way towards General Tang Sang-chi (his Human subordinate) coming up on the centre and striking a vital blow on Hanyang. Some of Chang's own troops also wheeled round from Wuchang, crossed the river under cover, and assisted in the subjugation of Hanyang.

Once the strategic heights above Hanyang had fallen, Han-kow was untenable.

What About Chang Tso-lin?

The net result of these captures is that Wu Peifu has lost the province which was essentially "his own." Crossing the Hupeh frontier, he goes into Honan, which is south of the Yellow River. Should he not make a stand there he will then be in the very North of China Proper.

In Honan are several thousand pro-Nationalist troops under Fan Chung-siao, better known as the "White Wolf Cub," as he is the successor of the former notorious bandit, the "White Wolf," whose men have now been embodied into an army.

There is as yet no evidence that the Fengtien party, of which Marshall Chang Tso-lin of Mukden is the head, has sent any troops into the field to help their ally, Wu Peifu.

On the other hand, developments are springing up in Kiangsi province which is to the south of the Yangtse River and to the east of Hunan.

Kiangsi comes within the domains of Marshal Sun Chuanfang, generalissimo of five provinces extending up to Shanghai and Kiangsu province.

Hitherto Marshal Sun has maintained armed neutrality. Chang Kai-shek seems to have ignored the possibility of a sudden sortie on his right flank and rear and continued to push ahead. At the moment it appears as if the Nationalists, instead of waiting for Sun Chuan-fang to come to Wu Pei-fu's aid, are "trespassing" on Kiangsi.

From Changsha, one of the southern bases, Nationalist forces.

headline: SOVIET WOMAN.
text:
MEXICO.

DOCTRINES IN AMERICA

一

A report from Mexico City says that Madame Kollombai, at present the Soviet Minister to Norway, has been appointed Soviet Minister to Mexico. "She is a most able woman."

Bolshevik-propaganda in Mexico, the United States and Latin America with considerable suc-

The appointment is regarded as indicating that the Soviet will make renewed efforts to spread their doctrines in the United States.—Reuter's American Service.

headline: REPORTS BY MAIL.
text:
Fighting for mastery of the central provinces which has been in progress for more than a week between the Cantonese forces and Marshal Wu Pei-fu became increasingly fierce yesterday. From Pagoda Hill, a mile south of Wuchang, the Cantonese fired artillery into the city and were repulsed in street fighting. The gunboats of the northern forces raked the Cantonese lines from the river, aiding the reinforcements from Honan, and stiffening General Wu Pei-fu's stubborn resistance.

A heavy attack is progressing and the Northern forces are holding their positions "at Wuchang, which has been invested for several days, although several times they have been forced to enter the city and to engage in street fighting.

Japanese Marines Land. General Wu Pei-fu crossed over the Yangtze River to Hankow day before yesterday. Martial law prevails at Hankow, the several military authorities preventing disturbances, despite the almost complete confusion. The British, French, and American consulates are guarded by their respective gunboats. The Japanese landed 200 marines, which had a salutary effect.

Nanking advices say that General Sun Chuan-fang is sending troops to Kangsha, but apparently they are not participating actively.—Associated Press.

Shanghai Worried.

The Chinese population is actively preparing for a siege which they feel is inevitable within the next three weeks unless General Sun Chuan-fang is able to stem the advance of the Cantonese army.

Troops are being rushed to the Kiangsi border and the Arsenal is working night and day turning out rifles, machine guns and three-inch cannon. The Hankow front is 700 miles away but there is a general feeling that the Cantonese are financed and equipped by Russia which gives them a distinct advantage over the northern defenders.

There are also unmistakable indications that General Chang Tsung-chang, Fengtian tuchun of Shantung, whom General Sun Chuan-fang drove out of Shanghai 18 months ago, is planning to attack from the north while General Sun's troops are busy helping General Wu Pei-fu defend Hankow. United Press.

headline: THIRD ACTION. / MUCH DISPUTED POKFULAM PROPERTY.
text:
A LADY PLAINTIFF.

A claim respecting a house which has already been the subject of much litigation was heard in the Summary Court this morning. The house in question is N.o. 31A. Pokfulam Road, the owner and former occupier of which, a Chinese lady, was the plaintiff.

Plustiff, Mrs. Chun Kwok Shi, claims from the Hang On firm, $950, $150 being 18 months' rent for a portion of the ground floor which she states was hired by the defendant for giving shelter to certain workmen and keeping their tools in; and $500 alleged to have been a loun.

Mr. D. McCallum, for the plaintiff, stated that plaintiff had owned houses in Kiu Yang Lane which she had pulled down for the purposes of re-erection facing Pokfulam Road. The Hang On firm were engaged as contractors for this work. The plaintiff was living at 31A, rokfulam Road in a completed house and in response to a request by the defendants agreed to let the workmen have a portion of the ground floor at $25 a month. With regard to the claim for money lent, Mr. McCallum stated that immediately after the contract between the plaintiff and the defendants had been entered into for the reconstruction of the houses, the defendants wanted money to construct some kind of a store for materials and the plaintiff accordingly advanced $500.

Guild Influence.

Neither the rent nor the loan had been paid, it was further stated. The arrangement with regard to rent and the loan were only verbal; there being nothing in writing. It was agreed that the plaintiff should deduct, from the money owing on the certificates, the respective amounts; Mr. McCallum stated. The house had already been subject of two court actions and an arbitration. The architect had not been satisfied with the progress of the work which was held up during the strike, and had put an end to the contract. The contractor, as a result of influence in the contractors' guild, had made it extraordinarily difficult for the plaintiff to get the work completed. There was a clause in the original contract, said Mr. McCallum, which stated that any dispute should go to arbitration. But the arbitrator could not deal with the matters relating to the rent and loan as they were outside the contract. It had therefore been necessary, to bring the matter to court again. Plaintiff went into the witness box and bore out the opening statement. She said that on the certificates she still owed, defendant $2,000. This had been adjudged at the arbitration but there had been a stay of execution for the present case to be decided.

Houses Reduced.

Cross-examined by Mr. W. B. Hind, plaintiff denied that all she had allowed the contractor was a portion of the yard of her house for the storage of materials. She also denied that the original contract price for the reconstruction was $43,750, and that she had stated "her partner" could not pay more than $42,750. She had not got a partner.

Plaintiff also denied that as she was not willing to pay, the original price she compromised by offering $500 not to be included in the contracted price but to be paid on the completion of the contract.

Plaintiff stated in reply to further questions that the original contract price had provided for five-storeyed houses but that the defendant had told her that the Government would not allow this. In spite of the fact that the houses were to be reduced in size, the defendant had wanted an increase. The case is proceeding.

headline: FURTHER DETAILS.
text:
Further details received regarding the Naval action at Wanhsien on Upper Yangtse (in which the casualties amounted to five British officers and about dozen other Naval ranks) make it clear that an extremely difficult operation was attempted with great gallantry and a considerable measure of success.

The object of the small Naval forces engaged was to free if possible the British-owned trading vessels "Wanhsen" and "Wantung" which were forcibly detained by General Yan Sen, and to obtain the release of six mercantile officers of these vessels, which were otherwise manned by Chinese crews.

(Continued on Page 6.)

headline: DIFFICULTIES IN WAY
text:
"Le Temps," in an editorial, dwells on the difficulties of con-ړed action in China.

1. “Says a — “Firstly, within China itself there exists the sentiment of political independence.

"Society, apart from internal resistance" which such a policy might provoke in a country "where the Government is without authority, it may be asked whether an agreement could easily be realised between the Powers directly interested" in the Far East. "Voices have already been raised in the United States protesting against a joint policy, the effect of which might be to throw China into the arms of Soviet Russia."

“Le Temps” urges that no hasty decision be reached lest a conflict might be let loose which would be graver than the present situation.— $ ^{9} $Reuter.

In view of the foregoing, the following cableg published yesterday are of particular interest:—

The Daily Express at Paris understands from the French Foreign Office that France will remain neutral in the event of a dispute with China.

“Les Temps” points out that this is not the first time that a common policy of the Powers (in China) has been contemplated; but hitherto difficulties were always encountered; preventing effective action in this direction.

That Japan is not making a decisive move at present is indicated in the following:—

This morning the Cabinet discussed the Chinese situation, but beyond agreeing to the necessity for maintaining a very vigilant watch on possible developments. It was decided that it was not yet time for Japan to consider any positive step, though it empowered the Foreign Minister to take any measure deemed necessary in the event of exigency—Reuter.

headline: RIVER SHOTS.
text:
ALLEGED FIRING AT JUNKS.

NO CASUALTIES.

At 4 p.m. on "Thursday two rice-boats, carrying passengers and cargo," are rumoured to have been fired on in Canton harbour.

The shots are alleged to have come from pickets' mauser pistols. In the darkness, a picket launch is surmised—says the Chinese report—to have ventured out on to the river, but this is open to doubt.

The crews of the boats say that they left the fish, depot for the Hong Kong bound steamboat. In the river they were challenged by a launch. Shots were fired and returned but there were no casualties.

Subsequently' a motor-boat is stated to have come on the scene and to have escorted the cargo boats to the steamer, without further incident.

The Indo-China s.s. "Fooshing" has arrived at Canton, being "ac" companies in China at the H.M.S. "Cicala." She went alongside Messrs. Jurdine's wharf at Honam. No pickets were in the vicinity.

headline: "SHOE" MONEY.
text:
TENANT'S PLAIN ON "OH, HONG KONG."

"MY DESPISED NAME."

“Please do not reveal my ‘de- pised’ name,” concluded a Chinese tenant who writes, "China Mail" about alleged unwarranted increases of rent and demands for "shoe money" (gratuity) by an agent.

"Oh, Hong Kong!" he exclaims, "trade is becoming more depressed every day and this is how heartless landlords treat occupants of over ten years' standing."

If the facts as stated are true, then the cause is evidently "no bad instance of ramp.

The writer says he is not sure but he believes that the owner is in Singapore and a son-in-law of Mr. Loke Yew.

headline: YANGTSE COMPLEX.
text:
"BEE'S" RAIL DENTED RY FIELD GUN

FIRE NOT RETURNED.

一

Further telegrams received today from central China report several more cases where foreign ships of different nationality on the Yangtse River have been fired at indiscriminately by bands of Chinese soldiers on the river banks.

Two American sailors are reported to have been wounded and two Chinese passengers killed as a result.

The British gunboat "Bee," when returning from oil installation near Hankow yesterday, was hit by a field-gun shell, but no damage was done beyond a dented rail.

The fire was not returned. British Wireless Service.

Wanhsen Incident.

American officials still disclaim any knowledge of the reported participation of American warcraft in the Yangtsze engagement.

A former British naval officer, now a pilot in the merchant service, Mr. Thomas Fairburn, arriving from Hankow on the "s.s. Kungwo" asserts that the American gunboat "Stewart" was attacked while passing Yanglo, fifty miles from Hankow, when two seamen were wounded, one being shot in the leg and the other in the ankle, and were taken to Hankow.

A report from Wanhnsien states that Lt. C. F. Ridge, of H.M.S. "Cockchafer," was shot down ashore when returning to his ship after a futile effort to negotiate with Gen. Yang Sen, preceding the battle.

It is authoritatively reported that all the foreigners have evacuated Chungking.—Reuter.

Mr. Douglas Jenkins, U.S. Consul-General in Canton, has been in communication with the Canton Foreign Office, it is reported, in connection with interference with American shipping on the Yangtse, allegedly by southern military orders.

The reply is quoted as being in the nature of a request that American ships do not go beyond a stated point, and that precautions be taken to see that non-American ships do not misuse the American flag. The name of M. Borodin, Soviet adviser to Canton, is mentioned as having made the suggestion.

headline: WUCHANG'S FATE.
text:
Counter-Offensive By Wu Pei-fu?

Fengtiên and Sun Chuẩn-fang Inactive.

Wuchang's fate still remains in mystery. The latest report, coming from Chinese sources, is that the city is defended by about 5,000 men under several Allied commanders.

It was at first stated that the fall of Hanyang and Tortoise Hill would render Wuchang untenable. The claim is now made that when the northerners retreated they took with them the vital parts of the guns on Tortoise Hill so that the southerners have to bring up heavy artillery before they are again able to shell Wuchang. Perhaps the presence of foreign warships may have had a desul

Wu Pei-ful is calling frantically for reinforcements and for half a million dollars to be raised by Dr. Wellington Koo in Peking.

Admiral Tu Hsi-kwen, the acting Premier, is reported to have gone South to rally the Navy and to urge Marshal Sun Chuan-fang to take the field against the southerners.

Southerners Hall. Marshal Wu has now made a definite stand but the southerners are not moving away from the north bank of the Yangtse River. Wu Pei-fu hopes to form a base at a certain point, rush down new forces from subordinates further North, cling to Wuchang, and send a detachment to attack the Nationalist flank. The breathing space of the last few days has given him time to take stock and he is not eclipsed, as far as appearances go.

The Fengtien party, although making boastful promises of an offensive against Chang Kai-shek, are clearing to Peking and the immediate vicinity.

Except at one point in Kiangsi province where a subordinate engaged the southern vanguard and then retired, Marshal Sun Chuan-fang has not entered hostilities.

The Chinese still give prominence to a series of communiques from Sun Chuan-fang, frantically asking for peace.

Riots Break Out. Hankow, Sept. 12. Wuchang is still holding out. Reuter:

Serious intercommunal riots broke broke out yesterday owing to reports that Honan troops, defending Wuchang, were ill treating the Hupeh people inside city. More than a dozen Honan coolies were beaten to death by mobs in Hanyang and in the Hankow native city. There, has always been bitterest feeling between these sections. The Honanese having the upper hand during the Wu Pei-fu regime while now the situation has switched over, the Hupehites are exacting revenge.—Reuter.

headline: EUROPEAN ROBBED. / THIEF STRUGGLES WITH WATCHMAN
text:
STABBED IN THE ARM

A gold wrist watch valued at $85 was stolen from the residence of Mr. G. A. Lawrence, manager of Messrs. A. S. Watson and Company's North Point factory, at about 1 A'clock yesterday morning.

The thief entered the house by an open window and commenced in contact with a chest of drawers in the grandish from which he took the wrist watch.

Apparently he was disturbed in his work, as he ran down a staircase leading to the main gate of the factory, where he was intercepted by a Russian watchman on the premises. A struggle took place between the two men and the thief eventually freed himself by stabbing the watchman in the upper part of the left arm. The wound was not serious, but it disabled the watchman for the time being and made him release his captive.

A report was made to the police and attempts to trace the man have so far proved unsuccessful.

headline: LOADED, PISTOLS. / ARRESTS AT DOUGLAS. WHARF. / CASE ON THURSDAY.
text:
Another remand was made at the Central Magistracy this morning in the case of two Chinese charged with unlawful possession of two automatic pistols, one revolver, and 43 rounds of ammunition.

The men were arrested during a watch kept by Senior Revenue Officer Watt and a party on the Douglas wharf on Thursday morning. One of the men came in a sampan alongside the vessel on which he was employed (s.s. "Hai Hong") with a bundle containing the arms. The two pistols were fully loaded. Whether the alleged attempt to bring the arms aboard was with a view to carrying out a piracy as is thought will be disclosed when the case will be heard on Thursday afternoon before two Magistrates.

Mr. T. B. Wilson, who was the Asst. Manager of the Admiral and Oriental line in Manila is passing through "Hong Kong to Yokohama to relieve Mr. F. W. Thompson of the Admiral line office there. Mr. M. Thompson, also connected with the same firm, is en route to Seattle on leave of absence. Mr. Thompson is accompanied by Mrs. Thompson. They are sailing this afternoon at 5 p.m. by the "President Grant."

General Sun Chuan-fang in the present fighting: While Hankow reports state that he has actually sent troops to the assistance of his old chief, Marshal Wu Pei-fu, there is nothing to show that he has departed from his announced intention of maintaining neutrality in the dispute.

"Sitting on the fence" is the local description of his attitude, "but it is admitted that he has mobilised his army and has an army of 40,000 men along the Kiangsi-Hunnan border, concentrated at Pingziang practically opposite Changsha. General Lu, Haiang-ting. Tupan of Chekiang, who will take command of General Sun's forces if he is swept into the war, is at Kiuiklang.

Continual troops movements are reported from different parts of the province and all available soldiers are being sent to Nanking, for despatch to the probable war front. It is reported in some circles that General Sun's plan is to strike at Changsha and cut the communications of the Cantonese army. Nothing definite, however, appears to have been done along these lines.

Agents of General Chang Kai-shek, the Cantonese leader, are unremitting in their efforts to induce General Sun to swing over to the south, and take a definite step to seal the bargain. This would mean attacking Marshal Wu Pei-fu, a thing he has refused to do. Nevertheless, the Southern agents are persistent in their efforts and it is reported that as direct agents of the south have failed, the local branch of the Knomintang have sent their own personal delegate to see General Sun.—"Shanghai Times."

headline: TO-DAY'S DOLLAR
text:
The closing rate of the dolln demand, to-day was 2/2 1/1

but directly the boarding party got aboard several machine-guns poured in a leaden hail; Darley and Higgins being amongst the first to fall.

It is estimated that 400 soldiers were packed on the Wanhisen's deck. A hot interchange of fire was kept up for some time, the Kiawo finally drawing off, having in the meantime rescued the ship's officers.

Chinese Guns Silenced. - Meanwhile several thousand troops, kept up a terrific fire from both sides of the banks, but the Widgeon going inshore, did tremendous execution with her quickfrers while the Cockchafer's six inchers, allenced the enemy fieldguns and destroyed Yang Sen's headquarters and other marked positions.

A conservative "estimate" places the Chinese casualties in the neighbourhood of 2,000 and in view of the tremendous odds the British casualties are extremely small. The engagement lasted one hour.

It was discovered afterwards that Yang Sen had decamped twenty miles inland, at two o'clock in the afternoon. It is reported to day that the foreigners on the Wanhsien are safe aboard a Japanese gunboat.—Reuter.

"Kiawo" Attacked Again. Hankow, September 10.

Firing on foreign steamers continues. The latest incident is Butterfield and Swire's S.S. Wuchang and the Japanese S.S. Yoyang; though fortunately there were no casualties. The S.S. Kiawo, from Ichang, bearing the naval officers and men wounded at the Wanhsien affair, was heavily fired on when passing Hanyang last night and was forced to turn back up the river. This morning another attempt was made but the fusillade was so severe that she again had to turn back.

The naval wounded were taken off by an American destroyer this morning; while this afternoon H.M.S. Cricket proceeded up the river and escorted the Kiawo to safety.—Reuter.

Further "Bee" Details.

Hankow, September 9.—Yesterday H.M.S. Bee returning from the A.P.C. installation, where she was taking/on fuel, was deliberately shelled by the southerners near Luchlamiao. In all six shells were fired one striking the armour plating diagonally and glancing into the water; fortunately not exploding, otherwise the consequences would have been serious.

The Bee did not return the fire but slewed a gun towards the shore observing which the soldiers retreated.—Reuter.

Observatory at 9 a.m. this morning:—4 p.m. 12th, typhoon in about Long. 127 E. Lat. 17 N., direction unknown.

Another message at 11.30 a.m. to-day reported the typhoon to be in about Long. 127 E. Lat. 18 N. moving North.

Rainfall for the 84 hours ending at 10 a.m. to day, 1.27 inch. Total since January, 77.16 inches, against as average of 70.29

Forecast until noon tomorrow:—East winds, moderate; rain at first, improving later.

headline: DISHONEST COOLIE / ROBBED HIS MASTER'S MONEY.
text:
CAUGHT IN THE ACT.

A coolia in the employment of the Rev. H. S. F. Rossiter, of No. 12, Broadwood Road, was the defendant in a charge of theft of money from his master. The case was heard by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Complainant stated that he missed small sums of money from time to time and set a trap by leaving one dollar worth of five-cent pieces inside a purse in a chest of drawers in a room, the door of which was left open. He entered the bathroom and kept a watch on the other room by the aid of a looking glass. By the reflection of the glass he was enabled to see the defendant take the purse and empty the content's into his hand.

The defence was that complainant purposely wanted to trap him by leaving two coins on the ground, but he picked them up and placed them on the table.

"You are a shameless hiar as well as a robber of your employer," said His Worship in imposing sentence of six weeks' hard labour.

headline: "Hawkins" and Admiral at Hankow.
text:
PRINCE GEORGE ON BOARD

The British warship "Hawkins" flying the flag of Vice-Admiral Sir Edwin Alexander Sinclair (as Commander-in-Chief, China Station), on board which is H.R.H. Sub-Lt. Prince George, has arrived at Hankow and already its presence has had a moderating effect on the tension of the last few days. Sir Edwin is at once opening negotiations with General Yang Sen.—British Wireless Service.

headline: "SPLASHED WITH BLOOD." FULL STORY OF WANHSIEN EPIC.
text:
DEAD SOLDIERS HEAPED UP IN PYRAMIDS.

Details of the Wanhsien incident make a story that is certainly unique in the annals of the Yangtze. Indeed it is unlikely that a bloodier fight has ever been fought in China waters. The whole scene as the survivors paint it does not belong in this age but in the 18th century, when muzzle to muzzle fighting was the rule.

The "Kiawo" was fitted with boiler plate, equipped with two pom-poms, fore and aft, and a number of machine and Lewis guns.

It was planned that four boarding parties should enter the four after cargo doors in the starboard quarter of the s.s. "Wanhsen," get on deck and stand off the soldiers until the three officers had made their escape.

The first man who stepped across into the cargo door was greeted with a riffle bullet. The second was also shot at and then

garrison troops under command of Gen. Tu Hsi-chun were yesterday disarmed and deprived of their uniforms by the southern troops. Without any previous arrangement they marched up the British Bund last night and boarded two Japanese steamers, the "Fengyang-Maru" and the "Suiyang Maru," hoping to be taken to Nanking whence they

The situation was delicate because they amounted to over 2,000 men while the Japanese steamers were able to take only 500 and the balance refused to return into Chinese territory. This predicament has now been relieved by other shipping companies who will take on board over 1,500 men to night.

As the result, of personal interviews between the American Consul, the Japanese Admiral Nagano and Gen. Tang Sui were "living on steamers here has been stopped. The American gunboat "Palos" and "Pigeon" with two steamers in convoy last night received a formal call from the officer commanding the batteries at Yochow who had boasted that he would allow no gunboat to pass Chenlingchi.

The British monitor H.M.S. "Cri-ket" took up her station to-dry at Chenlingchi without any incident.

Official telegrams from Chung-king give positive assurance that there is overt hostility against foreigners there, but nevertheless agitators are frantically working up a British boycott.

headline: YANG SEN'S REPRISALS
text:
Shanghai Sept. 17.

The Wanhien's military have occupied the China's Inland Mission there and are holding three British missionaries as captives. --Reuter.

The bugle sounded and the four boarding parties leaped across and were met with a terrific crisscross machine gun fire that seemed to come from every part of the steamer.

Machine guns had been placed to fire from every possible angle while riffemen by the score were concealed behind heaps of cargo. The fight began at 6.28 p.m. and lasted for just three quarters of an hour with the two boats bound together by the "Kiawo's" grappling hooks.

In the first few minutes the British sailors suffered all the casualties, but swarms of soldiers then appeared on the decks and the machine and Lewis guns came into full play.

The “Kiawo” edged up, until she was fully abeam of the “Wanhsien” and the after pom-pom got into action against the after deck of the “Wanhsien,” with the shells set so that they would ex-plode four or five feet from the muzzle.

The dead on the deck of the "Wanhsien" heaped up until they rolled off the pile and fell into the water.

Muck of Brains and Filth. On the forward hatch, which is a very big one, they piled up in a perfect pyramid as the "soldiers were driven on deck by the boarding parties below and mounted on the heap of corpses to get a shot at the "Kiawo" only to add to the heap. The whole port side of the "Kiawo" was splashed with blood until she appeared to have been newly painted with red lead and the deck of the "Wanhsien" was deep in a muck of blood, brains and filth.

The forward boarding party under a warrant officer got from the lower to the main deck and tried to find the ship's officers who were supposed to be locked in their cabins. It was discovered then that they were on the bridge, where they had fortified themselves against the pirates who had seized the ship.

How Darley Was Killed, Commander Darley was on the bridge with several men who were sniping at soldiers on the "Kiawo" while the Chinese pilot fed them ammunition. Having gone so far, and having seen so many of his men killed and wounded, he must have made up his mind to take the "Wanhsen" while he was about it, for he ran down to the main deck with a revolver in each hand, shouted to his men who rushed to follow him and leaped across. Before he reached the body of the "Wanhsen" he fired two shots and then dropped fairly, riddled by machine gun fire. The Chinese immediately rushed him, stabbed him everywhere with their bayonets and cut his throat. When about 300 out of the 400 soldiers on the "Wanhsen" had been killed, the rest grew frenzied in their desperation and made, a rush to board the "Kiawo."

headline: 5.000 CASUALTIES?
text:
Of the wounded on board the "Kiawo" taken over by the U.S. destroyer "Stewart", near Hanknow, there have been no deaths among the 14 and one man only is in a dangerous condition. Four were described as stretcher cases but all but the one man, who is shot through the kidneys, walked down the gangway.

All the dead, seven altogether, and the fourteen wounded, were carried away by the repulsed boarding party except Commander Darley whose body could not be recovered.

When the party returned decimated there was nothing to do but demonstrate to Yang Sen and his cut-throats that the threat to shell Wanhsen was not a bluff, so it was done and done thoroughly. According to an American report from Szechuan those killed in the bombardment numbered 5,000. The Japanese minimum estimate is 5,000.

Unfortunately for the “face” of the expedition and the security of foreign residents in Szechuan it was then found that none of the ships had more than enough fuel to take her back to Ichang so an immediate withdrawal from the scene was essential although it was fully realised

(Continued on Page 7.)

headline: ANTI-BRITISH.
text:
AGITATION BEGINS IN HANKOW.

Important despatches on the developments at Hankow and further up the Yangtze River have been sent by Mr. Rodney Gilbert.

The position of the British Navy following the Wanhaien incident, the result of firing by the southerners and agitation for an anti-British boycott, and other incidents are described, throwing considerable light on the situation.

The latest despatch to hand ends:—

headline: JAPANESE PRISONERS.
text: A message from Hankow under yesterday's date snys that the Japanese staff of the Talan Cotton Mill, Chiakow, have been made prisoners in the mill buildings by local labour union pickets. It is thought that this is a sequel to the present anti-Japanese agitation.

headline: OBITUARY: / OLD LADY RESIDENT'S DEATH.
text:
MRS. G. P. LAMMERT.

As we go to press we learn of the sad news of the death of Mrs. Geo. P. Lammert, wife of Mr. G. P. Lammert, Sr., the stockbroker.

Mrs. Lammert has for some time past been suffering from anaemia.

Yesterday, we are told, she was very cheerful and did not seem to be near such a serious turn that took place this morning.

The deceased lady died at 1.30 p.m. to-day.

Arrangements for the funeral will be announced later.

The sympathy of all will go out to Mr. Lammert and his family, and to other relatives, in this sad hour of their bereavement.

headline: END ON OCTOBER 10 OR BEFORE: THE OFFICIAL DESPATCH.
text:
Official intimation has come to hand regarding Canton's proposal to end the boycott in the next few weeks or so. In its place the Canton Government proposes to levy certain taxes. The designate is given in full below.

First, all it should be noted that Mr. Eugene Chen writes as Acting Minister for Foreign Affairs, of the Foreign Ministry, Nationals' Government, Republic of China. He adds that "the proper Chinese authorities will levy the taxes referred to."

Comment on the project is made in the leading article of this issue. It is also noteworthy to observe that Mr. Chen concludes his de-jatch to the Consul General by saying that the arrangements have been made with the Swike Committee.

The "de" is addressed officially to Mr. J. Fitzgerald Brennan, J. R.M's acting Consul-General, the Sharnock. It reads:

Rate and 5 per cent, on imported hurries together with a special production or produce's tax on exposure. It is proposed to calculate the new rates on Customs Memo, and to arrange for the Customs authorities to clear papers only on production of vouchers verifying payment of such new special taxes.

"I have to add that the arrangements referred to have been made with the Strike Committee."

Cunton Sept. 18.

"Sir, I have the honour to confirm the statement made to you yesterday that arrangements have been made to end the boycott on or before October 10 (most probably at the end of September) and that the proper Chinese authorities will levy a special consumption tax of 2% per cent on ordinary im-"

headline: CITY BURGLARY.
text:
PAWNSHOP ENTERED BY THIEVES:

$10,000 HAUL

(1)

The Kee Hing pawnshop at No. 105, Queen's Road Central, was selected as the venue for the latest city burglary which was discovered in the early hours of the morning.

When the employees woke up at 4 a.m. they were surprised to see some of the pledged articles scattered on the floor. Investigating further they found that the thieves had entered the shop through the basement, the door of which opens out into a side street. The haul amounted to about $10,000 in money and pledged valuables.

Investigations are now being made by the police following a report made by the shop.

headline: TRUCULENT WAITER
text:
FINED FOR STRIKING A CUSTOMER.

A misunderstanding by a tea-house waiter in not understanding the Shantung dialect was stated to have been the cause of this man striking a customer on the head with a stool.

The man was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning along with three customers for disorderly conduct. A long statement was made by one of the customers which pointed to the waiter having attacked one of them when he commented on the quality of the tea supplied to him. The waiter was fined $10 and the others were discharged.

headline: NEW CLERGY.
text:
ORDINATION AT ST. JOHN'S CATHEDRAL.

CANDIDATES' TRIP.

The Bishop of Victoria (Rt. Rev. C. R. Duppy, D.D.) held an ordination service at St. John's Cathedral at the close of Matins yesterday morning, the candidates for the Ministry being the Rev. Wong Fook-ping and the Rev. Mo. Yuen-in who were ordained priests and Mr. Kong Chai-ming who was admitted a deacon.

Long before the appointed hour for the service a large congregation, mainly consisting of Chinese Christians, assembled in the Cathedral and by 11.30 it was found necessary to bring in a large number of additional chairs from the Cathedral Hall.

The procession, which formed up in the Cathedral compound was long and imposing, the combined choirs of St. Stephen's and St. Paul's Churches being followed by nearly twenty of the local clergy. Among those noted were the Revs. V.H. Copley Moyle, M.A. (Chaplain), C. I. Blanchett, M.A. (Secretary, C.M.S.), W. T. Featherstone (Headmaster, Diocesan Boys' School), A. D. Stewart, M.A. (St. Paul's College) and G. E. Arrowsmith, M.A. (St. Andrew's Kowloon).

The Bishop of Victoria, who was vested in his Convocation robes, followed, being attended by the Rev. N. V. Halward, M.A. (Diocesan Chaplain) bearing his Lordship's pastoral staff.

The candidates for ordination brought up the rear of the procession, accompanied by the "Rev. Wang Tang-ng of Canton", who presented them to the Bishop. The “China Mail” understands that the three Chinese clergymen experienced something in the nature of an exciting time during the course of their journey from Canton, which was made by rail.

Considerable difficulty was experienced in obtaining the necessary permits in the first place and some opposition was met with when the party were stopped by a strike picket.

However, they managed to reach Hong Kong in safety and are hoping to arrange to leave for Canton in the course of the next few days.

headline: "BARBAROUS."
text:
STRIKE PICKETS' CONDUCT.

Although refraining from comment on the “disgraceful incident or on the character of a Government which allows such barbarous conduct to take place” under its very eyes,” the letter from H.B.M. Consul at Swatow to the Commissioner of Foreign Affairs there on the question of the treatment of a Chinese British subject, is couched in sufficiently strong terms to indicate the intense indignation felt over the matter in official and other circles.

The letter, together with one from the Acting Consul-General at Canton, has been forwarded to the Press for publication.

That from Mr. J. F. Brennan, Acting Consul-General at Canton, to the Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs at Canton, under date of September 16, is as follows:—

With reference to your communication of September 4 informing me that Mr. Sim Kye-sim had been released by the Swatow boycott pickets on the security of the Wan Sheng firm, I have the honour to enclose a copy of a letter addressed by His Majesty's Consul at Swatow to the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs at that place from which you will obtain a true account of Mr. Sim's imprisonment and the manner of his release.

headline: Picket "Scoundrels."
text:
I trust that you will bring to the attention of the Political Council this illuminating example of the methods employed by the count drels who, in the gaze of "strike pickets" have been committing every imaginable offence against decency and order for the past year and whose conduct must compromise seriously in the minds of all civilized people the legitimate aims and aspirations of the Chinese Nationalist party

The letter enclosed by the Consul at "Canton" is from Mr. Cecil Kirke, Consul at Swatow, to the Commissioner of Foreign Affairs at Swatow on Sept.8 and reads as follows:

I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 1st instant inform me that you had written to the strille committee to release Mr. Sim Kye-lim. This man was released on the 2nd instant.

In reply to my enquiries he informs me that at 10 a.m. on the 16th instant, as he was entering the office of Messrs. Bradley and Company he was attacked by about a dozen pickets in plain clothes who, in spite of his protests and the permit issued to him by Mr Hsu Fu, executive delegate, dragged him off with ropes to the headquarters of the strike committee.

Arrived there, he was immediately interrogated by two members of the committee who enquired what right he had to visit Messrs. Bradley and Company during the strike and boycott. He replied that as a British subject he had a perfect right to visit his employer's and he further explained the circumstances under which he obtained a permit from Mr. Hsu Fu which was valid until the negotiations between the Bund Reclamation Bureau and Messrs. Bradley and Company were complete. The strikers stated that they cared nothing at all for the executive delegate's permit.

After a few more questions had been put to him, Sim was flung into a dirty cell and a heavy rusty chain was padlocked tightly round his neck so that he could hardly swallow. For three days and nights he lay in that foul place chained to the wall. He could not, of course, sleep and all the food he received was the dirty scraps from his gaolers' table.

By the fourth day, he was worn out and sick with fever and not till he had been reduced to this condition was the chair removed from his neck. On the third day he was again interrogated by five scoundrels who appeared to be leaders of the gang when by TODAY'S DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar on demand to day was 2/1.11/16

threats of shooting him out of hand; they forced him to sign some document. (You will, of course, understand that as his signature was obtained by compulsion nothing that the document contains can be used against him).

He was then sent back to his filthy cell, a room about 18 feet by 12 feet, in which were incarcerated some 20 other unfortunate victims of these bandits; a room containing two open tubs used as urinals by the prisoners and no means of ventilation. In these disgusting surroundings Mr. Sim remained until September 2. At 1 p.m. on that day he was again chained and padlocked round the neck and interrogated by the same self-constituted "judges" who offered him the choice of either paying them $2,000 or of being sent to Canton for execution or indefinite imprisonment.

On his protesting against this outrage he was thrented with a rifle and the chain was twisted so tightly round his neck that he thought they were about to strangle him.

Finally, by this method of torture, they succeeded in extorting from him $800 and he was then released, his nerves and health much impaired.

Comment on this disgraceful incident or on the character of a Government that knows such barbarous conduct to take place under its very eyes is unnecessary. Suffice it to say that I am reporting the case to His Majesty's Minister in Peking who will no doubt see to it that the British Government and the International Commission on extraterritoriality are duly informed of the circumstances. In the meantime, I must lodge with you the strongest possible protest against the treatment accorded to Sim Kyeum and to reserve the right to claim full compensation, not only in respect of the sum of money extorted from him by the bandite who seized him, but also of all moral and material damage that he may have suffered at their hands.

headline: YANG SEN PROVIDES PILOT
text:
British Insist on Compliance Before Negotiations.

Received in London that as a result of negotiations conducted at Ichang by Rear-Admiral Cameron, (British Senior Naval Officer, Yangtse) and by Consular officers with relevant Chinese authorities, General Yang Sen has undertaken to hand back the two British-owned steamers. "Wanhien" and "Wantung" which were recently forcibly detained by him.

General Yang Sen is providing pilot and crew for the vessels which are being sent down river to Ichang where the British will take them over.

The British representatives insisted that the steamers should be given back as a preliminary to discussion of other matters in dispute over the vessels.

It will be recalled that General Yang Sen claims that he detained the steamers because another boat belonging to the same company (the "Wanlui"). had upset sam-pans causing loss of life and species.

This version was disputed, but the British authorities offered full inquiry and expressed their willingness to pay a sum into court pending a decision. General Yang Sen refused all such conciliatory offers and, in consequence, British Naval forces proceeded to Wanhsen where the vessels were held and in the course of a sharp action, rescued their European officers in the face of terrific fire from Chinese. —British Wireless Service.

A European. whose name is given in a police report as Mr. H. A. Stout, knocked down a small boy while motoring on the Taipo Road yesterday. The boy was taken to the Kwong Wah Hospital suffering from slight injuries, but was not detained.

The Note of His Majesty's Minister states that he has the honor to acknowledge the receipt of the Walchitopu's "memorandio" on September 10 and 14 on the subject of the seizure of the British merchant steamers at Wanhien, in which four complaints were made against the British steamers in connection with the sinking of junks of the Upper Yangtse as follows: Firstly, "the steamer "Tienkuang" on June 13 in the district of Wanhien, secondly the "Wanliu" on June 8 in the district of Fengju; thirdly, the "Chiall" on August 2 at Foutan; and fourthly, the "Wanliu" on August 29 at Yungyang.

Owing to the Interruption of regular communications, due to civil war conditions on the Yangtse, and the fact that His Majesty's Consul at Chungking is at present at Ichang, the British Minister hitherto has only been able to obtain telegraphic reports regarding these cases, but the British Consul at Chungking states that of the four cases alleged the first was never reported to him, the second was completely refuted, and the third was referred to the Steamship Company concerned for observation.

As regards the fourth the British Consul; on the day after the occurrence, telegraphed to General Yang Sen that any claim against the "Wanliu" should be brought through his Consulate, when it would be promptly and equitably dealt with, and in view of Yang Sen's high-handed detention of two British ships, which were not connected with the Yungyang incident he forthwith proceeded to Wanhsien in order to deal with the matter personally.

The British Minister has already discussed this last Wanhsien case and the grave incidents arising therefrom, and now places on record the following outline of the facts as they have hitherto reached him:—

The "Wanliu" on August 29 was discharging passengers at Yung-yang when she was boarded by sixteen armed soldiers seeking to commandeer accommodation for the transport of Chinese troops in violation of the regulations prohibiting British vessels, in the interests of strict neutrality in Chinese civil wars, from carrying armed Chinese forces, whilst simultaneously sampans containing troops approached the ship.

Proper Legal Inquiry. The “Wanliu” proceeded slowly in order to avoid the sampan when fire was opened from both banks of the Yangtse River and the troops on board rushed the bridge and engine-room, but fortunately were driven off by the ship's officers. Sampans endeavouring to come alongside the vessel fouled one another and eventually sank. On arrival at Wanhsien the troops were removed from the “Wanliu” by H.M.S. “Cockchafer” and the “Wanliu” proceeded on her voyage. On August 29 Yang Sen, apparently, as a reprisal, seized the “Wanhsien” and “Wantung,” putting at least 300 soldiers aboard. Yang Sen declined to discuss the matter with the commander of the “Cockchafer” whereupon the Consul hurried from Chungking to Wanhsien to take charge of the negotiations. Yang Sen refused to listen to his representations or release the steamers or the officers until the matter of “Wanliu” was settled. The Consul, acting under instructions from the Minister, in Peking, exhausted every possible conciliatory effort, including, naturally, an offer of a proper legal inquiry. Yang Sen declined to agree to any terms which did not permit him to exact compensation from the Company without regard to the actual facts of the case. On September 5, H.M.S. "Widgeon" and the "Kiawo" the latter manned by four naval officers and 60 men, proceeded to Wanhsien to assist the "Cockchafer" in effecting the release of the ships and officers.

Strict British Neutrality. As she approached the detained vessels the “Kiawo” met with murderous rifle and machine-gun fire without warning from the Chinese soldiers. Other British vessels were subjected to heavy rifle and field-gun fire from the troops

as here. The gunboats, in self-defence, were compelled to return fire against this point, including the town of Wanhien, from which they were being attacked and ultimately went down river, having effected the release of five of the six officers. The sixth was reported to have been wounded and presumed to have been drowned. The British Minister quotes the British casualties and goes on:—Pending the receipt of instructions the British Minister reserves, on behalf of His Majesty's Government, all their rights in connection with this grave incident. Meantime he draws the attention of the Wachiaopu to the fact that the immediate cause was the high-handed action of the Chinese military officer in attempting to commandeer a British ship for the transport of troops, and that the British Government, in pursuance of strict neutrality in Chinese civil wars, has consistently refused all British ships to be so used.

Strong Ignition Words. The Note points out Yang Sen's proper procedure, if he had a real or fancied cause of complaint. "It emphasises that the Chinese militaries place themselves entirely in the wrong if they endeavour to exact reparation by such menns as the forcible detention of British ships not connected with the case. It goes on:—His Majesty's Government is quite unable to tolerate such action. Yang Sen must be aware of the correct procedure in cases where he has a complaint against British subjects or ships. His action in seizing ships and posting armed soldiers aboard who open fire on British gunboats amounts to nothing less than piracy." His Majesty's Minister is convinced that the Walchinopu will not attempt to defend it. The Wachiapupu may rest assured that His Majesty's officers will endeavour to arrange on the spot an amicable solution of the difficulties which have arisen in connection with the case; but as a preliminary to discussion, it is essential that the two detained ships be handed over forthwith to the British authorities. (Signed) Ronald MacLeny. Peking, September 20.

headline: WAR ZONE SHIFTS.
text:
CHANG KAI-SHEK'S STRATEGIC ADVANTAGE:

WU CHANGES HIS MIND.

[By Our Special Correspondent.] Latest movements in the central China war portend the shifting of the main scene of hostilities from Hupeh province to Kiangsi.

The lull in the Nationalists v. Sun Chuan-fang zone continues with the southerners moving up troops as though preparatory to striking. Marshal Sun Chuan-fang's "five provinces" are still rushing up reinforcements towards the more flexible parts of their line.

Despatches from Kiangsi point to General Chang Kai-shek having taken up the position of a semi-circle, the middle of which threatens Nanchang. the capital of Kiangsi province.

The southern main force is in the centre of a large salient, having “bent back” the Kiangsi garrison to an extent whereby fresh divisions can be pushed forward rapidly to any part of the semi-circle.

Previous hesitation on the part of Marshal Sun Chuan-fang is blamed for having given the Nationalists this big advantage.

Military experts predict that Sun Chuan-fang will not fight seriously at least till another week

has passed by, when he will have put sufficient troops in the field to ensure numerical superiority over the southerners.

He is still waiting for Marshal Chang Tso-lin of Fengtien to give evidence of good faith as a professed ally, by taking the field in the north, on Wu Pei-fu's side. Native peace missions are still relying on Sun Chuan-fang's suspicions of a "back door" attack by Chang Tso-lin, and on the remote possibility of an understanding with Chang Kai-shek.

No outbreak has been reported from the Fukien-Kwangtung border.

To the north of Hankow, General Tang Sung-chee, commanding the 8th army, seems to be starting another offensive against Wu Pei-flu, who is now on the Hupeh-Honan boundary.

The Nationalists have already nominated a council of government for Hupeh province—on the lines of that in Canton—together with other officials who include Mr. Chan Kung-pok was Foreign Commissioner and Superintendent of Customs. Mr. Chan was head of the Labour and Agricultural organisation in Canton. His place on the Boycott Conference was taken by another at the last moment owing to his being ordered to the north.

At the eleventh hour, Wu Peifu seems to have changed his mind as to a counter-offensive to relieve the pressure on Wuchang. There is no official news regarding the besieged city.

A telegram from Hankow, dated September 19, states that missionaries of all denominations in Hankow and their property are safe, but that some fighting has taken place at Chikungshan, where there are missionary and Alliance missionaries from Wuchang. Bombs have been dropped on buildings adjacent to the Alliance Mission property.—Reuter.

Counsel also referred to a striking fact with regard to the boy's evidence. Never during the whole week he was with the people who rescued him from the island to which he had swum did he mention that he had recognised the man who had boarded his employer's boat and carried out the attack as the man with whom he had been previously acquainted, the first prisoner.

Counsel suggested that what had happened was that the two brothers who had been 200 to 250 yards away at the time and who had hastened to increase this distance as quickly as possible when they heard cities of "save life" had discussed the matter as soon as they thought they were far enough away to be safe. It was one of these who suggested that the "attacker must have been the first prisoner because he was known" to be connected with "a sampan" with a white sail.

As soon as the small boy got back to the two brothers' counsel submitted that it was not difficult for the lad to fall in with their suggested solution and for him to say "if you say it was number 1 prisoner it must have been" and for him to have identified them accordingly.

Counsel submitted that the evidence against the first prisoner was not enough to “hang a dog” on. It was a striking thing that this lad. if he had been convinced of the first prisoner's guilt at the time, should have kept his knowledge to himself for ten days.

Mr. H. G. Sheldon, for the second prisoner, referred to the alleged presence (according to Crown witnesses) of a fourth man and to the further evidence of the alleged wife of the first prisoner who had stated that the second prisoner was not on the host. She could have no object in shielding this man and he submitted that she had told the truth.

headline: FUTURE RELATIONS DEPEND ON BRITISH POLICY & ACTION.
text:
The boycott is to terminate arrangements having been made by the Canton Government with the Strike Committee.

This is officially announced by Mr. Eugene Chen who, in his latest "information" does not refer to the special, new taxes previously mentioned.

The Capton Information Bureau d'altz, however, that the restoration of relations will depend on British comprehension of Chinese Nationalism.

"Firstly, it should be noted that no specific condition is laid down, nor is there a stipulation as to those taxes."

[Note: A correspondent to the "China Mail" on Tuesday ("Merchant") has maintained that the settlement and Canton's intention to impose taxes, are separate issues.]

Through: Reuter, the Canton information Bureau has issued:

“The Foreign Office has authorised the publication of the following communique:—

"The Acting Minister for Foreign Affairs has informed H. B. M. Acting Consult General that arrangements have been made with the Strike Committee for the termination of the boycott"

"To what extent this step will lead to a restoration of Chinese-British trade relations must depend on British policy and action and on British comprehension of Chinese Nationalism, its idols and force as a principle of energy in the work of unifying and modernising China."

"Sir,—I have the honour to confirm the statement made to you yesterday that arrangements have been made to end the boycott on or before October 10 (most probably at the end of September) and that the proper Chinese authorities will levy a special consumption tax of 2% per cent. on ordinary imports and 5 per cent. on imported luxuries together with a special production or producers' tax on exports. It is proposed to calculate the new rates on Customs Memo. and to arrange for the Customs authorities to clear papers only on production of vouchers verifying payment of such new special taxes."

“I have to add that the arrangements referred to have been made with the Strike Committee.”

Home Paper's Comment.

London, Sept. 22. Commenting editorially on Canton's proposed luxury tax, the "Daily Telegraph" says it immediately raises the vital question of illegal interference with the long established international administration of the Chinese Maritime Customs.

It is calculated in defiance of the Treaty Powers with whom it lies to decide whether or not there shall be humble submission to this latest encroachment, which, if allowed to pass, must be succeeded by more serious encroachment.—Reuter.

History Repeats Itself. On the other hand, Wu Pei-fu is now definitely eclipsed. That leaves Chang Kai-shek and Sun, Chuan-fang clear to fight their issue, the winner to tackle Chang Tso-lin chaving drawn a Bye), in the final

History—and very modern history at that—has"repeated itself. Wu Pei-fu despised the Cantonese to an extent that he did not trouble to fight them till they had entered his domains and were always on the aggressive.

Sun Chuan-fang dallied. It did not pay him to restore Wu Pei-fu. His own position came first. Then there was always the possibility of a rear attack by Chang Tso-lin (the Fengtian party). Now the southerners are hammering at his door.

Politically and strategically, he has greater reserves to draw upon than Wu "Pei-fu had. But he will have to begin by fighting a rearg guard action against Cantonese who know no stopping when they have tasted of the fruits of victory. As I have previously pointed out, the Cantonese soldier is a wonderful fighter once having won. Raw recruits become seasoned veterans in a moment but once there is a reverse.....One need only look at the way the southerners lost heart over Wuchang, which will now succumb at any moment—not because of defeat, but because of starvation and dissent in the rank.

There has been little fighting on any scale. On small sectors there have been detached actions one of which 'proves my contention about the southerners' psychology.

Chan Kwing-ming's governor of Swatow) has fought many a battle. He has a small following in Kiangsi, on Sun Chuan-fang's side. Attempting to restore the fame of the anti-Reids, he stood his ground against a division of the 2nd Nationalist Army. After being nearly surrounded, he fought his way out, secured a temporary advantage—and then fled, simply because it was whispered that the Whampon Cadets were going up. All along the Kiangsi-Hunan frontier, southern units are marching up to take over fresh territory. The allies retreated and gave up Nanchang without a struggle.

Until Sun Chuan-fang definitely lays down a line where he will stand, the Nationalists will simply continue to push eastwards with Shanghai and the coast as their last objective.

Wu Pei-fu is no longer a power in the struggle. His most loyal generals have deserted him, preferring to throw in their lot with Sun, Chuan-fang.

This last development means that the southernors will have a clear run in central China up to past the Yangtse, and almost to the right tank of the Yellow River.

The majority of Wu. Pei-fu's fresh troops will trek south-eastwards to join the allies and a few may go over to Chang Tso-lin.

Worse than desertion, Wu Pei-fu has had to face open mutiny and he has fled to Puoting.

"Execute Me First." Two of the men who fought for Wu/Pei-fu at Hanyang till their regiments were decimated have refused orders.

A brigadier refused to march south because "Wu Pei-fu had no fixed plan of action in counter-attacking." The Marshal became furious and ordered his execution. The general concerned stepped in

the way and replied "execute me first."

At Wusing Pass and other points of entry into Honan province, the southerners are now moving up.

Meanwhile there is no news of any plan to strike at the Nationalists from their rear.

The fall of Nanchang (capital of Klang) province, captured by the southerners) has been confirmed.

Marshall Sun Chuan-fang has arrived at Klukiang (on the lower half of the Yangtse) from Nanking (his seat of government).

At Hankow there is no change in the local military situation.

headline: “FOR THE BEST.” / VIEWS ON BOYCOTT SETTLEMENT.
text:
PEACE WITH HONOUR TO BOTH SIDES: CONFIDENCE FELT:

"All for the best." This is the consensus of opinion in Hong Kong as to Canton's official announcement of the termination of the boycott.

"If it is a settlement, then it is 'pepe' with honour to both sides," said a leading merchant who is closely connected with Canton trade.

In view of "the many disappointments in the past, a number are still pessimistic" Besides the communiqué by the Canton Foreign Office, there is the following telegram, sent via London:—

The anti-British boycott has terminated Reuter.

There is also a statement that the strike pickets at the French and British bridges at Shameen were withdrawn yesterday morning. This may be the first step towards the end.

Discussion was rife in Hong Kong last night. Different points of view expressed were:—

Canton's communique only mentions the termination of the boycott. Does this include the "strike"?

If it does not, then will the strike be continued?

One reply to this was that there is an explicit reference to an arrangement with the "Strike Committee"

Negotiation to Follow?

On the absence of terms, a shipping man pointed out: Hong Kong originally maintained that negotiations should be preceded by calling off the boycott and curbing the pickets. Perhaps Canton's decision may be followed by a request for further parleys.

The best informed circles read the second paragraph of yesterday's communique as not being directly connected with the settlement, but as indicating Canton's foreign policy of the immediate future.

There has yet been no celebration among the Chinese merchants of Hong Kong, the majority of whom prefer to wait till communications are actually restored.

Nothing to Crow About. On all sides residents emphasise that even if the boycott is over there is nothing to crow about. Misunderstanding has been cleared, they say, and the best thing to do is to make up for lost time.

In spite of an element of doubt a quiet tone of improvement has set in but results will not be seen for some time.

Private cables from Canton, are practically unanimous that the Canton Government is sincere, predicting a complete restoration of normal conditions after fifteen months of bad times. Chinese owners of river shipping have already started to make up deficiencies in their crews. For a good many months a number of boats have been lying idle with skeleton crews at reduced wages. In addition to overhaul before re-entering the trade more men will have to be engaged.

Effects have already been felt in Hong Kong.

In the exchange banks there was a preponderance of buyers of foreign money, with few or no sellers.

Sterling and Shanghai taels were in great demand.

The Hong Kong dollar came down by 7/8ths of a penny (before tiffin time) and Shanghai money had appreciated 2 per cent. Several denominations of local shares also firmed up. Scrip did not change hands to any large extent but the tone is firm and sellers are holding off.

headline: MANSLAUGHTER CASE
text:
The varying degrees of manslaughter, which in some cases amounts (as the Attorney General stated, this morning) to little more than an assault and in others almost to the graveness of murder, were explained to the jury at the Criminal Sessions this morning. A scavenging coolie, employed by the Sanitary Department, is charged with the manslaughter of a man with whom he quarrelled as to some paper bags placed on the pavement outside a sweet stall.

The Attorney General quoted from law cases laying down that if two persons quarrelled and afterwards fought at a time when their passions were roused the charge of manslaughter must be brought against either one who caused the death of the other. If one killed the other some period after the quarrel when there was time for the passion to subside the charge was one of murder.

headline: MORE FIRING. / SOCONY SHIP ATTACKED ON YANGTSE.
text:
ANOTHER DEMONSTRATION

It is reported from Chenglin that the Standard Oil Co.'s ship "Neiying" was fired at, by No. 11 Crossing.

One quartermaster was killed. The vessel was stopped and asked to carry troops but refused. Other merchant vessels have been fired at near Shasi, presumably by northern units.

The Chungking situation is reported to be easier.

The Szechuan guild is organising an anti-Christian demonstration to-day over the Wanhsien affair.

Factories (in Hankow) including British are open again to-day. —Official despatch.

headline: CONFIDENCE IN SETTLEMENT.
text:
Conflicting Reports About Speci New Taxes.

Two definite moves have been made which point to the boycott being lifted within a week or two. The Canton Political Council has officially intimated to the Strike delegates that the boycott must end.

Then the Strike Committee held a meeting to decide what was to be done with the pickets.

An agreement was reached whereby they would be embodied in "labourers" (or army service) caps for duty with the northern expedition.

Not only have the pickets been withdrawn from the Shameen bridges but detachments on duty in other parts of the city—on both sides of the river—have considerably restricted their activities. Passengers coming down to Hong Kong yesterday on the s.s. "Fatshan" report that all the pickets who were seen had no arms—presumed to have been returned to the Government—and were carrying holes instead!

Still Some Pessimism. "There was no appreciable increase in the number of passengers or quantity of cargo," going either up or down river.

Canton merchants are almost wholly optimistic as to the outcome of the notification by the Nationalist Government, fully trusting in the ability of the authorities to call off the pickets. In Hong Kong a certain amount of pessimism still exists.

Some point to the opposition raised by a "political clique in Canton against "the "settlement." Others think that although the pickets will cease to function, that communication (both passengers and cargo) will be restored, but that a non-trading boycott may continue in which the Canton Government cannot interfere. To prepare for the re-opening, the Indo-China Co. is again sending up the "Cheongshing" which will be ready to take cargo for North China ports and Hong Kong.

No announcement has been made as to the possible running of night steamboats, nor has it been stated that the Steamboat Co.'s wharves will be used just yet.

Further improvement in the share market is recorded in Messrs. Moxon and Taylor's report published elsewhere in this issue.

From a reliable Chinese source, the “China Mail” learns that the present decision has the approval of General Chang Kai-shek and the majority of the administration can Canton.

Kumours are still current about the temporary taxes which Mr. Eugene Chen mentioned to the British Consul-General. Some say that the Canton Government has started the levy, either through the Customs, or through their own organisation (the latter converted from the former examination shed of the Merchants-Labourers' Association).

This is doubtful, else there would have been an official statement.

The consensus of opinion is that the pickets will be sent away on or shortly after October 1, when there will be no more interference with traffic. The restoration of normal conditions would then follow automatically.

What Has"Hong Kong to Say? The "Canton' Gazette" specifically mentions the new taxes but not as a term of settlement. It says:—

“The conclusion of the fifteen months' long boycott, however, cannot be satisfactorily and lastingly secured without sufficient funds for the'return to normalcy,' and for this purpose our Government will levy a temporary consumption tax of 2½ per cent. on ordinary imports, and 5 per cent. on luxuries. On exports a flat rate of 2½ per cent. will be charged.

The right of our Government to levy a consumption tax is unquestioned, and it has on numerous occasions throughout the country successfully maintained its position.

“Likewise on a production tax on its own citizens the foreign nations cannot raise the bugbear of infringing the integrity of the macro”

sinet Maritime Customs. What then, journalese Hong Kong says, has the new taxes to do with the ending of the anti-British boycott? Hint to Powers.

“The Maritime Customs, whatever its defects, is an institution of many years’ standing, with a developed organisation and well-recognised traditional standards of levying.

“For the Nationalist Government to organise a complete apparatus a new, there would undoubtedly ensure a period of confusion during which trade would suffer.

"It is to obviate this necessity that the Government desires the co-operation of the foreign-controlled Maritime Customs in the collection of the new tax, although it could create its own entirely independent organ or collection if necessary."

"With the conclusion of the boycott when a trade boom is on the offing, it would seem natural that foreign Powers, and particularly Britain, whose trade interests in South China are larger than that of any other nation, would be desirous of seeing that the new taxes be levied with the least disturbance of commerce."

On the settlement itself our contemporary observes:— "The projected sudden termination of the anti-British Boycott is in a way as dramatic as its gory beginning. What had precisely moved the powers that be to take the course, will always be subject for conjecture."

"Doubtless had they so desired they could have obtained various concessions from Hong Kong, as it is no secret that when the last Hong Kong delegation came up they offered concessions for a negotiated settlement."

"In acting as they did without the least reference to Hong Kong our people may well have been paraphrasing Dumas' Athos: For ourselves we want nothing, for China we have much to ask!" After hinting at the abolition of Ikin, the "Gazette" concludes:— "We, therefore, commend the new taxes to the business community, for not only is the Nationalist Government completely within its rights in levying them."

These three cases do not seem to exhaust all possible cases in which it might be desirable to call out the volunteers. For example, a local emergency is perhaps more probable than a national emergency. Again, it should not be necessary to delay the call out of the volunteers until serious local disturbances had actual broken out. Accordingly, clause 3 of the bill gives power to call out the volunteers in case of great local emergency, and in case it is desirable to take precautions against the possibility of serious local disturbance.

5. Section 13 of the principal Ordinance provides that when the volunteers are on actual military service they are entitled to pay and allowances and billeting in the same way as His Majesty's regular forces, so far as the regulations relating to the regular forces are by the Governor in council deemed applicable to the volunteers. Nothing is said about camp, and it is obvious that the circumstances of the volunteers and of the regular forces might often be very different. Clause 4 of the bill, therefore, proposes to substitute a section providing that the volunteers, when called out on actual military service, and when in camp, shall be entitled to such pay and allowances as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council. A proviso is added that no volunteer is to be entitled to

headline: LAST NIGHT'S STORM TAKES HONG KONG BY SURPRISE.
text:
Loss of life early this morning was one of the features of the week-end typhoon—the second to strike the Colony this season.

Although the layman, from appearances, thought that there could not have been much damage, there may be a more serious tale to be told when there has been time to look around.

First Alarm at Night. At the time of going to press the "China Mail" has already learned that one idle steamer "has been driven ashore by the fury of the elements and that another was in danger." Cargo boats were also having a hard fight against wind and wave, possibly through not having taken early advantage of the "stani" by "alarm" last night. Recent typhoons have hitherto been first "signalled" during the day with the result that small craft

Has had better time to get away. Signad No. 1 went up last night, just about the time when Macao excursion steamboats, picnic daunches and other vessels had just about tied up for the night.

Some left their wharves in the small hours, while a few of the hardier ones did not steam away till between 6 and 7 a.m. to day. One oferry crossed over from Hong Kong to Kowloon—very early—but did not return and Kowloonites were stranded till after tiffin. The sight of J.M.S. "Ambrose" being towed about the harbour—minus her funnels (after overhaul)—inspired awe into the minds of the few intrepid spirits who braved the elements to watch "the fun."

Even the "100 miles an hour" velocity mentioned below is not a record. We had over 130 miles an hour in 1923, but the blow this morning was wicked enough. It will be seen from the official statement that the centre of the cyclone passed near Gap Rock about 30 miles away at least. Had it been nearer we should not have got off as lightly.

Two deaths occurred at Yaumati this morning. "The wind had severed some electric wires which fell across the road." A Chinese girl of about eight years old became entangled in the wires, her brother went to her assistance and also became entangled. The father then went to their assistance but failed to help and got entangled himself. However, his fokis managed to extricate him but unfortunately the children both lost their lives.

The Chinese s.s. "Confucius" has run aground in Kowloon Bay. During the first typhoon of the season (in July) this same steamer was also in difficulties but was eventually pulled off.

At 2.15 p.m. to-day the "China Mail" was informed that she was "fairly high up" out of the water, just outside the KoWloon Dock at Ilunghom and appeared to be in a bad way.

Even then conditions were such that immediate assistance was well high impossible.

In the mist it was difficult to see if any other of the many ships which had gone there to weather the storm had got into danger. The “Confuclug” was formerly one of the “Lake” boats, operated by the U.S. Shipping Board on the feeder service and was sold to a Nam'Pak Hong rice firm a year or two ago.

A report was received at the Harbour Office this morning that the s.s. "Sui Tai" was drifting in the direction of Stonécutter's Island. The Government tug was sent to assist and the vessel was later stated to be under control.

The s.s. "Pekin' drugged anchor and drifted in the same vicinity, but a later report stated that her anchor was holding.

Nine cargo boats drifted towards the sea wall near the Harbour Office. Help was immediately sent and they were secured by ropes until the force of the wind died down.

Shortly after 10 a.m. two lighters and a motor boat were observed by watchers on the waterfront to be rapidly drifting from east to west. Owing to the spray it was difficult to observe the conditions on board the boats even with the aid of glasses. The lighters were probably reported safe near the Harbour Office.

headline: 100 MILES PER HOUR.
text:
Two Changes in Course: Then Hong Kong.

The following is the official report issued by the Observatory's this morning:—

On enquiry at the Royal Observatory later this morning, we were informed that until shortly before eight o'clock last night the typhoon was heading for Amoy, but it then took a sudden turn to the westward and passed close to the Pratas. At 8.30 this morning it passed within a few miles south of Gap Rock and persuming it continues its course it will strike the coast a little south and west of Macao.

The severity of the typhoon can be judged from the fact that the highest velocity registered in any one squall at the Observatory was 100 miles per hour, which occurred at 8.15 this morning. The approximate mean velocity between eight and nine o'clock was 60 miles per hour.

When the Guns Were Fired.

At 2.20 this morning a notification was issued from the Observatory to the effect that a severe typhoon had passed about ten miles south of the Pratas and the probability then was that it would pass 50 miles south of Gap Rock. Owing to a change in its course it came much nearest.

No. 1 Signal was hoisted at 9.10 p.m. No. 4 at 2.40 a.m. No. 6 at 4.43 a.m. and No. 7 at 6.37 a.m. A few minutes after the last signal was hoisted and the warning guns were fired.

The wind gradually died down during the course of the mcrning and the Observatory expects that by the evening only strong breezes will prevail.

The rainfall for the 24 hours ended at 10:30 this morning was 1.67 inches.

" Official intelligence was that at 6 a.m. the typhoon " was " about 50 miles east-south-east of Gap Rock, approaching that station rapidly. The meteorological observations at that hour were: — Barometers 29.29; wind direction: N.E.; force: 6; temperature: 77 degrees.

Ferry Pontoons Smashed. In addition to the high seas running, embarkation on the ferries when they commenced running was rendered the more difficult by reason of the fact that the floating pontoons on the Hong Kong side were smashed as a result of the severe buffeting of the waves, also the main floating pontoon at Kowloon. The tank of the latter was damaged and leaked considerably. An electric pump was soon got to work and kept pace with the flow of water eventually getting it down to a float of water (by two o'clock). A temporary structure was erected for landing and disembarking on the Hong Kong side.

When typhoon conditions were at their height at about six o'clock this morning, with waves breaking over the sea wall at "Praya East, three Japanese jumped into the harbour" at a spot near the Blue Buildings and swam out to one of their cargo "junks" about fifty yards away. The swim was watched by crowds on the Praya, who raised a cheer when the men fought their way through a boiling cauldron of water and eventually scrambled on board.

The crew of the junk had gone ashore overnight, and when the owners called for assistance to save the vessel from being carried away, the Japanese lads promptly volunteered to swim out to the junk.
