headline: BRITISH POLICY / TO DEFEND LEGITIMATE BRITISH INTERESTS.
text:
OUTLINED BY "THE TIMES."

In a leading article discussing generally British policy in China, the "Times" says it is important to recall that there is no central Chinese Government in existence. The number of military chiefs, great and small, wage endless war with one another and rule what are in reality independent states by the rifle. Many of these provinces that chiefs and governments and national dislike of the privileges of foreign residents in China is expressed in anti-foreign boycotts which for various reasons, but chiefly because British trade is most obviously vulnerable have usually become simply anti-British boycotts. Attempts have been made by numerous Chinese faction leaders including the Canton Government to obtain the help of Britain against their rivals. We should indeed be ill-advised to take sides in a sordid struggle. The only policy which the British Government can safely and honourably follow is to defend lives, property and legitimate interests of British subjects in China by force if and when they are endangered by political brigandage and when the use of force is practicable and easily local. Otherwise British policy must to remove legitimate chieves by negotiation with authority with whom negotiates possible. That appears to be course which the government is suing. It may be regarded in quarters as unnecessarily but by no legitimate use of can it be described as provocative of aggressive."—British Wheles Service.

headline: COAL STRIKE
text:
A FURTHER DELEGATES CONFERENCE.

NO IMMEDIATE CHANGE.

Rugby: Sept. 25.

No immediate change in the consultation is in prospect. The Miners' Executive met to day, however, and after considering the Prime Minister's letter, decided to call further a debate conference which will meet on Wednesday in London to consider the position. Additional interest will be lent to Monday's coal debate in Parliament, in view of the fact that the Miners' Executive will meet the Parliamentary Labour Party and Mining Members of Parliament on that day. They will also discuss the situation with the Council of Trades Union Congress.—British Wireless Service.

headline: " MR. COOK ON ORGANIZED RETREAT.
text:
The'secretary of the Miners' Federation, Mr. A. J. Cook struck a new note in his speech at Radstock last night, when he said he believed in organised retreat. This speech is of special importance in view of the fact that the miners' delegate conference has been summoned for Wednesday following upon the debate in the House of Commons, and the meetings between the Miners' Executive and the Labour Party Traders Union Council and the Miners' Members of Parliament. In the course of his speech Mr. Cook said, "If we have got to retreat and to recommend compromise we must do it in a disciplined way. I do not like compulsory arbitration, but I would accept arbitration because I know that wages cannot justly be reduced. It is the eight hours day which we do not like. We have to get round it somehow because it is there in an Act of Parliament. We are prepared to resume work on a reduced national minimum. We will accept the report of the Royal Commission and we will not quibble over it. We are prepared to allow people who drafted that report to interpret it. I wish we had not got to compromise, but compromise has to be faced."

The Prime Minister's Statement. The Prime Minister's statement Mr. Stanley Baldwin, will, it is understood make a full statement in the House of Commons which meets to-morrow on the negotiations of the last week and the reasons which actuated the Cabinet, in putting forward the offer of a tribunal, provided the miners returned to work. It is anticipated that the debate may extend over three days. Steady return to work of miners in various parts of the country continues and over one hundred thousand are now in their places. There has, however, been no return to work on part of miners in some of the largest coal areas notably Lancashire and Yorkshire and north-eastern countries.

Sir Philip Cunliffe Lister's Speech. Sir Philip Cunliffe Lister, President of the Board of Trade speaking at Warrington yesterday emphasised the urgency of an early settlement of the coal dispute being reached. Services which were essential to maintain the life of the country could he said carry on indefinitely, but at what a loss to all. He stated that the direct loss up to present time on output alone was not less, probably, than two hundred million pounds. In addition to that there was an indirect loss, which it would take time to recover, and in all that loss, the coal trade itself had been the greatest sufferer of all, the country was in need of a settlement. It must however be economic and fair. He had no doubt that economics and improvements in the coal industry could be made by amalgamations but no one with any real knowledge and appreciation of that industry would be quick to generalise on the magnitude of the savings that could be effected. Money for such developments and improvements could however only be found if there was peace stability and confidence.—British Wireless Service.

headline: Gunboat in Distress.
parent_headline: GUNBOAT DAMAGED: BUSINESS STOPPED THE WHOLE DAY.
text:
The Portuguese gunboat "Macao" had a distressing time in the typhoon. When seem after the typhoon her foremost was missing, having been blown away. It is believed that damage was also done to other parts of the vessel.

According to what ship's officers heard this morning after their arrival in Hong Kong, a rumour was current here that 2,000 lives had been lost in the typhoon.

Until accurate information is received from Macao, it is difficult to estimate the death roll and the damage done to shipping and buildings.

Hong Kong's Sympathy.

[Note: Each junk in the important industry of fishing at Macao employs an average of 15 persons, mostly men. These boats sometimes venture out, often at night, to 30 to 4 miles from shore.]

headline: BAG SNATCHERS. / ATTEMPT AT GARDEN ROAD.
text:
THIEF CAUGHT.

While Mrs. Hickey was returning from the Cathedral along Garden Road on Saturday, a Chinese youth tugged at her handbag, but failed to get it. Mrs. Parsons and Mrs. Hall were also with her at the time.

Sergeant Hopkins had his attention drawn to the runaway and chased him on his motor cycle. The youth attempted to get away by running across the parade ground, but the Sergeant ran on foot and caught him as he was getting through a hole in the railing near the matshed.

Defendant, who had two previous convictions, was sentenced to eight months' hard labour and to receive 15 strokes.

A small-boy who was pointed out by the defendant as a member of the same gang was ordered 12 strokes by the Magistrate.

headline: Picket5
text:
In the interval between the initial announcement and the actual termination of the boy-cott, rumourists are still busy as to the outcome.

Advice from Canton is that the native merchants are practically unanimous that "communications will be restored by October 1, or a few days afterwards. More than that, cannot be definitely stated.

In Hong Kong, on the other hand, a degree of pessimism prevails. The belief is that while normal conditions will be brought in, on appearances, there will remain.

headline: Sense of Uneasiness.
text: "A sense of uneasiness is felt at the absence of a further statement (firstly) as to whether the termination will depend on the institution of the level and (secondly) as to whether there will only be resumption of communications without the former trade."

According to a vernacular paper, this official is quoted as having denied rumours that the settlement was contingent on an understanding having been arrived at with Britain in regard to (a) a loan on the railway scheme as detailed at the peace conference (b) the allocation of the Customs Surplus of the south of China to Canton and (c) that the new taxes be collected through the Maritime Customs.

The reply of the official, as given, is that the Nationalist Government has now extended its scope to such an extent that a boycott is undesirable in general interests and that the presence of abnormal conditions in the "home area" is undesirable.

headline: Prosperity and Peace.
text:
As to the luxury and other luxes, the official is said to have maintained that their collection was outside of the scope of the Customs and that the co-operation was merely desired to ensure smooth and rapid working.

An unofficial view expressed is that the Canton Government has decided to end the boycott as it is now felt that former trade connections must be resumed to bring about prosperity and peace in Kwangtung.

Semi-official schemes have been advanced, and in some cases approved, for demobillsing the strikers, and pickets. Such comprise (a) each man to be given a Government bounty of $50 to seek employment (b) those unable to find work to be assisted (or recommended) to Kwangsi, Hunan and Hupeh, or to be attached to factories, public offices, etc. (c) pickets to be drafted into military service corps.

Conflicting reports continue to come in about picket activities in various parts of the province.

Attractive Pay.

In Canton there has been a considerable decrease in the numbers on duty, but batches have still made surprise appearances here and there.

General Ho Ying-yum of Swatow is stated to have naked the leading unions to supply him with 200 pickets, for transport service on the Fukden front at attractive rates of pay. Pickets there have not been disbanded yet but are in communication with Canton headquarters. Continued at foot of next column.

An interesting and important debate in the House of Commons is expected.

Mr. Cook predicted over the week-end that the twenty-second week of the stoppage would be the most critical in the history of the Miners' Federation.

The miners' proposals, just rejected, were a distinct concession, but the Miners' Executive realise that they must go farther. Mr. Cook has been telling the Somerset miners that, he believed in "Organised Retreat." "We have got to compromise. I wish we had not to compromise, but it must be forced." He added that whatever the Miners' conference on Wednesday decided, he would carry out or he would "clear out."—Reuter.

headline: STATEMENT IN PARLIAMENT.
text:
Beyond a statement that the matter had the attention of the Government, MS. Stanley Baldwin had nothing to say in Parliament yesterday on the settlement of the Canton boreott, pending the return of the British Foreign Minister to London.

There is little new to report since yesterday. In Canton the spirit of optimism prevails as to the outcome.

It is felt that communications will be restored by October 1, or next Monday at the latest, without interference, with the complete removal of the pickets.

Whether ships will be running again as usual remains to be seen. Predictions are that there will be no general start as soon as the boycott is lifted but that a gradual resumption will follow.

Whether the Government had taken notice of the fiscal conditions attached to the removal of the boycott.

The Premier said that in the absence of Sir Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary), who returns in a few days, all he could say was that the matter was at present engaging the Government's attention.]—Reufer.

Should a bounty be paid, it is thought that applicants will not be over 20,000 at the utmost. The sum mentioned is either $50 in money or $100 in treasury bonds (now current at par).

Members of the rank and file are now coming to Hong Kong to seek employment before the final call-off.

A restaurant waiter of West Point told the "China Mail" an interesting story yesterday.

Getting Back to Normal.

He had been drawing 60 cents a month, with free meals and a bed in a Canton dormitory, ever since the strike began but had not taken up duty as a picket.

A tip "from those who knew" had reached him, "hence his trip to Hong Kong to secure employment after Oct. 1 and to rent a cubicle for his family. He came down on a pass for a week, which also included free passage on the Chinese section of the railway. It was his intention to return in a day or two to be present at the demobilisation in Canton "so that he would be square with everybody."

headline: 90 Per Cent. Belief.
text:
The most interesting part was that many other strikers who had heard the same news were “90 percent... certain” that the boycott would be over and they were all coming down to look around.

Quicer tales are associated with the name of Tam Hoi-shan, now chairman of one of the Strike Committees. Previously he had hawked shoes in West Point and went by the name of "Shoe" Po. "People who had called him that in Canton had been thrown into prison. "Tam Po" was deemed a term of insult. The least that he condemned to be addressed by was "Tam old four," "Mr. Tam Hoi-shan" or "Head of Bureau Tam" was preferred.

headline: REPORTS BY MAIL
text:
A wireless from KiuKiang received this morning says, that according to the Chief of Police who fled from Nanchang and arrived there at 9 p.m., Nanchang was captured by 1,500. southern troops under command of General Chu Fei-teh, with whom the garrison stationed there as well as a larger number of students sided. The routed troops and rioters set fire to the houses in one part of the city, following the looting.

Troops Surrounded. General Teng Ju-cho's troops were enveloped by the Cantonese at Changshu, several miles downstream of Linkiang.

Upon arrival at Kiuklang, Marshall Sun Chuan-fang held a military conference. As a consequence, the Generals who participated set out for their posts on Sept. 22: A decisive battle against the southerners is expected to take place shortly.

The progress of a battle in the direction of "Lohuu is reported to be in favour" of the Allied forces.

There is a tendency among the inhabitants of Kiukiang to welcome the arrival of the southern troops, while the higher class is afraid of the invasion. Wild rumours are current in the city, following the entry of the Southerners' propagandists.—Shanghai Mercury.

Though Nanchang had fallen into the hands of southern troops for a time owing to the defeat of the Kiaugsi troops, Marshal Sun Chuan-fang's forces, which took the offensive, have now practically re-captured Nanchang, after very severe fighting. The southern troops, numbering some 3,000, are now in a fix in the delta below Nanchang.—Toho.

Chang's Movements. Peking, Sept. 22. General Chang Kai-shek arrived at Changsha from Wuchang on Sept. 18, and went on to Liling and Pinghejiang.

It is reported that he will direct an offensive against Nanchang.

Kukiang is full of rumours many of an alarmist nature and many rich people are moving their belongings from the native city into the foreign concession, and some of them are leaving themselves for Shanghai or elsewhere.

headline: GALLANT RESCUE BY BRITISH STEAMER "HYDRANGEA."
text:
Three thousand lives are believed to have perished in the typhoon, the victims being of the Yeung Kong fishing fleet.

The thrilling experiences of the crews of fishing fleets from Yeung Kong in Chinese territory (not far from Macao) were related by the survivors of ten junks who were rescued from the wreckage by Captain R. Elvidge of the s.s. "Hydrangea" between 2 and 6.15 p.m. yesterday, south of Hong Kong, the exact position being given at Lat. 21.7 No. Long. 111.10 E.

Captain Elvidge in his report stated that the ten junks were a mass of wreckage, four of them considered to be dangerous to navigation within a radius of five miles of the position given.

Rescue Under Difficulties Heavy-sens were running at the time and the rescue of 35 survivors who were clinging for dear life to the wreckage was effected with considerable difficulty—a fent accomplished with great gallantry and at the risk of the lives of the crew of the vessel. Wreckage was floating about all around.

Passengers on the vessel were moved to sympathy at the pitiful appearance of the survivors as one by one they were Huiled on to the deck clad in what little rags were left after the fury of the storm.

A voluntary subscription among the crew and passengers of the "Hydrangea" realised the sum of $200 which was handed to the survivors to help them in their sad "ghts". The recipients gratefully knowledged the gift.

When they were sufficiently recovered from their long immersion in the water and fluttering by the waves, with the careful attention given by the crew and passengers on board, the survivors related their experiences from the time they were caught by the typhoon until they were rescued.

It appears from their narrative that the 35 men were part of the crews of ten junks which were out at sea on Monday morning.

At that time there were about 130 other junk within sight of each other all carrying out their occupation with nothing to indicate the fate which was in store for them.

The typhoon struck the junk's at 10 o'clock in the morning and almost without exception as far as those who lived to tell the tale could see, all the junk's capsized in the terrific gale which kept on continuously for about 14 hours.

Those rescued formed only a small part of the crews of the ten junks which were carried away by wind and wave, as one by one dropped out exhausted. They had been allout for 36 hours.

Enormous Death Toll.

The survivors state that in their unit of ten junks there were 270 other spuls, who are all believed

The survivors have lost everything they possessed and it is their intention to stay here a few days before leaving for Macao from which place they hope to get to Yeung Kong.

Mr. Eugene Chen has announced that the Canton Government has made arrangements with the Strike Committee for the boycott to terminate.....possibly by the end of September. To-day is the last of the month. Above is "the cartoonist's conception of "Mr. Boycott" today. (See also page 6.)

Defendant pleaded that he had no recollection of what he did. headline: SWATOW & BOYCOTT
text:
EXTREMISTS TRYING TO WRECK THE NEGOTIATIONS.

CHINESE MERCHANTS HOPEFUL

The Swatow correspondent of the "N. C. Nally News" writes:

The outcome of the conference on the settlement of the boycott, now being held at Canton, is naturally the subject of much speculation in these days. Optimism as to the result seems to be much more pronounced among the Chinese than among the foreign community, which seems impressed with the truth of the beatitude pronounced on those who expect nothing. The Chinese merchants are said to be already making preparations for the resumption of business.

The strict censorship which is being exercised on the press at Canton while negotiations are going on is certainly not in force here; and there is a curious propaganda on foot which seems anything but conducive to a settlement. There appeared some days ago the manifesto of the latest addition to the number of the countless "hui" (societies) with which the place is plagued, this one having as its aim in life the extermination of rebels and brigands, and the maintenance of public peace, and its particular function being to search out rebels, reactionaries, and other enemies of the Knomintang and hand them over to the authorities.

Violent Attack on Hongkong Its manifesto contained a violent attack upon Hongkong as being the fount and origin of all the ills that affiet the province; it asserted that it was the policy of the Hongkong Government to keep the province in a chronic state of unrest, in order to weaken the "attack upon the north," and that for this purpose they were not only subsidising Wu Pei-fu to the tune of millions of dollars, but also financing the rebels and barbits all over the province.

This account of the outpouring of wealth from Hongkong hardly agreed, by the way, with the statement made at the beginning of the document that Hongkong had already been reduced by the boycott to the condition of a "desert island." It is difficult to believe that there is not official support somewhere to this sort of thing, and it makes one wonder where loyalty to the Canton government comes in. The British Consul has rightly protested against the publication of such stuff at the very time when the conference is in session. It would be a different matter if it were a free expression of opinion; but the newspapers, as well as all the numerous "hui" are of course mere organs of the officials, or at least of the Kuomintang. The crowning tout of humour is added by the loud protest of the leading "hui" against this attempt to suppress public opinion!

There has been in the past week a sudden outbreak of cholera, for the most part confined to the inmates of the pauper asylum which is temporarily housed in the old

stone fort on the shore of the harbour. Some months ago the beggans were cleared off the streets, housed there, and set to work at road-making and other useful employments—one achievement which must certainly be put to the credit of the present municipal authorities. The disease, which had appeared sporadically elsewhere in the city, broke out among them, and 15 deaths have already taken place. The authorities are now getting busy with arrangements for matshed isolation stations, and regulations about the sale of foodstuffs, drinks, and icecream. Apart from that centre of infection, there is so far little sign of an epidemje.

To-day's paper reports the sending to London of the sum of $1,087 as a gift from the labour unions of Swatow to their comrades in England who are on strike against Imperialism and Capitalism.

headline: SUCH IS FAME.
text:
MATINEE IDOL'S SUCCESS LOCALLY.

SEQUEL TO STRIKE.

Mr. Sit Kok-seen, the famous Cantonese matinee idol, who is the first "star" to perform in Hongkong since the strike began last year, has been playing to capacity houses this week. The attendance was such that queues lined up each night at the Kau-U Fong theatre and seats were booked up several nights ahead. Many had to be turned away.

When the strike began last year, all the leading troupes returned to Canton. Subsequently shows were given by amateur companies and by smaller troupes who got through or were assembled from other sources.

Mr. Sit (better known as Mr. S. C. Harrey) has been in Shanghai for over a year, where he holds the position of managing director of the Ideal Motion Film Co., He is on a short business trip to Hongkong. Starting as an amateur actor a few years ago, he rose very quickly to the top and his career has been meteoric.

Other "stars" have come to Hongkong, but only to sail for America, where there are several Cantonese companies. The cutting out of the Hongkong and Macao theatres from the itinerary of the Cantonese troupes has meant a fairly big exodus to America, and Malaya. Mr. Sit Kok-seen is the first actually to appear on a Hongkong stage since last June, except for a former colleague who appeared in charity shows here, while awaiting a steamer for Seattle.

headline: IDLE RICH.
text:
MUSSOINI CLASSES THEM WITH TRAMPS.

IN ROLE OF OUTCASTS

Signor Mussolini has declared who on the idle rich, who are included in the same classification as beggars and tramps in the new grouping system for electoral and industrial purposes of the whole Italian nation, which will be effected by legislation expected to come into force on July 1.

Unproductive, rich, vagabonds, and tramps will be excluded under this system from the benefits of Italian citizenship.

Italians will be grouped into fifteen categories. The sections of industry, sea transport, commerce, agriculture, land transport, and banking are further subdivided into employers and employees' groups, making twelve categories in all. There are also three more groups of independent workers, neither employers nor employees, such as doctors, lawyers, artists, and engineers. The classification of the idle rich with beggars and tramps has created much indignant comfort. Signor Muissolini, however, has often expressed his contempt for idlers, and a law against voluntary parasitism will, no doubt, be promulgated shortly.

All non-producers are to live “on the margin of the State,” that is, they will be treated as foreigners, not as Italian citizens.

headline: SENSIBLE TYPISTS.
text:
HAPPIER THAN £10-A-WEEK AMERICANS.

Mr. Roy S. Wildman, whose copper mills in America employ 35,000 men, dispelled some of the dreams about his country as the workers' utopia of high wages, when interviewed to-day before he sailed for New York.

"Shorthand-typists in America," he said, "earn from £6 to £10 a week, but the cost of living is proportionately high. They are no happier than their less-paid sisters in England, because in their feverish anxiety to maintain the standard of living they set themselves they are able to put only a little money in the bank."

"The craze for dress, which is the result of high wages, attains ridiculous heights. Shorthand-typists earning good money in New York and other great cities arrive at their offices dressed like revue stars. The English office girl's attire is much more sensible than that of the American girl."

headline: JAPANESE-SOVIET RELATIONS.
text:
Moscow, July 24.—In an interview with the press men shortly after his arrival here from Japan, Mr. Victor Kopp, the Soviet Ambassador to Tokyo, who is home on furlough, emphasised the normal development of Japanese-Soviet relations.

In illustration, he pointed to the successful settlement of a number of different questions, specifying the Soviet-Japanese agreement on Saghallen concessions among the successes and also predicting in the very near future the conclusion of a Fishery Convention between the two countries.

Mr. Kopp also insisted on the evidence of development of commercial relations between the Russian Republic and Japan since the installation of the Russian trade delegation at Tokyo and said he had been informed that before long there would be started parleys with representatives of the South Manchuria Railway, the Chinese Eastern Railway and with the Ussuri Railway for the regulation of railway traffic and construction in Manchuria.

headline: CHOLERA IN SHANGHAI.
text: The Chinese community of Chapei and Nantao is seriously alarmed at the rapid spread of the cholera epidemic. In a further petition to Dr. V. K. Ting on the subject, the Chinese merchants state that so long as the working classes are allowed to use creek water for cooking and drinking, the epidemic will continue. The petition states that the workers of innumerable cotton factories and silk flatures on the Chinese side of the "Soochow Creek" use water direct from the creek for all domestic purposes, including drinking. The petition adds that the factory management should be compelled to have sanitary wells dug. Dr. Ting has issued further orders in connection with the epidemic, and these, he says, must be obeyed. It is his stated intention to walk through the streets himself during the nights to see that the police obey his instructions and prevent the people from sleeping in the open. The regulations regarding the sale of unclean food must be tightened, and most important of all, corpses must be immediately buried, and not allowed to lie in the homes in accordance with ancient Chinese customs. Dr. Ting regards this particular custom as an especial evil.

and, being "duly supported" by their own good officials, try to get into possession of "properties," which are not theirs; viz., the Swatow case. What is the name for it? Treaties and agreements with foreign countries are being violated every day. There exists no proper jurisdiction in China, and all and everybody are more or less at the mercy of court officials, bandits or selfish military chieftains. The person or persons acting for a while in government offices, in order to curry favour with the ignorant and agitated mob, sometimes called "students," support the "patriotic" demand for tendition of "the foreign Concessions. When driven out of office by gentlemen as worthy as themselves these very patriotic heroes are the first to take refuge and find a yalum in the cursed Concessions, where they, as a rule, have taken due forethought to have their own costly residences erected. A few years ago it was repeatedly printed in huge letters in the "Peking Gazette": The A.B.C. of Chinese policy is and must be friendship and cooperation with Great Britain. But at that time the Bolshevik agents had not yet come to China. They were then busy in planning how to rob and murder most efficiently in their own native land. "The same man, who formed the above quoted rule for Chinese policy, and who, if I am rightly informed, but for English timely interference, probably would never have come outside the walls of Peking jails (now on account of the cited advice to his countrymen, but for some other trifling matter being an offence in the eyes of a certain Chinese) he is now head over ears in love with the Soviet hirelings and from Canton tries to poison the mind of his fellow countrymen with accusations of the British, in a bombastic manner. In Don Quixote, He appears to be utterly unable to admit his country's outrages, crimes and shortcomings. Being in league with the Bolsheviks he singles out England among all the foreign countries and tries to make her the scapegoat for the chaotic conditions in China. What a pity that among all the millions of China's population there shall be so very few honest, broadminded and fair-thinking men! Mr. Editor, the writer of this has not the honour of being English, nor British, nor many way related to your great nation; nor is it his intention to advocate the English cause in China, because such a thing is not necessary and not called for. We all know that you are good enough and quite capable of doing this yourself. I only want to send you my greetings and to tell you, that very few foreigners are being deceived by these concentrated and unjustified Chinese attacks on the English nation alone.

It is so astonishing that the Chinese are so completely out of touch with the actual conditions, that they cannot grasp this prominent fact, that the Bolsheviks are deadly enemies both of China and of the whole world, whilst the English nation, so far from being an obstacle to the national aspirations of China, is the first Power in the world able and willing to assist and co-operate with the Chinese better than anyone else. In league with Soviet Russia means poverty destruction, ruins, bankruptcy persecution, moral deformity, stagnation, misery and annihilation; in league with Great Britain means strength, prosperity, high ideals and salvation of the country, if salvation be possible at all.

The writer of these lines has been in China for a number of years. He feels happy in saying that he has many friends among the Chinese, by whom he also is counted as a true well-wisher of the Chinese nation. He has had many opportunities in siding with the Chinese, and the opportunities have been used, verbally and in writing, always protecting the privileges of a free and independent nation. He has met scores of foreigners of all nationalities, and he has heard their views and learned their theories. The result of it all may be summarised thus: The English nation is still the leading nation in the world, and there is no other nation existing to day better deserving the position. How very fortunate it would be, if my friends, the Chinese, would understand this and act accordingly.

headline: WORLD THEATRE.
text:
"THE MAN WITHOUT A CONSCIENCE."

"The Man Without a Conscience" is the story of a man who reached worldly success regardless of the hearts and rights of others. It is to be screened at the World Theatre to-day and tomorrow.

Determined to conquer money, power and position, Richard Mason's "unscrupulous methods leave broken victims behind him"—but on he goes, selfish, greedy and deaf to the warnings of those who love him. He engts his flancee aside, to marry a wealthy society girl whose love for another makes her life a thing of dull misery. Using another man's brains and achievements, he runs up the ladder of wealth, only to treacherously trick his partner out of his deserved gains. But retribution is relentless—it strikes at his weakest point, his sincere love for his tiny, deformed son and lands him in a prison cell.

The emotional character of Richard Mason has been entrusted to Willard Louis, whose past performances have marked him as one of the leading interpretative masters of the screen. June Marlowe and Irene Rich have been chosen to portray the shy country maid and the haughty society queen, Robert Agnew, John Patrick, Helen Dunbar, William Orlamond and others complete the cast.

“The Man Without a Conscience” was translated on to the screen by Warner Bros.; James Flood is responsible for the direction of the picture, which was adapted by Hope Loring and Louis Lighton.

3 OUT OF 21 WORKING.

steamboats formerly on the Hongkong—West River run are now employed, states a Chinese report. These 21 ships are owned by 17 different Chinese companies and are exclusive of the Hongkong-Canton boats.

Hitherto steps have been taken by some of the owners to play their craft on routes excluding Hong-kong—in preference to laying up—but have been deterred. Those under the Chinese flag will not be affected by the boycott and others under British registry can “change over.” However, the deterrent lies in the unsettled conditions “upcountry” and the danger from piratical attack.

Three boats in the "Kwong Ying," "Kwong Hung" and "Kock Ning" are now running between Canton and Wuchow.

The "Kwong Fook Cheung," "Fook On," "Tai Ming," "Ko Chow," "Chung On" and Sun On are lying idle in Hongkong harbour.

headline: ON CHARTER.
text:
“MONDEGO” ENTERS CATTLE

The s.s. "Mondego," (Norwegian flag) formerly known as the "Standard," has left Hongkong after overhaul and general repairs at the Hongkong and Whampoa Dock Company's shipyard, Kowloon.

At Saigon she will run under charter in the cattle trade between Phomphenh in Cambodia and Manila and Cebu in the Philippine Islands (for at least six months).

This vessel (built in 1906) is of the spar deck type, and in former years, when she had a Hongkong passenger licence, used to carry 12 first-class passengers and about 500 coolie passengers. Messrs: Karsten Larsen and Co. are the local agents.

headline: ANOTHER JUNK PIRATEI
text:

headline: THE BANK LINE, LTD.,
text:
In the first report the master of trading junk "Sze Leung" stated that he left on August 28 for Mau Chau, in the Po On district, with a cargo of coal dust and kerosene. On the following morning the junk was hailed by a steam launch flying the pickets' flag at Shek Wan Bay. The master refused to surrender and kept up a pitched battle with the arms on board for about an hour until the launch left in the direction of Bocca Tigris.

When making his report, the master applied for fresh ammunition to replace those used in the defence of his junk.

Another incident reported took place near the same spot on August 11. The trading junk "Man Tai" was stopped by a steam launch in which were about fifteen armed pickets. On the plea that they had come to search for coniraband, they stole the junk's armoury consisting of one cannon, one rifle, 9 muskets and a quantity of ammunition, in addition to clothing and money.

headline: “No Indulgence.”
text:
"Besides having separately notified our subordinates to take every precaution, we are specially writing to inform you that you should refuse to do anything in connection with declarement at the Customs, or loading of cargo on behalf of any steamer which may be contrary to the Trade Rules, and that intentional offence will entail arrest of the offender for severe punishment, and the confiscation of his property. headline: FINNISH SAILING SHIP SOCIETY
text:
The Finnish Mercantile Marine includes at the present time a relatively large number of sailing vessels, namely, 541 vessels of more than 20 tons each, representing a total of 83,392 tons, and it is now reported from Helsingfors that the leading owners of such vessels have formed a society for the protection of their mutual interests under the name of the Finnish Sailing Ship Owners' Association.

One of the first aims of the association will be to watch very carefully any proposed legislation in regard to the conditions and hours of labour at sea, this being one of the burning questions of the moment. The association is seeking to get the owners of sailing ships in all the Baltic countries to unite in forming a general association for the purpose of fixing and maintaining freight rates in that region at a remunerative minimum. At the present time the fleets of the owners affiliated to the association represent a total of between 50,000 and 60,000 tons of Finnish sailing ships.

headline: DANISH IDLE TONNAGE $ ^{1} $ REDUCED.
text:
A large reduction is reported from Copenhagen to have taken place in the idle tonnage laid up at Danish ports. On July 12, there were 34 steamers of a total of $7,000 tons laid up; on July 19, the figures were reduced to 10 and $5,000 tons respectively, and further to 12 and 21,000 tons on July 31.

The cause of the improvement in the Danish shipping position is attributed to the effects of the coast stoppage in England; since the outbreak of which about 900,000 tons of shipping is lying in English ports, which tomnage has to be replaced in another manner. At the same time the transport of coal from America has acted favourably in freight rates from transmarine port to Europe for corn and other goods. The freight routes of the Danish United Company, which had to be restricted to North and South America in the spring, are expected to be fully restored in the present month.

Cargo and passengers on the Hong Kong-Canton Steamboats yesterday were very encouraging, both on the "up" and "down" boat. It is felt that an improvement has set in since the withdrawal of the strike pickets from the river.

The reason for the "holding up" of foreign shipping (mostly Japanese and Norwegian) on the Canton River a few days ago is the institution by the Bocca Tigris Forts of a system of examination which has not yet been put into actual operation. Steamers (other than the Hong Kong steamboats) are made to stop there for examination, if necessary. This is a Canton Government and not a strike measure.

The small gunboat "Fook Hoi," after going out past Bocca Tigris on a minelaying expedition (to guard against possible attack by Northern warships), is reported to have been captured by pirates. Other pirates are active up the East River.

A search is now being made near Yungki for the many bodies of those drowned when the Cantou-Kungyick tow-boat foundered (as reported by the "China Mail" correspondent at Pakkai).

text: For failing to report the arrival of his trading junk, a Chinese master was charged and fined $5 at the Marine Court this morning. A Chinese coolie was sentenced to a month's hard labour for going on board the s.s. "Santhia" without permission.

headline: CLEAR THEM OUT!

Several reputable newspapers have given prominence to their activities, and, incidentally, rebuked the Labourites for belitting the tell-tale documents exposed in the House of Commons by the Government. As one paper puts it, too many of the members of the Labour Parliamentary Party are always ready to place the foreigner invariably in the right when any question arises between aliens and their own countrymen. The way that they try to gloss over every unfriendly act of the Soviet Government, which is the mildest term we can use, toward bringing about a revolution and the overthrow of the British Empire, is a scandal to their patriotism—that is, if they have the slightest particle of such a virtue. The disclosure of direct communication between Communists at Home and the blood-stained Soviet Executive at Moscow has been most conclusively proved by the mass of documents published in the Blue Book. As a nation we are not only being attacked from Moscow. The plotters are on our own sole, free to carry out the

orders of the ruffians who have reduced Russia to unspeakable depths of degradation.

One does not generally look to a paper like the Police News, which usually confines itself to reports and pictures of sensational crimes, to indulge in outspoken language on such a subject. It is, therefore, gratifying to find in a recent issue a smart rebuke to those who would bolster up the "Reds." It points out that there can be no longer any doubt that immense sums of money have been remitted from the Moscow Government for the sole purpose of creating anarchy and revolution in Great Britain. Their idea is that if they can only smash up the British Empire they will find little or no difficulty in smashing up the capitalistic portion of the rest of the world. If our own people are ready to take Soviet money for such a purpose they are traitors of the worst type and should meet with the punishment that such miscreants deserve. Malolos, Bulacan, July 26.—The passenger train from San Fernando, Pampanga, which left Malolos, at 9 o'clock this morning for Manila, while passing over the bridge under repair almost in front of the Guiginto station, fell into the river, as a result of the collapse of the bridge. The locomotive and one freight coach fell into the river. The freight coach was thrown straight on the river bed and served to stop the passenger coaches from falling. headline: CHINA'S TARIFFS.
text:
"REVOLUTIONARY SITUATION"

The Foreign Office in Canton has authorised the publication of the following reply to the communication of the American Consul-General in which he answered the note of the Acting Minister for Foreign Affairs protesting against the resumption of the Special Tariff Conference:

Sir, I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter, dated July 26, in reply to my note of protest against the resumption of the Special Tariff Conference at Peking. In no querulous sense do I draw your attention to the fact that the text of your reply was handed to Reuter's Agency in time for publication in Peking and elsewhere on July 24—48 hours before it was delivered at this Ministry. While I do not wish to stress this lapse in procedure, you will, I do not doubt, agree that its repetition should be avoided in the future.

I note that Mr. MacMurray views my Government's strong opposition to the resumption of the Conference as evidence of "a disheartening lack of unanimity amongst the Chinese people in respect to the efforts of the Government of the United States jointly with the other friendly Powers concerned to carry out its purpose of bringing into effect certain readjustments in its treaty relations with China." But what seems to Mr. MacMurray to be a "disheartening lack of unanimity" in understanding and appreciating the policy of the United States is, in truth, a convincing proof that that policy is wrong at once in conception and in application.

Foreign “Interference.” The policy is wrong because it is an expression of American failure to realise that the Chinese situation is fundamentally a Revolutionary situation and that, therefore, a Revolutionary i.e. a fundamental solution is necessary as opposed to a solution involving a series of so-called “evolutionary” re-adjustments. And the situation is Revolutionary because the principle change implicit in the Revolution of 1911-12 has not yet been worked out in the life of the Nation, particularly in its politico-economic aspect, owing to the constant interference and intervention, direct and indirect, of certain Foreign Powers who (to cite some signal instances) first supported. Yuan Shih-kai in his attempt to destroy the Chinese Republic and financed him with the Reorganisation Loan of 1913, next supported by Tuan Chi-jui in his Anfu days and financed him with the Nishihara and other loans, then supported Wu Pei-fu and financed him with Customs and Salt surplus, and are now contemplating the support of a composite strong man in the diversified persons of Wu Pei-fu and Chang Tso-lin and the financing of this brace of militarists with the proceeds of a loan to be secured on the promised Tariff surtaxes.

Persistence in such a policy makes not only for Chinese disorder and what is called "chaos" in this country but for the intellectual confusion and moral bankruptcy of the diplomacy of the Powers. And naught but a "disheartening lack of unanimity" will manifest itself whenever the Government of the United States is moved to apply its "evolutionary" policy to the Revolutionary facts of the Chinese situation.

Nationalist China insists on a fundamental solution of the group of issues known as the Chinese question. Internally, the means that the new military and political technique which has enabled the Nationalist Government to unify the Liang-kuang militarily, fiscally and politically must be applied on a national scale in order that the Chinese people may work out their own salvation in the interests of themselves as a whole and not to subordinate the same to such alien interests as foreign high finance and foreign trade. And externally, the dominating feature of a fundamental solution of the Chinese question is that America should revise its present policy of "bringing into effect certain readjustments of its treaty relations with China" and, re-cognising the necessity of a General Re-adjustment or such treaty relations instead of readjustments on the instalment plan, satisfy the demand of Nationalist China for the substitution of the unequal treaties for other treaties consistent with the real independence and sovereignty of China. This is a policy that has been definitely brought within the range of practical politics and proved to be both practicable and expedient by the

bold statesmanship of Soviet Russia.

In view of the fact that “at the moment there exists no central government supported by all sections of China and recognised by the interested Powers with which to deal on a basis of mutuality of responsibilities,” it would be proper and pertinent for Mr. MacMurray to ask with whom is America, either alone or in conjunction with other Powers, to negotiate regarding a general re-adjustment of China's treaties relations with Foreign Powers. The Foreign Powers can only negotiate, in the interests of all concerned, with a National Government of China whose authority and power is a reality.

As there is not such a government at the moment, I have the honour to repeat the warning that the Nationalist Government, whose authority is now extending to Central China, will repudiate all and every loan to be concluded with the agents of Wu Pei-fu and Chang Tsc-lin in Peking, and to add that the resumption of the Special Tariff Conference will be viewed by my Government as a deliberate attempt on the part of the United States and the other interested Powers to convert the Chinese Maritime Customs from a politico-fiscal organ into an engine of war-finance and foreign intervention in China's civil or rather Revolutionary wars. In this event the Nationalist Government will be compelled to take certain defensive measures.

Foreign Affairs. The Honourable Douglas Jenkins, American Consult General,

headline: STRIKE ECHO. / EFFECT ON SANITARY DEPARTMENT. / FORMIDABLE PROBLEM
text:
In his report on the Sanitary Department for 1925, Mr. N. L. Smith says in his concluding paragraph—

Reference has been made in several of the preceding sections of this report to the effects of the general strike, which was the most notable feature if the year under

notable feature if the year under review and which perhaps affected the Sanitary Department more nearly than any other branch of the Government. Apart from the emergency measures necessary to counteract the wholesale desertion of butchers at the slaughterhouses and the almost complete stagnation of the markets, for several weeks, the maintenance of the essential sanitary services called for very long hours of trying labour on the part of the small non-Chinese staff of the Department. The defection of the regular night-soil coolies was anticipated by selecting a suitable number of stormwater manholes for the reception of excreta, marking these with paint, and notifying the public. By this means there was comparatively little dislocation when the collectors finally deserted. The supervision of this work and the flushing of the sewers in question was in the hands of the European Sanitary Inspectors, who also had the work of seeing to the clearance of dry public latrines. The Hill District nightsoil coolies, who are supplied by the conservancy contractor did not go on strike at any time.

The collection and disposal of refuse was also a formidable problem. Out of 771 scavenging coolies over 600 deserted between July 2 and 7. At the latter date there were left only 5 out of 64 bullock drivers, 5 out of 111 bargemen and no launch engineers. The entire fleet of launches and barges was laid up until July 31 from which date it was possible gradually to recruit fresh staff and to resume the normal methods of refuse disposal. All Kowlcom refuse was meanwhile taken by motor lorries to the Cheungshawan dump. In Hongkong, where a number of bullock and hand-drawn dust-carts still survive, it was necessary to supplement the Department's refuse lorries with motor lorries borrowed from the Public Works Department. Refuse dumps were started on the Praya East Reclamation and at Kennedy Town and the refuse was burnt, covered with chloride of lime or covered with earth as circumstances dictated. On both sides of the harbour the lorries were driven by European volunteer drivers who deserve the gratitude of the community for the efficient manner in which they worked for very long hours daily at this nauseating task. All the normal work of the Department was of course temporarily dislocated and it was not until August 15 that the routine of house-cleaning, etc. could be resumed.

headline: OVERWORKED!
text:
In the publication of the report for 1925 on the Sanitary Department will be found overwhelming evidence in support of recent articles in this paper contending that this all-important Department is grossly under staffed and overworked.

These annual reports rarely get into the hands of the average reader, who has to be content with whatever excerpts are published in the newspapers. For that reason it is not surprising to find a lack of appreciation in many quarters of the work of the Sanitary Department. But the more one studies the latest annual report the more one is driven to the conclusion that, in view of the shockingly low European personnel, the Department accomplishes truly marvellous work—work that would be a credit to the most thorough and up-to-date business establishment at Home.

Everywhere the hand of the Sanitary Inspector is seen—and felt. It is easier to enumerate what he does not do than what he does. There is routine work under the Public Health and Buildings Ordinance; there is work under the Food and Drugs Ordinance; there is scavenging, refuse removal, and nightsoil removal to supervise; there are public bath houses to be seen to; there are water closets and public conveniences to be looked after; there are cemeteries, mortuaries, and crematoria that require supervision — and right on through the whole gamut of the sanitary requirements of the Colony. Strikes may—and do—occur; floods come and necessitate volumes of extra work on the part of the Sanitary Inspectors and their gangs; but everything is performed as if the unusual were just the normal.

The report for 1925 discloses a staff of one Chief Inspector, four Senior Inspectors, and 38 Inspectors. With an army of 1,500 subordinates they look after the sanitary needs of practically the whole Island and Kowloon. Last year alone they had 16,866 "nuisances reported" to deal with (including 554 outstanding on December 31, 1924). There was not one nuisance reported in which action was not taken.

There were premises to inspect summonses to be taken out, prosecutions to be initiated, and Police Courts to attend—all eating into an otherwise very busy day's work. How it is all done is a mystery that baffles us. With even treble the present European staff the verdict would be that they do wonders in a community in which the Chinese lower classes predominate and in which, therefore, widespread ignorance obtains in regard to sanitation and hygiene. There were no fewer than 441 prosecutions, the fines totalling $4,324. Moreover in the sanitary districts on the Island, 90,567 floors were cleansed, the number in Kowloon being 44,800. There were 27,557 cases of limewashing on the Island and 11,997 in Kowloon.

Thus we might go on! Even were we to reproduce a Sanitary Inspector's notebook for one day's duty it would give an inadequate conception of the amount of labour of the European personnel as a whole. Nothing more has been heard of the project to increase that staff commensurate with the growing sanitary requirements of the Colony; but

something must be done in this direction even if only to cope with emergencies. Whilst the P.W.D. rightly earned a meed of praise for its fine work as the result of the recent floods, its confreres in the Sanitary Department were not one whit behind. It is as well that this fact should be known; indeed, to make no mention of it would be invidious. But the point is that the present strength of the Europeans in this Department cannot be expected to go on from year to year, emergencies or no emergencies, with only a very trifling increase. There may arise an emergency for which even three times the existing personnel could not possibly cope with. in which event — well, Heaven help Hongkong!

The origin of the Imperial Conference may be traced to the presence in London in 1887 of the Premiers of the self-governing Dominions, representing their nations at the celebrations of the Jubilee of Queen Victoria. Similar gatherings were held in 1897, 1902, 1907, and 1911, and in 1907 the title of "Colonial" Conference was changed to Imperial Conference. At the earlier meetings the Secretary of State for the Colonies presided, but with the change of title additional importance was given to the assembly by the assumption of the Presidency by the British Prime Minister. The Secretary of State for the Dominions and Colonies has invariably attended the Conference, but naturally Dominion as opposed to Colonial questions have ever been paramount and predominant.

sence of the Colonial Secretary in this capacity of Dominions Secretary is not sufficient. The Crown Colonies and Dependencies ought to be directly represented. Not that there is any fear of their interests otherwise being jeopardised. That is unthinkable. But, if it is to be truly a family gathering to consider Empire problems as a whole and not only of those of the Dominions it does not seem right that the Crown Colonies should be ignored. An invitation should be extended to the Governors of the Colonies to attend personally or by deputy. It would at the very least be an excellent opportunity for Empire propaganda. It would at least make the Crown Colonies feel that it is not only when the call to war comes that they are remembered by the Mother Country. The same arguments hold good in regard to the Empire Parliamentary Association. There is, of course, no Parliaments in the Crown Colonies but there are Legislative Councils. These could well be represented at the Empire Parliamentary Association Conferences. Such representation would tend in some degree to dissipate a lot of that parochialism that exists in the Crown Colonies. It would induce a livelier interest in British Parliamentary institutions as a whole that could not but react favourably on the whole Empire. Why should Hongkong and other Crown Colonies always be left out of the picture?

headline: OBITUARY. / MISSIONARY WORKER IN CANTON.
text:
MRS. M. N. KERR.

After 53 years of missionary work in China, Mrs. Martha Noyes Kerr, of Canton, passed away at the Matilda Hospital, Hongkong, on Saturday, at the age of 86 years.

Under the American Presbyterian Mission, Mrs. Kerr for some years after her arrival in China, was a teacher and director in the True Light Seminary for Women and Girls, together with her sister, Miss Harriett Noyes. Twenty-seven years ago, as the wife of Dr. J. G. Kerr, she helped in the foundation of the J. G. Kerr Hospital for the Insane in Canton and although her husband died a few years after its foundation Mrs. Kerr carried on with the work until last year when conditions in Canton made it impossible for her to remain there. The remains of Mrs. Kerr will be taken to Canton to be laid to rest beside those of her husband and of her brother, the Rev. Henry V. Noyes, D.D. in the “White Cloud” cemetery.

headline: P.I. AGITATION.
text:
INDEPENDENCE MOVEMENT SHAKES EAST.

BOTH SIDES AIRED.

Williamstown, Issachusetts, Aug. 2.

Widely divergent views on the Philippine question were expressed by eminent international authorities participating in "Philippines day" under the auspices of the Williamstown Institute of Politics.

George H. Blakeslee, professor of history and international relations at Clark University, presided over the meeting in his capacity as leader of discussion on Far Eastern topics. He made an address in which he declared that the Filipinos' insistence on independence threatened grave consequences in the Orient. He said that "harmonious, efficient administration" in the islands was impossible so long as agitation in favour of separation from the United States continued.

headline: Fairfield Bill Backed.
text:
Dr. Stephen Pierce Duggan of New York, former member of the Monroe commission, supported the plan embodied in the Fairfield Bill authorising a plebiscite in the Philippines twenty years hence, on the issue of independence. “Pedro Guevara, Filipino resident commissioner in Washington, said “that if the United States was unwilling to grant the islands immediately freedom,” the American government should at least grant them “the privilege of formulating their own constitution and conducting their own domestic affairs without interference.”

Vicente a Villamin, Filipino writer and lecturer, recommended a status for the Philippines similar to that of Canada—and Australia. He called this solution "independence without separation" and said that a majority of the Filipino leaders would be satisfied with this condition.

Sir Frederick Whyte, former president of the legislative assembly of India, made his second speech before the entire institute and argued that the final authority in India must always rest with Great Britain as the dominant power. He said that India would disintegrate and be torn by internal conflicts if England loosened her grip.—United Press.

headline: "Independence Without
text: Williamstown, Mass., Aug. 2.: Pedro Guevara asserted that "in view of the pledge of the United States, the Philippines are entitled to independence." He said the mistrust between the Filipinos and the Americans was hindering the economic development of the islands.

headline: Duggan Question Ability.
text: Prof. Stephen P. Duggan of New York University, member of the Monroe Educational mission which made a survey of the schools of the Philippines last year, said the ability of the Filipinos to conduct their governmental affairs was open to debate. He said he favoured the Fairfield bill presented in the last congress providing that after twenty years the people of the Philippines vote on severing or retaining their connection with the United States.—Associated Press,

headline: QUAKE SHOCK.
text:
The Manila Bulletin of August reports:—

An earthquake of considerable intensity which shook Maniln yesterday afternoon at 1.03 o'clock had its centre in the Pacific Ocean north of Camarines Sur and Albany, the observatory has discovered. In those two provinces, and in the Catanduanes Islands, the shock was quite strong, but no casualties nor damages have been reported.

Ten Shocks Recorded. Ten distinct shocks were recorded by the observatory instruments after the one big one. The last of the series occurred at 3.51. The main one, which came while many Manilans were sitting at lunch, was distinctly felt. Electric light fixtures described unusual areas, and wooden buildings creaked a bit.

Nagasaki, August 4. — Rajah Patrap, counsellor to the King of Afghanistan and a delegate to the Pan-Asatic Congress, which has just closed in Nagasaki, cannot leave Osaka because he does not have a passport. The Rajah alleges that while he was passing through China British spies robbed him of some of his baggage containing his passport.

headline: MEXICAN TROUBLE.
text:
BANKERS URGE CALLES TO END FIGHT.

PEOPLE CUT RATION.

Ten of the leading bankers in Mexico City called on President Calles to-day and urged immediate steps toward mediation of the government's quarrel with the Catholic church as the only means of preventing a nation-wide financial panic.

They informed the president that millions of pesos were being withdrawn from deposit banks for safekeeping and that, consequently, the financial situation was becoming more acute each day. They estimated that 50 per cent. of the deposits were in the hands of the church or directly controlled by the church.

Against Plebiscite Plan. The pressure of the economic boycott instituted voluntarily by Catholics as a means of passive resistance against the government's decrees, is beginning to be felt in all commercial lines. Catholics are purchasing only their actual requirements.

Official and public sentiment is apparently against the proposal to hold a plebiscite on the religious question. Discussion of this solution has almost died out.

It is reported in official circles, but not yet confirmed, that an American protestant clergyman was lynched by indignant citizens in Prapuato because he took the stand that the anti-religious decrees did not apply to protestants. Archbishop Del Rio suspended the Reverend Maurice Calvo, at

on the charge of attempting to conduct religious services in violation of the archbishop's pastoral letter.

headline: Moderation is Counselled
text:
Mexico City, Aug. 3. Counselled by the leaders to keep within the paths of peace and moderation, Mexico's Catholics continued to day to pray for a solution of the problems resulting from the government's religious regulations and the withdrawal of priests from the churches.

The people in many parts of the country are buying only essentials as a protest, although the effects of the economic boycott fostered by the League for the Defence of Religious Liberty is not applicable in Mexico City. Theatres and bull fights continue to draw the usual crowds. Influential persons still are seeking to bring about informal exchanges between the Episcopate and the government, believing that an accord is yet possible. The government believes that danger of serious disorders has passed but armed forces are ready for an emergency.

headline: LOOKING AHEAD.
text:
ISLANDS SHOULD BE AUTONOMOUS.

Williamstown, Mass., Aug. 3. A “Philippine Free State” with a dominion status similar to that of the commonwealths of Australia and Canada was recommended as a permanent solution for the Philippine problem by Charles Batchelder, former chief of the forestry division of the department of commerce, in an address before the Institute of Politics. He believed that the Philippines would achieve “a satisfactory place in the family of nations” on this basis, particularly if the United States should become a member of the league of nations. In this case, he said, the Filipinos would be entitled to a representative in the assembly just as each British dominion is now represented.

For Protectorate, Plan. He also suggested that American sovereignty in the Philippines should take the form of a protectorate with a Filipino governor and a cabinet entirely responsible to the legislature. Under these circumstances, he pointed out, it would be advisable to create a commission of appeal empowered to arbitrate disagreements between America and Filipino officials. He expressed confidence that the Filipinos would be contented with such an arrangement.

Norbert Lyons of the American chamber of commerce mission to the United States, followed Dr. Batchelder and argued that permanent retention of the islands by the United States was the only way to free America from depended on British rubber, Brazilian coffee and other national monopolies. Separation from the United States, he said, would result in the economic ruin of the islands and possibly, their political ruin.

Judge Santos Heard. Judge Jose Abad Santos delivered one of the principal addresses on the subject, "International Aspects of the Philippine Question." He said that the Philippines, if granted independence, would accord the United States all rights necessary to safeguard her special interests, in the islands "including a special treaty permitting her to maintain a suitable naval base."

He was confident that the Philippine government, in the event of independence, would be willing to grant compensation for American officials and employees who would be discharged or retired.

“As soon as the Philippines are given independence,” said Judge Santos, “and their new status recognised by the powers, we shall make application for membership in the league of nations. It is fair to assume that the Philippines would receive the same treatment as is already accorded Cuba, Haiti and Irish Free State.”

He urged that the United States government authorise the Philippine legislature to call a convention for the purpose of framing a tentative constitution, guaranteeing religious tolerance and economic security.—United Press

headline: WAKE UP!
text:
extended toward certain British firms in the Colony as a result of the "past year's stagnation is wasted. Trade may not be "humming." Frankly it will take a considerable time to revert to the conditions prevailing before June of last year. But—have certain large firms and many small retail shops not missed opportunities of extending trade by the sheer pushing of British goods? Go into any shop you like for a certain article and what is the result—you are offered a foreign article—anything but British. We may compliment others on their commercial enterprise. But that is no reason why British firms should fill the unenviable role of mere spectators while other agents and can-vassers are mopping up all the business with the myriads of retail shops in the Colony. A personal inquiry at a Chinese store a few days ago regarding the overwhelming proportion of foreign goods and the paucity of British elicited the explanation that the others "come round and book" orders, but not so the British." Is it any wonder that British trade in the Colony is feeling the pinch? Why put all the blame for the past year's trade losses on the strike and the boycott? If one door has been closed for a time, is there no opportunity of extending trade already gained in other directions? Is there not ample scope in the confines of this Colony itself for forging ahead in business and of pushing one's wares on to the consuming public through both Chinese and non-Chinese retail shops? Has a systematic canvass ever been made with one particular line — provisions, groceries, or wearing apparel? Have British traders the faintest idea of local sales and of the proportion that goes past them into

headline: AGITATORS FLEE. / AVOIDING CHOLERA AT LUTCHOW.
text:
EYEWITNESS'S NOTES.

A correspondent who has just returned from Luichow's after spending over a week in that district reports:—

The local people were very friendly and practically no anti-foreign or anti-Christian spirit was manifested.

The agitators were either absent or on vacation. Perhaps they left when 80 per cent. of the people of Luichow city fled in terror from the epidemic of cholera that has ravaged the place for the last two months.

Several hundred men, women and children have died from that disease. At one time, on the main street, the only establishments that opened their doors were the Baptist Chapel, a Christian bookshop and one other shop. The epidemic is abating and the inhabitants are slowly returning.

The district is now entirely governed from Canton. Hongkong and Kwong-chow-wan are “under the boycott” ban yet grass mats and bags are allowed to be exported. Otherwise, trade is at a standstill and many people are suffering the pangs of hunger.

Luichow is a district in the southern peninsula of Kwangtung province.

headline: COMPENSATION. / FOR DETECTIVE CAPTURED BY PICKETS.
text:
FINANCE COMMITTEE VOTE.

$1,250 will be asked for at tomorrow's Finance Committee meeting to cover the cost of expenditure of and compensation to a Chinese detective who was arrested by strike pickets in Canton last year. This detective, P.C. C626 Mak Po-tai, was sent to Canton on duty, and on June 28, 1925, was arrested and detained by strikers at Canton. He was severely assaulted and lost his watch and clothing. He was taken over from the strikers by the Police Department in Canton and detained until February 28, 1926, when he was sent to Macao. He had thus been a prisoner for eight months, and suffered severely at the beginning of his detention as a result of ill treatment. He was attended daily by a Chinese doctor for between two and three months, and was supplied with Chinese medicine. He was obliged to borrow money for food, medicine and comforts from friends and relatives including members of the Police Department in Canton. His friends also expended certain sums with view to securing better treatment for him.

In addition to these expenses the Government consider it reasonable to allow him compensation. A sum of $247.70 has therefore been added making a total of $1,250. Doctor and medicine.... $786.00 Food..... 90.00 Expended by friends.... 110.00 Loss of clothes and watch Compensation..... 247.70

$1,250.01

headline: CHINESE FESTIVAL. / SEVEN HEAVENLY VIRGINS RE-UNION. / FRIDAY'S CELEBRATIONS.
text:
This Saturday is the seventh day of the seventh moon, the day of the festival of the Seven Heavenly Virgins who are believed to meet the Young Cowherd on the Silver Stream (Milky Way) the previous night.

This festival is observed by nearly all Chinese girls and also by Chinese ladies.

Half of the shops in Lyndhurst Terrace are purveyors of haberdshery and other articles which only interest the fair sex. A week before the festival, these establishments display tableaux made of rice paper and tissue paper in which allegorical references are made to the Seven Sisters and the Cowherd. Girls in their teens buy these pieces for the ceremony on Friday night. The joss-paper shops make large seven-cornered trays of paper with boudoir requisites (also in paper) which are burnt as offerings to the Heavenly Maidens.

headline: Social Gossip.
parent_headline: CHINESE FESTIVAL. / SEVEN HEAVENLY VIRGINS RE-UNION. / FRIDAY'S CELEBRATIONS.
text:
Families vie with one another in getting up elaborate displays in which wild and edible fruit, corn grown in small dishes with minute lanterns inside the stalks, form the major port of the decorations. A common greeting on Friday will be “How many tables have you set up?”, numbers being “a sign of affluence”.

Last year there was a celebration at Lee Garden, East Point. This spacious Chinese amusement park was packed to the limit. Special sets of display, in honour of the occasion were constructed and placed in different parts of the garden for ladies and girls to admire.

This Week's Opportunity. Some of the adornments were exceedingly clever and very attractive as works of sheer art. Beyond the workmanship they cost little.

The sterner sex also turned up in force," not so much to see the articles put up, but to inter-mingle with the crowd.

The “China Mail” is informed that the “show” on Friday night will exceed in grandeur that of twelve months ago.

European who go down will find much that is instructive and pleasing. At the same time they will be able to get an insight into Chinese life when everybody is in the festive spirit. A visit will be well repaid and only a nominal gate fee is charged.

headline: A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.
text:
To be in a position to read, whilst within a few degrees of the equator, of heat waves surpassing in intensity anything experienced locally is but one of many phases of the-freakish ways nature seems to delight in evidencing. But although the temperature may be higher in other places, we are scarcely entitled to the position of sympathisers in Hongkong, having regard to the humidity which is almost as taxing to health as greater direct heat. Shanghai has been suffering from an intense heat wave which has severely handicapped curative and preventative work in connection with the serious outbreak of cholera. The heat cannot be myself, of course, be blamed for the actual outbreak and an investigation carried out there seems to have established beyond doubt that the outbreak was caused through disgraceful conditions obtaining in Chinese territory with regard to the water supply. Now that foreign helps has been called in to deal with the situation it should be possible to strike at the root cause of the outbreak and it is to be hoped that Shanghai is within sight of the end of her trouble both for her sake and that of neighbouring ports to whom the danger of carried infection is a serious one.

In some of the cases submitted by, Kowloon residents to their Association in reference to increases of rent, the Association has come to the conclusion that such increases are excessive but further information is requested from other tenants if the Association is to put forward a strong case for a Fair Rent's Board on the ground of general unfair increases. The week has seen further correspondence on this subject and a strong argument is put forward by a correspondent who points out that the Government exercise control over public utility companies the cost of whose services play far less important a part in the household budget than does that of rent. Once given the rightness of the principle that Government control is desirable in services affecting the public, he argues, no consideration

of the difficulty involved in setting up a Fair Rents Board should influence them in ignoring the necessity for its institution.

The grounding of yet another steamer on the shoal near the Kowloon Clock Tower is all the more serious in view of the evidence it furnishes of the rate at which this shoalis silting up. It was only to be expected that a heavily laden vessel like the "Danmark," drawing twenty-nine feet of water, would ground if attempting to pass over the shoal at a time when it was practically low water. But the "President McKinley" was drawing but twenty-four feet when she stuck. If, as stated, this shoal has at some time or other been dredged to a depth of over thirty feet (presumably at high water) it is about time it was dredged again, for although it is easily possible to enter and leave the harbour without passing over the shoal it is not in the interests of an important seaport to ignore a menace to the ships it harbours; particularly when it has the facilities for carrying out the necessary work.

Official figures have been published this week, showing the tremendous loss in revenue to the nation that the coal stoppage has entailed. Later cables indicate that prospects of settlement are brighter in spite of the rejection by the mining districts of the proposals submitted by the Churches. These proposals, even if they had been accepted by the miners, would hardly have been a satisfactory basis of renewal of negotiations for settlement in view of the fact that they incorporated the continuation of a subsidy against which the Government has steadfastly set its face. Mr. Cook, the Miners' Secretary, who has been the greatest stumbling block to effective settlement, seems to have moderated his tone somewhat and now agrees that it is vital that the miners should secure an agreement enabling them all to resume work together.

headline: AFTER 26 YEARS.
text:
RETIREMENT OF MR. J. McMURRAY.

OF INDO-CHINA S. N. CO

After an association with the Indo-China S. N. Company extending over 26 years, during half of which he has filled the responsible position of Engineer Superintendent, Mr. J. McMurry, who is leaving by the "Empress of Asia" on Thursday on retirement, was the guest of honour yesterday at a tiffing given in his honour by the Jardine Matheson and Hongkong Whampoa Dock management.

Mr. R. Sutherland was in the chair, supported by Mr. R. M. Dyor.

The Chairman referred to the loss to the Indo-China S. N. Co., and to the engineering fraternity which the departure of Mr. McMurray entailed. Mr. McMurray had succeeded Mr. Angus Sinclair in the position of Engineer Superintendent and his task had been no sinecure. He (the speaker) was afraid that it was in Mr. McMurray's unfalling devotion to duty lay the reason for what he hoped was merely a temporary breakdown in health. All present would join in the wish that once more, invigorated by the heather scented breezes of bonny Perthshire, Mr. McMurray would soon regain his usual good health.

Mr. R. M. Dyer also added a tribute to the engineering ability and personal qualities of Mr. McMurray and presented him with an English silver salver which he hoped would serve too remind Mr. McMurray of the friends he had left behind in Hongkong.

After Mr. Murray had suitably replied further, remarks were made by Mr. Russell, "Government Surveyor, Mr. Lang, of Lloyds, and Mr. D. Gow, an old schoolmate and co-worker in Hongkong shipping interests.

Amongst those present were:—Messrs. R. M. Oyer (Hongkong and Whampon Dock Co.), R. Sutherland, J. W. Sanderson, P. Tod. Captain I. H. Rolfe, Captain D. Skinner (Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd.), Messrs. E. L. Hosie, H. H. Scott, P. Gow, J. S. MacIntosh, J. W. Mathews, W. Forsyth, S. Steel, G. Duncan, J. M.
