headline: SEVEN YEARS. / SEQUEL TO "SUIYANG" ARMS SEIZURE.
text:
A heavy sentence was applied for yesterday afternoon at the Kowloon Magistracy on four Chinese convicted on charges of unlawful possession of six fully loaded revolvers. They were arrested on board the B. and S. vessel "Suiyang" as it was about to proceed to Shanghai and it was stated by Sub-Inspector Andrew, who had charge of the prosecution, that "the D.S.P. was convinced that the men intended to commit a piracy. All were experienced seamen.

The case was tried before two Magistrates, Mr. J. H. B. Nihill and Major C. Willson.

Evidence was given as to the purchase of four tickets for the voyage by the third defendant, these being found in the course of the police search in the possession of the first, third, fourth and fifth defendants. Five men appeared to answer charges of possession of arms and it was stated in the course of the case that they were the only Chinese travelling by the vessel. The others were all Northerners.

Two of the defendants made statements when arrested admitting ownership of the boots in which the arms were found concealed. The third prisoner, who was absent when the police carried out the search on the vessels but who was afterwards found on a junk which was lying alongside, said that he was going to Shanghai to take the fourth defendant to pursue his studies.

The statements made by the prisoners were read over at the hearing yesterday, that by the second defendant including the statement that the first defendant had asked him to go to Shanghai to "rob things." Questioned with regard to the Chinese expression ("fat yeung choi") from which "rob things" had been translated the Court interpreter said that it meant to "procure" foreign wealth." Asked if the character "yeung" did not also signify "ocean," the interpreter said that that also was a translation and it was possible that the defendant had meant to "procure ocean wealth."

After the defendant had made statements in court denying possession of the arms, the first four defendants were all convicted and the fifth man acquitted. Sentence of seven years' hard labour each was passed

headline: BOLSHEVIST ACTIVITY.
text:
Prominence is given in the Indian papers to a question in the House of Commons on July 12 when Sir William Davison asked what action the Government of India was taking with reference to the Bolshevik activity in Afghanistan where, according to the statement "of Colonel M. Saunders," the Director of Military Intelligence in India, an Afghan Air Force was being formed with Russian pilots and mechanics, and also new aerodromes and new military roads and railways. Commander Kenworthy asked whether this was a proper question seeing that Afghanistan was an independent friendly State which was represented at the Court of St. James. Sir William rejoined that surely the Commons was entitled to enquire with regard to a report by a British official. Earl Winterton replied that Lord Birkenhead was enquiring by whose authority the published statement was made, and added that the Government was carefully watching the situation in Afghanistan.

For the benefit of those of our readers who have not fully appreciated the magnitude of Moscow's machinations and the subtlety of detail underlying her campaign against Britain and ultimately against civilisation as a whole, it may be well to quote from the Rangoon Times some of Gol. Saunders's revelations, which were first given to the public at the Saturday Club in Calcutta. The most significant of the Colonel's

statements may come as a shock to the many who still believe that in cultivating friendly relations with the Soviet the British Empire would be taking the most practical step towards the institution of a permanent world peace. Yet it has been amply proved by the speeches and writings of almost every Bolshevik leader who has given his attention to international affairs that "The Third International has declared war on the British Empire." To quote Zinovieff, "Our first weapon is propaganda and our second, force of arms. The Achilles heel of the British Empire is India." We must therefore make every effort to develop all possible lines of advance leading on India." In a later speech he added: "What we planned for India has come to pass in China, but we have hopes that India may make up leeway in a sudden and unexpected fashion."

In addition the Soviet aims at the absorption of Afghanistan. Large subsidies, mostly in the form of arms and munitions, have been given to the Afghans. The Afghan Air Force, with Russian pilots and mechanics, is being developed. It has its main aerodrome at Kabul, and landing grounds have already been made at Kandahar and Jellalabad besides those on the Termez-Kabul air route. From their present aerodromes, therefore, Russians can bomb the Indian frontier stations. The great barrier of the mountains of the North-West Frontier, so long thought to be impregnable to Russian invasion, has been metaphorically razed to the ground by aerial development and the attack on India has at last become a possibility.

It is a fact; declares Col. Saunders, that the Red Army is a more efficient fighting force than the pre-war Russian Army. It is well equipped with mechanical weapons, and great stress is laid on the use of tanks, armoured cars, aeroplanes, gas and chemical warfare. The Red Army has a large and efficient air force. It is worth noting that, whereas other nations are economising on military expenditure, the Soviet this year is increasing its military budget by fifty per cent. These are striking disclosures, and it is little cause for wonder that the movement against Bolshevism has taken concrete shape in Shanghai, for instance, and that in Great Britain itself the popular clamour is increasing for the expulsion of the “Red” aliens, whose presence there is a perpetual menace to the whole Empire.

headline: IRREGULAR?
text:
SUMMONS SERVED BY A BOY.

MOTORIST'S POSITION.

When summoned before Mr. J. H. B. Nihill, at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday for driving a car without a licence, Mr. C. M. Manners said that he always observed the regulations, but he had no idea when he took the car out that he had left his licence behind.

Regarding the serving of the summons, Mr. Manners thought it peculiar that it should have been done by a small Chinese boy. On it being pointed out that the Court Sergeant served summonses only when the drivers could not be found, His Worship remarked that the boy evidently knew Mr. Manners.

A fined of $3 was imposed. LANDLORD'S CLAIM.

Mr. H. H. Fox, Commercial Counsellor of the British Legation at Peking, will be passing through Shanghai on the 24th instant. We understand that he has accepted a luncheon invitation from the Union Club of China to be held on that date.

headline: BETTER PAY. / AMERICA'S, ADVICE TO FRANCE.
text:
OR MAY OWE MOVE.

Although officially ignoring George's Clemenceu's open letter to President Coolidge complaining of America's war's debt demands on France, the Washington authorities pointed out to day that if France fails to ratify the Mellon-Berenger agreement it will owe $407,000,000 in principal on its war supplies, debt in 1929. The war supplies purchased from America after the war while Clemenceu was premier, now bear five per cent. interest. Under the Mellon-Berenger settlement this obligation will be consolidated with other war debts, bearing a much lower rate of interest.—"Associated Press."

Secretary Mellon, who is now here to visit his daughter, said that he saw no reason for commenting on the open letter from ex-Premier Clemenceau of France to President Coolidge asking for tolerance toward the French debt. Only one paragraph of the letter was published in the newspapers of Rome and it aroused only slight comment.—"United Press."

Versailles, France, Aug. 10. The Senate and Chamber of Deputies, sitting as the National Assembly, to-day approved the ed placing a measure creating offer- ed placing a measure creating a sinking fund into the constitution, Shortly before the vote the session was temporarily suspended because of a demonstration by Communists who sang the revolutionary anthem, Premier Poincare, urging the adoption of the measure, declared: "Our creditors will find this a proof of our determination to pay all of our debts, because of our capacity."—"Associated Press."

headline: CANTON'S CONNIVANCE.
text:
It must now be taken for granted that a deadlock exists in regard to the negotiations for the settlement of the boycott, and that little hope exists for any change from the present position unless through one of those dramatic developments for which China is notorious.

After many months of discreet silence, maintained with the excellent object of giving the negotiations every possible chance of success, freed from the embarrassment of criticism, the voice of Hongkong has again been heard. His Excellency the Governoror, in his speech yesterday, referred to the Canton tangle in terms that are nothing, if not significant. There was no beating about the bush and no leaving the Colony to guess his meaning. In seathing terms he denounced “the attempts made by a band of organised banditti and pirates, miscalled the Canton Strike Committee, to do injury to this Colony.” In plain words he regretted that “the Canton Government even now has not realised that the first and essential duty of a Government is to maintain law and order.” Moreover, his outspoken criticism of the Canton Government comes straight from the shoulder:

"It connives at organised piracy and brigandage in the provincial capital itself, and it allows an unlawful tyranny to be imposed by strike pickets upon the Cantonese people." This outspoken 'condemnation of the Canton Government naturally recalls the grave warnings uttered by the Governor before the official negotiations were commenced. "His Excellency warned the Canton Government of the risks of permitting a breach of Treaty rights and of attacks upon British lives and property. That warning passed unheeded. Then came the overtures for a settlement of the boycott, which augured well for a time. Now it would appear that we are back to the

position in which we were at the time of the Governor's serious warning to the Canton Government at the beginning of the year. The infringement of Treaty rights continues. The unlawful activities of the Canton Strike Committee are unabated. The Canton Government connives at organised piracy and brigandage in the provincial capital itself!

Nothing is to be gained by endeavouring to read into Sir Cecil Clementi's statement yesterday something that may not exist. Nor would it be in the slightest degree helpful at the moment to venture on any surmises as to the reason for His Excellency himself being the first to break the long silence in this Colony in regard to the boycott. The blame for the continued activities of the Canton Strike Committee has once more being rightly placed on the shoulders of the Canton Government. The Governor's indictment is also a warning, but what can it lead to if the Canton Government — unrecognised, be it noted, by the Powers—persists in being ruled by the miscalled Canton Strike Committee? That is what we would like to know!

headline: ALLEGED ASSAULT.
text:
SEQUEL TO INCIDENTS ON “ASIA.”

DINING ROOM DISPUTE.

There was a sequel at the Kowloon "Magistracy" yesterday to a dispute in the dining room of the "Empress of Asia" which occurred prior to the liner's voyage to Manila. On the return of the vessel to Hongkong yesterday a charge of assault brought by the engine-room store keeper against the deck storekeeper was heard.

headline: DIRE PROPHECIES.
text:
CLAIMS TO FORETELL THE FUTURE.

A PREACHER VISITOR.

Believing that he is the chosen instrument of God for conveying warning of disasters to come, the Rev. Francis James Highett has arrived in Hongkong.

Mr. Highett, who claims to have foretold many events of world-wide import prior to their happening (including the War and its outcome in the overthrow of the Kalser, also the earthquake in Japan and the recent coal strike) predicts that the most calamitous period in history is about to begin and that 1927, 1928 or 1929 will see many places destroyed by fire, the sinking of certain portions of China in the sea and the occurrence all over the earth of "dreadful disasters and cataclysms."

Mr. Highett prophesies that "the end of the present age is at hand" and that "God has already descended to take charge of this planet." The Bible, he states, foretells these events. "I have been in communication with 'the Master' for 46 years and it is He who tells me that these catastrophies are to happen although I have not definite dates for them."

Mr. Highett, who is a firm believer in spiritualism, has come to China to preach his religion which he calls the "Universal Church of God." He claims to have founded centres in virtually every country on the globe in the course of his world travels which have taken him round the world three times already.—Mr. Highett is a man of independent means owing to his ownership of a lucrative sheep station in Australia.

headline: CHINESE Y.M.C.A. / EXHIBITS OF HAND WORK.
text:
Yesterday at the Chinese Y.M.C.A., Bridges Street, the closing exercises were held for this summer's Daily Vacation Bible Schools. Sixteen schools have been in session, for four full weeks, with 165 volunteer teachers, and more than 1,600 pupils. The teachers are all students of the various middle schools of Hongkong, who freely gave their mornings to this form of helping younger boys and girls to get some education. About three quarters of the teachers were girls and one quarter boys. Most of the pupils are "poor" children, that is, children from the streets, or children who have had only a few months or so of school, and are not occupied with any work.

The daily programme of the schools included Chinese reading and writing, geography and hygiene, and hand work, as well as Christian instruction and music. The handwork for the boys was basket weaving, and for the girls, sewing and knitting. The cost for the entire work was about a dollar a pupil, or $1,600, which has been raised, from the friends and supporters of the work, almost entirely Chinese. This money goes for text books, materials for handwork, some entertainment and social, riches for teachers, and advertisement and printing, etc.

At the closing exercises at the Y.M.C.A., exhibits of the hand work were shown, some being of a high standard. The waste paper baskets and trays were sold for ten or twenty cents. The socks,

sold for small amounts. About 100 pieces of the wicker ware were sold and a couple of hundred pieces of sewing and knitting.

Credit for this fine piece of work goes to the Daily Vacation Bible School Committee of Hongkong, which is composed of the younger Christians of the churches, together with the pupils in the middle schools and some of their teachers. The faculties have given great aid by urging their pupils to do the teaching and a service to less fortunate children.

Mr. Chang King-shung, principal of the Y.M.C.A. Day School, has been executive secretary for the work thir summer. Mr. Wang Siu-pun has been chairman of the committee of eighteen who have done such fine work.

The closing of the school, following the morning exhibit, took place yesterday afternoon. The schools, which had been held in sixteen different places, sent representatives to the central gathering, each school contributing some item to the programme.

In former years, Hongkong once had eighteen schools, but considering the difficulties of the recent months, the committee is to be congratulated on the report now present. In all China last summer, the number of these

now present in an summer, the number of these Bible Vacation Schools was 2,100.

headline: OLD MAIDS." / ARE THEY THE BEST WORKERS?
text:
Mr. Herbert D. Brown, chief of the United States Bureau of Efficiency, whose business it has been for twenty-three years to study employees in American Government offices, states that widows and large fat men are the world's worst workers, while "old maids," tall, slim men, and little men are the best type of workers for an employer to have in his office.

"Of women, considered as workers, the 'old maid' is the most loyal and efficient," says this American expert.

"Once settled in spinsterhood, a woman is not distracted by thoughts which constantly engage the minds of young girls, which are in eager chase of husbands. She does not stop her typewriter to powder her nose; the arrangement of her shingle is not causing her incessant anxiety, and her lipstick, if she has one, is reserved for occasional use.

"The widow is not so good," Suya, Mr. Brown. "She thinks of her past, looking backward rather than forward. She is often a 'trouble-maker' in an office.

"Slender women are, as a rule better workers than those of more substantial physique." When a slim woman puts on flesh she is liable to lose some of her energy."

Mr. Brown has some equally hard truths to say about the so-called sterner sex.

"The best men workers, generally speaking, are of two physical types," he declares. "One of them is tall, slim and wiry." The other is small, perhaps not more than four inches above five feet in stature.

"There is an unmistakable relation between physique and mentality. The fat, placid man is not likely to forge ahead. He is too easy-going. The large, husky man is not usually successful in commercial life. Married men, as a rule, are better workers than bachelors."

Another variety in Mr. Brown's inexhaustible catalogue is the redeaded worker, who, he says, is dynamic on his job, but less easy to manage than others.

A “Daily Express” representative toured a number of London offices to find out whether English workers come under this category. Some of his inquiries proved illuminating.

"It is impossible to generalise," said an official of a business training college. "The capability for work does not depend on the physical qualities of either a man or woman. Fat women often prove better workers than thin ones. Everything depends on the mentality of the person concerned."

"Spinsters, who are resigned to spinsterhood, are among the best workers," said the manager of a large store. "The trouble with them; however, is that their ideas become

settled and they lose their sense of proportion. Married women are not usually good workers, because their time is occupied in thinking about their homes. There is not much to choose between a bachelor and a married man. "Short men are generally efficient, but most red-haired men are full of bluff."

headline: “DULCIPEL”
text:
Keeps the skin fresh cool and fragrant Prevents and cures "Hongkong Foot"

try and to mitigate the uneconomic effects on the whole country. A month or so ago, Mr. Garvin, in the Observer, expressed the opinion that the only alternative to peace by negotiating was for the Government to call the Coal Commission together, and consult with that body as to the most feasible method of ending forth with a most deplorable situation. Since then the Anglican Bishops and the Free Church leaders have endeavoured to effect a conciliation between the coal owners and the miners, but even their proposals were turned down on a district vote of the miners.

For the moment there appears only one ray of hope. The miners in an important colliery in Notts have accepted the owners' terms—a 7½ hours week at the old wages—and are signing on immediately. The Derbyshire and other Notts owners have intimated their intention to re-open their pits on the same terms. This example will doubtless be followed by others, in which case it will be tested whether Mr. A. J. Cook's vitriolic eloquence fails against the cry of the miners themselves for work in order to keep themselves and their families from starvation.

A hint is given in to-day's cables of a probable development when the House of Commons resassemblies at the end of this month to sanction a continuance of the Emergency Regulations. But no great reliance can be placed on a cursory statement of this kind. The miners' leaders having failed to effect a peaceful settlement, it only remains for the "ment themselves to have a turn at saving themselves and the industry in which they are employed.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
In accordance with the old pro- ver's expectation hath failed where most it promised. After a grim silence of two months the coal owners and the miners' leaders have met at the round table; talked for an hour and a half; and separated without com- ing a fraction of an inch closer to each other.

From the reports cabled to-day, both sides appear to have been implacable and obstinate, neither would concede one point to the other. In these distressing circumstances it would certainly have been futile to have kept up a mere semblance of negotiations without a practical Basis. And so, at the beginning of Autumn the whole country is faced with the possibility of the stoppage being carried on through the long cold Winter months with calamitous results to the women and children of the miners and of the families of men in other industries affected by the mining dispute.

The breakdown in the conference yesterday is to be deplored. It is not for "us at this distance to "reason why." The populace at Home, however, have a right to demand intervention by some means to save the mining industry.

headline: LOST A WATCH? / TWO WALTHAMS IN POLICE HANDS.
text:
POSSESSOR CONVICTED.

Arising out of a case before Major C. Willson at the Central Magistracy this morning, two American, Waltham gold wrist watches are now in the hands of the police awaiting claimants. One watch has the makers' name on the dial and is complete with a flexible band. The other, slightly smaller, which has hooks designed for use either as a wrist or pocket watch, may be the valued possession of some person, whose initials appear in woven characters at the back (decipherable as F.C.S.C.), the date April 10, 1917 on the inside of the back cover, and the makers' name and number (Waltham, U.S.A., 186755) on the works.

These watches were found in the possession of a young Chinese who visited a pawnshop at a time when Sergeant Brittain and a detective were there making investigations in another case. In answer to a charge of unlawful possession, defendant stated that he purchased the smaller of the watches in Shanghai and the other from a local shop. An employee of the latter shop refuted this statement in evidence.

His Worship was not satisfied with—the explanation—and sentenced defendant to three weeks' hard labour. Order was made for the waiches to be held by the police pending claimants.

headline: RENT TREBLED. / GOVERNMENT DISPENSARY ISSUE. / THE CONTROL PROBLEM.
text:
Sir,—I am very pleased indeed to see that others are taking up the cudgels on behalf of the public dispensary in Kowloon. If you, Sir, will kindly look at the register you will appreciate the work done by this Government institution. Many have recourse to it and will be sorry to see it go.

Supposing that it is argued that the Government does not mind a few hundred dollars more. Had a Fair Rents Board been established it will be the implied duty of the Government to appeal against the landlord's increase. There is a strong precedent. Some years ago, the landlord put up the rent of some premises at Wanchai, leased by the Government for housing sanitary coolies. Sir Edward Stubbs was so incensed that the Rents Restriction Ordinance followed.

Although you assure us that the dispensary may be incorporated with the Kowloon Hospital I strongly urge the Government to shut down on principle. If the house owner be so heartless there is no option. The public ought to be made to forego such a boon if it is too heartless to stand for rights. When such a situation arises, I have no sympathy for either the Government or the public.

, Yours, etc., DISGUSTED. Hongkong, August 19.

headline: ASSAULT CASE.
text:
ATTACKED WITH CHOPPER.

A Chinese was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with causing grievous bodily harm to two others.

P�lending guilty to the charge, def- fendant said that the complainants were the aggressors.

A dispute was stated to have arisen owing to an alleged refusal of the complainants to join a workmen's guild in the course of which the defendant slashed a man in the abdomen, necessitating his removal to hospital, and cut another in the back with a chopper. One-of-the complainants retaliated with a boat hook to such good purpose that defendant also had to enter hospital.

Defendant was sentenced to three months' hard labour.

headline: NIGHT RAID. / LOTTERY TICKET PRINTER FOUND. TWELVE ARRESTS.
text:
As a sequel to a raid carried out by Det-Sergeant Meadows and a party of police on a matshed hidden among trees on the hillside near Cape D'Aguilar Station, last night, twelve Chinese were charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with being concerned in the printing of lottery tickets.

Three of the defendants were charged in addition with keeping a common gaming house for the purpose, but a question arose as to whether there was sufficient evidence on this point. Two of the men, however, were found to be old offenders, and were fined $100 each, or four weeks' hard labour, while the third, who was a proof reader and as such held a responsible position, was fined $50, or two weeks.

Two others were discharged, as they were merely servants, and the remainder received a fine of $25 each, or two weeks.

headline: DID NOT KNOW. / USUAL EXCUSE IN ARMS CASE. / EMIGRANT FINED.
text:
A Chinese gardener who had spent the greater part of his life in Australia pleaded that he was unaware of the regulations when charged before Major C. Willson at the Central Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession of a revolver and 109 rounds of ammunition.

In answer to His Worship as to whether the regulations were posted up on the Japanese vessels, Inspector Pain said that he was not quite sure whether the arms notice was exhibited on the particular "vessel by which the defendant arrived in the Colony, but it was pointed out that the arms were found in the false bottom of a wooden case claimed by the defendant at the Kin Shan wharf yesterday.

A fine of $250, or three months' hard labour, was imposed, and order was made for the arms to be confiscated.

A rifle and 40 rounds of ammunition were found in the possession of a master of a junk at Deep Bay yesterday. He was arrested and charged this morning before Mr. J. H. B. Nihill at the Kowloon Magistracy, who imposed a fine of $100 or two months' herd labour in default.

headline: Another Editor Arrested.
parent_headline: EDITOR SHOT. / NO SEMBLANCE OF A TRIAL.
text:
Chen, Shi-wu, proprietor and editor of the "Shih, Chieh W. n. Pao" and the "Shih Chieh Jih Pao," was arrested by the local gender-merie at three o'clock t'dis morning and is now held in the headquarters of General Wang Chi, Commander of the gender-merie. Efforts are being made by Chen's friends to save him from the fate which overtook Mr. Lin Pai-shu yesterday morning.

The arrest was effected by General Kang, Aide-de-camp to General Wang Chj. with the assistance of about thirty gendarmes; Chen had already gone to bed when the military visitors called at his house, but was wakened and carried to the headquarters in a motor car.

It is "not known what are the charges against him, as his two publications are rather friendly to the anti-Kuominchun cause. Previous to the arrest of Mr. Chen, the gendarmies seiled the "Ming Li Wan Pao" and took all the employees of the papers into custody. They made a thorough-going search of the editorial offices

for Chen Chi-an, manager of the evening paper, but as Chen happened to be out, they failed to set hold of him. It is understood that Chen has fled to the Legation Quarters for safety.

The "Ming Li Wan Pao" was a recent addition to the family of evening papers in Peking and had a rather limited circulation. It was the first paper to publish the text of a circular telegram alleged to have been issued by General Sun Chuan-fang advocating peace. Whether this is the cause of the suppression of the paper remains to be seen.

The "Shih Chieh Jih Pao" and the "Shih Chieh Wan Pao" are probably two of the largest morning and evening papers in the capital. The evening edition may appear as usual this afternoon, as the military authorities did not suppress the two sister publications, although they have taken their manager into custody.—"Kuo Wen."

headline: AMERICAN ASIATIC UNDERWRITERS
text: H.E. the Governor's outspoken reference during the week to a policy directed from Canton conniving at piracy and brigandage and the maintenance of a state of affairs which was not in accordance with the views of the majority should disillusion any under the impression that the Government in opening negotiations on, the boycott issue was condoning a position which it has claimed as illegal from the outset.

headline: A NEW CAMPAIGN.
text:
The Miners' Federation sat privately for three hours and agreed to send the Government a verbatim report of the proceedings of yesterday's meeting with the owners after which the members returned to their respective districts.

The executive of the Miners' Federation met in London. A grave view is taken of the situation, and a member expressed the opinion that the attitude of the owners would prolong and embitter the struggle. Far from disintegrating the Federation, it would stiffen the backs of the rank and file. He anticipated another ten weeks' struggle.—Reuter.

The "Times" in a leader says that the coal owners' objections to a national agreement on economic grounds are not substantial, and ought to be removed. "Here is the first obvious contribution the coal owners can make toward an agreement. The miners on their part must be prepared to make concessions in respect of wages and costs of the industry required by the circumstances of the industry."—Reuter.

headline: Cook's Campaign:
text:
Mr. A. J. Cook, interviewed as regards the reported break away of miners from the Federation in Notts and Derbyshire, said that a campaign would be started immediately in that area. "We have no fear that the owners move will succeed there."

He declared that the movement at Mansfield was 'unofficial' and referred only to the Bolsover Colliery. Sixty thousand miners were concerned in the Nottingham area, of whom only half were members of the Federation before the stoppage and the remainder had joined the lot of the Federationists. The campaign would be directed to maintaining this united front.—Reuter.

headline: More Trickling Back.
text:
Reports are coming in of miners trickling back to work all over the country.

Four hundred men resumed at Sherwood to-day, 500 at Cross Farm, and 600 at Rufford. Hundreds are signing on at Mansfield, and many have resumed at Cannock Chase.

It is early to determine whether the new terms offered by individual Companies in Notts and Derbyshire will be accepted generally," but scores signed on this morning, on terms varying at different pits. Most provide for the April wages rate and 7½-hours' day with seven months guarantee.

To-day there are 6,525 miners working in Warwickshire compared with 6,350 yesterday.—Reuter.

headline: CONFERENCE REPORT
text:
The Miners' Federation Executive has communicated to the Government a verbatim report of the proceedings of their meeting with the mine owners at which an attempt to re-open the negotiations for a national settlement of the ccal dispute proved unsuccessful.

The Prime Minister, who had intended returning this afternoon to his Worcestershire home prior to leaving on Sunday for his holiday at Aix les Bains, decided to remain in London in order to study the report.

It is stated that the miners' leaders, after further meetings of their Executive to-day in London, dispersed to their districts; and no immediate new negotiations are in prospect.

Meanwhile the chief interest in the coal situation is centred in the areas where the men are showing a desire to return to work in response to local offers by the colliery owners. The members affected by this movement are relatively small, but the development is regarded as significant. It is reported that 2,000 men signed on for work in the Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire area to-day in pursuance of a local agreement which is contrary to the decision of the miners of the national organisation, and provides for seven hours and a half per day instead of seven hours. In certain other coal fields the steady drift back to work, which has been going on for some time past, continues; but in all the larger areas, such as Yorkshire, Lancashire, Northumberland, Durham, and South Wales the pits are still idle.—British Wireless Service.

headline: Troop Train Dynamited.
parent_headline: A LITTLE REVOLT. / CAPTURE OF SEVERAL TOWNS.
text:
Mangua, Aug. 20. The Nicaragua revolutionaries attacked Sun Antonio and killed the assistant superintendent, and several employees of one of the largest sugar estates in the district.

They also dynamited a troop train between Managua and Corinto. Nobody was killed, but a few soldiers were injured.—Reuter.

headline: MILL TROUBLES. / STRIKERS THWARTED IN SHANGHAI..
text: Attempts of strikers at Japanese mills to create trouble this afternoon were averted by the police. It was intended to march on the Japanese Consulate, but this did not materialise. The agitators had planned a demonstration both in Nanking, and Whangpoo Roads—the Japanese Consulate being situated in the latter street. An attempt to execute the plan was begun in the western district, but it was nipped in the bud by the police. Trouble has been fomenting ever since the alleged murder of a Chinese hawker aboard a Japanese vessel, when docked at Pootung. It is stated that the sailors—who chased the hawker, when the latter is alleged to have accidentally died by falling down a hatch—are being held in custody at the Japanese Consulate, awaiting trial. 2,400 employees at Japanese mills struck this morning, bringing the total of those away from work to 5,000.—Reuter.

headline: TURKEY YIELDS. FOREIGN CHAMBERS AGAIN. OPEN.
text: Constantinople, August 20. The foreign Chambers of Commerce dispute is at present the subject of diplomatic discussions. Meanwhile the Chambers have been allowed to reopen.—Reuter.

Then another gang attacked Ha Liu village, which is between Pakkai and Ngoi-hoi.

The sortie was made at midnight when the villagers were taken by surprise. Over forty persons were marched away to captivity, pending payment of ransom.

The echo of firing from machine-guns and the native field pieces was heard distinctly in Pakkai.

Among the passenger's who will leave the Colony to-day, on the P. and O. s.s. "Kalgann" for Home, will be Mr. J. Cleiland, of the Kowloon Dock. Mr. Cleland is one of the newest hands at the Dock, but has been forced to go Home on account of a serious breakdown in health. As a token of the esteem in which he is held at the Dock, his fellow employees have presented him with a silver tea set, and a blackwood tray as parting gifts. Mr. Cleiland's friends wish him a speedy return to health and strength.

headline: ARMED THREATS.
text:
FINE OF $100 INSTEAD OF IMPRISONMENT.

At the Central Magistracy on Saturday, Mr. R. E. Lindsell reconsidered a sentence of six months' hard labour imposed on a member of the Labour Maintenance Bureau for assault. The case was one in which the defendant with another man were

alleged to have escaped trom the police by pointing revolver at them.

The Hon. Mr. E. D. C., Wolfe (C.S.P.) said that he investigated the matter thoroughly and had received an assurance from the officers concerned that such a thing would not happen again. In asking His Worship to consider the imposition of a fine, Mr. Wolfe remarked that these men had rendered valuable help during a critical time and, although the offence was a serious one, the police officers averted trouble by acting discreetly.

Defendant was fined $100. The other man concerned in the case was discharged.

headline: KILLED AT POLO.
text: Colonel Herman Harjes, the famous American banker, was thrown while playing polo and died of his injuries. Harjes was a partner in the J.P. Morgan Company and managed their Paris agency. He conducted all the negotiations of his firm and the Banque of France, which resulted in the Morgan credits.—Reuter.

They were instantly pilloried in Canton as “hunting dogs of British Imperialism”, their assassination was openly advocated, and despite censorship threatening letters ‘continually found their way to their addresses. Nevertheless there were no defecitions and the failure of the Moscow-Canton attack before this line of defence may fairly be said to have been the turning point of the campaign. The crisis was over, and we settled down confidently to a war of attrition.

Following are extracts taken from a report under the heading of "Labour":—

From April onwards reports of violent and inflammatory speeches were received almost daily, the texts being the oppression of China and China's labouring masses by the "Imperialism" and "capitalism" of the foreigner and his "hunting dogs," the "compradore" class and the general colour being "Red" of the hue associated with the "Third International." The Hoi Yuen (Sèamen's Union) and the Head Labour Union (Association of Labour Unions) took a very prominent part in this agitation.

On June 15 ten representatives from the Head Labour Union and Hoi Yuen went to Canton, where they had an interview with Liu Chung Hoi, a powerful member of the new Government with strong communist views. It was reported that this man had instructed the Hongkong delegates to set a general strike in motion. Financial assistance was promised also support, food and shelter to all strikers coming to Canton. 24 hours after this meeting many secret meetings were reported to be taking place in unions and Boarding House in the Colony. Rumours were set about to the effect that pitched battles would take place in Hongkong and that the Colony would be burnt to the ground. People were advised to leave the Colony at once, otherwise they would be shot down by British Imperialists.

There were slight material changes in the general situation in September compared with August. The Boycott continued. Practically all factories in the Colony with the exception of the Nanyang Bros. Tobacco Co. who were working overtime, were working with half their pre-strike staff. The labour supply was, however, quickly approaching a parity with the reduced needs of the Colony and all serious anxiety on this score was definitely over by the middle of October, although there was still some shortage in the more skilled branches of labour.

headline: A PROUD DISTINCTION.
text:
It was only becoming that the Chinese community should arrange a gathering at which to express their congratulations to Sir Shouson Chow on being honoured with a Knighthood and a seat on the Executive Council of the Colony. Honour, like troubles, apparently never come singly, and the gratification of the Chinese community will by no means be confined to them. In view of the unique "double event" there is no reason why the non-Chinese community should not likewise invite the new Knight to be the guest of honour, and thus further in an appropriate and practical manner that spirit of Concord which His Excellency the Governor dwelt upon some months ago.

The Chairman at last night's dinner, Mr. Li Yau-tsun, Chairman of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, struck a good note when he remarked that Hongkong has been passing through difficult times, and that, thanks to the cooperation of Sir Shouson and Dr. Kotewall with the authorities, peace and order have been successfully maintained that the Chinese have been able to pursue their occupations peacefully. The history of the recent—and indeed the present—crisis through which the Colony is passing amply demonstrates that the best Chinese thought and opinion are ever on the side of the flag that gives them the surest protection—the Union Jack. Whatever may be the end of the present troubles in China itself it can be forecasted with the same confidence that the Chinese as a whole shall never turn their backs on the Power that has done so much through the ages to secure for them a worthy place in the comity of nations and to further, by all honourable means that position in international trade for which her unrivalled resources so admirably entitle her. That by the way.

headline: PICKET PIRATES. / JUNK HELD UP IN CHINESE WATERS.
text:
CARGO & PROPERTY TAKEN.

The master of a trading junk. (T4684) which left Hongkong for Hoihow with a "general cargo on August 18 and returned to the Colony yesterday made a report of a piracy "by strike pickets whilst on the outward voyage.

When the junk was at Shek Wan Bay, in Chinese waters, at midnight of the day after leaving Hongkong, eight men armed with rifles and revolvers approached in a boat flying the strike picket flag. Five of the armed men boarded the vessel and questioned the master regarding his movements and the nature of the cargo he had on board.

Ten bags of flour valued at $100, clothing to the value of $100 and $40 in Chinese money was taken by the armed gang before they rowed away in the direction of the shore.

The junk continued her voyage to Hoihow and reported, the incident at the Harbour Office on her return.

headline: "SAD HANDICAP:" / EDUCATION DIRECTOR ON PLAYGROUND. / REPORT FOR 1926.
text:
In this 'Colony where lack of playing fields is such a sad, if inevitable, handicap to our schools, states the 1925 report of the Director of Education, to be placed before the Council to-day, it is pleasant to be able to report that a football ground and a ground available for tennis courts, both in King's Park were placed at the disposal of the Central British School at the end of the year. It is hoped that a good ground in King's Park will also be provided for Yaumati School; where the pupils who are keen sportsmen may not only play football and hold their sports but also if it can be arranged, be taught to play cricket.

In spite of lack of school grounds, it should be possible to arrange for cricket matches between the bigger schools, Government and Grant-in-Aid, by borrowing certain Club grounds.

Queen's College are fortunate in having a football ground at Causeway Bay, and much is expected from the new Queen's College playing fields, but that lies in the future. The Indian Recreation Club has done much for the pupils of the Ellis Kadoorie Indian School by placing its ground frequently at their disposal.

Growing Requirements

The report goes on to state that the Quarry Bay Junior School, started in 1924, had a most successful year under able management. The new buildirly is well advanced. Our thanks are again due to Messrs. Butterfield and Swire for their kindly interest in the welfare of the school and for their loan of its present premises. The Central British School is already finding that the 5 new class rooms built in 1924 are not enough to provide for its natural expansion.

Similarly the Kowloon Junior School needs accommodation if it is to meet the growing requirements of the neighbourhood.

With regard to English-Teaching Government Schools (for other than British pupils), a comparison of the total roll in May and in December shows how these schools were affected by the troubles that began for the Colony in June.

In May the numbers were 3,190 and in December they were 1,898. At the same time it must be remembered that numbers are not necessarily a measure of efficiency.

The sudden fall in numbers chiefly affected the higher classes, and instead of admitting large numbers of younger pupils to the lower classes, it is recognised that the sounder method is to build the school up gradually, allowing it to reconstruct itself by natural stages and avoiding a temptation to emphasise the importance of mere numbers.

The only Revenue collected by the Education Department comes from school fees, which amounted in 1925 to $94,416.00 as against $121,478.00 in 1924.

The Expenditure was $1,019.905.23, an increase of $86,980.58 over the previous year. These figures do not include Expenditure on School Buildings or Furniture which are debited to Public Works.

The increase is mainly due to an increase of $36,500 in Personal Emoluments caused by the employment of more staff in the first half year; of $15,000 for Fees and Maintenance for Students in Training at Hongkong University: of $5,400 in Rent: of $11,400 under Capitation Grants: of $8,400 in the subsidies paid to Vernacular Schools: and of $10,000 under Building Grants.

Kowloon Apathy? REPORT.ON 1925.

Following are extracts from the report of the Secretariat For Chinese Affairs for 1925, submitted to Council today:—

The outstanding event of the year was, of course, the General Strike and subsequent Boycott work in connection with which tended to dwarf completely the ordinary activities of the department. An outline of the history of this fanatical outburst is given elsewhere in the report, but it will not be fitting to let the year pass without special record of the wonderful spirit of loyalty and solidarity shewn by the Chinese intelligentsia of the Colony in face of this great crisis.

Offers of service began to come in even before any calls were issued, and thereafter there was never the least difficulty in obtaining suitable volunteers for such varied posts as, postal, press and cable censors, assistants to the Foot Controller, special police, special street guards and ferry-pass officers.

It is not my province to point out in what manner they might be overcome but I suggest that if these cuttings on these roads were faced with stone or cement, if these huge retaining walls were properly built and properly supervised during building so that they should not act merely as dams, if these nullahs could be trained or diverted, and if these threatening boulders could be removed by blasting, a great risk of the monotonous recurrence of these damages every year would be removed a great saving of money effected as well as loss of life and discomfort avoided.

A Modern "Atlas" I was told the other day that a report was made to the Public Works about a boulder which was sitting up a hill and threatening a house. The Public Works were warned that they would be held responsible. I believe. The reply that was received was that the Public Works were keeping it under observation. Now, when such possible danger has been pointed out to them, does it not seem rather casual that a department like the Public Works should make a reply of that kind, if I am correctly informed. One is almost tempted to think of the Director of Public Works watching this boulder and rushing to bear it on his shoulders like a modern Atlas when it shows signs of slipping.

Then, also, it seems to me that evident lessons to be derived from these damages are not always learned. For instance, the nullah that goes down Pedder Street and that wrecked the street during the storm is being re-built to the same dimensions as before, although on a previous occasion this nullah was also heavily damaged. Why could not the dimensions be made wider?

It is said that these rainstorms occur during high water and that the rising tide meets the rush of storm waters and so prevents it escaping into the sea. But surely if the nullah were made on a proper size from experience already gained this ought not to be a factor.

Saving in the End. “I have also seen that these landslides occur pretty nearly always at the same place or in places closely adjoining previous ones and apart from the removal of the slipped soil nothing seems to be done. I have watched with great interest for months and months, every day, coolies on Stubbs Road near the Peak tram station, where there has been a notable slip not yet righted; I have watched these coolies sitting and gently patting the internet with mud in the hope that the Fzvptian sun would harden it so that it might last for centuries. But the same thing occurs every time. The next heavy rain that comes along causes a wash-out in the same place. And thus, not only is safety not secure but we have every year very large sums of money, voted to effect what prove to be only temporary repairs.

I maintain that if a Commission was formed who would examine all these danger spots, they would be able to make recommendations which if acted upon might obviate these recurrent storm damages. It might be costly, but in the long run it would be cheap. I have therefore no hesitation in putting forward this resolution for the approval of the Council and for the consideration of the Government.

headline: Hongkong, Tuesday, August 31, 1926.
text:
Very soon the "London Times" will be retrieving the reputation for consistency that was associated with it for decades before the blight of the Northcliffe influence began to make itself felt. For the second time in succession it has advocated the policy of force, or concerted diplomatic intervention, in China, after previously posing as a warm champion of "peace and conciliation." In its latest article on the subject, as cabled by Reuter, the "Times" dwells on the Bolshevik activities in China, and expresses the opinion—as if it was something absolutely original and never dreamed of by anybody else!—that the Bolsheviks wish to keep China weak, divided, and unstable by setting province against province and General against General. That, of course, has long been known out here, so that it is nothing in the way of a discovery that the "Times" has made now, although its reiteration cannot possibly do any harm. Anything that can be said and done counter to the "Bolshevik propaganda is all for the good. It is apparent from recent happenings at Home that the full extent of the present and possible Bolsheviks mischief in the Orient is not dully appreciated or understood throughout Great Britain. If, as the "Times" says, China has hitherto lost the opportunity of forming a stable State, it can be predicted with equal truth that if Great Britain does not really awake to the dangers of the Bolshevik menace at Home and overseas, she may lose the opportunity of curbing their wings and limiting their activities whilst it is comparatively easy to do so. Therefore anything that can be published in the "Times" or any other Home paper to expose that danger is to be welcomed.

When the “Times,” however, proceeds to speak of the imperative demand for concerted displot

matic action on the part of the States principally interested in the recovery of China it is tread-ing on ground that, whilst it has been covered many times already, has already been chuked by these same Powers as "delicate" and "dangerous." The reason for this is exactly what the "Times" in its great wisdom surmises: "it would seem that the British, Japanese, and American Governments cannot agree to take such action." In any event, even supposing that the three Powers could agree merely on "concerted diplomatic action," that alone would be quite incapable of curing the internal sores from which China is at present suffering. That alone would be quite insufficient to rid China once and for all of the cancer of Bolshevism. Nor would it bring to an end one day sooner the civil warfare that is at present waging throughout practically the whole country—with the aid of arms and ammunition supplied by or stolen from foreigners.

It was only recently that the "Times" itself deplored the lack of a stable Central Government with whom the Powers could deal, not in relation to the question of the recovery of China, but in regard to the protection of foreign lives and foreign property and the fulfilment of all existing Treaties. Where, then, is the use of talking of the imperative necessity of concerted diplomatic intervention to be confined to the one phase of the recovery of China? If the "Times" thinks it has made out a good case for its plea let it demonstrate in which direction the Powers can move with the hope of ultimate advantage. Let it give us concrete instances of where concerted diplomatic intervention would bring healing balm to the present very disrupted China. For the Powers to interven, diplomatically or otherwise, in China in order to secure the fullest protection of their nationals and for the upholding of Treaty rights is one thing—and a very proper thing in certain circumstances—but to intervene only in order to assist in the recovery of China would simply give the world another exhibition of diplomacy running

headline: Embargo on Money.
text:
As from to-morrow people may take out of the Colony any money they please without fear of a prosecution following. Such a construction can be placed on the “Government Gazette” announcement of last week. On June 22, last year, an embargo was placed—under the Emergency Regulations—on the export of Hongkong money. Since then residents going elsewhere have been only permitted to take with them, a certain sum—believed to be not more than $5 in coin, and the same sum in local banknotes. Europeans were not much affected because they carry little ready money, preferring to deal in cheques and other negotiable documents. Not so the Chinese masses. For them silver and gold were always preferable and notes of repute ran a good second. Police officers on wharf duty always had to explain regulations to people who did not always appreciate their kindness in doing so. In extreme cases, prosecution was

necessary. One way of getting over things was—if one was going to Macao for example—to change the money into Macao banknotes and silver. The same applied "to other destinations." Accusations have been made against the alleged harshness of this regulation. When the "strike" first became apparent last June it was necessary to prevent a "run" on local banks, especially the native banks. If bullion, specie and coin could not be carted away, what was the use of withdrawing it from the bank just because other people were in a panic? The order certainly had the desired effect. Conditions have now changed to an extent when the ordinary flow of money is unlikely to harm Hongkong—hence the notification that the regulation "shall cease to have force and effect." There is one point that we wish to draw attention to. We believe there is still some restriction regarding silver (Mexican, as they are sometimes called) Hongkong dollars, but we are open to correction. This has been in force for years.

headline: CHINESE STUDENTS. / INTERESTING ANNUAL CONFERENCE.
text:
The annual conference of Chinese students in Great Britain and Ireland which was held in mail week at Kingsmead, Selby Oak, Birmingham, attracted some attention. Although only between sixty and seventy in number, the conference had a big programme, the general theme of which, as stated, was "The Students' Share in National and International Reconstruction," with the motto taken from the sayings of Confucius that "Within four senses we are brethren."

In his speech at the preliminary welcome meeting on July 24, Dr. W. C. Chen, the Chinese Charged Affairs, after recalling his own student days in America, exhorted his young compatriots, who enjoy the privileges of Western education, to keep before them their responsibilities with regard to China's future. That the small body of students in Britain are fully alive to their responsibilities in this respect is evidenced by the nature of the discussions. Great interest centred in the debate, "That Socialism is Beneficial" to China. Among the addresses was one, "Our Aim in Life," by Rev. T. S. Tso, M.A., while Mrs. C. C. Chen, Vice-President of the National Committee of the Y.M.C.A. of China, spoke of "China's Challenge to Her Students." Among the foreign speakers were Dr. Lionel Giles, M.A., D.Litt., the Deputy Keeper of Oriental Printed Books at the British Museum, who gave an address on the "First Fruits of Tunhuang," illustrated with lantern slides; Mr. G. E. Lerrigo, Secretary of the National Committee of the Y.M.C.A. of China, who discussed "The Responsibility of Chinese Students in Foreign Lands," and Sir, Denison Ross, C.I.E., PhD., Director of the School of Oriental Studies, who spoke of "China and the West."

On July 29 and 30 the chief speakers were Mr. Nelson Britton, Home Secretary of the London Missionary Society, whose subject was "A New Beginning;" Dr. L. C. Martin, D.Sc., of the Imperial College of Science, London University; and Dr. C. Stubbs, who gave an address on the subject of "The Challenge of Christian Education in China."

headline: A RADIO SET. / CONCERTS WHICH DID NOT MATERIALISE.
text:
SUMMARY COURT CASE.

A claim in respect of a wireless set sold to a Chinese customer, By Mr. Bird, the Manager of the S. China Development Syndicate, was heard in the Summary Court this morning.

The claim was "for $266 still outstanding on the price charged, according to the claim. Mr. W. B. Hind represented the plaintiffs and Mr. J. T. Prior, the defendants.

It was claimed on behalf of the defendant that a guarantee had been given that the cost of the set would be probably $200 or a little more and would not in any event exceed $300. The set was stated by plaintiffs to be complete but it was claimed that further parts had had to be bought and that considerable cost had to be incurred in endeavouring to get the set working. It was also claimed by defendant that a guarantee had been given by Mr. Bird to have the set installed "in working order and that he (defendant) should be taught. A guarantee had also been given with regard to a Government permit and assurance that the set would get Manila and certain concerts broadcasted at the time by the Hongkong Hotel.

The date of the sale was in dispute, plaintiffs stating that it was in May, 1924 and defendants that it was in June, 1923.

On this point, Mr. Prior had indicated that he would plead the Statute of Limitations in favour of the defendant but on Mr. Bird being examined and, referring to his books, stating that the sale took place in May, 1923, His Honour (Mr. Justice Wood), stated that he was satisfied that plaintiffs had made out their case sufficiently as regarded the date and Mr. Prior withdrew his pleading.

Mr. Bird also denied in the box that any guarantee had been given as to installation, permission from the Government, or as to the Hongkong Hotel broadcast concerts which had ceased shortly after the transaction. Defendant was the brother of the Company's treasurer and brother-in-law of the Company's compradore. Defendant had for a period attended often at the office but had not been officially connected with it and drew no salary. There was no contract in writing about the sale. Defendant had simply asked witness to get him a receiving set. The plaintiff knew as much about the radio business as he (plaintiff) did. After hearing the evidence His Honour found that the plaintiff had succeeded in his claim and that it was no part of the plaintiff's contract to install the set, to obtain the permission of the Government, etc. Judgment was therefore given for $260.

headline: Mission Hospital Property.
text:
One point in Canton's "mission hospital" despatch provides special food for thought. It says that the office of the commander-in-chief has been ordered to instruct the Wuchow authorities immediately to return the Stout Memorial Hospital to the American Baptist Mission for reopening. "First of all, a teen observer may query that part about the Nationalist Government ordering the commanding general to do something. Is it not generally recognised that the word of Chang Kai-shek has been the law

In Canton for some time. The series of famous resolutions and other "coups" by the commander-in-chief still bear testimony as to where orders come from. Then again the Wuchow authorities profess allegiance to the Canton rulers. Why is it necessary for the Nationalist Government to instruct Wuchow through military headquarters? Presumably the answer to this is that a minor general is in virtual charge at Wuchow and that orders have to pass through certain channels. It is easy to comprehend the peremptory order to troops to protect foreigners and evacuate mission buildings. That, of course, would come within the province of the general's office. Hitherto mission hospitals in the two Kwang provinces have closed down because of anti-foreign agitation although the patients were almost entirely Chinese. The step taken by Canton will be deemed highly commendable. Because they were cut off from supplies and their servants were intimidated from them, the mission staffs had to leave. We now learn that the union of the workers has been told to negotiate for a speedy re-opening of the Canton Hospital. Other issues aside, it is only fair to point out that the trouble at the hospital was certainly not of the mission's making. The personnel was picketed and there was no alternative but to suspend operations. However, the despatch published yesterday is welcomed as a step in the right direction. May those concerned see that justice is done and that former beneficial intercourse is resumed without delay.

headline: A SAD TALE. / MISFORTUNES OF A YOUNG BRITON.
text:
CHARGED AS STOWAWAY.

Charged with stowing away on board the s.s. "Linan" from Shanghai, Victor Simpson, of British nationality, born in Riga, related a sad story of his misfortunes to Mr. J. H. B. Nihill at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday.

Simpson said that he was taken to Tsingtao by his parents, both of whom died there. On the death of his mother, three years ago, he was left with $500, with which he intended coming to Hongkong in search of his uncle, Mr. William S. Simpson.

Whilst on the voyage to Shanghai, the balance of the money was stolen. Simpson then went on board the s.s. "Linan" to see the second officer, who was entertaining some friends and asked him to wait. It was 11 o'clock at night and he fell asleep. The ship left at 4 o'clock the following morning, but it was not until some time later that he was found asleep by one of the sailors.

Captain T. G. Beer, master of the vessel informed the Magistrate that Simpson had told him the same story and it was correct that he had seen the second officer, who apparently forgot about Simpson after the guests had gone.

In view of Simpson's youth, His Worship said he would not like to send him to prison. Orders was made for him to be kept in the House of Detention while the police made enquiries to locate his uncle.

The mining crisis at Home looks more hopeful of settlement than at any period in this long drawn out struggle which has cost the community so much loss and inconvenience. The hint which the miners' leaders have given that providing assurance was given that any agreement reached would be on a national basis they would consider modifying the hitherto adamant attitude they have adopted on the question of hours and wages has been followed up by Mr. Winston Churchill and it is significant that the Opposition listened attentively to his speech in the House of Commons and even cheered references to the relation of district to national agreements. Even more cheering is the announcement that the miners' delegates conference have agreed to the Executive's recommendation for plenary powers and an open mandate to negotiate a settlement of the coal stoppage and to approach the Government for a new conference with that object. This is a decided modification of the positive attitude hitherto taken up that no negotiations could be countenanced which did not guarantee non-interference with the eight-hour day or the scale of wages in operation before the strike. It is to be hoped that the owners will display a similar conciliatory attitude and not prejudice the negotiations by holding strictly to the letter the local agreements entered into in certain districts.

headline: A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.
text:
As succeeding military leaders have obtained supremacy in the North the new regime has been hailed as the forerunner of a competent and effective federal Government which will solve the questions outstanding between China and the Powers. Not for a long time had the prospects been brighter than when the Chang-Wu Pei-fu alliance outlasted the ousting of General Feng's Red Government from Peking and the defeat of the Red or Kuominchun forces. The South was keenly interested in the outcome of the struggle which it was generally understood would have a bearing on the local boycott question in that Canton would await developments before resuming the negotiations with Hongkong begun at the Boycott Conference. The assumption was that once Wu Pei-fu was in a position to turn his attention to the South there would be danger of the minor victories won by the allies of the South being checked and an extensive campaign entered into against the ascendancy of the Nationalist Government. Wu Pei-fu has, in fact, launched an offensive against the Nationalist forces on the Hankow front and reports indicate that he has been none too successful. Now comes news from a reliable source that he has been deposed by subordinates and held a prisoner. The Southern forces claim victories and whilst their claims as to the fall of Hankow and Wuchang seem without official confirmation it appears that the arrival of Wu Pei-fu's forces from the North, so far from establishing an immediate supremacy over the Southerners, has still further complicated matters. What effect it will have on the Southern situation it is difficult at the moment to state. It is doubtful if the treachery against his ally on the Hankow front had the acquiescence or even knowledge of Marshal Chang-but it is hardly likely (with his position in the North still far from being safely assured) that he is in a position to forsake the North to render active assistance. headline: War Effects on Hongkong
text:
Will General Chang Kai-shek now rest on his laurels or push northwards to Peking? That is a question which many who are "following" the trend of events in China's civil war are now asking themselves. Canton's soldier of the hour has declared that he will establish a joint government in

fact and in name, for the whole country. Politics in China being so liable to take the most unexpected turn, it is rash to predict what the future holds in store. Chang Kai-shek may tackle Chang Tso-lin or even Sun Chuan-fang of armed neutrality fame; or he may enter into an alliance with one or the other. Time was not so long ago when the Fengtian party and the Kuomin-tang were in alliance against Wu Pei-fu who was then in Peking. From the British point of view there will be much speculation as to whether the hostile attitude will spread to the territory newly conquered by the Nationalists. It is not denied that propagandists are accompanying the armies in the field to spread the new doctrine. The presumption that follows is that anti-British agitators will be at work. How far it will take root and what response the people will make remains to be seen. Hankow's trade is well known enough to Hongkong. There are Chinese merchants who do a fairly extensive business with that part of China. Sugar and medicinal herbs are two commodities which come to mind to speak of no others. Intermediate ports are situated between Hongkong and Hankow. If an embargo is placed against Hongkong we venture to say that it will not be so effective as, say, at Swatow or Kongmoon. On the other hand, British shipping may have to cope with pickets if the movement takes any root. The fact that a number of unruly students were executed only recently at Hankow by Wu Pei-fu may be taken to indicate that there exists fertile ground on which to sow the seed of feeling against Britain.

headline: What It Does.
text: Prior to the demonstration, Mr. P. A. Rosario explained that the Panatrope was the result of a few years of scientific research in the laboratories of the Radio Corporation of America, the General Electric Company, the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company, and the Brunswick Phonograph Company. He said it was different from other conventional makes of gramophone in that it had no sound box or horn. In place of the sound box there was a device called the magnetic pickup. The scratches on the record were conveyed by wires to a power amplifier and by electrical energy converted into sound and the sound amplified in different stages by means of radio valves.

headline: Records Used.
text:
The machine is primarily designed for Panachord records, rione of which was available at the demonstration, but that the machine gives pleasing results on other makes of records was convincingly proved. Among the Victor and Brünswick records which were used on the instrument and much appreciated by the audience were "Lights Out" March (Victor), Fox Trot-Valencia (Brunswick), Voice Duet, contralto and tenor (Brunswick), Pibroch Solo — Angelus, and Piano Solo (Victor), Cello Solo (Columbia), quartettes, jazz, etc. At the end of the demonstration the members of the audience availed themselves of the invitation to inspect the instrument and ask questions on points which needed explanation.

headline: FATAL QUARREL. ALL OVER A HAWKER'S BAGS.
text:
MANSLAUGHTER CHARGE.

How a quarrel between a scavenging coolie and a hawker as to two bags which had been placed in the street to dry resulted in "a fight and how later the hawker was found on a doorstep suffering from internal injuries which later led to his death was described at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday when the scavenging coolie in question appeared on a charge of manslaughter.

Inspector Pincott prosecuted, while the defendant was unrepresented.

It was stated for the prosecution that defendant in the course of the fight used his broom and prodded deceased in the stomach. The defendant himself appeared at the time to have got the worst of it as he showed signs of having been struck below both eyes. It was further stated that the deceased accompanied friends of his from the scene and that it was not until they turned round a corner that they found the deceased missing. Turning back, they found him on a doorstep. He was still alive then but by the time his relatives were called he had died.

Dr. Newton gave evidence of having performed the post mortem examination. He said that the deceased had a scratch near the spleen just below the ribs. The scratch was very slight and might have been caused by a prod with a stick or even by the deceased's own finger nails. The spleen was ruptured, with a considerable amount of haemorrhage, which was the cause of death. After further evidence the case was adjourned.

headline: OUR NAVY IN CANTON.

It is clear now there is a complete end of pourparlers between the Governments of Hong Kong and Canton in respect to a settlement of the boycott by negotiation. Canton has been challenged to do its worst, but the British naval authorities have made it quite clear at the same time that that "worst" shall no longer include the molestation of passengers and cargo going to the Hong Kong steamers. The pickets may continue to be "cocks of the walk" on purely Chinese territory, but they will menace British lives and British property with impunity in future. That is the plain and very welcome message to be read into the action by the British gunboats at the British-owned wharves in Canton. The position is one that will be followed with interest. A period has been put to the policy of passive resistance to the annoying and illegal acts of the boycott pickets and the miscalled "Strike" Committee in Canton. They have had a long and a merry innings. They have now been told in the plain language of decisive action that that innings is at an end so far as it concerns passengers and cargo for the Hong Kong steamers. Any further illegalities in this direction have now been made impossible.

headline: Balance of Power in China.
text: Much that is informative has passed through the wires during the week-end but as yet “conflicting reports” is the only apt description of news about the war in China. During the last seven days Wuchang has “fallen” and “held out” several times. There seems less doubt about Hankow and the Hanyang arsenal; these being also immediate objectives of the southern Nationalists. One factor which will be noted by those who are hoping for peace in China is that the struggle seems to be spreading to other parts of the country. From far-off Szechuan province comes a report of merchant vessels being seized to convey troops to Wu Pei-fu's aid. Marshal Sun Chuan-fang, ruler of the five provinces around Shanghai, seems to be moving at last, on the side of his professed superior. As his vanguard is rather far inland it will take time to discover whether he had actually entered the war on Wu Pei-fu's side. With the armies at his command, the supply of munitions and his strategic position, Sun Chuan-fang may become the deciding power. How much truth there is in his supposed gesture against the southerners remains to be seen. It is true that he can strike a vital blow and the rear flank of General Chang Kai-shek, by marching on Changsha in Hunan province. But, on the other hand, vernacular papers still give prominence to his emissary being in conference with Canton. Nearest to Hongkong is the possibility of hostilities on the Kwangtung-Fukien border. For a month, at least we have been told by private sources that the Fukien army was going to cross the frontier, having long cast covetous eyes on the richer territory of Kwangtung. It should be borne in mind that Chow Yam-yan, the Tupan of Fukien, is a subordinate of Marshal Sun Chuan-fang. Unless Chow (or his man on the spot) is acting without instructions, then it has to be assumed that Sun is helping Wu Pei-fu from a motive of loyalty, or he is out to preserve the balance of power.

headline: GLOBE & RUTGERS
text:
FIRE INSURANCE CO. OF NEW YORK.

FIRE-WINDSTORM -MARINE INSURANCE.

What the Canton Government have deliberately funked doing for fourteen months a small party of British bluejackets have done in about fourteen minutes. Saturday's landing on the wharves of the Hong Kong, Macao and Canton Steamship Company may not have been spectacular, but it was absolutely effective. On their appearance the pickets instantly melted awry like snow in a thaw. Their talons have been cut and

they are now harmless so fair as concerns British shipping.

The sequel should be easily imagined: With the pickets no longer in command of affairs on the river, the Chinese merchants in Canton may be expected to disregard any further attempts at blackmail and to set in motion in their own quiet way the necessary steps toward trading with Hong Kong as of yore. The moral effect of the discomfiture of the pickets cannot be lost on them, and it ought to be comparatively easy within a very short time for cargo and passengers to be conveyed to the Hong Kong steamers without any fear of intimidation even on shore.

Chapter I. of the “beginning of the end” of the boycott has been closed. The succeeding chapters should follow in rapid sequence, when it will be found that they make no less cheerful reading to all in Canton itself who honestly desire a restoration of normal trade relations with this Colony.

headline: GAS FATALITY.
text:
PEDDER STREET NULLALIL ACCIDENT

DEATH INQUIRY:

One of the results of the flood was an inquiry conducted by Major Willson at the Central Magistracy yesterday into the death of an earth coolie.

Addressing the jury, Major Willson said the man was overcome by gas in the mullah at Peder Street on July 25, sent to the Government Civil Hospital for a short time and then discharged as cured, and died the following day. The jury would have to consider whether the man had sufficient and skilful treatment.

In the absence of Dr. Valentine in Shanghai, a statement made by him was read to the jury. The statement showed that the man was admitted to hospital in an unconscious condition on July 25. He was discharged the following day. Coal gas poisoning had been diagnosed.

The father of the man said that on his return from hospital on the evening after the accident, his son complained of pains in the abdomen. A Chinese doctor was called and he said the man had no pulse, and did not prescribe for him. An ambulance was sent for, but his son died before it arrived. Dr. Craig said the man was taken to the mortuary on July 27 during the afternoon. The body was in an advanced state of decomposition. Witness saw it on the morning of the 28th when it was impossible to tell the cause of death. An accompanying deit diagnosed sewer gas poisoning. The history of the case was given as "coal" gas poisoning, but when blood was taken from the heart and tested there was a negative result. The report went to show that it was not a case of carbon monoxide or coal gas poisoning.

The overseer of the coolies engaged on the work "in Pedder Street said the man was working in a drain five feet below the surface. He had a rope round him. Major Willson: Is it safe to send men down drains?—Yes. Why is the rope tied round them?

In reply to other questions witness said the man could be pulled up by the rope. They did nothing else to ensure that it was safe for them to go down. Witness had had several years' experience of similar work and had never had a similar case before. The enquiry was adjourned until to day.

headline: KOWLOON TONG CASE
text:
MR. MURPHY'S DEFENCE.

At the continued hearing yesterday afternoon of the case in which Mr. A. E. Murphy is sued by six Chinese coolies for damages for alleged false Imprisons, Mr. Wadleson, for Mr. Murphy, submitted that he had no case to answer.

His Honour Mr. Justice Wood, finding against him Mr. Wndeson submitted that given "if defendant was personally responsible for the arrest of the plaintiffs he was justified for the reason that there had been or was likely to be a breach of the peace.

Mr. Murphy had arrived home at about 5:40 p.m. on the day in question (July 27), said Mr. Wadeson, and saw a large number of men, about 20 or 30, at the entrance to the nearby scavenging lane. They were against the wall and two Indian guards were facing them with levelled rifles. There was a great

As he could not make out what the trouble was Mr. Murphy suggested that they all go to the Estate office. "This they did, continued Mr. Wadeson, and here they met Mr. Ramsay, the chief storekeeper," Mr. Ramsay asked what was the matter and defendant replied that he didn't know, but that the Indian guards had two men whom the crowd had been trying to set free.
