headline: CARRY
text:
Government Ready For New Proposals

The report of the meeting between the members of the Government and the officials of the Miners' Federation reveals no advance toward a settlement of the coal dispute. The meeting dispersed without arrangements being made for a further interview, but Mr. Winston Churchill urged at the close the Government's readiness for such meeting if the miners have any new proposals to advance, and Mr. A. J. Cook cordially agreed with Mr. Churchill that a negotiated settlement would be better for all concerned in the dispute.

Mr. Herbert Smith, President of the Federation, was the spokesman for the miners at the opening of the conference. He reviewed the result of the miners' recent conference with the owners who had, he said, decided to take advantage of the Eight-Hours Act to the fullest extent and were determined to insist on a district as opposed to a national agreement and were opposed to applying for help from the Government. They (the miners, now approached the Government to ask what help the Government could give not only in the negotiations but financially for a period.

Mr. Churchill, in replying, repeated what has several times been said on behalf of the Government, namely, that the question of giving financial help had long passed out of the sphere of practical politics. The Government had last year given £23,000,000 to secure the nine months in which to settle, and that was the end of Government's assistance apart from the £3,000,000 reserved in this year's Budget. What was left out of the latter sum, after various expenses incurred owing to the stoppage had been defrayed, would be available for aiding the movement of the miners from any pits that might be closed, and £250,000 had been earmarked for the development of scientific research. What amount would be left he could not say, but perhaps half of that £3,000,000 would be available for the purpose for which it was set aside. No subsidy, however small or temporary and nothing in the nature of a loan by the Government would now be possible.

Mr. Cook urged that the ultimate loss to the country must be greater by the indefinite continuance of the dispute than by a grant of financial assistance but he agreed that the cost would exceed £3,000,000.

headline: Plain Speaking.
text:
Dealing with the prospect of the stoppage continuing, Mr. Churchill said that he could not see how the Federation's position would be improved for negotiating a favourable settlement by allowing force of circumstances to end the dispute. As for the country, much had been learned during the stoppage, and if he had been asked at the outset what would be the result of even two weeks' stoppage he would have given figures ten times as high as those he now knew to be the case. Except in the great basic trades, the country had shown extraordinary power of carrying on. The exports for July, for instance, were better than a year ago, making allowance for the fact that no coal was exported. Unemployment was better, although the harvest had something to do with that. Since the general strike 50,000 fewer were unemployed. People were buying coal. The Government was not called upon to buy coal to any extent now. Coal imports could be easily increased, no doubt, if cold weather came. On the other hand, there was a certain output here and outcrop workings were being worked. There was no doubt, whatever that the country was in a position where no difficulty was found in carrying on the life of the country, a large proportion of the trade of the country, and all vital services.

No Desire To Humiliate. The Government had no desire to humiliate the Federation officials or miners. There was nothing that it would rejoice in more than seeing the miners again working. Whether it should be by national or district settlements was not for it to decide, but he could not see why both parties could not be reconciled. He had thought that the miners might advance new and definite suggestions; and if they gave a promise of a solution Government offices would have been available in whatever way they might prove useful.

headline: Miners' Adament.
text:
Mr. Smith said that in the circumstances it seemed unnecessary to prolong the interview. They were not prepared to agree to an extension of hours or to district agreements.

There was, however, further discussion on various aspects of the dispute and in the Inter stage of the proceedings Mr. Cook suggested that, whilst they could not agree to extended them there might be

room for accommodation on a national settlement. He was not prepared in response to Mr. Churchill's invitation, to make any new proposals.

Eight Hours Act. Mr. Churchill said that the Government felt that the miners ought to have a choice, in certain districts between working an extra hour or half an hour and receiving a very low rate of wages. Under the old law they had no such choice, and the Act merely moved that restriction.

Answering suggestions that the Government's proposals for the reorganisation of the coal industry, particularly those of collieries' amalgamation, would not promptly be carried out, Mr Churchill said that it was the Government's sincere belief that apart from the question of buying out the owners of royalties, which would not be of any financial service to the miners at present, their proposals fully met the recommendations of the Coal Commission and it was determined to put them into operation to the utmost of its power.

A full report of the interview has been despatched to the Prime Minister at Aix les Bains, and it is anticipated that it will be discussed during the debate in the House of Commons on Tuesday.

The situation in the coal fields remains unchanged. The news builds right that we order prevails, and the Police arrangements have proved quite adequate to protect from any threats of molestation those men returning to work. —British Wireless Service.

headline: OSMENA'S MISTAKE.
text:
OFFICIALS THINK HE “UNINTENTIONALLY EXAGGERATED.”

COOLIDGE HASNT CHANGED.

Officials of the War Department believe that Senator Osmena "unintentionally exaggerated President Coolidge's views on Independence" when he quoted the President saying that the United States would withdraw as soon as the islands were sufficiently developed economically. General Frank McIntyre, chief of the bureau of insular affairs and Secretary of War, Davis conferred this afternoon on the subject of the Coolidge-Osmena conversations, which led to the declarations attributed to Senator Osmena in his Cebu speech.

It is pointed out that the President's attitude on Philippine independence has been known to be indefinite, due entirely to doubts as to the islands' ability to achieve economic independence.

“Although President Coolidge may feel that the Filipinos are entitled to independence,” said one spokesman for the War Department. “That does not mean that he would advocate the immediate adoption of this course; because circumstances may arise which would shape the administration’s policy to more material ends.”

New York, August 20. Senator Osmena's Cebu speech quoting President Coolidge on independence and economic development, with subsequent denials and reiterations, moves the "New York World" to another editorial on the Philippines, this time chiding the administration for trying to move two directions at once and urging "honesty about the Philippine question."

"It is not a happy position," says the "World," "for a new Englander with a conscience to be caught between the past" promises of government heads and the present demands of a faction of his party which is wholeheartedly for rubber and colonial expansion.

"After the promises we have been giving, it is ours, not their, to prove that we can at least be honest; and if it is rubber we want and a peon labour system, say so." —"United Press."

San Franchisco, August 19. Judge Jose Santos, adviser to the Philippine mission in the United States, to-day voiced prayers to the American people to give place to another race for an independent government. "Like the Americans of: 1776 we are a separate people with separate conditions," said Judge Santos.

He declared that the Filipinos have reached the point where they are able to govern themselves. He said there was no need to fear that Japan would step in as "Japan has no interest in us as we have nothing to offer save the needs for a strategic position. Her development must be toward Manchuria and Korea and not toward us." Judge Santos leaves for Manila

headline: ALLIES' DEMANDS
text:
IS IT INOPPORTUNE?

Berlin: Aug. 27.

"Strange" and "Trivial" are the adjectives applied in German circles to a Note from the Conference of Ambassadors to the German Government demanding:— Firstly—An unambiguous legal decree terminating the military activity of the Nationalist organisations.

Secondly — The discontinuance of legal recruiting for the Reichswehr.

Thirdly—The fulfilment without delay of the demands of the Inter-Allied Military Commission. It is pointed out that over 2,000 Notes regarding disarmament have already been received from the Inter-Allied Military Commission and the Ambassadors' Conference. The latest is regarded as most inopportunef in view of Germany's impending entry into the League.—Reuter.

headline: GERMAN CONSUL'S RECEPTION.
text:
Singapore, August 12.—Dr. O. Weber, Consul-General for Germany, received a number of guests in his office in the Union Building yesterday, when the German constitution day, the anniversary of the establishment of a republic in Germany, seven years ago, was celebrated.

Amongst those who attended the reception, at the consular office, were:—Lieutenant Bourke, representing His Excellency the G.O.C., the Bishop of Singapore, the Rt. Rev. C. J. Ferguson-Davie, Mr. C. R. Howitt, representing the Hon. Mr. Hayes Marifott, the Governor's Deputy, representatives of the different consular bodies and many others. Dr. Weber and his chancellor, Mr. Raedler received the guests, and the occasion was duly honoured.

SECRET ARSENAL IN A JUNK?

headline: CUT AND DRY. / TANGIER QUESTION TO BE DEFERRED.
text:
LEAGUE COUNCIL FIRST

It is confirmed in well-informed sources in London that Spain has suggested a conference at Geneva on Wednesday to consider the Spanish claim to Tangier on the eve of the League Council meeting.

It is understood that Great Britain will reply at the earliest. There is a natural reluctance at present to discuss the terms of the reply, but the general impression is that no useful purpose will be served by a conference at short notice which should be postponed till after the League Council meeting, the primary object of which is to arrange for Germany's admission to the League and no extraneous issues should be permitted to interfere.

It is expected that France will support Great Britain.—Reuter. Italian Support.

Italy has replied to the Spanish Note, assuring her of Italy's desire to meet all Spain's just demands, and agreeing to Spain's suggestion that "the Tangier problem should be submitted to an International Conference of the Powers interested. Italian political circles infer from this that the Italian Government is unwilling that the problem should be submitted to the League of Nation's Reuter.

headline: RED STRIKE. / STUDENT
text:
SHANGHAI SCENES.

Student demonstrations took place locally in connection with the "Red Strike propaganda." Students gathered in Nanking Road, waving flags and making demonstrations against the Japanese mill owners.

The Police were fully prepared and dispersed the demonstrators, but at one time it was necessary to make a baton charge.

"In the northern district the position looked serious, but the Police succeeded in controlling attempts at rioting, the agitators retreating to the Chinese territory."

Several students have been arrested for distributing Red pamphlets.

The demonstrations emphasise the seriousness of the labour situation in Shanghai. Reuter.

Against the Japanese.

Judging by the handbills distributed during the disturbances yesterday, as the result of the agitation after the death of a Chinese howker, about a Japanese ship, they were directed only against the Japanese.

Eighteen of the agitations have been arrested, and the total arrests during the weekend number thirty-four. The mill situation in Shanghai is unchanged, but it is better at Footung.—Renter.

headline: MINERS' EXECUTIVE MOVE.
text:
The Miners' Executive met this evening to discuss fresh proposals for ending the dispute. At the close of the meeting they proceeded to the House of Commons to confer with the Parliamentary Labour Party Executive.

Referring to the business before the House of Commons M. Ramsay MacDonald suggested that instead of proceeding to discuss the general situation in the coal dispute before the discussion on the renewal of the regulations, the general debate should be taken to tomorrow as certain conferences were being held to day and certain explorations were being made regarding the situation.

This course was adopted.

Sir William Joynson Hicks, Home Secretary, moved a resolution for the continuance of the Emergency Regulations, and his speech was much interrupted from the Labour Benches, one member, Mr. Jack Jones, being suspended after refusing to accept the ruling of the Speaker.

Sir W. Joynson. Hicks said that the chief value of these regulations was in their preventive effect. On the whole the mining disغriets had remained quiet and orderly, and he paid a tribute to the excellent behaviour of the great emission of miners most of whom were suffering under what they considered a great sense of grievance. During last month only 64 cases had been taken under the provisions of the Emergency Regulations; and the bulk of those concerned in such cases were not miners.

Mr. Ramsay MacDonald contended that no case of continuing the regulations had been established. The country was peaceful, and there had been nothing in the history of this or any other country of such a quiet and orderly prosecution of an industrial dispute. The worst that had happened could, he said, be dealt with adequately under the ordinary law.

The debate is proceeding. British Wireless Service.

headline: Buldwin's Message.
text:
When the House of Commons reassembled for the special purpose of renewing the Emergency Regulations in connection with the coal dispute Commander J. M. Kenworthy (Liberal Central Hull) asked whether Mr. Baldwin's message to the American newspapers as regards the condition of the miners and their families had been sent through our Ambassador in Washington in consultation with the Foreign Office.

Sir Austen Chamberlain replied that the message was not sent through the Ambassador but, "with my knowledge and full concurrence." (Conservative cheers).

Sir W. Joynson Hicks, in moving the resolution authorising the continuance of the regulations for a month, said that "there had been only 64 prosections. Thereunder in August. Their chief value was preventive. The mining districts generally were quiet and orderly." headline: OBITUARY
text:
DR. STACY A. RANSOM

Dr. Stacy A. Ransom one of the best known men in Shanghai and certainly one of the oldest residents among the American Community at Shanghai died at 8 o'clock last night (August 26) in the General hospital from Bright's disease at the age of 59 years.

Dr. Ransom had Been a sufferer from the disease for some considerable time past, but it was not until last week while on a holiday in Peitain to that the symptoms grew worse necessitating a quick return to Shanghai and an immediate entrance into hospital.

Born in Washington D.C., Dr. Ransom was educated at the University of Georgetown and at the age of 26 graduated in Medicine.

Prior to coming to Shanghai in 1902 Dr. Ransom served with the colours in the Spanish American War.

Immediately on reaching Shanghai Dr. Ransom was appointed Quarantine and Medical Officer to the American Consulate General and since then has been the United States Public Health Officer in Shanghai.

A popular member of all the principal clubs, sporting and social, the late doctor was also well-known and esteemed for his public works the chief of which were President of the Shanghai Medical Society. President of the American Association, Chairman of the Board of the Shanghai General Hospital and member of the Shanghai Municipal Council.

In 1903 Dr. Ransom was appointed second in Command of the Shanghai Volunteer Corps which rank he held at the time of his death, and in 1906 he organised and founded the American Company which he commanded for 14 years and which is to-day one of the foremost companies of the Corps.

A crack shot with the rifle Dr. Rainsom was for a considerable time, Chairman of the Executive Committee of the Shanghai Rifle Association and helped the local team considerably time and time again in a interport rifle matches. At one time Dr. Ransom, who was a Shriner, was District Grand Master of the local Masonic Lodge.

Dr. Ransom leaves a wife who is now in Shanghai and one son who is at present serving with the American Infantry having graduated from the West Point Military Academy. To both of the bereaved the sympathy of the community will be extended.—“China Press.”

headline: CATHOLIC CONGRESS
text:
CHICAGO ECLIPSED BY MADRID AND VIENNA.

While the Eucharistic Congress of Chicago was gigantic in dimension and emblematic of America in its democratic setting and "biggest in the world" spirit for magnificence and pomp, it would be hard to surpass the congress held in Madrid in 1911 and Vienna in 1912. A special solid silver monstrance, wolching seven hundred pounds, placed on a state carriage laden with roses and jasmin and attended by King Alfonso featured the congress of Madrid. In Vienna, the papal legate, Cardinal Van Rossum rode in the golden carriage of the Empress Maria Teresa, drawn by eight pure white Hungarian steeds, followed by the "Emperor Franz Josef in his state coach with emblazoned outriders, accompanied by the Archduke. Ferdinand and the entire court. Ninety thousand persons participated in the procession. In the course of the final meeting of the Madrid Congress of 1911, King Alfonso made an important speech in which he recalled the historic claims of Spain as a Catholic country. The King and Queen of Spain got down from their state coach to receive the Eucharistic procession when it reached the portals of the royal palace.

The procession which terminated the Viehna Eucharistic Congress, of 1912 was, especially magnificent. More than 8,000 priests, 2,800 officers of the Austrian army, 3,500 state employees, 92 deputies, 260 bishops and 12 cardinals took part in it.

The first Eucharistic Congress was held at Lille in 1881; the second at Avignon, 1882; the third, Liege, 1883; the fourth, Frieburg, Germany, 1885; the fifth, Toulouse, 1886; the sixth, Paris, 1888; the seventh, Antwerp, 1890; and the eighth at Jerusalem in 1892.

The tenth congress was celebrated. ed 'lt Parahonial in 1896; the 11th, Brussels, 1896; the 12th, Lourdes, 1890; the 13th, Angers, 1900; the 15th, Angenlame, 1904; the 16th, Rome, 1905; the 17th, Tournai, 1906; the 18th, Metz., 1907 and the 19th, London in 1908.

On this latter occasion, Pope Pius X sent Cardinal Vannutelli, new dean of the sacred College, as his legate. Cardinal Vannutelli, who is in his 90th year, has represented the Holy Father at more Eucharistic Congresses than any other living prelate.

The twentieth congress was held at "Cologne in 1900; the 21st, which was the first to be held on the continent of North America, took place at Montreal in 1910, and on all these three occasions Cardinal Vannutelli was the papal legate.

The 22nd congress was celebrated at Madrid, in 1911, the 23rd at Vienna, 1912, and the 24th and 25th at Malta and Lourdes respectively in the year 1913 and 1914. During the War no Eucharistic congress was held.

In 1922, the first post-war congress was held in Rome. It was inaugurated by the present Pope in the Vatican in the presence of 23 cardinals and some 20,000 persons.

Following in the wake of the Times the Daily Telegraph is seriously perturbed by the chaotic conditions prevailing in China and more particularly the anti-foreign developments. The Daily Telegraph is a sound journal far removed from the Chauvinist type, and is not in the habit of raising the cry of "Wolf" for the sake of mere amusement. It would be idle, knowing the reputation of the Daily Telegraph, to inquire whether its volatile pronouncement on China, as cabled by Rêuter to-day, has been inspired or not. It may or it may not be. It is all a matter of surmise, and, in any event, that does not affect the issue at stake—the need for some form of intervention to protect the lives and property of foreigners in China.

CHEUNG CHAU ISLAND Beautiful scenes of all parts of this part of Hongkong.

Orders for photos can be placed with our representative at Cheung Chau, MR. JACKSON LOWE, House No. 11.

The list of outrages committed by Chinese boycott pickets and by Chinese soldiers and banditti during the past three months alone makes formidable and almost incredible reading. There is no end to which the Chinese of to-day will not go to humiliate the foreigner and to encompass either his ruin or his death. Well may the Daily Telegraph re-echo the views of the men on the spot that the so-called policy of "pence and conciliation," about which we have heard so much during the past year and a half, is actually nerveless submission which has only made the position worse:

Times the Daily Telegraph does not state the exact form of the suggested intervention. It goes, however, a step further than the Times by suggesting that Great Britain should send out a special Plenipotentiary — for instance, the Marquis of Reading — who "will show that Great Britain is in earnest."

Unfortunately for the suggestion of the Daily Telegraph, it is one thing to say that Great Britain is the only Power able to bring Japan and the United States together with herself and others in a common policy of intervention, and another thing altogether to transform that idea into concrete form. Up to the present the main anti-foreign propaganda in China has been directed against Great Britain and Japan, and whilst their joint case for some form of intervention is unassailable they comprise only two of the Powers interested in China.

One is tempted to ask what does the League of Nations stand for if it is not to meet such cases as exist in China today? Only yesterday China made a special plea for a permanent seat on the League Council, in which she was strongly supported by Japan. Is it not time that the League was induced by Great Britain and Japan to "sit up and take notice" of what is transpiring in China against the interests of the nationals of members of the League other than China? If any form of intervention, diplomatic or otherwise is feasible, it ought surely to come from the League of Nations. That, on the whole, appears at the moment a better suggestion than that of sending out a special Plenipotentiary who might be in no better position than the British Minister in Peking—that is, in the absence of a common understanding with Japan, America, and the other Powers interested in China.

headline: H.E.'S BIRTHDAY. / ENTERTALNED AT TAIPO MARKET.
text:
GUEST OF KAI FONG.

In a specially erected matshed at Taipo yesterday members of the Kai Fong met to do honour to H.E. the Governor, Sir Cecil Clementi, who many years ago held the position there of District Officer. The occasion was His Excellency's "birthday".

The matshed was erected between two "Flame of the Forest" trees which Sir Cecil and Lady Clementi planted at Tripo Market on a somewhat similar occasion a year ago when the villages of the New Territories united in doing him honour shortly after his arrival to take up the duties of Governor of Hongkong.

Taipo Market was decorated with flags for the occasion and a Chinese band played during the afternoon in an specially erected bandstand. Strings of crackers were fired upon His Excellency's arrival, also a 17 gun salute. The vicinity was thronged with Chinese.

The proceedings opened with the singing of Chinese students of the local schools and the guests were then entertained to a Chinese dinner consisting (with the exception of the ingredients of the inevitable sharks' fin soup) of products in-digenous to the New Territories. H.E. the Governor sat at the head of the table under an illuminated address containing a congratulatory Birthday message and behind a silver replica of the symbolic god of longevity.

In reply to Mr. Lee Chung-chong, who offered His Excellency the congratulations of his hosts and read an illuminated address in Chinese which he handed to the chief, guest. His Excellency thanked his hosts for the congratulations and hoped that they too would enjoy long life and good health.

His Excellency expressed the hope that the elders of the New Territories would always keep him informed of affairs in their district particularly of anything which they considered might promote the interests and happiness of the people. He would always be very glad to help them in such matters. (Applause).

At the conclusion of the dinner group photograph was taken outside the building.

Ambing those present were the Hon. Mr. W. T. and Mrs. Southern, the Hon. Mr. J. H. Kemp, C.B.E., K.C., the Hon. Mr. C. McI. Messer, O.B.E., the Hon. Mr. H. T. and Mrs. Creasy, the Hon. Mr. E. D. C. headline: ALICE HOSPITALS:
text:
COMMUNITY'S SHARE OF BURDEN.

Last week mention was made in these columns of the "Alice and Memorial Hospitals and information was given about the being of the work.

At the very beginning Christ Chinese and missionaries of London Missionary Society, particularly the late Dr. John Chalmers, assisted in the work when Sir Kai Ho Kai built the Alice Memorial Hospital. The London Missionary Society was asked to provide the medical superintendent, which they agreed to do. Several doctors have acted in this capacity and many local doctors have given willing assistance. The L.M.S. was later asked to provide a matron, and to this they also agreed, but they felt that this was all they could afford to do in connection with the work

The local community has borne the burden of this charitable enterprise for these many years, taking a growing share of the financial responsibility as the demands of the work increased. The intimate relations of the Hospitals to the Chinese philanthropic community were strengthened when the Chinese Public Dispensaries were formed, and for many years the medical and other supplies of the Dispensaries have been issued through these Hospitals.

A few years ago a new constitution was formed under which the local Committee and Executive of the Hospitals have full control and management of the affairs of the Hospitals, and are responsible for all funds required for the work, except those guaranteed by the L.M.S.

headline: OBITUARY. / MR. O. R. COALES.
text:
Shanghai, August 31.—We regret to announce the death, news of which was received by telegram on Saturday, of Mr. O. R. Coales, H.M. Consul at Changsha. To a great number of people in Shanghai this will occasion great regret, for he had been stationed here in more than one capacity, and had family ties with the port.

Mr. Coales came to China as a student interpreter in 1901, having been born in 1880. After completing his course as student interpreter, he was appointed assistant in the Chinese Secretary's office in Peking, and thereafter was appointed assistant in the Shipping Office in the Consulate-General in Shanghai, holding this position from 1908 to 1909. From 1911 to 1913 he was acting Consul at Wuchow, and returning to Shanghai in the latter year took up the position as assistant in the Land Office. He was promoted to the rank of Vice Consul in 1914, and as such was in Shanghai until 1917, when he went to Tengyueh in Yunnan, becoming Consul there in 1919. Subsequently he went to Tachienlu in Szechuan, and such a station seems undoubtedly to have suited his character, which contained in it a great love for exploration. He is known to have done several hazardous and strenuous journeys on foot in these little known regions, and as a reward for the information he gained he was made a Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. Probably his greatest achievement was the crossing of the Gobi Desert and making contact with the Siberian Railway—a feat accomplished, we believe, prior to his travels on the Tibetan frontier.

"Mr. Coales leaves a widow—a sister of Mrs. E. T. Byrne—for whom the deepest sympathy will be felt." "N.C. Daily News."

headline: VICEROY'S ADDRESS
text:
GOVERNMENT DETERMINED TO DO ITS DUTY.

COMMUNAL RIOTS

Simla: August 17.

Striking observations on matters constitutional and communal were made this morning by Lord Irwin in his first address to the Central Legislature.

The Viceroy said that they could no more deny the fundamental duty of Parliament to assist India and judge of the progress made than they could deny the ultimate claim which India made and for the satisfaction of which they worked. But before this claim could be fully realised many obstacles imposed by history, circumstance and nature would need to be surmounted. While the past achievements of progress had been the happy fruits of joint Indian and British effort, so now in the solution of the present difficulties, each race had an indispensable part to take. He was the last to ask those who criticised reform to abandon the principles which they revered. The British did not seek to force India into a mould unfriendly to the main features of Indian life and character.

The Viceroy emphasised that events between now and the Commission's statutory enquiry could not fail to exert a great influence upon the conclusions of that body regarding the efficiency, or otherwise with which the policy of 1910 had proceeded.

Unhappily, 'the burning question remained. of the feeling between the communities. He admitted that time was required to heal the wound.' Meanwhile the Government had obligations to law-abiding citizens. Although the matters were the primary concern of the provincial Governments, the form in which they were now emerging made them of all-India interest, intenible claims of rights and exaggerated opposition from time to time had caused anxiety to the authorities. The Government had no intention of allowing any unjust or "unreasonable claims, still less any violence, or threat of violence, to deter them from their duty of maintaining the public peace, and, so far as was compatible with the rights of others, to assure the right of the individual citizen to pursue unhampered-his lawful avocations. India had an abundance of ability but some of it in the past had been directed along lines that could at best lead to no useful result. 'n the future the whole of India's resources were needed for one of the most constructive tasks which had ever enlisted human energies and hopes.

headline: Imperial Affair
text:
Referring to foreign and imperial matters, the Viceroy touched on the friendly relations with Afghanistan and Nepal, and his satisfaction at the solution of the Mosul problem.

As regards the South Africa, a question, there would be a delegation to the forthcoming Conference shortly, which would satisfy the Indian public on the question of Indians in South Africa. He declared that the Government was not susceptible to an easy decision by coerive force. The solution must be based upon mutual accommodation and carry the free assent of both communities.

The Viceroy next advised the Assembly to examine the Currency Bill, not in the light of local interests, but with reference to its ultimate reaction upon the economic and commercial prosperity of the whole country.

Alluding to the policy of the development of railway traffic in rural areas with the view to stimulating agriculture, the Viceroy mentioned that the railways had planned to add 6,000 miles of railway, which would be remunerative and a boon to the country. He also referred to the changes in public services based on the Lee Report and declared that shortly all action on the Lee recommendations would be complete and the re-organisation of the services of a very striking nature will have been accomplished.

The public galleries were packed to overflow, and the House was f., and the Viceroy on concluding was loudly cheered and applauded.

headline: SHANGHAI.
text:
PREPARATIONS TO PROTECT.

Numerous rumours continue to be circulated locally about the civil warfare in Central China and the attitude of Marshal Sun Chuan-fang, which is causing considerable speculation.

" Marshal Sun has issued a proclamation pointing out that too many false and malicious rumours are rife, all of which tend to disturb the peace. There is no foundation whatever to them. He, Mشرpal Sun, has hitherto adopted a policy of "pao ching an min" (armed neutrality), and this is a stand which he will continue "to take. Rumours cannot be permitted to pass with impunity and so all are strictly warned against disseminating false reports, otherwise he will adopt severe measures in dealing with them. The local authorities are ordered to keep watch for rumour-mongers and to arrest them and punish them to the fullest extent of the law.

Arrangements for the defence of the Woosung Forta and the

Kocharigmiao Arsenal have been completed, due precautions having, Legn taken against possible attacks, Chinese gunboats, loyal to Marshal Sun, have been posted at Woosung and on the upper reaches of the Huangpu River, near the Arsenal, and no boats are permitted to moor near either of these places at night. Arrangements are being made for the search of vessels coming from Canton, it being thought that professional Bolshevik propagandists have been arriving with Red literature and arms.

Gen. Lu Hsiang-ting, Tupan: of Chekiang, again passed through Shanghai early yesterday morning on his way from Hangchow to Nanking, to confer with Marshal Sun once more on the situation. It was only on Saturday morning that he returned to Hangchow from Nanking. According to reports, Gen. Lu has completed arrangements for the defence of Chekiang and he will be sent to the war front. His family are due to arrive here today. Rumours were prevalent yesterday to the effect that the press gang was busy in Shanghai but these were officially denied.

These men are being paid $30 a piece for expenses whilst on their way to Tsinanfu. Already some 80 have been enrolled. Marshall Chang has 3,500 White Russians in his army at the present time.—“N. C. headline: COCAINE CHARGE. / NINE MONTHS' HARD LABOUR.
text:
Henricus Augustus Boom, a Dutchman, aged 28, describing himself as independent, was brought up on remand at Westminster Police Court and charged with being in possession of a large quantity of cocaine. Boom was arrested at Victoria Station on July 21, when, according to the police evidence, a brown paper parcel alleged to contain cocaine was found in his pocket. Mr. Muskelt prosecuted for the Crown and Mr. F. W. Perkins appeared for the accused.

Mr. Muskett said the authorities agreed to the case being dealt with summarily, and Mr. Perkins announced that Boom would plead guilty.

Mr. Muskett stated that the accused was a drug suspect, and had been watched by the police. Analysis of the contents of the parcel found in his possession showed that they consisted of 89% per cent. pure cocaine. The parcel was an extremely large one. The Magistrate: I have never known a case with so large a quantity.

Mr. Muskett: Now nor have I, and we know that when this pure cocaine is diluted, as it is, for sale to women of a certain character and others, it fetches enormous prices. The man is a trafficker in the drug. An order for his deportation has already been made by the Home Office.

Detective-inspector Burnby said Boom had been in this country about twelve months, and had made frequent journeys between here and Holland and France. The police information was that the journeys had been made for bringing cocaine to this country and for arranging to bring foreign women of ill-repute here.

The Magistrate (to accused). You will go to prison with hard labour for nine months, and I shall recommend you for deportation.

“Ours is the discontent of optimists and not the dull despair which afflicts a decaying civilisation.”—Bishop of Birmingham.

headline: DANGER OF DIVORCE.
text:
BROKEN VOWS RESULT IN SHORTER LIFE.

The statement made by Professor G. M. Robertson, president of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh, that the incidence of insanity among married people is low, but that it is increased in a marked degree by the loss of a husband or wife, gives an added interest to the sensational disclosures of Dr. Herman N. Bundesen, the famous Health Commissioner of Chicago, who declares that married men live virtually twice as long as men who have been divorced.

Dr. Bundesén bases his revelation on new completed statistics compiled by his department on the comparative longevity of bachelors, married men and men who have

The scribbles show that out of every thousand divorced men between the ages of twenty-five and thirty-four, fifteen died last year; that out of the same number of single men five died, and out of a thousand married men only four died.

In the group between the ages of thirty-five and forty-four, out of one thousand in each class, eighteen divorced, fourteen single, and only seven married men died.

The age between forty-five and fifty-four comes next. Statistic here again reveal that whereas thirty-seven divorced and twenty-three single men died in each thousand of this class, only fourteen married men succumbed.

Forty-nine bachelor, fifty-six divorced men and only twenty-nine married men, further, died in Chicago last year between the ages of fifty-five and sixty-four in their respective groups of one thousand. "Consider finally the age of sixty-five," says the Health Commissioner. "No fewer than 116 divorced and 112 single out of one thousand over this age died last year, against only eighty-year-old."

headline: GALLANT RESCUE. / DROWNING SWIMMER SAVED BY DR. A. H. SWAN.
text:
AN UNKNOWN MAN

Shanghai, August 30. — At Tsingtao during the past week, Dr. A. H. Swan was instrumental in rescuing a Mr. Eames, according to word received in Shanghai yesterday, from drowning and a buffeting to death on the wild coast at Itis Hook, Mr. Eames went swimming off the point during the heavy sea subsequent to the typhoon and became exhausted, being dragged away from the coast. His condition was noticed and many people rushed to the beach. Women became frantic.

The men seemed powerless to do anything.

The drowning man was swept against the rocky projections but managed to keep afloat although the waves dashed him time after time against the rocks. Dr. Swan

came on to the beach and seemed to grasp the situation immediately. He rushed for a life preserver and, despite the heavy seas, dashed through the surf into the swells beyond. Towing the life preserver, he gradually made his way toward Mr. Eames, who was weakening fast. It was after he had put the life preservor around Mr. Eames that the real struggle began. The rescuer had not been a physical director in vain, and his past experience stood him in good stead. Struggling with the waves, he gradually neared the beach, where he was assisted by the others present in dragging the victim of the waves on to dry land. First aid measures were applied and it is understood that Mr. Eames is getting along nicely.

We have been informed that another foreign gentleman, name unknown, either partially or wholly assisted Dr. Swan in the long swim and rescue.—“N. C. Daily News.”

text:
ARTILLIERY DISAFFECTED

headline: - Drastic Action.
text:
The Government has announced that in view of "recent events, necessitating crustic action, it has requested the King's authority to proclaim martial law throughout Spain and enforce suitable measures.

London, September 6. " Needs from Madrid in regard to the proclamation of a state of war is the sequel to recent rumours, which are semi-officially declared to be alarmist and unfounded, in regard to disorders in Spain and

It is now confirmed that martin law is due to indiscipline in the Army.

headline: "SAVE YOUR JOBS."
text:
ADVICE OF WARWICKSHIRE OWNERS.

At length there is a prospect of a settlement of the protracted coal trouble on lines which, it is hoped, will bring enduring peace to Great Britain's basic industry.

Although the owners are still irrevocably opposed to the principle of a national agreement, holding that the freedom resumed by the districts on the abandonment of control by the Central Council of the Mining Association should be maintained, it is declared that the District Associations of Coal Owners will resist a renewed abrogation of their powers of negotiation and wages settlements. Therefore, if a national wage basis is agreed to between the Government and the miners, it may be necessary to obtain legislative power to impose it.

On the other hand it is possible that such a situation may be created that the coal owners' negotiating Committee may bring influence to bear on the districts to modify their attitude.

"It is noteworthy that the Warwickshire coal owners have notified the miners that a national wage scheme would put them on a level with the lowest paid district and ask them if the reduction is worth fighting for." Save your jobs and let the other districts do the same."—Reuter.

London, September 5. The Mining Association represents the Joint Conference between both parties in the dispute.—Reuter. London, September 5. Although representatives of the Mining Association and the Cabinet Council Committee are meeting on Monday, the textsof Letters exchanged with the Miners' Department reveal that the Association is theidedly against the miners' desire for a national settlement.

The Secretary of the Association, the Miners' Federation and the Government, declared that the Association had no authority to discuss and negotiate on behalf of District Owners' Associations questions relating to terms of employment with workmen; they, therefore, declined to attend a tripartite meeting. The reply, further to the letter from the Miners' Mining Association secretary, agreed to meet the Cabinet Coal Committee on Monday.—Reuter

The Central Council of the Soviet Labour Unions are transmitting "to the British Mirers' Federation all available sums collected by means of a levy". The members, in addition, advance on account of future levies, a total remittance of three million roubles.—Reuter.

headline: The Miners' Letter
text:
Late last night the Miners Executive sent a communication to Mr. Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, containing a formula which has enabled the Government to request the mine owners to resume negotiations. The letter to Mr. Churchill, which was signed by Mr. A. J. Cook, the miners' secretary states that the Executive Committee and a special delegate conference of the Miners Federation having again carefully considered the present deadlock in the mining dispute "have resolved to ask you to convene and attend a conference of the Mining Association and Federation. We are prepared to enter negotiations for a new national agreement with a view to a reduction in costs to meet the immediate in costs to meet the immediate necessities of the industry." An official announcement states, "The Government considers that this letter constitutes a basis sufficient to justify them" in requesting the Mining Association to resume negotiations and they are communicating with them accordingly. The Prime Minister is being kept fully informed of the course of

The Miners Executive's letter constitutes a distinct advance upon their previous attitude. The phrase "reduction in labour costs" is sufficiently comprehensive to permit discussion on hours as well as wages and reorganisation of industry. At the moment, however, the statement that the miners are prepared to negotiate for a "new national agreement" is of primary importance in view of the decision of the mine owners not to negotiate nationally and to take separate agreements in districts as the only basis for the settlement of the dispute.

A full conference of mining owners will probably be called to consider the letter from the Government suggesting a reopening of negotiations with the miners' national body.

Owners will be invited and expected not to impede a settlement by rigid adherence to this attitude.

headline: Position Reviewed.
text:
As a result of the correspondence between the coal owners and the Government Minis Department, representatives of the Mining Association will attend meeting of the Coal Committee of the Cabinet to-morrow to discuss the question of calling a joint conference of the parties to the coal dispute.

The association had in a previous letter informed the Mines Department that they were unable to meet the miners in three-corner conferences to discuss a national agreement as they "had no authority to enter into any discussions of negotiations on behalf of the District Colliery Owners' Associations on questions of terms of employment of workmen."

The general belief is that the insistence of the coal owners to settle terms in the districts and, not on a national basis will not be allowed to block the way to a settlement.

The Government view that this matter is capable of equitable settlement by a national agreement, with district variations in accordance with the conditions existing in the different apels, was expressed by Mr. Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, in parliament last week. This view was expressed strongly by the Goal Commission's report, and the negotiation of such an agreement is now the sole limitation placed by the Miners' Executive on the scope of the discussion at the joint conference which they requested Mr. Churchill to convene.

Pesumably the Cabinet Coal Committee, at their meeting with the Mining Association to-morrow will invite that Body to obtain from the District Coal Owners' Associations a mandate to enter upon discussions on a national basis. British Wireless Service.

headline: NOTE TO CHINA. / SOVIET AND MUKDEN WAR LORD.
text:
M. Chichigrin has handed the Chinese Charge d'Affaires in Moscow, for transmission to the Chinese Government, a Note protesting against Marshal Chang Tsolin's demand to the Board of the Chinese Eastern Railway to hand over to the Mukden authorities all vessels belonging to the Railway, also a demand for a liquidation of the training department of the Railway and to transfer all schools to the control of the Mukden authorities.

The Note points out that the Government has repeatedly attempted to adjust its differences with the Railway in an amicable spirit, but, for reasons beyond Soviet control, all such attempts have been futile. The Soviet is again ready to enter into the question of all differences, but emphatically protests against the one-sided action of the Chinese Government in violating the essential Treaty rights of Soviet Russia in North Manchuria.

The Soviet awaits the immediate withdrawal of the demand and insights on the submission of the questions through diplomatic channels to both Governments.

headline: SWATOW OUTRAGE.
text:
CHINESE EMPLOYEE OF BRITISH FIRM CHAINED.

Swatow, August 23.—Last week was reported the outrage, committed on a leading Chinese British subject by the police here. This has been followed up by a still more dastardly attack upon another man by the strike pickets. The victim in this case is the head Chinese in the employ of Messrs. Bradley and Co., with whom he has been for 30 years. Like other Chinese employees, he, of course, had not been working in the office since the boycott began; but recently, as the firm had business to transact with the Reclamation Bureau, he was given a special official permit to attend the office. In the face of this he was, some days ago, on his arrival at the office, laid hold of by a body of pickets, and carried off to one of their dens, where he has been chained up and kept on the verge of starvation since—in the hope, no doubt, that he will come to the point of paying some huge sum for release from his misery. So much for the value of the pledged word of the official. So much also, alas, for the value of the once boasted British citizenship. So much, again, for the justice which we are assured China is going to met with open hand when extraterritoriality goes. The official position is that Chinese are Chinese, and have no right to call themselves citizens of other countries. It looks as if the British government had decided to take the same view. If so, it is at least due to the Chinese who think they can claim British protection that the government should enlighten them.—“N.C.D.N.”

headline: Policy of Conelliation.
text:
The opening speech of the Czecho-Slovakian Premier, M. Benes, at the Assembly of the League has been wirelessly broadcast. A Geneva report states that M. Benes said that the League ever since its creation had been concerned with the problem of disarmament which was appreciably nearer the goal. The members of the league, in response to the Assembly's recommendation, were inaugurating among themselves a vast new political system based on the principle of conciliation and arbitration.

As regards organisation the Council report, which had been adopted, seemed to hold out a prospect of a, unanimous speedy agreement. They were saddened by the thought of the departure of Staples which were very dear to them, but they had not yet lost all hope.—Renter.

headline: FASCISM OPPOSED / TO BE DRIVEN FROM FACE OF EARTH.
text:
ENEMY OF HUMANITY

“The Federation will stand and work with the Anti-Fascist Alliance of North America until Fascism is driven from the face of the earth” declared Mr. William Green, President of the American Federation of Labour, in addressing 500 delegates at the first annual convention of the Alliance.

Mr. Green said that he had come purposely to show the deep sympathy of the workers with anti-Fascism, declaring that Fascism was an enemy of society and humanity.--Reuter.

headline: STRIKE" PICKETS. / WHAT THEY HAVE DONE SINCE SATURDAY.
text:
ACTIVE ON SHORE?

Since Saturday when the British senior naval officer of the West River dislodged the Canton strike pickets from the Steamboat Co.'s wharf, there have been several movements. Several of the pickets were arrested for trespassing, it is stated. The examination shed' established by the "Labour and Merchants' Examination Bureau," on the Tung On Co.'s wharf, has closed down; but a similar establishment may have been erected elsewhere.

Pickets have now taken up positions, near the bund, but at a safe distance from the Naval detachments and patrols.

Canton police and gendarmes are preserving order in the neighbourhood.

The Canton Foreign Ministry has communicated with the Strike Executive which has, in turn, instructed members not to enter foreign buildings.

The Executive has asked the Ministry to lodge a protest.

Ministry to lodge a protest. The pro-Kuomintang (four) Chambers of Commerce of Canton have passed four resolutions, asking for a protest and the withdrawal of the warships and British armed launches.

Telegrams from, Canton state that there is complete cessation of firing by pickets' boats which disappeared at the first sign of activity by British naval vessels. The latter found it unnecessary to fire a single shot.

Although ejected from the British wharf alongside which gunboats have been stationed, pickets are still showing activity ashore. British Wireless Service

headline: RAILWAY PERILS. / THREE FRESH ACCIDENTS REPORTED.
text:
An express travelling to London from Glasgow over-ran the buffers at Leeds station "early this morning. The engine crashed through two walls and demolished the end of the station, stopping within a few feet outside a cab rank opposite. The hotel roof at the station end fell on the engine. There were no casualties.—Reuter.

Eight persons were killed and over a hundred injured in a collision at Courtlan Street Station between two passenger trains. Two wooden cars at the rear of a stationary train, containing holiday makers, were telescoped.—Reuter.

Vancouver, September 7. Four persons were killed when a goods train jumped the rails of a bridge a hundred miles east of here. Fire broke out destroying the bridge. Twenty-six cars were partially burnt and precipitated into a canyon a hundred feet below.—Router.

headline: ONE BIG UNION
text:
LIVELY DISCUSSION AT "CONGRESS.

OVERNMENT CRITICISED.

A lively discussion at the Trade Union Congress centred on the resolution of the General Workers' Union demanding the discouragement of the formation of new organisations with "One Big Union" as their ultimate goal.

The Congress finally adopted an agreement asking the Council to call conferences of trade groups in order to promote the merging of separate unions.

Thereafter an emergency resolution was carried expressing concern at the tendency of the present Government to interfere needlessly with the liberty of the subject and to utilise methods of repression in industrial disputes, and protesting against the unwavering application of emergency powers notwithstanding "the peaceful atmosphere of the mining dispute."

The proposal of the General Council to impose a penny levy per member for the next three years in connection with the Easton Lodge labour education scheme, for which £50,000 is required for alterations and developments, was rejected by 2,441,000 votes against 1,481,000. Countess Warwick had donated Easton Lodge for labour education. Reuter.

headline: MILLION AND A HALF ON THE LIST.
text:
Rugby, September 7. The Ministry of Labour announces that on August 30, the total number of persons recorded unemployed in Great Britain was 1,549,800. This was 9,198 less than a week ago, but 1,954,08 more than a year ago.

It is exclusive of the persons who have ceased work in the coal mixing industry on account of the dispute.—British Wireless Service.

headline: A LEGAL POINT. / CLOSED RESTAURANTS AND COURTS. / MR. LO'S ARGUMENT.
text:
Arguing for the defence of a Chinese restaurant keeper who was summoned before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning for keeping his premises open after regulation hours, Mr. M. W. Lo said that the condition of the licence was that the restaurant should be closed at 2 a.m., but nothing was mentioned about the door. It was necessary, he said, for the inmates to open the door in order to get some air, but so long as customers had not been served with drinks he thought no offence had been committed.

To further illustrate his point, Mr. Lo said that the doors of a court house may be open, but the court will be “closed” so long as a Magistrate is not sitting there. His Worship thought that a technical offence has been committed and imposed a fine of $10

were pursuing a deserted and entered a house. A large crowd collected among whom were several Japanese. The soldiers emerged and, brandished loaded rifles, the crowd seatings in all directions. headline: OUT WITH THE REDS!
text:
A REFERENDUM PROPOSED.

A great crowd filled the Royal Albert Hall, Kensington, W., on July 15, at a mass meeting to protest against Soviet interference in British affairs.

Col. John Gretton, M.P., presided, and others on the platform included Lord Clive, Lord Struthspey. Commander O' Locker-Lampson, M.P., Mr. G. Havelock Wilson, the President of the Seamen's Union, and many Conservative M.P.'s.

Mr. Joseph Martin, who was blinded by the treatment he received in Russian prisons and whose case was mentioned in the House of Commons, sat behind the speakers, Commander: Oliver Locker-Lampson, M.P., who commanded armoured-car contingents in Russia during the war when that country was an Ally of Great Britain, said:

The Soviet owes private British creditors alone more than £250,000,000, and I ask. What right had we to recognize this swindling syndicate until it had owned up and paid up?

It can establish companies in Great Britain for trade, like Acros, and Arcos can issue a writ for libel, as it has done against the "Daily Mail." But no Englishman can bring any action in our Law Courts for damages for his losses in Russia.

Why, an Englishman can even watch wood coming into the country from Russia and he can actually identify it as his own timber because it bears his mark, but he cannot recover one rouble.

Petrol which is ours has been sent over and dumped below cost price upon the British market. It is disposed of by the agency known as Russian Oil Products, Limited.

Plotters' Stolen Gold. It first steals our goods; secondly it sells them to us; and, thirdly, our money, realised from the sale, returns in the form of subsidies to encourage chaos throughout the Empire and to undermine constituted civilisation. It pours in gold to irrigate the thirsty palms of spouters in the park, agitators in every strike, and even to nourish anti- English candidates in elections. The English Communist Party would not live a day if you closed down the cash-box at Moscow. If the English Communist Party is an illegal organisation, as the Attorney-General has declared it, and if Englishmen who conduct it are criminals, are not those aliens who furnish it with the sinews of war criminals also?

The Government fears that a withdrawal of recognition might be treated as tantamount to a declaration of war. I should like to ask if the persistent Bolshevik meddling in our affairs is not tantamount to ten declarations of war?

headline: Diplomatic Slobber.
text:
I am tired of hearing the Soviet referred to by his Majesty's Ministers as a "friendly State," and sick to death of the diplomatic Slobber with which we fawn upon these fiends. There was a ringing mandate from the constituencies at the last election to kick them out, and we should long since have swept the stable clean. But our Government does not propose to act. And yet the peril is as grave as any since the war.

Will the Government forthwith take a referendum in this grave emergency? If to each citizen, simply and straightly, the question "is put—Yea or Nay, under which flag will you live; the bloody banner of Bolshevism or the Union Jack? I know in advance what England's answer will be.

At one point in Commander Locker-Lampson's speech a well-dressed woman shouted some remarks that were inaudible. There were cries of "Up the Reds!" and counter-eries of "Put her 'out!'" Waving her arms and shouting "Up the Reds" the woman was escorted from the hall by stewards.

A Mountain of Murder

Brigndier-General Sir Henry Page Croft, M.P., proposed a resolution protesting against the activities of the Soviet agents in the Empire and supporting the Government in any steps they might take to deal with the menace. He said that in Russia anti-Christ was enthroned upon a mountain of murder.

I warn you that the Soviet Governments are making war on our country every day and that several great trade unions have passed, without the knowledge of their members, under the control of the Minority Movement, which is the British branch of the Red International. We feel for the miners because we see they are being used by Mr. Cook to achieve his vainglorious aims. Those people who have come to make trouble in our midst should be given 48-hours notice.

headline: TSINGTAO.
text:
LIQUOR AND BEER TAXES PAID UNDER PROTEST.

TREATY RIGHTS:

Foreign importers, including British, Germans, Russians and Japanese, have been paying the liquor and beer tax under protest since it was put into effect on August 23, and are obtaining receipts, hoping to recover their tax payments when the impost is abolished. Representations have been made to Peking by the British, American, German and Japanese consular officials protesting against the tax which is collected by a specially organised bureau called the Kiao-no Territory, Wine, Spirit and Tobacco Tax Bureau. As no tobacco has been moved since the tax became operative no taxes have been paid on that commodity.

The method by which the authorities were able to enforce payment of the tax was to detain imports in what's godowns whither they were removed upon arrival until receipts showing that the tax had been paid to the tax office were presented.

headline: Wrongful Arrests.
text:
The enforced collection of such a tax is considered a further indication of the disregard of the local Chinese authorities for foreign treaty rights. This was hitherto apparent in the arbitrary arrests of

recent being the Lock case, where a British subject on three occasions was forcibly removed to the Chinese police station to be questioned in connection with the murder of Mr. Carb Fischer, "wealthy German jeweller. The last time he spent the night there in a cell of the type reserved for common criminals." The Japanese have found direct action effective in such cases.

headline: The Cholera Scourge.
text: Cholera has made serious inroads here and Tsingtao has been declared an infected port. Few foreigners have contracted the disease but the daily number of deaths among Chinese is from five to 30. The British Consul has warned his subjects against sea bathing, while the American squadron in port has issued orders to the officers and sailors to refrain from eating raw fruits and vegetables. The entire crew of the U.S. Seaver has been kept on that vessel for the past two days because of a case of cholera among the crew. It is learned that the sailor was almost on the point of death, but rallied and will recover.

headline: LORRY FATALITY. / EARTH COOLIE'S FALL FROM VEHICLE.
text:
POKFULAM ACCIDENT.

An earth coolie in the employment of the Sang Fat contractors at Pokfulam Road was fatally injured in a fall from a motor lorry yesterday.

The vehicle was taking a sharp corner when the coolie who was seated at the back overbalanced himself and fell on the roadway, alighting on his head.

The accident happened at 10 o'clock yesterday morning and the injured man was immediately taken to the Government Civil Hospital, but he expired soon after admittance.

The resolution was seconded by Mr. R. Mitchell Banks, K.C., M.P.

More attention should be paid to the men of the scen, as British soldiers had been fighting "the Bolshies for 9 years. What was wanted was a great league, composed of all classes, to join in a great effort to preserve what our forefathers had left to us from being stolen by the microbe of Bolsheviks. The resolution was carried

The resolution was carried unanimously.

headline: THIEF'S EXCUSE.
text:
SPENT ALL ON A BIT OF WOOD.

MAGISTRATE'S REMARK.

When charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession of a piece of wood, a Chinese claimed that he paid 70 cents for it to a man with whom he struck a bargain on a vacant piece of ground.

In answer to a question as to how much money he had with him now, defendant said he had not a single cont.

His Worship: No money at all, yet you spent your last 70 cents on a piece of wood! What is the good of telling lies?

Defendant, who was identified as a previous offender, was sent to prison for four weeks with hard labour.

headline: NAVAL EOSSES
text:
ANOTHER VERSION OF THE INCIDENT

YANG SEN'S THREAT.

The British steamer "Wanliu," belonging to Messrs. Busterfield & Swire, on August 29 was discharging passengers at Tungying when she was bonded by sixteen armed soldiers and at the same time a sampa in containing troops approached the ship. The "Wanliu" proceeded slowly in order to avoid the sampa. The was opened from both banks of the river and the troops of board rushed to the Bridge and the engine room. The ship's officers drove them off. Meanwhile, another sampa containing about eight people tried to come alongside, but fouled with another boat and drifted "a�stern, eventually sinking.

On August 29, Yang Sen sent three or four hundred solidic saband both the "Wantung" and "Wanhsien," when lying at Wanhai. "In addition, he lined the banks of Eno river with troops and refused to allow only inter-house with the two steamer; I've been by H.M.S. At Wanhsien negotiations through the British Consul at "Chingking" failed after Yang Sen's attitude and it was decided to send "newal" expedition to Wanhsien to effect their release. This expedition was under Consumander Barley of H.M.S. "Depatch," who had been sent from Hankow with a party of officers and men. They arrived at Wanhsien on the evening of September 5, but owing to a warning having been received by Yang Sen, no attempt was made on the occasion to release the ships.

The Wannisier attempt was renewed on a date missing in the message received by the naval authorities, but the expedition, apparently set out in Messrs. Jarding, Matheson's steamer "Kiawo," which the British Navy had taken "piver for that purpose. The "Kiawo" encountered the heaviest fire alongside the s.s.
