Mrs. Ross, the wife of Mr. S. H. Ross, of Messrs. Percy Smith, Seth and Fleming, has given birth to a daughter at the Peak Hospital.

The Rev. and Mrs. Frank T. Woodward, who are residents of Cheung Chau Island, have been congratulated on the birth of a daughter.

Mr. William Nowell, the Assistant-Director of Agriculture in Trinidad, has been promoted to be Director of Agriculture in British Guiana.

Sympathy will be extended to Mrs. and Mrs. R. C. Wilson in the loss of their first child, which died yesterday morning, shortly after birth. The funeral took place yesterday afternoon at Happy Valley.

Professor J. Anderson of the Hongkong University and Dr. Arthur Woo were passengers on the U.S. "Empress of Asia" which left Hongkong yesterday for the North. They will represent Hongkong at the joint conference of the China Medical Association and British Medical Association at Peking.

The death occurred at the General Hospital, Singapore, on August 12 of Captain Frederick James Stack, who was a well-known figure in local shipping circles. The late Captain Stack, who was 66 years of age, came up from Australia twenty years ago and took charge of one of the ships operated by the Ho Hong Steamship Company. Twelve years ago he joined the Straits Steamship Company and was in the Kinta when he retired fifteen months ago on account of ill-health.

Friends of Mr. C. M., McDonald, editor of the "China Mail," will be pleased to learn that he is recovering from the effects of an accident, while on his way Home on leave. He was a passenger on the B.S. "Largo Bay," Entering the Gulf of Aden, the ship was in a heavy sea and Mr. McDonald was thrown so badly that he broke two ribs near the spine. The heat and pain were very trying but recovery was quick and Mr. McDonald on July 15 expected to be able to go ashore at Port Said. He is now in London.

Tokyo, August 5,—The Home Office announces that 490 labour disputes, involving 36,000 labourers and including 152 strikes, occurred during the first half of this year. This indicated an increase of 340 over the same period of last year.

Rome, August 11.—The authorities to-day refused to issue permits to 630 pilgrims on the way to the fete of Madonna del Sasso in Switzerland. Last week 800 pilgrims also were stopped at the frontier. Switzerland's hotel keepers are getting anxious.

Shanghai August 12.—The price of rice, which has been advancing steadily at the rate of 10 cents a day for the list four days, yesterday took a 40 cent jump and closed with quotations at from $16.80 to $18.80 per picul. A week ago yesterday the price was $15.70 to 17.70 per picul.

H.M.S. "Plover," used as a hulk at Gibraltar, is to be placed on the sale list for breaking up. For many years the "Plover" has been employed on harbour service at Gibraltar. She was one of a class of gunboats launched in 1888 at Penbrooke, and at the beginning of the century was serving in China. Although of only 755 tons, the "Plover" mounted six 4-in. guns.

The Ministry of Finance has handed down a set of regulations governing the examination of the capital of Chinese banks, together with the instructions that no official ratification for the opening of any banks should be given unless a thorough investigation is made as to their capital in accordance with the stipulations. This step is taken as a precaution against unscrupulous merchants organising banks with little capital thus creating disorder in the financial market.

Shelfield police force boasts of a constable, Charles Milner, who has just joined up after taking degrees of Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Laws at Cambridge University. He appeared in his first case recently. With other officers he made a raid on a local hotel, where'setting was being carried on. Milner told the Court that the place' had the atmosphere of "betting" when he entered. The licensee was fined £30; a book-maker £50, while fines totalling another £50 were imposed on frequenters.

Another new case of onterle fever was notified on Thursday. The patient was u Chinese from the city.

A Nationalist resolution requesting the Bavarian Government to make representations to the Reich Government with a view to the re-examination of the Dawes Report has been adopted unanimously by the Bavarian Diet.

Berlin, August 11.—Perhaps the ex-Kaiser is beginning to fear that another vote on the question of confiscating his properties may not turn out well for him, for to-day, his attorney general, suggested "new negotiations". He hinted at a possible compromise in his answer to a letter of the Prussian Premier, Herr Brauns.

The “Observer” understands that the Wembley Exhibition site will be developed as a self-contained industrial unit. Two of the largest buildings are virtually sold to an American motor manufacturing company, which is not Ford's, which will provide housing for thousands of its British employees.

As a sequel to a caning administered by his father, a Tamil school-boy, aged 16, named Raju, attempted to commit suicide by drinking about an ounce of iodine. He was unable to speak and was sent to the hospital. He was charged before Mr. W. J. H. Hughes, the Kuala Lumpur magistrate, and was bound over in $50 for three months to come up for judgment if called upon.

Vice-Admiral Crawford Maclachlan, C.B., has been placed on the retired list, at his own request, in order to facilitate the promotion of junior officers. Vice-Admiral Macluchlan first saw service as a naval cadet of the Agincourt during the Egyptian War of 1882, and was in China during the Boxer outbreak in 1900. He served on the Admiralty Committee on Bertking Accommodation of his Majesty's ships at home ports in 1910. Promoted to flag rank in 1920, he held the post of Rear-Admiral, Reserve Fleet, Rosyth, until the following year, afterwards being appointed Senior Officer, Yangtse. In the late war Admiral Maclachlan was a Grand Fleet Captain in the Royal Oak at the Battle of Jutland.

Another auction sale of household furniture in Kowloon is announced by Messrs. Lammert Bros. This is to take place at Nos. 6 and 7, Aimai Villas (ground floors), Kimberley Road, at 2,45 p.m. next Friday.

Temperature of 93° degrees, in the shade, was recorded at Pakkai, the port of Kongmoon, on Monday. Last week there was a fairly heavy rainstorm which lasted 20 hours without a stop. Our Own Correspondent.

Additional "bus facilities for bathing parties are now provided by the Kowloon Motor 'Bus Company'. The ordinary service to Laichikok between 3 to 7 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays has been supplemented by extra vehicles specially for the purpose.

In answer to a protest from the City Council of Niagara Falls, where Sunday dancing is now permitted in one restaurant, the Attorney-General of Ontario, Mr. Nickle, states that "public dancing cannot be tolerated in a Canadian city" on Sundays," and gives assurance that all such dances will be "prohibited.

As from last Sunday, the city governor of Kongmoon, “enforced” the construction of modern roads. By this is meant, states the “China Mail” correspondent at Pakkai, that an order has been given to subordinates to start the laying out of thoroughfares which had been contemplated some time ago but left in abeyance.

A warning to wives who neglect to consult their husbands before visiting the hairdresser to have their hair shingled was given in a Paris Court. Madame Chaplin left home because she alleged that her husband insulted her after she had had her hair shingled, M. Chaplin obtained a deed of separation for desertion. The wife brought in a counter-suit, but to-day "judgment was given against her on the ground that "however insulting the epithets used by the husband might have been, they were justified by the fact that the wife had her hair shingled without her husband's permission."

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL NEWS.
text:
A Malay Ismail, was fined $25 in the District Court, Singapore, for exhibiting uncensored films. The films were exposed for sale in an auction room and were traced to the accused.

The mortality returns for the Island of Singapore for the week ending July 31, show a total of 322 deaths giving a mortality rate of 32.83. There was one cholera death but no plague or small-pox cases. Four European deaths were recorded.

A number of leopards, which were being transported through New York, escaped from their cages when passing through a suburb, and have fled into the woods. The militia has been called out to capture them. The people are panic-stricken.

Bills have been laid before the Austrian Parliament for the ratification of alterations to the existing tariff agreements with Czecho-Slovakia and with the Belgian-Luxembourg Customs Union. The proposed tariff alterations in the agreement with Holland have also been laid before Parliament.

Six of the men who were accused of manslaughter for having secreted a number of "Arab stowaways in the ballast of the Sid'Ferruch, bound from Algeria to Marseilles, of whom 11 died from heat and suffocation, have been found guilty and sentenced to two years' imprisonment, 600f. fine, and to pay the costs of the case.

The arrival in Bogota, Colombia, of an official of the National City Bank of New York has given rise to the report that a substantial loan will be made to the Government after the inauguration of the new President. It is stated that the money will probably be used for financing public works and for railway construction.

It is reported by the Academy of Science in Leningrad that a geological expedition led by Professor Nenadkevitch along the banks of the River Amur, in Siberia, has discovered near Ust Kara, the skeleton of a mammoth, of great size and in excellent preservation. Steps are being taken to convey the entire skeleton to the Leningrad Zoological Museum.

Chief Inspector John Ryder, from Tampin, takes Chief Inspector Doel's place at Ipoh headquarters, Mr. Doel has been transferred to Tampin, as Officer-in-Charge of that police district. Mr. Doel has served in Perak for twenty years,

Stuttgart, Germany, August 9.— Marshal Mackensen; hero of one of the major offensives of the World War, was feted to-day by the population of this city when he arrived here to attend the wedding of his son. He is an old man now but he walks with the soldierly erectness of a youth. He seemed much gratified at the demonstration given him.

Mr. W. R. Mowell, of Reuters' Far Eastern organisation, has arrived in Batavia from Shanghai. The object of his visit is to investigate trade conditions and to establish a service for the distribution of financial and commercial reports of the world markets in the Dutch East Indies. Mr. Mowell is expected to be in Java about a month and a half, and in the course of his stay he will also visit Semarang and Soerabaya.

Washington, August 7.—Presidential Coolidge explained at "his Vermont farm yesterday that there could be no American recognition of the Soviet Government without a settlement of the debts of the latter. He added that if the debts and property rights were honoured the Soviet would be automatically recognised without conference. President Coolidge had not heard that the Soviet was making plans to recognise its debts.

Amongst the passengers passing through Singapore on August 12 on the Dollar Liner "President Van Buren," from Hongkong to Marseilles, were Colonel, Main Magalhues, who has retired from the Governorship of Macao, accompanied by his wife, daughter and A.D.C. They stayed on the steamer whilst she was in Singapore, but were entertained at the Parsonage of the Portuguese Mission in Victoria Street, at which were also present the Portuguese Consul-General and Madame Ferreira.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL NEWS.
text:
On Wednesday two further cuses of enteric fever (typhoid). were notified. Both patients were Chinese, from the city district.

The “Times of Malaya” understands that the Government is reducing the charge for electric light in Iph to 20 cents per unit as from August 1.

The "Times" contains an advertisement for assistant engineers for P.W.D. of the F.M.S. for four years' service on a beginning salary of $400 a month.

Thirty bags of letters dated London, July 29, were included in a total of 133 bags brought by the s.s. "Tilawn" yesterday. The Home paper mail of the same date is due on Sunday.

Shop fittings, furniture, tables, bedstands, carpets, etc., will be sold by auction at Messrs. Lane, Crawford Ltd.—old premises — by Messrs. Lammert Bros., at noon tomorrow.

Nairobi, August 12. — The lengthy trial of a native, charged with outraging an elderly European lady, aged 70 years, twice in a single night, and also with brutally assaulting her, concluded to day when the accused was found guilty and sentenced to 14 years' imprisonment and 24 lashes. This case, which occurred in Kijube on May 17, was one of the chief causes of anxiety regarding the safety of white women, which resulted in Government action and the revision of the law recently "any unced.

London, August 12. — Mr. Havelock Wilson, addressing seamen at Middlesbrough, said that one of the greatest misfortunes of the Labour movements was its entry into politics. The Trades Unions were now in a very serious condition, nearly everyone of them being bankrupt; worse still, hundreds of thousands of men had declared that they would never pay anything more into the Unions. Labour and Capital were mutually indispensable. "Let us try and foster a better understanding with the employers," added Mr. Wilson. "This is the one way in which the Unions can recover. I am glad to say that we have arrived at something like an intelligent position in the shipping industry."

Further evidence was taken at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday afternoon in the case in which four men are charged with committing an armed robbery at the residence of in Chinese merchant, his wife and daughter, from whom they are alleged to have stolen valuables and money to a total of $1,500. The case will be continued this afternoon, when it is expected it will be concluded.

In the Cooperative Hall, Methil, Fifeshire, five miners who were sent to prison under the Emergency Regulations during the general strike for holding up traffic and throwing stones at the police, were acclaimed as heroes and presented with medals provided through the International Class-War Prisoner's Aid. There was a large gathering, and the speeches were interspersed with the singing of the Red Flag.

A distingħed officer of the Indian Medical Service recently undertook an enquiry into "Heat-stroke in Allahabad Independent Brigade Area in relation to meteorological conditions." The following is an extract from his report which has just been published:—"Unfortunately meteorological conditions in 1925 were unfavourable for the occurrence of heat-stroke and only one "case occurred in Benares during June."

Dairen, August 16.—Through the Japanese Consul-General at Mukden, the Kwangtung Government tendered a formal protest to-day to the Mukden authorities against "the drastic measures taken by them to check the steady decline of the Mukden notes. The protest, pointing out the arrest of the clerks of the Japanese exchange brokers and the temporary closing of the Japanese exchanges, demanded that the authorities take more moderate steps in future.

Sentence of six months rigorous imprisonment was on August 19 passed on E. D. Sykes who was convicted by the Singapore District Judge, Mr. P. F. David on three charges of cheating by tendering cheques in payment of debts when he had no funds in the bank to meet the cheques. Sykes had a sum of $1,700 in the bank, it was said, and during history in Singapore, doing business as an import and export broker, he had distributed cheques amounting to over $18,000.

The Hongkong Radio Society is transmitting a programme of gramophone records between 7 and 8 this evening.

London, August 13. — Mr. Quaritch on behalf of an English customer has again acquired the "Pilgrim's Progress" copy for a smaller amount than auctioned on July 26. The price is not disclosed.—"Times of Ceylon."

Geneva, August 6.—Tass, the official Russian news agency will not be represented at the League of Nations Commission of News Agencies to convene at Geneva on August 19 for the purpose of securing improvements in international press facilities.

London, August 10.—Rome.—Commenting on the Italian and Spanish Treaty, the “Glornal d’Italia” remarks that many countries have Mediterranean interests, notably, Great Britain, whose watchfulness towards communications to India nobody can dispute, but defines the principal aim of the present Treaty to be the shifting of the equilibrium in the Mediterranean by a joint effort of two sister nations.

London, August 12.—There has been an unusual sequel to the sale of “Pilgrim's Progress,” mentioned in the message of July 26, the buyer having returned it to the auctioneers on the ground that it was not a first edition, but a second issue of the first edition. The existence of this issue, which is distinguished by a five-line errata at the end, was hitherto not generally known to bibliographers. The book is still worth a thousand sterling, but is scarcely as valuable as the original first edition.

A reference to a mounted white tiger being on "show in India," called forth a letter to the "Statesman," Calcutta, from a correspondent who says that recently two such white tigers have been shot in the Pasan Zemindary, Central Provinces, Bilaspore District. The skin is practically white chocolate (not black) stripes very prettily marked, a most handsome specimen, all else is normal including the eyes. Information frequently comes in of other tigers of the same colour having been seen, in the same forests. The correspondent raises the question of whether this is a distinct species.

headline: BETTER THAN A LETTER. / BANDITTI AND PIRATES.
text:
His Excellency the Governor recently described the miscalled Canton Strike Committee as a band of organised banditti and pirates, and criticised the connivance of the Canton Government.

This has, we are told, aroused “great natural indignation” in Kwangtung, and the developments are reported in the OVERLAND CHINA MAIL.

The full story of the piracy of a local picnic party off Lantau Island is graphically told in the OVERLAND CHINA MAIL.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL NEWS
text:
To-morrow is the anniversary of the beheading of Sir John the Baptist.

Local cricket clubs are remind- ed of the League annual meeting at 6.15 p.m. on Monday.

The pilot and two passengers were killed at Kulamazoo, Michigan, on August 22 when a stunt-flying plane fell 2,000 feet. The dead were Victor Arnold, the pilot, William Burns and Claire Elodgett, residents of Kulamazoo.

New York, August 21.—The "New York Herald Tribune" publishes a dispatch under the date line. Dumaguete saying that it may be stated with some degree of certainty that Colonel Thompson's report will oppose the granting of further autonomy to the Philippines. The dispatch says that any extension of autonomy will be unjustifiable because the Filipinos "have more now than they can handle effectively." The report will also say that the "independence move" is directed by politicians not representative of popular sentiment," according to the "Herald Tribune" dispatch.

A Washington cable from the "United Press" says:—The Department of Justice is sponsoring a national investigation of juvenile crime which is increasing at an alarming pace each year. Many in official circles are frankly worried over the prevalence of bankruptcy, murder, and "other" crimes committed by boys and girls under 18 years of age. A preliminary study of the situation in widely scattered sections of the country prove conclusively that this sort of lawlessness is increasing. There has also been a marked increase in the proportion of illegitimate birth.

San Francisco, August 22.—The Scripps-Howard chain of newspapers publish an editorial to-day "on the crisis coming in the Philippines" in which it is emphasised that American sovereignty in the Philippines is not a question that concerns only the United States and the Philippines, but involves important international factors, such as peace in the Far East and the open door in China. It advocates a policy of non-interference in the domestic affairs of the islands and the maintenance of a military protectorate over the islands, together with supervision of their foreign affairs.

The Mexican Army on August 8 dismissed 1,000 army officers including three Colonels and 28 Lieutenant-Colonels. These officers were dismissed on account of overstaying their leaves of absence, or devoting their time on other activities than army duties.

Paul Smith's, New York, August 21.—President: Coolidge does not consider feasible any proposal to except companies importing Rubber, tobacco, etc., from the provisions of the Sherman Anti-trust act as exporters are exempted under the Webb-Pomerene act, it was learned today.

"An official announcement wired from Sydney by the "United Press" states that two giant radio stations will be ready to establish regular commercial and press communication between Australia and Canada and Australia-Britain in October. These stations will both operate directs with the Canadian and British stations in a 300-metre wavelength."

Summer White House. August 13.—President Coolidge approved plans for two commercial air lines, the first to be established in the United States. One route will pass through the southern states and the other through Chicago, hence to Dallas. Both will terminate in San Francisco. It is planned to inaugurate both lines within six months.

To meet the expenses and costs arising out of the General Strike it is proposed to impose a special assessment of nearly £30,000 in Glasgow, an amount equal to about two-thirds of a penny per £ sterling. One hundred claims for damage to property and looting have been admitted by the Corporation. The police expenses incurred during the strike period exceeded £26,000, and the loss in Glasgow trumway revenue was estimated at £50,000.

Dr. Wirth, former Reichs Chancellor, has written an article in the "Berliner Tageblatt" in which he asks the German Republicans to oppose any reactionary manifestations, saying that the fusion of Germany and Austria must be consummated, but only after the lapse of a few generations Dr. Wirth urges the necessity of entirely clearing the atmosphere of European politics, especially with reference to the relations between Germany and

In view of the recent increase in the number of applicants for permission to conduct excavations for ancient relics in the Loland tombs, the Government General of Korea has decided to prohibit all such work. Special prohibitions will concern the 1,376 tombs in the old Loland District. 16 historical buildings in Seoul and other places, which are to be registered as historic monuments and are preserved for future generations. Among the structures to be designated are the Nandalmon and Todaimon Gates.

The American secretary of Labour, James J. Davis, addressing the Lodge of the Order of Moose on August 19 denounced the immigration of Asiatics into North America. He said: "China with her 400,000,000 people; India with her 300,000,000; Japan with her 70,000,000; and other Asiatic lands with their millions, will swoop over you, keep your wages low, and your racial development questionable, until eventually, the white man will be submerged in North America, unless preventive measures are taken."

Nauen, August 5.—Twenty-two German youths living in Italian South Tyrol have been arrested by the Italian authorities on a charge of high treason. It is claimed that the youths plotted for the autonomy of South Tyrol. Professor Rosse, leader of the organisation "Heimatbund," which is striving to get autonomy for Alsace-Lorraine, has been condemned by the French court to immediate dismissal from office. Rosse thereupon was immediately elected secretary-general by the Alsace Lorraine school teachers' organisation.

At the Old Bailey the Recorder, Sir Ernest Wild, K.C., said he had always understood that every member of the Junior Bar in court in robes was bound to take a dock brief if selected by a prisoner. He had noticed of late that there had been a practice of some members of the Bar, who did not wish to be selected by a prisoner to defend him, of removing their wigs. That was contrary to the practice as he knew it. and he thought it would be a pity if it continued. "Sir Travers Humphreys, senior counsel for the Treasury," said the matter would be brought before a special meeting of the Bar Mess.

headline: BETTER THAN A LETTER. / BANDITTI AND PIRATES.
text:
His Excellency the Governor recently described the miscalled Canton Strike Committee as a band of organised banditti and pirates, and criticised the connivance of the Canton Government.

This has, we are told, aroused "great natural indignation" in Kwangtung, and the developments are reported in the QVERLAND CHINA MAIL.

text:
A sense of typhoid fever (Chinese) is notified in the health return for Friday.

A report issued by the Glasgow Corporation Tramways shows — despite tradition — how easily the Scot and his money may be parted. During the year ended May 31 no fewer than 2,186 sums of money were found in the corporation's tramway-cars, "besides 918 parcels of clothing.

Despite the robbing at Messrs. Mackintosh's Ltd., reported elsewhere in this issue, the three days' sale, announced to commence there to-day, will be held in accordance with the original arrangements. The robbery will now be allowed to make the slightest different in connection with the sale of the prices.

The sharp shower which came down on Saturday afternoon did not more than spoil sport—it brought streams of water and several feet of mud across the road near the Nursing Home and the Cemetery, impeding traffic. Trum cars could not get round the Valley and came back the same way as they had been used to for a month until Monday last.

Sydney. — In view of the precarious position of many Tasmanian fruit growers as the result of the low prices prevailing in the London market, the Hobart Chamber of Commerce has appealed to the Federal Government to come to their relief. The Chamber of Commerce calls attention to "the extreme distress suffered by a large number of orchardists through the failure of the English market's in consequence of the general strike" and declares that many are penniless as a result of the failure and unable to prepare the soil for next season's crops.

Mr. Coates, the Prime Minister, in an address to the women's branch of the New Zealand Political Reform League, said that anyone knowing the active propaganda conducted at present, by people aiming at the disintegration of the Empire must realise how supremely important it is to maintain a Government in office which stands for King, Constitution, and country. His Government was endeavouring to inculcate among all citizens those basic principles of loyalty, patriotism, and respect for law and order without which no British people could really progress.

Shareholders are reminded of the annual meeting of the United Asbestos Oriental Agency Ltd., at 12 noon to-morrow, at the offices of Messrs. Dodwell & Co. Ltd

Sir Samuel Houru (Secretary of State for Air) has, by written answer, informed Colonel Day (Lab. Soc., Southwark, C.) that, approximately, 3,500 gallons of petrol were used by aeroplanes for the Air Force at the recent display at Hendon.

'Mr. Bridgeman' (First, Lord of the Admiralty) stated in the House of Commons in reply to Major Glyn (U., Abingdon), that during present financial year twenty ships would be removed from the effective list of the Royal Navy. These vessels included Ajax, Thunderfer. King George V., and Agamemnon.

Dresden.—The German army appears to have obtained a new gas. Experiments were carried out recently near Dresden by an artillery regiment with this gas, which produces a dense fog over a large area. The thickness of the fog is such that it is impossible to see for more than a couple of yards. The new gas is stated to have no poisonous effects.

A hole about the size of a pin's head in lead casing deep in the ground below. Trafalgar Square, caused by vibration set up by the traffic overhead and a leaking water main, recently put out of service one of the largest telephone cables in London and rendered temporarily useless 240 telephones in the hotels, shops, and offices at Charing Cross. The exchanges affected were Gerrard and Regent.

Johannesburg. — Golf has been distinctly perilous at Beira lately owing to the presence of a lion and lioness, who made the links their home. Irate golfers objecting to this new hazard organised gun parties, and, accompanied by half the inhabitants of the town, armed with anything, had been scouring the links for several days. The animals were seen several times, but it was impossible to shoot at them for fear of hitting one of the hunters. Finally, a lucky shot on the part of the town's best golfers killed the lion, which was borne into the town amid great rejoicing. The lioness is still at large, and has taken up her residence in some bushes near the fourteenth hole.

text: London, August 12. — Lord Lloyd and his wife and son were involved in a motoring accident near Inverness. Sir John Harrington, who was passing, took them in his motor car to Inverness. In- irmary. Although suffering from shock and cuts, they were able to go home.

headline: ALI BABA. / INDIANS STORY OF GEMS & IDOLS OF GOLD.
text:
New York, July 23.—A weird story of a enve filled with idols made of the purest gold comes from Mexico.

It is related by the director of the National Museum in Mexico City, who has commissioned a party of explorers to seek for the cave, which is situated somewhere in the Santa Clara Mountains.

The director says that some time ago an old Indian visited his office and offered to lead him to the mysterious cave. The man explained that he was a charcoal "burner," and happened to come upon the treasure while seeking shelter from a storm.

Entering a long tunnel, he suddenly found himself in a cave, which was lighted by a ray of light from the roof.

The ray, falling on two huge idols, caused them to shine as the sun, and at first filled him with terror.

The cave, which was of large dimensions (so the man continued), was filled with golden images and armour of gold, set with precious stones.

On leaving the cave the covered the entrance to prevent its rediscovery, and had journeyed to the capital to enlist the assistance of the museum director, whom he offered to lend to the spot.

The director was unable at the time to accompany him. When later he sought the Indian he found that the old man had died.

“Woman’s mission in business is to inject into it more idealism.” —Mrs. Lee J. Rountree.

“Until the workers are given a share, and a direct share, in the profits of the coal industry, there will be no inducement for them to regard their work as anything but a task.”—Sir Alfred Mond.

Another dog bite was reported yesterday. A coolle employed at the Peak when passing the residence of Mr. Martin, No. 6, The Peak, was attacked by a terrier. The animal was removed to Kennedy Town.

headline: "WENT TO SLEEP." / BRITISH SUBJECT FOUND ON SHIP
text:
"LOOKING FOR UNCLE."

Victor Simpson, a British subject, was charged this morning before Mr. J. H. B. Nihill at the Kowloon Magistracy with having had a "free transportation" from Shanghai to Hongkong without the consent of the owners or master of the as. "Linan" of the China Navigation Company.

The defendant, in relating his story to the Magistrate, said that he came from Tsingtao en route to Hongkong via Shanghai with $500 and on arriving at Shanghai all his money was stolen from him. He made several attempts to see the British consul at Shanghai, but the latter postponed his interview several times, while he ran short of funds.

He sold some of his personal belongings to support himself, continued defendant. To continue

his trip to the colony, he appealed to the second officer of the steamer who asked him to wait. According to the defendant, he was so tired that he went to sleep underneath a life-boat while he

waited for the second officer. He did not wake up until the next morning when the steamer was already sailing. A sailor inquired what he was doing on the ship and reported the matter to the master.

In conclusion, defendant told his Worship: "I am looking for my uncle named William Simpson who is staying in Hongkong and I want to find him as he is supposed to look after me."

The master of the "Linan" gave evidence, corroborated the testimony of the defendant as to he circumstances under which he was found.

His Worship, in passing sentence, informed the accused that the regular "penalty" for the charge against him was imprisonment, but that he took into consideration his age (defendant was scarcely twenty) and gave credit to his story, and would not therefore send him to jail.

therefore send him to jail. In conclusion His Worships said: I therefore order you to be detained in the Detention House pending inquiries, which the police will make as to the whereabouts of your uncle. As soon as your uncle is found, you shall be released.

headline: BOBBED HAIR. / CRAZE ENDED IN BERLIN.
text:
Berliners, like gentlemen, "prefer blondes."

This is shown (writes the Berlin correspondent of the London "Daily Chronicle." under date of June 10) by the fact that Berlin has chosen a "blondine" as the city's "Summer Queen of Beauty." She is Fraulein Grete Reinwald, a pretty young firm actress.

Fashion journals are more interested in the "fact that the queen" has not bobbed or shingled air.

Little more than a year ago the short hair craze reached here. Almost in a night it captured the fair sex of Berlin.

It was exceedingly unpopular with the male population. Callous employers dismissed their women secretaries, clerks and typists for no other reason than that they had bobbed or shingled hair. Hundreds of engagements must have been broken off for the same reason. Yet, for weeks, there were queues outside the barbers' shops.

But Fraulein Grete's election is a sign of the times. There is little doubt that she was chosen because she had not yielded to the "un-womanly and un-German fashion."

The reaction against short hair has set in with that impetus with which the new fashion originally conquered Berlin. Actresses and film stars are flocking to lonely holiday resorts—determined to come back capable of playing Juliet or Marguerite without false hair.

Though the burber laments that the “ladiés” salon” is now almost deserted, he has begun to do n' roaring business in hair restorers!

headline: OWNERS' ATTITUDE.
text:
Although no fresh move in the coal dispute is to be expected until after to-morrow's delegate conference, further interviews took place to-day with a view to facilitating direct negotiations.

The Miners' Executive met in the morning and later had a long discussion with Mr. Ramsay MacDonald and other leaders of the Labour Party. Although nothing tangible emerged, importance is attached to this meeting in view of Mr. Winston Churchill's appeal to the miners to formulate fresh proposals.

No report has been issued in regard to the interview of Mr. Churchill "and other members of the Government with the goal owners' organisation. The Government's decision—that the claim of the miners for national negotiations is "reasonable so long as the latter are prepared to advance helpful suggestions as a basis of discussion—was, it is assumed, discussed with the owners.

On the owners' behalf it was recently stated that their central organisation had no longer power to discuss wages and conditions with the Miners' District Associations.

the responsibility for such negotiations. It is not yet known whether this will constitute a definite bar to proceeding with efforts to secure a national settlement.

Meanwhile the miners are returning to work in increasing numbers in the Midlands, and it is reported that Lancashire and Cheshire coal owners have invited the men to discuss a local settlement.—British Wireless Service.

headline: SOVIET CUNNING. / SIGNS A TREATY WITH AFGHANISTAN.
text:
NON-AGGRESSIVE PACT.

A Russo-Afghan Treaty of neutrality and mutual non-aggression has been signed with great ceremony at Pagman, the Summer residence of the King of Afghanistan, by M. Stark, the Soviet Plenipotentiary, and the Afghan Foreign Minister.

It provides for neutrality in the event of an armed conflict between either and third Powers, mutual non-aggression and abstention from entering into hostile agreements with third Powers, and mutual non-interference in home affairs.—Reuter.

headline: VIOLENT STORM.
text:
LIGHTNING'S HAVOC IN LONDON.

TRAMCAR ON FIRE.

A brief but violent thunderstorm, which broke over London this morning, did considerable damage. "There were many narrow escapes, but no lives were lost.

The streets in the low-lying localities were flooded, and the electric railway service between the City and Kew was disorganised owing to the current being cut off through the flooding of the track.

The buildings struck included elementary school buildings and ten houses.

Two tramway cars, of which one was set on fire, were also struck, and owing to the floods it became necessary temporarily to change the route of certain bus services.—British Wireless Service.

An enterprising crocodile, says the "British North Borneo Herald," recently got into one of the drains off Penampang Road, Jesselton, and seized there a Chinese coolie. As his only access to this spot was through the Simbulan stream which bisects the golf course it is not surprising that caddies hesitate before searching for mishit balls therein.

Tientsin, August 15.—The Civil Governor of Tientsin has just "issued" orders to the Chief of the City Police, the Foreign Commissioner, the Taoyin and also the Tientsin magistrate instructing them to form a committee to take up the question with the French-Belgian Company concerning the rendition of the Tientsin electric Tramway and electric light to the Chinese by purchase without delay.

Mr. J. H. Nieuwenhuis, resident of Solo, Java, has resigned. His successor has not as yet been appointed.

Bishop, Titus Lowe, D.D., of Singapore, received the honorary degree of Doctor of Laws (LL.D.), at the recent Commencement exercises of Nebraska Wesleyan University.

Tientsin, August 17.—Owing to the suspension of schools at Tientsin, more than four hundred Kuomintang students have lately left for the South to join the anti-North expedition.

Mr. O'Hara Hickson, one time Chairman of the Incorporated Society of Planters of Malaya, gave recently an address on the history and work of the Society to a large number of North Borneo planters and others at the residence of Mr. Fitz-Gerald Day of Kinarut Estate.

In connection with the departure of Mr. C. P. Goodhue, at Batavia, owing to indifferent health, for England at the end of last month, the office of the American Trade Commissioner will be in charge of Mr. Don. C. Bliss, Assistant Trade Commissioner.

Mr. J. Marvin Howes, for the last six years a resident of Shanghai, was on August 26 inducted into the office of clerk of the United States Court for China, succeeding Mr. William A. Chapman, now under arrest in Seattle, Wash., on charges of having embossed about $30,000 of Government funds there.

The "Straits Times" understands that Mr. Aw Boon Haw, of Singapore, who has the interests of his poor. decrepit countrymen very much at heart, is willing to donate $10,000 towards the erection of a public home for aged poor Chinese. Mr. Aw Boon Haw, who is the proprietor of Eng. Aun Tong and Co., has been always ready to assist when there is need for help, and he has been considering new means by which to be friend, poor and helpless men and women.

text: The Secretary of State for Air has announced that during the twelve months ended June last seventy aeroplanes of post-war design and 192 of war design had crashed. The value of the machines involved was, roughly, £500,000. The Air Force personnel killed and injured were 65 and 89 respectively. The casualties compared favourably with those of other air forces.

During the year ended June 30 last, 11,260,000 deposits were made in Yorkshire Penny Bank, representing a total amount of £35,648,000 and an average deposit of £3 3s. 2d.

Summoned by the P.W.D. for deviating from plans submitted and approved by the department, the owner of No. 16, Wing On Street, and of another building in Gilman Street, was fined $50 at the Central Magistracy yesterday.

One N.C.O. in the Polish Army was killed "and several privates were wounded when three "75" field guns of French make exploded during artillery target-practice near Nowy Targ (Neumarket) by troops of the Cracow garrison.

This year's conference of the International Law Association met in Vienna to the great satisfaction of the Austrians, who attach importance to the fact that this is the first meeting since the war outside what was Allied territory.

During Norwegian air manœuvres off Christiansand, two hydroplanes about to land collided, with the result that one sank immediately. The pilot, Lieutenant Troye, was seriously injured. The other machine was only slightly damaged.

The Council of the University of Paris has sanctioned the foundation at the Sorbonne of a wireless telephony institute, which will enable listeners in to follow lectures in their own homes. The new wireless institute will be opened in November.

The Recorder at Hull Quarter Sessions quashed the sentence of three months' imprisonment with hard labour passed by the Stipendiary on John William Dodsworth, a railway fireman, for throwing a missile, which the appellant contended was a ball of paper, at a volunteer during the general strike. Paulsmiths, N.Y., September 2.—Will Hays, President of the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America, informed President Coolidge to-day that American movie fans annually spend approximately one thousand million dollars in admission fees at 20,233 theatres in the United States.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL NEWS.
text:
The Yugoslav Prime Minister, M. Ouzounovith, has requested all the Ministers to revise their departmental estimates so as to secure a reduction in the Budget expenditure of 10 per cent. for the current year.

" Mr. Robert Mond and a family party of ten people, including nurses and several children engaged a giant super-muring Napier flying-boat of Imperial Airways to fly them from Southampton to Dinard, where they spent a holiday. This is the first time a family party has chartered a big flying-boat to take them on their holidays.

At Boston (Lincolnshire) three Wrangle youths were fined £2 each and ordered to pay costs for gross cruelty to a stray dog. They admitted taking the dog into a barn, fastening its jaws with a horse twitch, and pricking its hindquarters. They said it was done "for fun." The dog went mad, and had to be destroyed.

Four of the directors of the Jo-no Muslin Company in Tokyo have been prosecuted on the charge of having embezzled their employees' fund at the time of the dissolution of the company. About 2,000 workers who have been thrown out of employment are now appealing to the prefectural Governor for help.

The Chinese Delegation to the Seventh Assembly of the League of Nations is as follows:—First Delegate: H.E. Mr. Chao-Hsin Chu, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary in Italy; Second Delegate: H.E. Mr. Wang King-ky, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary in Belgium. The Third Delegate has not yet been appointed. Mr. Chao-Hsin Chu was Chinese Acting Minister in London, 1922-1925.

A private luncheon was given on August 5 at the Midland Hotel, Manchester, at which the President of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce (Sir Percy Woodhouse), the directors and the executive of the China section were present to welcome Mr. K.D. Stewart, a leading member of the China section, on his return from China. M: Stewart addressed the gathering on the results of the China Tariff Commission and the outlook for the Lancashire cotton trade in that country.

Mr. J. Nienhuys, one of the founders of tobacco-growing in Deli, Sumatra, recently celebrated his ninetieth birthday. This pioneer of one of the most flourishing cultures in the Dutch East Indies, started for the D.E.I. at the age of twenty-three. Native labour was proved a disappointment; and success only came when he recruited Chinese in Penang. In 1869, the Deli Co. was founded. Mr. Nienhuys personally directed affairs in Deli until 1871, when he returned to Holland. He is still, however, a Director of the Deli Co.

His Excellency Chao Phya Rama Raghob, the favourite and A.D.C. of the late King of Siam, is expected to arrive in Britain shortly. He is described by the Bangkok correspondent of the "Morning Post" as a figure in many ways recalling the days of "Grand Viziers" and the Thousand and One Nights. A few years ago Chao Phya Ram, as he is generally known, was the most powerful man in Siam. At the beginning of the present reign he was superseded in his position as A.D.C., the new king having no favourites, and his motto being "retrenchment," Chao Phya Ram is still a young man, only a little over thirty. He is bringing with him on his first visit to Europe a young wife of seventeen. He intends to make an extended stay in Britain, and it is understood that he may go into residence at Oxford. headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL NEWS.
text:
The Anderson Music Co., Ltd. announce their latest list of new process records. There is a nice variety for different tastes.

A fresh case of enteric fever (typhoid) was notified on Thursday. The patient is a Chinese from the city district.

Further evidence was taken at the Kowloon Magistruey yesterday in a charge of manslaughter against a sanitary coolie. It was alleged that he caused the death of a hawker by prodding him with a bamboo broom. The case will be continued this afternoon.

The Eastern Extension Telegraph Co., notifies that telegraphie communication with Hankow is totally interrupted. Telegrams to Hankow and places beyond are now being transmitted by wire from Shanghai to Wuhu and thence by post. They are subject to heavy delay and are accepted at sender's risk only.

Mrs. Hayley Morriss, who is to be released from Holloway Gaol, was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment in December last for conspiring with her husband—who was sentenced to two years' hard labour and twelve months' imprisonment for offences against young girls. Mrs. Morriss's release is on account of a remission of two months for good behaviour. During his imprisonment Morris's estate, Pippingford Park, has been in the charge of a friend.

In connection with the reported discovery of giant Monitor lizards in the Dutch islands of the East Indies, the Times publishes a photograph of the Two-Banded Monitor now in the London Zoo, which is 7 ft. 7 in. long. But the Banded Monitor is insignificant compared to the giant lizard of the same genus, which has been known to a few zoologists and to a few Dutch officials and sportsmen since 1912. These creatures, found on the island of Komodo, are said to attain the length of 30 ft., and to be extremely dangerous to man.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL NEWS.
text:
Tsinanfu, September 3.—Mr. Kang Yu-wei, “modern sage of China,” arrived at Tsinanfu from Tsingtao on the night of September.

The Council of the Society of Incorporated Accountants and Auditors have elected Mr. Thomas Keens as president, and Mr. Henry Morgan as vice-president for the ensuing year.

Matheson Lang bade farewell to London at the King's Theatre, Hammersmith, in "The Chinese Bungalow," and will not be seen again in the metropolis till his return, late in March next, from his Canadian tour.

Mr. Percival, A. R. Leith, chief civil and mechanical engineer, Smith's Deck Company, Limited, South Shields, has been appointed chief engineer to the River Tees Conservancy Commissioners, and will take up his new appointment on October 1.

The death is announced, in his 80th year, at Schonenwerd, of M. Edward Bailly-Prior, senior director of Bailly. Limited, one of the largest shoemaking firms in the world, who was a member of the Swiss National Council from 1902 to 1917.

Being held responsible for the assault case of Mr. Chao Chin-pa, an adviser to Marshal Chang T8-lin, by the Fengtian authorities, Mr. Wang Yung-pao, the Chinese Minister to Tokyo, has applied to the Waichiaopu for his return home for recuperation.

headline: 답변
text:
Shanghai, September 2.—Sergeant Short was one of the principals yesterday afternoon at a ceremony at Holy Trinity Cathedral when he and Miss Mary Hoffman were married in the presence of a small gathering of friends. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. A. C. S. Trivott, Sub-Dean.

Mr. Stewart Becker and Mr. Stuart Allen, who were graduated from Princeton University in the class of 1926, have arrived in Peking to teach English on the faculty of the Y.M.C.A. School of Finance and Commerce. Both young men were active in their undergraduate days, taking positions of leadership in student affairs. In his Senior year Becker was manager of the Princeton Commons, a dining hall for 1,200 students. They are living with Mr. Robert R. Garloy, former General Secretary of the Y.M.C.A. in Peking.

headline: GREEN ISLAND CEMENT CO., LTD.
text:
The giant arum of. Sumatra, which produces a leaf one year and a flower the next year, is in full bloom at Kew Gardens and is attracting much attention not only for its size, but for its beauty.

The wife of the Russian General Ataman Semienoff, has been arrested in Paris on a charge of fraudulently converting to her own use of funds and other articles obtained by her on credit. A young Pole, named Langehewski, is being charged as an accomplice.

SHEWAN, TOMES General Managers HONGKONG.

British Museum acquisitions include a Japanese panel painting showing a figure portrait, which is probably seventeenth-century work, and four fine colour prints. One of the principal of these is by an artist named Kiyonaga and another is by the author better-known Hokusai.

Paris, July 30.—A few weeks ago a patient in hospital at Tarbes accidentally swallowed a tube containing radium to the value of 30,000 francs. The obvious measures for its recovery proved unavailing. The patient has now died, but an examination of the body has failed to reveal the missing object.

"Moscow," August 27.—The strike of the employees of the Indo-European Telegraph Company continues. London is working India via the "Eastern Telegraph Company, paying daily over £500. The five days' strike has caused the concessionaries a loss of £25,000, whereas the salary raise demanded by the staff amounts to only £1,350 per annum.—Rengo.

Chicago, August 13.—The zoological section of the Capt. Marshall Field Brazilian Expedition obtained during its first week, a wolf-spider, a mouse-oppossum of a species hitherto not represented in an American museum, and many other valuable specimens to the number of 300. This was reported to D. C. Davies, director of Field Museum of Natural History here, from which the explorers departed for Tuama recently, Mrs. Field is taking an active part in the work, a communication stated, accompanying George K. Cherrie, leader, each morning on collecting expeditions.

headline: OUR NAVAL CASUALTIES.
text:
The events leading up to the Naval action on the Yangtse, details of the casualties suffered by the British in an heroic attempt to uphold prestige, will be found in this week's issue, together with names of ships taking part and other information.

The Diploma in Tropical Medicine and Hygiene of the Royal Colleges of Physicians and Surgeons of England has been conferred on W. Z. C. Yuen, M.B., B.S., Hong Kong.

headline: PICKETS AS PIRATES.
text: The Marquess and Marchioness of Reading left London on August 10 for Scotland, where they will be the guests of Viscount and Viscountess Inchcape at Glenapp Castle, Ballantrae.

Marlingville, Indiana, September 2,—The condition of Senator William "McKinley of Illinois, who is confined in a sanitarium suffering with serious congestion of the lungs, has shown marked improvement during the last 24 hours. His physicians say that he has survived the crisis and his recovery" is probable.

Those who remember Mr. Ian Greig, M.C., at one time, of Aylesbury and Nutter, Ipoch, will be integested in a picture in the "Sunday Pictorial" showing Mr. Greig and his bride, Miss Ailsa Maclean, leaving the church of St. Mary Abbots, Kensington, after their marriage on July 31, says the "Times of Malaya." Mr. Greig was a keen rugby and hockey player when in Perak.

Mr. B. W. Fleisher, publisher of the "Japan Advertiser" of Tokyo and widely known throughout the Far East, will sail for the United States within a few days to undergo treatment for an arterial disease which has kept him bed-fast for nearly a year. Mr. Fleisher will enter the Mayor Brothers sanitarium Rochester, Minn. He plans to return to Japan as soon as corvalescence is complete.

Among the passengers who leave on the Dollar liner "President Pierce" for San Francisco tomorrow is Dr. R. W. Hart, the United States Public Health Officer in Manila. Dr. Hart is accompanied by his wife and is going on leave. Mr. E. C. Waterhouse, a big rubber planter of Sumatra, is also leaving on the same liner for Honolulu. Lieutenant Commander G. W. Dugger, of the U.S.S. "Helena," with his family is proceeding on Home leave by the "President Pierce."

Archbishop M. J. O'Doherty of the diocese of Manila arrived in Manila on the "President Pierce." Mons. Jose Bustamante, vicar-general of the archdiocese of Manila, superiors of the different religious orders, rectors of Roman Catholic colleges, high government officials, laymen and students were members of the general reception committee that welcomed the returning prelate. At the close of the reception at the pier. a Te Deum was sung in the Roman Catholic cathedral in the Walled City. Archbishop M. J. O'Doherty during his stay in the United States attended the Eucharist congress at Chicago and later visited many of the larger cities in the middle west.

On the afternoon of the 2nd alt. two Chinese presumably students, threw a bomb from the top of Snake Hill, Wuchang. The bomb was thrown with the object of creating panic, and it succeeded in a certain extent as a large number of the populace mistook it for the sound of a southern gun. The two however were arrested by the military police and executed publicly.

Messrs. Colgate and Co., American perfume and soap manufacturers of New York, obtained judgment against the China Chemical Works of Shanghai on the ground that its "Vioris" trademark for soaps had been infringed By the defendants. The latter were fined $500, with the option of imprisonment at the rate of a dollar a day —(500 days). Assessor Spiker and Magistrate Kwan heard the case in the Mixed Court. Mr. A. Krisel appeared for the plaintiffs and Mr. A. M. Preston for the defendants.

Peking, August 25.—A “persecution of education” in China has progressed to such a point where any student or teacher displaying independence of thought is likely to be suggested. Like a criminal, carryon the Nationalist organ “People's Tribune” which is published in English in Peking. According to the “Tribune,” a regular grant is being conducted in educational institutions for the alleged purpose of cradicalizing bolshevik influence, but the term bolshevik subject to such wide interpretation that the ban on free thought has spread beyond all reason.

Omaha, Neb., September 1, 11 William, Corcoran, American Consul at Cologne, Germany, shouted "Hurrah for Prohibition" aid if Ben passed champagne to his guests, including Gertrude Ederle, "the American girl who swam the English Channed, the Omaha Women's Christian Temperance Union wants him recalled, according to an an- nouncement to-day. "The State Department to-day was without official word from Cologne, Germany, as to whether William Corcoran, American Consul there; shouted for prohibition and then served champagne to his guests. It was indicated, however, that all the reports are nothing would be done about the incident.

headline: OBTAINABLE EVERYWHERE / A WEEK'S PAPERS IN ONE. / OVERLAND CHINA MAIL
text:
Outstanding events of the week up to this Wednesday (inclusive) are graphically described in the Overland China Mail.

People at Home want to know all about the historic occurrences concerning sojourners in China. Better than writing a letter is to send along a copy with all the news. OUR NAVAL CASUALTIES.

text: How, action was taken against the Canton "strike pickets by forces of H.M.'s Navy at Canton and Swatow—and the sequel to the incidents—is also described in the Overland's China Mail. The "protest" of the Canton Foreign Ministry is included.

CHEUNG CHAU ISLAND Beautiful scenes of all parts of this part of Hongkong

Messrs. Lammert Bros. are selling by auction at their sales rooms, Duddell Street, on Friday, a quantity of "ship fittings and miscellaneous goods."

The offices of the P. and O. Banking Corporation will be in Prince's Building, Chater Road (the premises until recently occupied by the Yokohama Special Bank), on and after Monday, September 20.

A telegram has been received in Tientsin stating that on appeal the sentence on the Compradore and shroff of the Lienshing at Weihaiwei was reduced from one year's hard labour to six months' simple imprisonment.

Mr. Roy E. DeLay, Managing Director of the Kellogg Switchboard and Supply Company, announces that his Company has just signed a contract with the Manchurian Provincial Government to erect a Radio Telephone Broadcasting Station in Harbin. This is the first contract to be let for a Government Broadcasting Station in China. The power of the Harbin Station will be 1,000 watts.

The following has been sent to the members of the residents of the Peak by the "Peak Residents' Association": Bearers of all public chairs have been instructed that on their arrival at any "house, after having been sent for, they are to ring the door bell and inform the No. 1 Boy of their arrival, and that they are on no account to shout out that they have arrived. Any infringement of this regulation should be reported to Inspector Shannon, Gough Hill Police Station.

Hong Kong is to have another visit from Dick "Norton's company, the "Globe Trotters," who are returning from a successful tour in Java where they have strengthened their organisation by the addition of three new artists. Two of these, Dr. Ralph Lynne and Miss Gladys Cathie, recently concluded a successful continental tour as speciality dancers, securing second prize at the international competition held in Paris when 400 competitors from all parts of the world took part. Mr. Dimoff, the other new artist, is a clever exponent of the Balalaika, an instrument with three strings.

Mr. Hiroji Uyemura has been appointed Sub-Manager of the local office of the N.Y.K., vice Mr. J. Wada, transferred to the Head Office, Tokyo.

Prince Louis Ferdinand of Prussia, second son of the former German Crown Prince, has arrived at Buenos Aires on the steamer "Madrid."

The forthcoming wedding is announced "of John O'Brien, accountant, residing at No. 530, Nathan Road, to Beatrice Maria Castro, residing at St. Joseph's Building.

Names of children are wanted for the charity pantomime performance of “Little Red Riding Hood” at Christmas. They should be sent to Mrs. Gay Cuming, No. 6, Observatory Villas, Kowloon (phone K863) who is kindly taking charge, in co-operation with Miss Daisy O'Keefe.

Peking, September 6.—Advices from Mukden state that Suiyuan will be governed by Yen Hishash, Governor of Shansi, as a compensation for his vigorous efforts, or driving out the Kuominchun. The recent visit of General Chang Hsuehliang to Tatung is said to have a bearing on the problem of Suiyuan.

Madame Chang Kai-shek, wife of "Canton's dictator, arrived in Hong Kong by the "Fatshan" yesterday. It is believed that she is going to Shanghai by the "Empress of Russia." The "China Mail" reported yesterday that General Chang's brother had come down on Tuesday by the "Lungshan."

The marriage took place at All Saints' Church, Tientsin, of Stanley Daniel Kemsley, of the Chinese Maritime Customs, Tientsin, and Ivy Margaret Elinor Poye, of Shanhaikuan. The Rev. C.W. Scott officiated. A number of friends were present. A reception was afterwards held at 14 Via Vincenzo Rossi. There were many present. The homymoon is being spent at Peking. Another Russian aeroplane belonging to the Soviet aviation company "Aviatchim" arrived at Berlin from Moscow via Koenigsburg. The plane is making a Central European round trip and will visit four capitals.

Berlin, September 2. "A strong campaign has been opened in Czecho-Slovakia against the Foreign Minister, Dr. Benes, by Fascist party organs. The "Prave Lidu" claims that the campaign is inaugurated and backed by Italian money.

Three were killed and many wounded in a daring Bank robbery at Warshaw. The thieves who entered the bank in broad daylight, threatened the employees with revolvers. They stole $8,000, which later were recovered when one of the bandits was killed and another captured. The third escaped.

Moscow, September 4.—The Communist organ, "the Pravda, declares that Marshal Chang Tsolin is determined to cripple by violent means the Chinese Eastern Railway, as the railway during the last few months, has carried considerably more traffic than the South Manchuria Railway, which is controlled by the Japanese, whom the Soviet Press accuses of supporting the Marshal for their own ends." The paper says the Soviet Government will submit to no provocation, but will continue its policy which is exclusively in defence of the workers of Russia and China.

Harbin, August 28.—In view of the fact that the Chinese Military Wireless Station in this city is intercepting radio news, broadcasted at Nauen and other places, and selling it to local newspapers, besides handling a private telegraph service for the purpose of money-making, the local Japanese Consul-General has filed a protest with General Tsai, Taoyin of Harbin, requesting him to suspend the handling of the private telegraph service on the ground that such conduct on the part of the Chinese Military Wireless Station is contrary to the Shuang-chiao Wireless Contract.

headline: MAKING NAVAL HISTORY.
text:
Officers and men of the China Squadron have been making history on the Yangtse. All the despatches published daily, with copious foot-notes to tell strangers what the names of persons, places, &c. stand for, are reproduced.

Our reports give prominence to the rescue, the names of those concerned (also the mercantile marine officers), the effect of the bombardment and reprisals, and the steps towards negotiation.

Side issues at Hankow where warships and steamers have been fired upon, and in some instances retaliated, combine to make an impressive pen picture.

"Action's" in which American destroyers took part are also described.

This week's issue also contains:—General Chang Kai-shek's manifesto to foreigners, the circular to shipping by the Strike Executive, reports of "scraps" with Canton, and a lengthy review of the past year's complications.

headline: POLICING THE RIVER.
text: Step by step, the activities of the British Navy are described up to strike pickets leaving the Canton River. Explanations are included in this issue as to how Canton has begun to realise responsibilities.

One of the two Indian guards who was seriously wounded in the Salkung ferry "pirney alfair has" since died in hospital. A charge of murder will "now" be preferred against the five men now in custody and alleged to be the pirate gung.

Home mails and parcels arrived by the F. and O. "Morey" yesterday. The total mail amounted to 299 bags and there were 133 bags of London parcels of August 12. The "President Taft" brought 488 bags of letters and "papers" from the U.S.A., Honolulu, Japan and Shanghai.

A Chinese was charged at the Central Ministry yesterday with intimidating another man to join the Wai San Society. Det. Sergeant Carey stated that although they were not able to prove it, the police knew the Society to be an unlawful and dangerous one. Defentant was remanded for one week.

Rign. August 29.—According to the Soviet Press the measure hitherto adopted by the Soviet to meet the loss of output in factories owing to the enormous number of malingerers among the workers have entirely failed. Physical assaults on doctors for refusing to grant them opportunities for carousing instead of working are rapidly increasing. Many doctors have been killed or injured in carrying out their duties. The Council of Soviet Trade Unions is appealing to all members energetically to fight such hooigans.

Peking, September 3.—An in-starice of Chinese 'filial piety' is reported from Mengtuan Hutung, where Miss Huan Yi, the only daughter of Mr. Huang Fu-chow, aged 19, believes she has cured her sick mother with her own "flesh and blood. The mother has been in the bed for a long period. Re-calling acts of many dutiful children in past history, the girl took a knife and cut a piece of flesh from her left arm and mixed it as a medicinal dose for her mother to take." Strange to say, the woman soon felt comfortable and now is in good health. The girl, it is said, is now in the P.U.M.C. Hospital for medical treatment, and her recent action is highly respected in some circles. —"N. C. Standard,"

An (aquatic) night fete will be old at the V.R.C. to-morrow:

The Peak Church Sunday School will hold sports and tea at Kelley Crest, the Peak, at 4 p.m. to tomorrow.

Reminder.—C.R.C. "at home" for: n:orrow, Chuseway Bay, 3 p.m., when Lady Clementi will prerupt the prizes. The 5/2nd Punjab Regiment band will be in attendance.

The Infantry Company of the Volunteers will hold a promenade concert on the parade ground at Corps Headquarters next Friday. Tickets at 50 cents each may be obtained at Headquarters.

Mrs. Inglis, who did splendid work in Perak as District Commissioner of the Ipoh Girl Guides, has been appointed District Commissioner of the Seremban Girl Guides.

Sir James Craig, the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland, who is to spend a two-months' holiday touring Canada, left Liverpool for Montreal in the White Star liner "Doric."

The Middlesex Hospital is to receive a sum of £10,000 from an anonymous donor, who has also promised to add to this sum as circumstances permit, for the special purpose of building a new home for the nurses.

Cologne.—Prince Joachim Albrecht of Prussia (a son of the ex-Kaiser), forsaking martial aspirations in order to woo the Muses, has attained some distinction as a musical composer. He is shortly to conduct, on behalf of charity, an orchestral concert at Bad Gastein, at which several of his own compositions will be performed.

Mr. Clement Shorter has been compelled through prolonged illhealth to resign the editorship of "The Sphere," which he founded and has edited for twenty-six years. Mr. Clement Shorter has been a pioneer of illustrated papers, with which he has been associated for nearly forty years, and he has founded three of the most successful of these.

On Thursday a Chinese case of diphtheria (wns) notified from the city

A private firm is negotiating with the Admiralty for the purchase near Rosyth dockyard of a site on which to erect a glass making factory, where 1,000 men would be employed.

Chicago, September 10.—The strike of 3,000 musicians in 400 Chicago movie theatres ended today by an agreement reached providing for an increase in pay from forty dollars to fifty dollars a week, the agreement to run two years, with an additional three dollars a week thereafter.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL NEWS.
text:
Among the passengers who returned to the Colony to-day by the "Aki Maru" were: Mr. and Mrs. A. J. Lane and Miss Marion Lane, Professor J. L. Shellshear, Mrs. H. M. C. Shellshear, and Mr. R. H. Skelton.

The Requiem Mass for the late Mother Superior of the French Convent, Causeway Bay, which should have taken place on July 19, but was postponed on account of bad weather, is being held to-morrow morning at the Catholic Cathedral at 8 o'clock.

The forthcoming weddings are announced of Roland Forusworth Griffin, of No. 21 Yu Yuen Road, Shanghai, to Lillithe Crossley, of Malvern Terrace, Leeds, England; George Sinclair, clerk of works, residing at 115 Avenue Road, Shanghai to Mary Lillian Gibson Inkster, who is due to arrive in the Colony by the s.s. "Mantua."

Salt Lake City, Sept. 11.—Senator Reed Smoot was re-nominated to-day as Republican candidate for the senate, by the state convention which is meeting here. Senator Smoot is now serving his fourth term in the Senate, having been elected for the first time in 1902. He is chairman of the committee on finance. Senator Smoot recently announced his intention of retiring from politics, but was persuaded to accept the nomination for a fifth term. He is 64 years old. Berlin, August 31.—The late Fritz Ebert, who starting life as a saddle maker, became the first president of the German Republic, as a socialist, and then was thrown out of the radical saddle-makers' union because of the charge that he had lapsed into conservatism, "has postnumously been readmitted to membership in the union." The unique resolution, striking from the records all mention of Ebert's expulsion, was passed at the recent saddle-makers' convention in Hamburg. It declared among other things that "in the course of time the union's members have come to regard even this post-revolutionary period in a different light."

The marriage took place in Penang, on Wednesday, September 8, of Mr. R. M. Latham, J.P., manager, Ratanne Rubber Estate, Limited, Teluk Anson, Perak, with Mrs. Gorman, who arrived from Home by the "Patroclus." A reception was afterwards held at the E. and O. Hotel, when the customary toasts were proposed and duly pledged. Mr. Latham being a popular figure among the planters of Lower Perak, there was a large attendance at the tiffin which was included in the reception. Mr. P. G. Short was the best man, and Mrs. F. E. de Paula was the matron of honour. Mr. and Mrs. de Paula were the host and hostess at the large gathering in the Hotel.

It is estimated that in Singapore there are 25,774 children of school age, states, the annual medical report for last year. To deal with this large number of children there are in the Settlement 28 Government English and Vernacular Schools: 13 Government Aided Schools and 37 Private Schools Examinations of school children during the year shewed 78.7 per cent. to have good general condition; 13.3 per cent. had a generally fair condition, and 11.1 per cent. had distinctly poor condition.

Nairobi, August 28.—During the last five years a local syndicate has been exploring concessions for oil and coal in the coastal area of Kenya. It has now succeeded in interesting financial groups in Johannesburg, who have provided considerable capital for further investigation and have sent up experts and drillers, who are already working. Should coal be found in Kenya in payable quantities, it might revolutionise the whole future of the country.

A denial was given at the office of the Shell Company by one of the directors to a statement that the distribution of Soviet Petrol in England has been largely limited to supplies bought by the Shell group from the Russian Oil Products Ltd. The Royal Dutch Shell group, it was stated, have not handled Russian oil for more than a year, as the Customs would show, nor would the group be likely to facilitate the distribution of oil derived from properties which have been confiscated by the Soviet Government without compensation being paid to the former proprietors.

“I regret to have to report that the younger'men' who are coming to the Colony do not display on the whole, any great desire to enrol. This reluctance seems to be associated with a general lack of athletic powers. Further, the decreases in the numbers under 25 is largely due to discharges for inefficiency,” states the G.O.C. (Major-General Sir T. Fraser) in his report on the Volunteers for 1925. “In my opinion it would help greatly if the Government would draw the attention of employers to the very great importance of the volunteer forces and to the necessity for inducing their young European employees to take their share in preparing for the defence of the country.”

It is not affected by another's oscillation. The tone is quite good despite the volume. It is claimed to be as simple to operate as a gramophone.

headline: THE CAFE - RESTAURANT PARISIEN
text:
Couched in exaggerated terms, an appeal has been issued by the Chinese Young Communist League who have sent copies to the "China Mail." They claim to be the leading organisation of Chinese young workers, peasants and student! The nations singled out as Imperialistic are Britain, Japan, United States and France. The appeal talks about the red banners of the Communist International which is no more Chinese than it is Hottentot. Comment is superfluous.

Special Musical Dinner and Dancing Bring Your Partners

Cairo, September. — The Finance Commission decided not to recommend the Chamber to authorise the payment of interest on the Ottoman 4 per cent. loan of 1855, the guaranteed Egyptian tribute, on the ground that payments hitherto were made at the express demand of the Ottoman Government which no longer was suzgraim. The Commission recommends that the interest should be deposited in a bank until the State's liability is settled in the Court.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL NEWS.
text:
Mr. G. G. Seth, Solicitor-General of the Straits Settlements, returned from leave by the "Morea."

Probate of the will of Mr. Eric Munro Ross has been granted in the Supreme Court. Mr. Ross was a chartered account of Shanghai who died at sea in the s.s. "Morea" on January 12, 1926. His estate in Hong Kong amounted to $94,400 Among his bequests were the following, to the Shanghai St. Andrew's Society Tls. 1,000, and to the Scottish Company, Shanghai Volunteers Tls. 1,000.

Pin-money as a factor in restricting industrial output was mentioned by Mr. A. Angles of the National Institute of Industrial Psychology. Among reasons for restricted output he said was satisfaction with present earnings. This was generally the case with pin-money girls, who kept most of their earnings for dress allowance. That type, he said, had a harmful effect on the real worker and in one particular instance a well-known firm decided not to employ such girls.

Sylvia Gaines was mysteriously beaten to death while visiting her father near Seattle. A new English elementary school is to be built at McNair Road, Singapore.

Moon-cake. feast " falls tomorrow. " The "China Mattle" article on the festival appears on page 6. The Chinese Maritime Customs will be closed for the day.

The French Government requested Mr. Chen Lu, Chinese Minister at Paris, to inquire whether the Chinese Government would take any interest in the Betheloe Institute in Paris. After careful consideration, by the Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Education, it has now been decided that an annual sum of Francs 15,000 be subscribed by the Chinese Government, which amount will immediately be remitted to the above mentioned institute.

headline: ST. LAMOI PILSNER
text:
Sydney, August 5th The movement for the secession of Western Australia from the Federation which has been in the air for several years has now been launched definitely by the formation, at a large public meeting at Perth, of an organisation provisionally entitled "the Secession League," officials have been appointed and fighting fund has been opened. The position is probably not serious, but it is interesting in view of a similar movement, in Tasmania.

Mr. F. C. Jenkin sailed for England in the s.s. "Malwa" on Saturday.

Yesterday was the anniversary of the date of the opening and dedication of the Union Church. Kowloon. The anniversary serves, however, are being held next Sunday.

Cairo, September 1.—A wife of the ex-Sultan of Turkey, Shemed Vahieddin, deposed in 1922; who came to Egypt when the Sultan left Turkey, jumped into the Nile to end the misery of destitution. She was rescued, and recently was given shelter in a charitable institution. She has not received a pension from Angora for the last three months. The Rev. Hugh John Embling has been nominated "Assistant Bishop of the Diocese of Korea.

text:
Peking, September 7.—H. R. H. Prince George, now in this city, expects to visit the Nankow battlefields to-day accompanied by Gen. Chang Hsueh-liang, son of Marshal Chang, who will return to Mukden after returning from the trip to Nankow. The Prince returned here this morning from an extended tour through Kalgan and Tayuan, Shansi province, where he called upon General Yen Hsi-shan.

London, August 29.—Nuremberg.—The organisers of the Nationalist demonstration telegraphed to President Hindeburg, whom they joyfully acclaimed as the leader of the greatest battles in the world's history. General Ludendorf was a notable absentee. He was not invited to participate in the demonstration owing to his breach with Prince Rupprecht and the Envarian Officer's Corps whereby he has been subjected to a social boycott.

CHEUNG CHAU ISLAND Benutiful scenes of all parts of this part of Hongkong.

Mr. J. Nienhuys, one of the founders of tobacco-growing in Deli, Sumatra, recently celebrated his ninetieth birthday. This pioneer of one of the most flourishing cultures in the Dutch East Indies, started for the D.E.I. at the age of twenty-three. Native labour was proved a disappointment, and success only came when he recruited Chinese in Penang. In 1869, the Deli Co. was founded. Mr. Nienhuys personally directed affairs in Deli until 1871, when he returned to Holland. He is still, however, a Director of the Deli Co.
